units.la: C[?]Anticum Canticorum explanandum suscepturus, usus sum instituto meo, ut tum ex Sacrarum Literarum fontibus ipsis, tum ex aliorum veterum & recentiorum quasi rivis haurirem quicquid ad illustrandum sensum Literalem attinere mihi videretur. Est autem in hoc Sacro dramate Literalis sensus duplex; nempe materialis, sive rei gestae inter sponsum & sponsam quae per parabolam stylo bucolico inducitur; tum etiam spiritualis quem Spiritus-Sanctus significare voluit perpetua quadam allegoria declarans mutui Christum inter & Ecclesiam amoris aculeos, locutionibus ad nostras dicendi formulas accommodatis; primus sensus dicitur grammaticalis, secundus vocatur realis; ille est cortex, hic medulla inde eruenda, nisi velimus iis esse similes, qui negligentes historiam in tabella depictam solis se coloribus oblectant, nihil in hoc Cantico Canticorum praestan-
units.tr: As I am about to undertake the explanation of the Song of Songs, I have followed my usual plan: to draw from the very fountains of Holy Scripture, and, as it were, from the streams of other writers, both ancient and recent, whatever seems to me to bear on illustrating the literal sense. In this sacred drama the literal sense is twofold. One is the material sense, namely the event that took place between the bridegroom and the bride, introduced in pastoral style through a parable. The other is the spiritual sense, which the Holy Spirit wished to signify by declaring, through a continuous allegory, the mutual sting of love between Christ and the Church, in expressions adapted to our own ways of speaking. The first sense is called grammatical, the second is called real. The former is the bark, the latter the marrow to be extracted from it, unless we wish to be like those who, neglecting the history depicted in a painting, delight themselves only with the colours, and achieve nothing in this Song of Songs

units.la: Proœmium.

units.la: præstantissimo divini esse, sed profanis omnia plena voluptatibus, sententia erat Theodori Mopsuestiani, damnata in synodo Constantinopolitana II. Collat. IV. Hanc hæresin renovarunt Anabaptistæ, nescientes perpendere Dei benignitatem et misericordiam, qui ut nos ad sacrum ipsius amorem vividius excitet, usque ad carnalis amoris verba sese inclinat. Nihil in hoc sacro Epithalamio, quod sanctum, castum, pudicum, et immaculatum non sit; sed ignitum eloquium capere non potest cor algidum, & lingua divini amoris ei, qui cœlestem animarum sponsum, omnis castimoniæ magistrum medullitus non amat, barbara erit. Hinc Philo Carpathius, Quicunque omni occasione carnis præcisa, remotisque atque depulsis illecebris voluptatum, mente tranquilla, corpore castus, & animo, temperantiæque viribus vallatus erit, is Cantica Canticorum intrepide adire potest. Quia vero in hoc nuptiali carmine palea frumentum tegunt, cavendum inprimis duxi, ne sic belluarum instar paleis immorarer, ut frumentum electorum & rationalem cibum quærere, vel tantisper desisterem. Atque ita mea commentatio sic distribuitur, ut subjecta verbis sententia dilucidetur, & mysticus Christi Jesu sponsi, atque Ecclesiæ sponsæ dialogus, exponatur quam fieri potest accuratissime. Siquis autem, ut Hieronymi verbis in Mich. 2. utar, in Lege Domini die ac nocte meditatus, majus habuit Studium,
units.tr: The Anabaptists renewed this heresy, which Theodore of Mopsuestia held, that the most excellent parts of the divine things are full of pleasures for the profane, a view condemned in the second Synod of Constantinople, Collation IV. They did not know how to weigh the kindness and mercy of God, who, in order to stir us more vividly to his holy love, stoops even to the words of carnal love. Nothing in this holy wedding song is not holy, chaste, modest, and spotless; but a cold heart cannot grasp the fiery speech, and the tongue of divine love will be barbarous to anyone who does not love from the heart the heavenly bridegroom of souls, the teacher of all purity. Hence Philo of Carpathus: whoever has cut off every occasion of the flesh, put aside and driven away the allurements of pleasure, and has a tranquil mind, a chaste body and soul, fortified by the powers of self-control, may approach the Song of Songs without fear. But since in this nuptial song the chaff covers the grain, I thought it above all necessary to take care that I do not linger among the chaff like beasts, and so cease, even for a while, to seek the grain of the elect and the rational food. And so my commentary is arranged so that the meaning, set under the words, is made clear, and the mystical dialogue between Christ Jesus the bridegroom and the Church his bride is expounded as accurately as possible. But if anyone, to use the words of Jerome on Micah 2, meditating on the Law of the Lord day and night, has had greater zeal,

units.la: Studium, majus ingenium, otium, gratiámque, & potest de Cantico Canticorum probabilius aliquid dicere, non invideo, non aspernor, quin potius cupio ab eo discere quod ignoro, & libenter me discipulum profitebor, dummodo doceat, & non detrahat ; nihil enim tam facile, quàm otiosum & dormientem de aliorum labore ac vigiliis disputare. Idem dictum volo de aliis scripturæ libris quorum Literalem explicationem, vel jam typis mandavi, vel deinceps, Deo juvante, sum mandaturus.
units.tr: Whoever has greater zeal, greater talent, more leisure and more favour, and can say something more probable about the Song of Songs, I do not begrudge, I do not disdain. Rather, I desire to learn from him what I do not know, and I will gladly profess myself his pupil, provided that he teaches and does not disparage; for nothing is so easy as to dispute, while idle and asleep, about the labour and watchings of others. I wish the same to be said of the other books of Scripture, whose literal explanation I have either already committed to print or shall, God helping, commit to print hereafter.

units.la: Explicatio Litteralis CANTICI CANTICORUM SALOMONIS.
units.tr: Explanation of the Literal Sense of the Song of Songs of Solomon.

units.la: SAlomon Bethsabee ex quatuor filiis postremo genitus à patre suo David Rege post annos imperii tres supra triginta regni hæres decernitur impulsu Nathanis Prophetæ. Adhuc adolescentem Sadoc ungit, rejecto ipsius fratre Adonia, qui se Regem jactabat. Tantam à Deo in somnis obtinet sapientiam, ut sciat dispositionem orbis terrarum, & virtutes elementorum, initium & consummationem & meditatem temporum, vicissitudinum permutationes, & commutationes temporum, anni cursus, & stellarum dispositiones, naturas animalium & iras bestiarum, vim ventorum, & cogitationes hominum, differentias virgultorum, & virtutes radicum, & quæcumque sunt absconsa & improvisa. Templum juxta traditam à patre constructionis ichnographiam, & Regiam condere incipit, illud absolvit annis septem: hanc tredecim. Templi dedicatio inchoata die octavo mensis septimi, in illudque postmodum arca illata. Hiramo Tyri Regi transfert viginti Galileæ oppida, velut honorarium pro lignis & operariis, quos ad extruenda Templum & Regias domos miserat. Pharaonis filiam ducit, & urbem ultimam Chananæorum Gazer in dotem accipit. Ex quo totam Promissionis Terram possident Israëlitæ, annis quadringentis quinquaginta post incœptam à Josue Terræ divisionem. Regina Sabæorum Arabiæ, adeoque terrarum extima occupantium ad Oceanum & mare Rubrum, ex urbe sua metropoli Saba, quæ & Mariaba, venit ad Salomonem ipsius auditura sapientiam. Hæc Regina vocatur à Geographo Nubiensi Clim. 1 part. 6. Belkis, à Rabbi Abraham Zaccuth Salmanticensi in libro יוחסין, genealogiarum, ad annum 1502. Scripto sol. 136. editionis Cracovien sis An. 1580. appellatur Nicolaa. Christus hanc nuncupat Reginam austri, quia quod Hebræis regnum Saba, & Romanis scriptoribus Arabia aromatifera, hoc Arabibus Jeman, & cum articulo Aljeman, ut videre est loco laudato Geographi Nubiensis, in Itinerario Rabbi Benjamin, Juchasin sol. 14. 135. & 139. Aben-Ezra in Dan. 11.
units.tr: Solomon, the last born of the four sons of Bathsheba, was named heir to the kingdom by his father, King David, after David had reigned thirty-three years, at the urging of the prophet Nathan. While still a young man he anointed Zadok, and rejected his brother Adonijah, who was boasting that he was king. From God in a dream he obtained such wisdom that he knew the arrangement of the world and the powers of the elements; the beginning, end and middle of times; the changes of the seasons and the alternation of times; the course of the years and the arrangement of the stars; the natures of animals and the rages of beasts; the force of the winds and the thoughts of men; the differences among plants and the powers of roots; and whatever things are hidden and unforeseen. He began to build the temple according to the plan of its construction handed down by his father, and also the royal palace. He finished the temple in seven years and the palace in thirteen. The dedication of the temple was begun on the eighth day of the seventh month, and afterwards the ark was brought into it. He handed over to Hiram, king of Tyre, twenty towns of Galilee as payment for the timber and workmen whom Hiram had sent to build the temple and the royal houses. He married the daughter of Pharaoh and received the city of Gezer, the last city of the Canaanites, as her dowry. From this time the Israelites possessed the whole Promised Land, four hundred and fifty years after Joshua began the division of the land. The Queen of Sheba of Arabia, whose people occupied the outermost lands, reaching to the Ocean and the Red Sea, came from her metropolis, the city of Saba, which is also Mariaba, to Solomon to hear his wisdom. This queen is called Belkis by the Nubian geographer (Clim. 1, part 6); by Rabbi Abraham Zacuto of Salamanca, in his book Yuchasin, a book of genealogies, written in the year 1502 (p. 136 of the Cracow edition of 1580), she is called Nicolaa. Christ calls her the queen of the south, because what the Hebrews call the kingdom of Saba, and Roman writers Arabia Felix, the Arabs call Yemen, and with the article Al-Yemen, as can be seen in the passage of the Nubian geographer cited, and in the Itinerary of Rabbi Benjamin, Yuchasin (pp. 14, 135 and 139), and Aben-Ezra on Daniel 11.

units.la: v. 6. &c. Ut autem ימין jamin Hebraicè, ita ימן jeman, & cum articulo אלימן aljeman austrum sonat. Secundæ res quæ sapientium animos fatigant, ut loquitur Aug. lib. 17. de Civit. c. 20. magis Salomoni obfuerunt, quàm profuit ipsa sapientia, etiam nunc & deinceps memorabilis, & longè latèque laudata. Nimirùm diviti æ ducunt Salomonem ad delicias, delicia ad insatiabiles libidines, quas ut expleat contra præceptum Domini Exod. 34. v. 16. & Deut. 17. v. 17. septingentas uxores, concubinas trecentas undique accersit, à quibus ad idola senex conversus, ne amasias offenderet, illis templa miser extruit. Fecit, inquit. Aug. 11. de Genesi ad literam cap. 42. quod sciebat non esse faciendum, ne suas, quibus deperibat atque diffluebat, delicias contristaret. Annos quadraginta Mortalium sapientissimus & opulentissimus, si tantæ gloriæ libidinis maculam non intulisset, regno perfunctus, vitâ defungitur, ætâ pœnitentiâ, ut colligitur ex 2 Sam. seu Reg. 7. v. 12, 13, 14, 15. & 16. & 2. Paral. 11. v. 17. Ex omnibus libris à Salomone conscriptis, quorum meminit Scriptura 3. Reg. 4. v. 32, & 33. & Josephus 8. Antiq. 2 nunc extant tantummodo tres, de quibus nulla est dubitatio quin illius sint, nempe liber Proverbiorum, Ecclesiastes, & Canticum Canticorum. Ex mente S. Bernardi Serm. 1 in Cant. in Proverbiis pellitur superfluus amor sui, in Ecclesiaste vanus amor mundi, in Cantico Canticorum præscribitur castus amor Dei. In Proverbiis, ait Paphnutius Abbas apud Cassianum Collat. 3. c. 6. Concupiscentiæ carnalium rerum ac terrena vitia resecantur; in Ecclesiaste universa quæ aguntur sub sole vanitas pronuntiantur; in Cantico Canticorum mens visibilia transcendens Verbo jam Dei cœlestium rerum contemplatione conjungitur; cùm totus hic liber qui Canticum Canticorum inscribitur, amores sanctos Christi & Ecclesiæ figurata locutione commendet, & prophetica pronuntiet altitudine, ut loquitur B. Aug. in Speculo.
units.tr: v. 6, etc. But the Hebrew yamin, so yemen, and with the article al-yemen means south. The things that trouble the minds of the wise, as Augustine says in book 17 of The City of God, chapter 20, did more harm to Solomon than wisdom itself did him good, though his wisdom is still remembered and widely praised. Namely, riches led Solomon to luxury, luxury to insatiable lusts, and to satisfy these, contrary to the Lord's command (Exod. 34:16 and Deut. 17:17), he gathered from everywhere seven hundred wives and three hundred concubines; and, grown old, he turned to idols, and to avoid offending his lovers he wretchedly built temples for them. He did, he says, Augustine, On the Literal Meaning of Genesis, book 11, chapter 42, what he knew should not be done, so as not to upset the delights to which he was addicted and in which he dissolved. Solomon, the wisest and richest of mortals, reigned for forty years, and, if he had not stained so great a glory with lust, he would have died a happy man; as it is, he died in old age in repentance, as is gathered from 2 Sam. or Kings 7:12, 13, 14, 15 and 16, and 2 Chron. 11:17. Of all the books written by Solomon, which Scripture mentions (3 Kings 4:32 and 33) and Josephus (8 Antiq. 2), only three now exist, and there is no doubt that they are his: the book of Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, and the Song of Songs. According to St Bernard's first sermon on the Song, in Proverbs superfluous self-love is driven out; in Ecclesiastes vain love of the world; in the Song of Songs chaste love of God is prescribed. In Proverbs, says Abbot Paphnutius in Cassian (Conference 3, chapter 6), the desires for carnal things and earthly vices are cut away; in Ecclesiastes everything that is done under the sun is pronounced vanity; in the Song of Songs the mind, passing beyond visible things, is joined to the Word of God in the contemplation of heavenly things, since this whole book, which is entitled the Song of Songs, commends in figurative speech the holy loves of Christ and the Church, and proclaims them with prophetic loftiness, as St Augustine says in the Mirror.

units.la: Grande sacramentum, quo nubit Ecclesia Christo, Et simul est Domini sponsa, sorórque sui. Hinc soror & conjux, quoniam sine corporis usuMente coit, cui vir non homo, sed Deus est.
units.tr: A great sacrament, by which the Church is wed to Christ, and at the same time is the Lord's bride and his sister. Hence sister and wife, since they unite in mind without bodily use, whose husband is not a man but God.
