units.la: CANTICUM CANTICORUM SALOMONIS.
units.tr: The Song of Songs of Solomon.

units.la: QUod ex Hebræis pro primo versu Lxx. reddidere, hoc Vulgatus rejecit in titulum hujus libelli, qui specie Dramatis ordinatus, ut loquitur Hieron. personarum imitatione contexitur. Mirificè autem Regum sapientissimus Salomon divinitus inspiratus Christi sponsi & Ecclesiæ sponsæ laudes, sacri amoris gratiam & æterni commercii cecinit Sacramenta sub persona pastoris, ast Regio sanguine procreati castam puellam congenerem sibi desponsatam maximè, sed casté adamantis. Unde libellus hic vocatur Canticum Canticorum, id est, Canticum excellentissimum, quo nihil suavius, nihilque divinius. Quia verò pluribus constat odis, inscribitur à benè multis Cantica in plurali.
units.tr: What the Septuagint rendered from the Hebrew as the first verse, the Vulgate moved into the title of this little book, which, as Jerome says, is arranged in the form of a drama and woven together by the imitation of persons. Solomon, the wisest of kings and divinely inspired, sang wonderfully of the praises of Christ the bridegroom and of the Church his bride, of the grace of holy love and the sacraments of an eternal fellowship. He did this under the person of a shepherd, and of a chaste maiden born of royal blood, akin to him and most surely betrothed to him, yet a chaste lover. Hence this little book is called the Song of Songs, that is, the most excellent song, than which nothing is sweeter or more divine. Because it consists of many odes, many writers give it the title Cantica in the plural.

units.la: CAPUT PRIMUM.
units.tr: CHAPTER I.

units.la: Sponsa loquitur primò sola intra se, dein occurrentem sponsum alloquitur.
units.tr: The bride speaks first alone to herself, and then addresses the bridegroom who comes to meet her.

units.la: 1. OSculetur me osculo oris sui: quia meliora sunt ubera tua vino,
units.tr: 1. Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth, for your breasts are better than wine.

units.la: 2 Fragrantia unguentis optimis. Oleum effusum nomen tuum: ideo adolescentulæ dilexerunt te.
units.tr: 2 Fragrant with the finest ointments. Your name is oil poured out; therefore the young maidens have loved you.

units.la: 3. Trahe me: post te curremus in odorem unguentorum tuorum. Introduxit me Rex in cellaria sua: exultabimus & lætabimur in te, memores uberum tuorum super vinum: recti diligunt te.
units.tr: 3. Draw me; we will run after you into the fragrance of your ointments. The King has brought me into his cellars: we will exult and rejoice in you, mindful of your breasts above wine. The upright love you.

units.la: 4. Nigra sum, sed formosa, filiæ Jerusalem, sicut tabernacula Cedar, sicut pelles Salomonis.
units.tr: 4. I am black, but beautiful, daughters of Jerusalem, like the tents of Kedar, like the curtains of Solomon.

units.la: 5. Nolite me considerare quòd fusca sim, quia decoravit me sol: filii matris meæ pugnaverunt contra me, posuerunt me custodem in vineis: vineam meam non custodivi.
units.tr: 5. Do not look at me because I am dark, for the sun has looked upon me. My mother's sons fought against me; they made me keeper of the vineyards, but I have not kept my own vineyard.

units.la: 6. Indica mihi, quem diligit anima mea, ubi pascas, ubi cubes in meridie, ne vagari incipiam post greges sodalium tuorum.
units.tr: 6. Tell me, you whom my soul loves, where you feed your flock, where you lie down at midday, lest I begin to wander after the flocks of your companions.

units.la: EXPLICATIO.
units.tr: EXPLICATIO.

units.la: 1. OSculetur me osculo oris sui. Heb. ad verbum, osculetur me ex osculis oris sui, in quo loquutionis genere præpositio videtur, ut sæpe aliàs, separationem denotare; quasi diceret Osculetur me osculo illo exoptato, quod, ut Bernardus loquitur, matrimonii signum & initium est. Sic Ecclesia sub Lege jam diu promissò sibi per Prophetas Dominico adventu, cùm moras ejus diutiùs ferre non posset, rogat ut citò veniat per incarnationis mysterium, quo non jam quasi desponsata, sed quasi nupta intime uniatur & adhæreat Deo Verbo; ut enim ait Greg. Mag. Hom. 38. in Evang. In hoc Pater Regi Filio nuptias fecit,quo ei per incarnationis mysterium sanctam Ecclesiam sponsi sibi acquisi- avit. Porro nemo nescit in desiderio matrimonii honesti & liciti nihil esse, quod dedeceat puellam jam desponsatam, maxime sub Lege viventem, cujus tempore fides in Christum secundum carnem nasciturum, plerosque justos ad conjugium incendebat. Inducit itaque Salomon in hoc cantico (quod unum ex mille & quinque ab ipso compositis, ut dicitur 3 Reg. c. 4. v. 32. habet authoritatem & est in Canone Scripturarum divinarum apud Hebraeos & Christianos) puellam amantem jam pridem desponsatam diuturnioris nuptiarum dilationis impatientem, quae vix suam impatientiam verbis testata percipit sponsum caste quidem, sed ardenter amatum, quem statim alloquens, ipsi impatientiae causam & vehementis nuptiarum desiderii rationem simpliciter & candide, ut pastoritiam puellam decet, aperit dicens: Quia meliora sunt ubera tua vino. Haec esse verba sponsae ad sponsum, non vero sponsi ad sponsam, praeter literae seriem & connexionem indicat pronomen tua, quod in veritate Hebraica est affixum masculini generis. Sensus autem est idem ac si diceret, Idcirco tibi jamjam matrimonio jungi tantopere expeto, quia suaviores sunt blanditiae tuae quibusvis lautitiis. Sic Ecclesia dicit vilescere sibi omnes delectationes & jucunditates prae suavitate ineffabili coelestis sponsi in se amoris.
units.tr: 1. Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth. The Hebrew, word for word, reads: "let him kiss me with kisses of his mouth." In this idiom the preposition seems, as often elsewhere, to mark separation, so that the sense is: "Let him kiss me with that longed-for kiss, which, as Bernard puts it, is the sign and beginning of marriage." Thus the Church, which under the Law had long been promised the coming of the Lord through the prophets, and could no longer bear his delay, asks that he come quickly through the mystery of the incarnation. By this mystery she is joined and cleaves inseparably to God the Word, no longer as one betrothed but as one wed. As Gregory the Great says in Homily 38 on the Gospel: In this, the Father made a marriage for the King his Son, in that by the mystery of the incarnation he joined the holy Church to him as his bride. Nobody doubts that in longing for honourable and lawful marriage there is nothing unbecoming to a girl already betrothed, especially one living under the Law, when faith in Christ who was to be born according to the flesh kindled the desire of many righteous people for that union. Solomon therefore brings in, in this Song (which is one of the thousand and five works composed by him, as 3 Kings 4:32 says, and which has authority and stands in the canon of the divine Scriptures among the Hebrews and Christians), a girl who is in love and long since betrothed, impatient of the longer delay of the nuptials. Scarcely able to express her impatience in words, she addresses her bridegroom, whom she loves chastely yet ardently, and at once declares, simply and frankly, as befits a shepherd's girl, the cause of her impatience and the reason for her intense longing for the wedding, saying: For your breasts are better than wine. That these are the bride's words to the bridegroom, and not the bridegroom's to the bride, is shown, apart from the sequence and connection of the text, by the pronoun your, which in the Hebrew is attached as a masculine form. The sense is the same as if she said: "I so eagerly desire to be joined to you in marriage at once, because your caresses are sweeter than any delicacies." So the Church says that all delights and pleasures become worthless to her beside the ineffable sweetness of the love of her heavenly bridegroom towards her.

units.la: Duplex est hic Hebraismus. Primus est in voce ubera, quae idiotismo Hebraeis familiari hic blanditias seu amores significat, quia ubera sunt amoris illices, & quia cor, quod amoris est sedes, uberibus quasi stipatur & continetur. Sic Ezech. 23. v. 17. Cubile mammarum, id est, amorum, seu amoris. Prov. 5. v. 14. Ubera ejus inebrient te in omni tempore, id est, ut ipse Salomon interpretatur ibidem in altero mox sequenti hemistichio, in amore ejus delectare jugiter. ibidem c. 7. v. 18. Inebriemur uberibus, id est, amoribus, quomodo interpretantur Hellenistae & Chaldaeus. Licet ergo ubera in primitiva significatione non soleant tribui viro, unde nec infra c. 5. hujus praestantissimi cantici inter sponsi membra enumerantur; apte tamen in praesenti versiculo tribuuntur sponso in metaphorica & tralatitia significatione amoris & blanditiarum. Sic in metaphorica significatione tribuuntur & alia quae mulierum sunt Deo & viris passim in sacris Eloquiis, puta lactare Esa. 66. v. 16. Ose. 2. v. 14. parturire Esa. 46. v. 4. Gal. 4. v. 19. ex utero gignere Ps. 109. v. 3. &c.
units.tr: There are two Hebraisms here. The first is in the word breasts, which, in an idiom familiar to the Hebrews, here means caresses or loves, because breasts entice love, and because the heart, which is the seat of love, is as it were cradled and contained by the breasts. So Ezekiel 23:17 has bed of breasts, that is, of loves or of love; Proverbs 5:19 has let her breasts satisfy you at all times, that is, as Solomon himself explains in the very next half-verse, delight continually in her love; and in Proverbs 7:18 let us be drunk with breasts, that is, with loves, as the Hellenists and the Chaldee paraphrast render it. Although breasts in their proper sense are not usually attributed to a man, and for this reason in chapter 5 of this most excellent Song they are not counted among the bridegroom's members, nevertheless they are fittingly attributed to the bridegroom in the present verse, in the metaphorical and transferred sense of love and caresses. In the same metaphorical way, other things that belong to women are attributed to God and to men throughout the sacred Scriptures: for example, to suckle (Isaiah 66:16; Hosea 2:14), to be in travail (Isaiah 46:4; Galatians 4:19), to beget from the womb (Psalm 110:3), and so on.

units.la: Alter Hebraismus praesentis versiculi est in voce vino, quae hic, ut & alibi passim sumitur phrasi Hebraica pro quovis delectabili, seu deliciarum genere, ut observant Rabbini; quemadmodum panis eodem idiotifmo sumitur pro quibusvis vitæ necessariis, quo sensu in oratione Dominica, quæ, quantum substringitur verbis, tantum diffunditur sensibus, ut ait Tert. de Orat. dicimus, Panem nostrum quotidianum da nobis hodie. Nec incongruè etiam dixeris amoris & blanditiarum bonitatem passim in hoc sacro Dramate cum bonitate vini veri & proprië dicti conferri, quia & amoris & vini bonitas in suavitate & fortitudine sita est.
units.tr: The second Hebraism of this verse is in the word wine, which here, as elsewhere throughout, is used in the Hebrew manner for any delight or kind of pleasure, as the rabbis observe. In the same idiom, bread is used for any necessities of life; and in this sense we say in the Lord's Prayer, which, as Tertullian says in his treatise On Prayer, is as much spread out in meaning as it is compressed in words: Give us this day our daily bread. Nor would you be wrong to say that the goodness of love and caresses is throughout this sacred drama fittingly compared with the goodness of true and properly so-called wine, since the goodness of both love and wine lies in their sweetness and strength.

units.la: 2. Fragrantia unguentis optimis. Id est, odor tuus præstat odore ex optimis aromatibus exhalante. Est autem fragrantia hic nomen fœminini generis sonans suaveolentiam, & responsdens Hebræo Reach, non vero participium plurale, quod etiam plus satis indicat versuum distinctio.
units.tr: 2. Fragrant with the best ointments. That is: your scent surpasses the scent of the finest spices breathing out. Here fragrance is a feminine noun, signifying sweetness of smell, and answers to the Hebrew reach; it is not a plural participle, as the division of the verses also sufficiently indicates.

units.la: Oleum effusum. Id est, sicut oleum nulli vasculo inclusum longè latéque serpit.
units.tr: Poured-out oil. That is: just as oil, not enclosed in any vessel, spreads far and wide.

units.la: Nomen tuum. Q d. Sic famæ tuæ longè latéque spiras fragrantia.
units.tr: Your name. That is: in the same way you breathe fragrance far and wide over your reputation.

units.la: Ideò adolescentulæ dilexerunt te. Id est, fama tua bona ubique sparsa, vel ipsarum adolescentularum (quæ Heb. dicuntur Alamoth, quia quoad fieri potest latitant, ne oculus viri, maximè externi ipsas videat) animos in tui amorem rapit. Sic Ecclesia dicit, tam longè latéque diffundi famam cœlestis sui sponsi, ut gentes, quæ vix ipsum nosse cœperint, in ipsius amorem rapiantur.
units.tr: Therefore the young maidens love you. That is: your good name, spread everywhere, or perhaps the young maidens themselves (called in Hebrew alamoth, because they keep themselves hidden as far as possible, so that a man's eye, and especially a stranger's, does not see them), carry their hearts away into love of you. So the Church says that the fame of her heavenly bridegroom is spread so far and wide that the nations, who have only just begun to know him, are carried away into love of him.

units.la: 3. Trahe me. Supple, ad te, ut quantocyùs tibi, à quo separata vivere nequeo, arcto jungar amplexu, & indissolubili matrimonii vinculo adhæream. Ardens suum accelerandarum nuptiarum desiderium sponsa exprimit, dum trahi à sponso in uxorem appetit, ne si vulgari more duceretur, ductus ille aliquam parvam moram nuptiis afferret.
units.tr: 3. Draw me. Supply: to you, so that I may be joined to you in a tight embrace as quickly as possible, since I cannot live separated from you, and cleave to you in the indissoluble bond of marriage. The bride expresses her ardent desire for the nuptials to be hastened, as she asks to be drawn by the bridegroom as his wife, rather than led in the usual manner, since that kind of leading would bring some small delay to the wedding.

units.la: Post te curremus. &c. Q. d. Tam suaviter fragras, ut velimus ego & adolescentulæ comites meæ te gressu quàm velocissimo sequi, quocunque ieris.
units.tr: We will run after you, etc. That is: you give off such a sweet fragrance that I and my young companions wish to follow you with the swiftest possible step, wherever you go.

units.la: In odorem unguentorum tuorum, Hæc verba in textu Hebræo subaudita, suppleverunt Interpretes Hellenisstæ & Vulgatus.
units.tr: Into the odour of your ointments. These words are implied in the Hebrew text; the Hellenist translators and the Vulgate supplied them.

units.la: Introduxit me Rex in cellaria sua, &c. Hebraicè, ad verbum, introducat, &c. Sensus est q. d. Etiam si introduxerit me Rex aliquis in ipsa penetralia thesaurorum suorum, non tantum gaudii & voluptatis inde accedet, quantum ex tui fruitione accedit mihi & comitibus meis, nec unquam oblivi scemur amores seu blanditias tuas esse quibusvis deliciis suaviores.
units.tr: The King has brought me into his storerooms, etc. In Hebrew, word for word, let him bring, etc. The sense is: even if some king were to bring me into the innermost chambers of his treasuries, there would not come to me from that as much joy and pleasure as comes to me and my companions from enjoying you. Nor shall we ever forget that your love and your caresses are sweeter than any delights.

units.la: Recti diligunt te. Id est, quotquot sunt æqui rerum æstimatores, tot habes tui amatores. Ecclesia illecta coelestis sponsi fama veluti fragrantis cujusdam unguenti bono ac suavi odore optat non more solito duci uxorem sed trahi, ut quantocyùs spirituali cum sponso conjugalis usûs dulcedine perfruatur. Addit paratam se cum omnibus gentibus sponsum adamatum velocissimo gressu sequi, ita ut nullis rerum creatarum oblectamentis ab ipsius fruitione avocari possit, memor adeò cœlestis sponsi suavitatem præstare maximis quibusque deliciis creatis, ut qui ejusdem suavitatis amore non rapitur, perversum habeat judicium necesse sit. Obiter hic adverte gratiæ efficacis cum humana libertate combinationem. Trahit nos Deus, cùm infirmissimæ voluntari nostræ gratiam medicinalem, efficacissimam, & vorticordiam adhibet; quo autem fortius trahit, eò suavius & liberius currimus.
units.tr: The upright love you. That is: as many as are fair judges of things, so many lovers you have. Drawn by the fame of her heavenly bridegroom, like a fragrant ointment with its good and sweet odour, the Church desires not to be led in the customary manner as a wife but to be drawn, so that she may as quickly as possible enjoy the sweetness of marital intercourse with the spiritual bridegroom. She adds that she is ready to follow her beloved bridegroom with the swiftest step, together with all the nations, so that she may not be drawn away from his enjoyment by any pleasures of created things. She remembers that the sweetness of the heavenly bridegroom surpasses the greatest of created delights, so that whoever is not carried away by the love of that sweetness must necessarily have a perverted judgement. Here, in passing, notice the combination of efficacious grace with human freedom. God draws us, applying to our weakest will a healing, most efficacious and, as it were, whirling grace; yet the more strongly he draws, the more sweetly and freely we run.

units.la: 4. Nigra sum, &c. Q. d. Colorem meum insuavem abundè compensat elegans ac venusta totius corporis, membrorumque singulorum figura, & dispositio. Potest verti ex textu Hebræo, fusca sum, sed expetita. Sic Ecclesia licet nigra peccatis, decora tamen est fide suâ in eum qui populum suum a peccatis eorum salvum est facturus.
units.tr: 4. I am black, etc. That is: the elegant and graceful figure and arrangement of my whole body and of each of my limbs abundantly makes up for my unpleasant colour. It can be rendered from the Hebrew text as: I am dark, but desired. So the Church, though black with sins, is nevertheless comely through her faith in him who is going to save his people from their sins.

units.la: Filiæ Jerusalem. Sacrorum horum bucolicorum scenam exhibet Salomon in montibus & convallibus civitatis Jerusalem; unde sponsa hic inducitur filias Jerosolymitanas amatoriis ipsius excessibus quasi attonitas alloquens. De etymo nominis Jerusalem egimus in commentario nostro in Mat. 2. v. 3.
units.tr: Daughters of Jerusalem. Solomon presents the scene of these pastoral sacred poems on the mountains and in the valleys of the city of Jerusalem. Hence the bride is here introduced addressing the daughters of Jerusalem, who are astonished, as it were, by the ecstasies of her love. We have treated the etymology of the name Jerusalem in our commentary on Matthew 2:3.

units.la: Sicut tabernacula Cedar. Id est, juxta Chaldeum paraphrasten, ut filii Chus, qui habitant in tentoriis Cedar: immo ut Cedrei, qui & Cedareni, seu Cedranitæ dicuntur, & Arabiam felicem incolunt, nomé que habent à parente suo Cedar secundo Ismaelis filio. Sonat autem Cedar Hebraicè fuscum, qui ferè Arabum color est, quia sunt à sole adusti, quales proprie dicuntur Cedarim. Unde est quod Job c. 30. v. 28. queritur se קדר Cedar, id est, fuscum ambulasse quamvis à sole intactum, ut luctum in se doceat idipsum omninò præstitisse, quod in aliis solis adustio.
units.tr: As the tents of Kedar. That is, according to the Chaldee paraphrast, as the sons of Cush who dwell in the tents of Kedar; or rather as the Kedreans, who are also called Kedarenes or Kedranites, and who inhabit Arabia Felix and take their name from their forefather Kedar, Ishmael's second son. Now Kedar in Hebrew means dusky, which is nearly the colour of the Arabs, because they are burnt by the sun; they are properly called Kedarim. Hence Job (30:28) complains that he walked "dusky" [קדר], that is, though untouched by the sun, so as to show that in his mourning he had himself suffered exactly what sunburn does to others.

units.la: Sicut pelles Salomonis. id est, sicut tapetia Salomonis, cujus supellex omnis pulcherrima. Porro ordo præsentis versiculi esset, nigra sum sicut tabernacula Cedar, sed formosa sicut pelles, seu tapetia Salomonis. Sed hæc transponuntur per figuram, qualis χιασμός. Similis Metathesis occurrit Joel. 1. v. 11. & 12. in his verbis. Confusi sunt agricolæ, ululaverunt vinitores, super frumento & hordeo, quia periit messis agri. Vinea confusa est, &c. ubi ordo esset: Confusi sunt agricolæ super frumento & hordeo, quia periit messis agri; ululaverunt vinitores, quia vinea confusa est.
units.tr: As the curtains of Solomon. That is, as the hangings of Solomon, whose furnishings were all very beautiful. The order of this little verse would be: I am black as the tents of Kedar, but beautiful as the curtains or hangings of Solomon. But these words are transposed by a figure of speech, such as chiasmus [χιασμός]. A similar metathesis occurs in Joel 1:11 and 12: The farmers are ashamed, the vinedressers wail, over the wheat and the barley, because the harvest of the field has perished. The vine is dried up, etc., where the order would be: The farmers are ashamed over the wheat and the barley, because the harvest of the field has perished; the vinedressers wail, because the vine is dried up.

units.la: 5. Nolite me considerare. Heb. ad verbum, ne videte me, id est, ne despicite me. Sic Job 41. v. 25. de Leviatan, id est, de crocodilo, dicitur Omne sublime videt, id est, despicit ea animalia, quibus corpus procerius est, & longiora crura, quorum ad miniculo eriguntur in sublime. Ut ut enim sese efferant, eorum maxima quaeque uno ictu caudae prostrata nullo negotio jugulat & dilacerat crocodilus, ut videre est apud Horum lib. 1. Hieroglyphicorum c. 67. Petrum Martyrem Legat. Babylonic. lib. 3. Dalechampium Historiae plantarum lib. 18. c. 99. &c.
units.tr: 5. Do not look at me. In Hebrew, word for word, do not see me, that is, do not despise me. So Job 41:25 says of Leviathan, that is, of the crocodile, He sees everything that is high, that is, he despises those animals whose bodies are taller and whose legs are longer, which they raise up on high with their help. For however much they raise themselves, the crocodile easily throws down the greatest of them with one blow of its tail, and tears them apart, as may be seen in Horapollo, Hieroglyphics book 1, chapter 67; Peter Martyr, Embassy to Babylon book 3; Dalechamps, History of Plants book 18, chapter 99, etc.

units.la: Fusca. Heb. [illegible, ~6 letters], quod non est subfusca, ut multi volunt, sed valde fusca, qualem se fatetur esse sponsa, quia sol illam exuflerat, dum custodiebat vineas. Literarum quippe radicalium in vocibus Hebraeis geminatio non minuit vim vocis, sed intendit, ut apud nos superlativus gradus.
units.tr: Dusky. In Hebrew [the word is illegible in the scan], which does not mean somewhat dusky, as many suppose, but very dusky; this is what the bride confesses she is, because the sun has scorched her while she was keeping the vineyards. For the doubling of the root letters in Hebrew words does not weaken the force of the word but intensifies it, as the superlative degree does among us.

units.la: Filii matris, &c. Q. d. Cum vineam meam custodiendo, libera essem a solis ardore, fratres mei coegerunt me, ut relicta vinea mea custodirem vineas aliorum, in quibus dies, noctesque sub dio agens, aestu gelúque adurebar. Rogat Ecclesia ne despiciatur ob nigrorem contractum, dum aestu Libidinis abrepta, vineam Legis sibi a Deo traditam non custodivit, studio placendi hominibus.
units.tr: The sons of my mother, etc. That is to say: while I was keeping my own vineyard I was free from the heat of the sun; but my brothers compelled me to leave my vineyard and keep the vineyards of others, where, living out of doors by day and night, I was scorched by heat and cold. The Church asks not to be despised for the darkness she has contracted, since, carried away by the heat of lust, she did not keep the vineyard of the Law given to her by God, but sought to please men.

units.la: 6. Indica mihi, &c. Id est, verum, o sponse dilectissime, haud aegre omnium praeteritorum malorum, quanta quanta sunt, oblivicar, dummodo indices mihi ubi te invenire possim, ut tuo fruar amplexu.
units.tr: 6. Tell me, etc. That is: tell me, O most beloved bridegroom, and I shall gladly forget all the past evils, however great they are, provided you show me where I may find you, so that I may enjoy your embrace.

units.la: Ubi cubes. Heb. recubare facias, supple, gregem tuum.
units.tr: Where you lie down. In Hebrew, make to lie down, supply: your flock.

units.la: In meridie. Id est, sub meridiem. Solebant autem pastores in calidis regionibus pecora horis meridianis ad umbram & aquas subducere, ne lac per aestum corrumperetur, & ipsa pecora in periculosos morbos inciderent. Vide Virgilium Georgic. 3. Hinc & illud Menalcae apud eundem Eclog. 3.
units.tr: At noon. That is, about midday. Now shepherds in hot regions were accustomed to lead their flocks to shade and water during the noon hours, so that the milk would not spoil in the heat and the flocks themselves would not fall into dangerous diseases. See Virgil, Georgics book 3. Hence also that line of Menalcas in the same poet, Eclogue 3:

units.la: Cogite oveis pueri, nam si lac praeceperit aestus, ut nuper, frustra pressabimus ubera palmis.
units.tr: Boys, drive your sheep; for if the heat has spoiled the milk, as it did lately, we shall press the udders with our palms in vain.

units.la: Ne pagari incipiam, &c. id est, ne incerta ubi fis, dum te quaero, ut vaga circumire cogar per singulas sodalium tuorum caulas cum dedecore & probro. Ecclesia Sollicita quaerit ab ipso sponso ubi cum ovibus meridietur, seu degat in clara & orthodoxa fidei luce. Non enim, ut ait. B. Leo Ser. 5. de Nativit. Domini, in sola opere virtutum, aut in sola observantia mandatorum, sed etiam in tramite fidei angusta & ardua via est, quae ducit ad vitam, & magni laboris est, magnique discriminis inter dubias imperitorum opiniones, & verisimiles falsitates, per unam sanae doctrinae semitam inoffensis gressibus ambulare, & cum undique se se laquei erroris opponant, omne periculum deceptionis evadere. Praeclare autem B. Ambrof. lib. 4. hexaëm. cap. 5. Meridies, inquit, praesentis seculi Ecclesia, est, ubi justitia splendet, ubi fulget judicium sicut meridies, ubi umbra non cernitur.
units.tr: Lest I begin to wander, etc. That is: lest, not knowing where you are while I seek you, I be forced to roam from one of your companions' folds to another, to my shame and disgrace. The anxious Church asks the bridegroom himself where he rests at noon with his sheep, that is, where he dwells in the clear and orthodox light of faith. For not, as St Leo says, Sermon 5 on the Nativity of the Lord, only in the works of virtue, or in the observance of the commandments alone, but also in the path of faith, the way that leads to life is narrow and steep; it takes great labour and great care, amid the doubtful opinions of the unskilled and the plausible falsehoods, to walk with unstumbling steps along the single path of sound doctrine, and, since snares of error stand in every direction, to escape every danger of deception. St Ambrose too says admirably, Book 4 of the Hexaemeron, chapter 5: The noon, he says, is the Church of the present age, where justice shines, where judgement blazes like midday, where no shadow is seen.

units.la: Sponsus.
units.tr: The Bridegroom.

units.la: 7. SI ignoras te, ô pulcherrima inter mulieres, egredere, & abi post vestigia gregum & pasce hœdos tuos juxta tabernacula pastorum.
units.tr: 7. If you do not know yourself, O fairest among women, go forth and depart after the footsteps of the flocks, and feed your kids beside the tents of the shepherds.

units.la: 8. Equitatui meo in curribus Pharaonis assimilavi te, amica mea.
units.tr: 8. I have likened you, my love, to my company of horses among the chariots of Pharaoh.

units.la: 9. Pulchrae sunt genae tuae sicut turturis: collum tuum sicut monilia.
units.tr: 9. Your cheeks are beautiful as those of a turtledove; your neck is like strings of jewels.

units.la: 10. Murenulas aureas faciemus tibi, vermiculatas argento.
units.tr: 10. We will make you chains of gold, inlaid with silver.

units.la: EXPLICATIO.
units.tr: EXPLANATION.

units.la: 7. SI ignoras te. Heb. ad verbum, si non cognoscis tibi, seu, ut vertit Munsterus, si ignorans es apud te. Sensus est, si domi apud te manens detegere ubi pascam & recubare faciam gregem meum in meridie non potes.
units.tr: 7. If you do not know yourself. In Hebrew, word for word, if you do not know to yourself, or, as Münster renders it, if you are ignorant with yourself. The sense is: if you remain at home with yourself, you cannot discover where I may feed my flock and make it lie down at noon.

units.la: Egredere. Supple, extra domum & civitatem.
units.tr: Go forth. Supply: outside the house and the city.

units.la: Abi post vestigia gregum. Id est, insiste vestigiis per greges relictis.
units.tr: Go after the footsteps of the flocks. That is, tread in the footprints left by the flocks.

units.la: Et pasce hœdos tuos (Heb Capellas tuas) juxta tabernacula pastorum tuorum. Id est, & inter pascendum hœdos tuos, ne recedas à tabernaculis pastorum, & invenies me meridiantem cum ovibus meis. Itaque si Ecclesia in detegendis veris fidei & morum dogmatis aliquâ difficultate laborat, insistat oportet vestigiis Patriarcharum, nec recedat ab eorum doctrinâ, ad quos sermo Dei factus est.
units.tr: And feed your kids (in Hebrew, your she-goats) beside the tents of your shepherds. That is, while feeding your kids, do not stray from the tents of the shepherds, and you will find me resting at noon with my sheep. So if the Church labours under some difficulty in discovering the true doctrines of faith and morals, she ought to follow the footsteps of the Patriarchs, and not depart from the teaching of those to whom the word of God was spoken.

units.la: 8. Equitatui meo, &c. Sponsae decor commendatur. Q. d. Decor tuus, ô sponsa mulierum pulcherrima, mihi videtur non absimilis Regiis illis equis curulibus, mihi ex Ægypto adductis. Hic satis indicat Salomon, Regiae suae dignitati in hoc sacro bucolico carmine pastoralem personam accessisse, non succes-sisse.
units.tr: 8. To my company of horses, etc. The beauty of the bride is commended. As if to say: Your beauty, O bride, most fair among women, seems to me not unlike those royal chariot horses brought to me from Egypt. Here Solomon clearly indicates that, in this sacred pastoral song, a pastoral figure has been joined to his royal dignity, not substituted for it.

units.la: In curribus Pharaonis, Id est Regiis. Pharao enim ; teste Iosepho, Ægyptiis sonat principem. Licèt autem, ut dicitur 2. Paralip. 9. v. 16. equi Salomoni venissent ex Ægypto & omnibus terris, tamen hoc ipso, quod ibidem fit Ægypti mentio specialis, docetur plerúsque ipsius equos ex Ægypto venisse ; quod etiam colligitur ex 3. Reg. 10. v. 28. & 29. 2. Paralip. 1. v. 16. & 17,
units.tr: Among the chariots of Pharaoh, that is, among the royal ones. For Pharaoh, as Josephus attests, means "prince" in the Egyptian tongue. Although, as is said in 2 Chronicles 9:16, horses came to Solomon from Egypt and from all lands, nevertheless, from the very fact that a special mention of Egypt is made there, it is taught that for the most part his horses came from Egypt. This is also gathered from 1 Kings 10:28–29 and 2 Chronicles 1:16–17.

units.la: 9. Pulchræ. Id est, ornatæ. Comparat sponsus varium splendorem gemmarum sponsæ genas adornantium cum plumis turturum, quæ circa collum ad singulas conversiones colorem mutant, sicut & plumæ versicolores columbæ. Neque obscurum est, quomodo gemmis ornentur genæ, nempe si ex auribus pendeant, aut si inspergantur mitrarum redimiculis, id est, latis fasciis, quæ per malas productæ, mento subligabantur.
units.tr: 9. Beautiful. That is, adorned. The bridegroom compares the varied splendour of the gems adorning the bride's cheeks with the plumage of turtle-doves, which change colour at each turning about the neck, just as the many-coloured feathers of the dove do. Nor is it obscure how the cheeks are adorned with gems: namely, if they hang from the ears, or if they are scattered over the headbands of mitres, that is, the broad bands which, drawn across the cheeks, were tied under the chin.

units.la: Sicut turturis Scilicet plumæ, non vero genæ ; nam ut ait Philosophus lib. 2. de partibus animalium c. 16. Avis pro malis id habet, quod rostrum vocant. Frustrà Ovidium objeceris reliquas aves invitare ad genas lacerandas in morte psittaci sui lib. 2. Amorum Elegiâ sextâ.
units.tr: As of a turtle-dove. Namely, its feathers, not its cheeks. For, as the Philosopher says in book 2 of On the Parts of Animals, chapter 16: A bird has for its cheeks that which they call the beak. You will vainly cite Ovid, who in book 2 of the Amores, elegy 6, invites the other birds to tear their cheeks at the death of his parrot.

units.la: Ite pia volucres, & plangite pectora pennis. Et rigido teneras ungue notate genas.
units.tr: Go, dutiful birds, and beat your breasts with your wings, and mark your tender cheeks with your stiff claws.

units.la: Hæc enim ille poëticâ profopopeiâ ad aves accommodans, quæ hominum in luctu propria sunt. Proinde idem Tristium lib. 3. Elegiâ tertiâ,
units.tr: For he, applying to birds in a poetic personification what is proper to men in mourning, says this. Accordingly, in book 3 of the Tristia*, elegy 3:

units.la: Parce tamen lacerare genas, nec scinde capillos.
units.tr: Yet spare to tear your cheeks, nor rend your hair.

units.la: Et Tibullus lib. 1. Elegiâ primâ,
units.tr: And Tibullus in book 1, elegy 1:

units.la: Tu manes ne læde meos, sed parce solutis, Crinibus, & teneris, Delia, parce genis.
units.tr: Do not harm my spirit, but spare, Delia, your loosened hair and your tender cheeks.

units.la: Et Artemidorus onirocriticôn lib. 1. cap. 30. Genas (in somnis) habere graciles aut exulceratas, tristitiam & luctum significat. Graciles quidem tristitiam, exulceratas autem luctum. Nam in luctu homines genas dilacerant. Horus lib. 2. Hieroglyph. cap. 50. ait de Ægyptiis quòd mulierem lactantem & bene nutrientem ubi significare volebant, τρυγόνα, id est, turturem pingebant. Sola enim inter omnes volucres, hæc dentes ac mammas habet. Quæ si vera sunt, malas etiam habet & genas. Sed à doctis jam observatum hæc ad vespertilionem pertinere. Itaque τρυγόνα in τρυγόνα nonnulli mutant : quo nomine vespertilionem appellari conjectant, quia illius est proprium τρίζειν stridere, ut author est Julius Pollux. Alii μεsitus in νυκτερίδα ; quæ cur permutata fuerint, causa est obvia. Proximè antecesserat, imbecillum hominem & magna molientem significare volentes, vuxtepi'Ala, vespertilionem pingunt, qua fine pennis volat. Et proxime sequitur, hominem qui saltatione & tibia demulcetur, designaturi pingunt τχυγο'να, turturem, scilicet marinum, qui Latinis dicitur paslinaca. Neque enim turtur avis, sed turtur piscis marinus, (quem praeter morem Graecorum Horus lib. 2. Hieroglyph. cap. 51. & 105. Turturem appellat sine addito) id est, pastinaca, tibia & saltatione delinitus in nassam inducitur, ut pluribus narrat Aelianus lib. 17. de animal. c. 18. Philes tamen id quoque refert ad turturem avem.
units.tr: And Artemidorus, in book 1, chapter 30 of the Oneirocritica: To have slender or ulcerated cheeks (in dreams) signifies sadness and mourning. Slender cheeks indeed signify sadness, but ulcerated ones mourning, for in mourning men tear their cheeks. Horapollo, in book 2 of the Hieroglyphics, chapter 50, says of the Egyptians that when they wished to signify a nursing and well-feeding woman, they painted a τρυγόνα [trygona], that is, a turtle-dove. For it alone among all birds has teeth and breasts. If these things are true, it also has cheeks and jaws. But learned men have already observed that this applies to the bat. Therefore some change τρυγόνα into τρυγόνα [trygona] (sic), by which name they conjecture the bat is called, because it is peculiar to it to τρίζειν [trizein], to squeak, as Julius Pollux attests. Others change the word into νυκτερίδα [nykteris], the bat; the reason for the change is obvious. Just before, wishing to signify a weak man attempting great things, they paint a bat, which flies without feathers. And next, wishing to designate a man who is soothed by dancing and the flute, they paint a τρυγόνα [trygona], a turtle, namely the sea turtle, which in Latin is called pastinaca. For it is not a bird, the turtle, but a sea fish, the turtle (which Horapollo, contrary to the usage of the Greeks, calls simply "turtle" in book 2 of the Hieroglyphics, chapters 51 and 105), that is, the stingray, which, charmed by the flute and dancing, is led into the net, as Aelian relates at length in book 17 of On Animals, chapter 18. Philes, however, also refers this to the turtle-bird.

units.la: Collum tuum sicut monilia. Q. d. Collum tuum adeo usque quaque speciosum est, ut rotunditate perfectissimum adaequet monilium circulum, & candore non cedat eorumdem monilium candidissimis margaritis, ex quibus connecti solent, proindeque nec adscititiis egeat monilium ornamentis. Hinc praeclare B. Bernardus Serm. 41. in Cantica: Solet collum monilibus ornari, non ipsis comparari: sed hoc illae faciant, quibus quia de proprio non inest decor, aliunde necesse est ut mendicent, unde speciosas se mentiantur. Nam sponsae collum in seipso tam formosum, & tam decenter, quasi natura formatum est, ut extrinsecus non requirat ornatum. Ceterum in textu Hebraeo habetur ad verbum, pulchrae sunt genae tuae batorim, [id est, in turturibus, vel quod aliis magis placet, in ordinibus scilicet, gemmarum) collum tuum bacharouzim, id est, in catenulis, seu, monilibus; haec enim vox Hebraeis aliunde ignota, ex Arabica lingua est notissima, qua verbum charaza est filo conserere, subula confuere. Unde Charazath, grana filo conserta, spinae dorsi vertebrae in homine; in scorpione caudae spondyli & internodia, quae Talmudicis chomare & Hebraeorum aliis Chulijoth. Alcharaz, spina dorsi, cujus spondylia tanquam consuta & conserta sunt. Item monile ex gemmis confertis. Vulgatus itaque & Helleniftae interpretes vel pro batori & bacharoufim legerunt Hebraice catorim & cacharoufim, vel non curantes de versione ad verbum reddidere sensum. Ut Ezech. 16. v. 10. Et seqq. Sic hoc versiculo commendat Deus varia a se dona in Israelitas collata, sub figura sponsae pulcherrimae, quae ad nuptias ornatur.
units.tr: Your neck is like necklaces. As if to say: Your neck is so beautiful in every respect that in roundness it equals a perfect circle of necklaces, and in whiteness it yields nothing to the most gleaming pearls with which such necklaces are usually strung; therefore it needs no borrowed adornments of necklaces. Hence the blessed Bernard admirably says in Sermon 41 on the Song: The neck is wont to be adorned with necklaces, not to be compared with them; but those women do this who, since no beauty is in them of their own, must beg it from elsewhere, so that they may pretend to be beautiful. For the bride's neck is in itself so lovely and so becoming, as if formed by nature, that it does not require outward adornment. Moreover, in the Hebrew text it reads word for word: Beautiful are your cheeks, batorim (that is, among the turtle-doves, or, what pleases others better, in rows, namely of gems), your neck, bacharouzim, that is, in little chains, or necklaces. For this word is otherwise unknown to the Hebrews, but from the Arabic tongue it is very well known, in which the verb charaza means to string together with thread, to sew with an awl. Hence charazath, grains strung on a thread; the vertebrae of the spine in a man; in a scorpion the joints and segments of the tail, which the Talmudists call chomare, and other Hebrews chulijoth. Alcharaz, the spine of the back, whose vertebrae are as if sewn and strung together. Likewise, a necklace of closely set gems. Thus the Vulgate and the Septuagint translators either read catorim and cacharoufim in Hebrew instead of batori and bacharouzim, or, not troubling about a word-for-word rendering, gave the sense. Compare Ezekiel 16:10 and following. So in this verse God commends the various gifts he bestowed upon the Israelites, under the figure of a most beautiful bride being adorned for her wedding.

units.la: 10. Murenulas aureas, &c. Murenulae, Inquit Cassiodorus, ornamentum sunt colli virginalis & puellaris: videlicet, virgulae auri perplexae, intermixtis nonnunquam pulchra varietate subtilissimis argenti filis. Pollicetur itaque in praesenti versiculo sponsus ornamentum congruum sponsae collo, cujus pulchritudinem in superiori versiculo commendaverat. Vocem Hebraicam tore in praesenti versu non sumendam pro turture ave, sed pro ornamento indicant adjuncta. Vermiculatas argento. Id est, ut patet ex textu Hebraeo, punctis argenteis affabrè intermixtas, seu ut loquitur mox laudatus Cassiodorus, in modum vermium terrenorum, quos lumbricos dicunt, distinctas & inter se conjunctas. Jam promittit Deus Israelitis dona longè majora, & pretiosiora hactenus collatis sub figura ornamentorum pretiosiorum & multò magis affabrè factorum. Hactenus quippe Ecclesiæ sub Lege ornamenta erant adoptio filiorum, & gloria, & testamentum, & legislatio, & obsequium, & promissa, ut loquitur Apostolus. Rom. 9. At jam ipsi promittitur decus longè majus, nempe brevi ex ipsa nasciturus secundum carnem Christus, qui est super omnia Deus benedictus in secula, Amen.
units.tr: 10. Golden little chains, etc. Murenulae, says Cassiodorus, are ornaments of a virgin's and a girl's neck, namely little threads of gold intertwined, sometimes with the most delicate silver threads interwoven in a pleasing variety. The bridegroom therefore promises in this verse an ornament suited to the bride's neck, whose beauty he had commended in the previous verse. The Hebrew word tore in this verse is not to be taken for the turtle-dove, but for an ornament, as the accompanying words indicate. Worked with silver. That is, as is clear from the Hebrew text, skilfully interspersed with silver points, or, as the same Cassiodorus, just quoted, puts it, distinguished and joined together in the manner of earthworms, which they call lumbrici. Now God promises the Israelites gifts far greater and more precious than those hitherto bestowed, under the figure of more precious ornaments and much more skilfully made. For hitherto the ornaments of the Church under the Law were the adoption of sons, and the glory, and the covenant, and the giving of the law, and the service, and the promises, as the Apostle says, Romans 9. But now there is promised to her a far greater honour, namely Christ, who was shortly to be born of her according to the flesh, who is over all, God blessed for ever, Amen.

units.la: Sponsa.
units.tr: The Bride.

units.la: II. DUm effet Rex in accubitu suo, nardus mea dedit odorem suum.
units.tr: 2:1 While the King was at his table, my spikenard gave its fragrance.

units.la: 12. Fasciculus myrrhæ dilectus meus mihi, inter ubera mea commorabitur.
units.tr: 2:2 A bundle of myrrh is my beloved to me; he shall lie all night between my breasts.

units.la: 13. Botrus cypri dilectus meus mihi, in vineis Engaddi.
units.tr: 2:3 My beloved is to me a cluster of henna blossoms in the vineyards of En-gedi.

units.la: EXPLICATIO.
units.tr: EXPLANATION.

units.la: II. DUm effet Rex &c. Q. d. Quamvis odor meus fragret, ita ut Rex mihi desponsatus, cùm esset in accubitu suo inter fragrantissima unguenta, nardum meam fit odoratus; tamen longè fragrantior; multóque suavior est odor sponsi; est enim ut myrrhæ fasciculus, & cypri prope balsameta Engaddi nascentis botrus adeò odoratus, ut eum peroptem jugiter habere inter ubera mea. Per nardum humilem calidæ naturæ herbam designatur humilis ac fervens Ecclesiæ oratio cœlos penetrans. Vide Bernard. Ser. 40. in Cantic.
units.tr: II. "While the King was..." etc. The sense is this: although my fragrance is pleasant, so that the King to whom I am betrothed, while he reclined among the most fragrant ointments, was perfumed by my spikenard, yet the fragrance of the bridegroom is far stronger and much sweeter. For he is like a bundle of myrrh, and like a cluster of henna blossoms from the vineyards of En-gedi, so fragrant that I would wish to have him continually between my breasts. By the humble spikenard, a plant of warm nature, is signified the humble and fervent prayer of the Church, which penetrates the heavens. See Bernard, Sermon 40 on the Song of Songs.

units.la: In accubitu. Heb. ad verbum, in circuitu. Hebræorum mos erat mensæ accumbere in circuitu; unde illud pf. 127. Heb. 128. Filii tui sicut novellæ olivarum in circuitu mensæ tuæ. Eadem vox accubitus eodem sensu accipitur. Tob. 2. v. 3. Exiliens de accubitu suo, relinquens prandium, jejunus pervenit ad corpus.
units.tr: "In accubitu." In Hebrew, word for word, "in circuitu." It was the custom of the Hebrews to recline at table in a circle; hence that verse of Psalm 127 (Hebrew 128): "Your sons like young olive shoots around your table." The same word "accubitus" is taken in the same sense in Tobit 2:3: "Leaping up from his reclining place, leaving his dinner unfinished, he came to the body fasting."

units.la: Nardus. Ex nardi spicis fieri unguentum odoratissimum, proindeque pretiosissimum, eóque olim convivas perfundi solitos litos non colligitur ex præsenti tantum versiculo, sed & ex Evangeliftis. Mat. 26. v. 7. Marc. 14. v. 3. Luc. 7. v. 46. Joan. 12. v. 3. Indidem etiam patet muliebre fuisse officium convivas præcipuos unguentis perfundere. Hinc. 1. Sam. seu Reg. 8. v. 13. Samüel prædixit Regem filias Israël unguentarias esse facturum.
units.tr: "Nardus." That a most fragrant, and therefore most precious, ointment was made from the spikes of nard, and that guests were formerly accustomed to be anointed with it, is gathered not only from this verse but also from the Evangelists: Matthew 26:7; Mark 14:3; Luke 7:46; John 12:3. From the same passages it is also clear that it was women's work to anoint the principal guests with ointments. Hence in 1 Samuel (or 1 Kings) 8:13, Samuel foretold that the King would make the daughters of Israel perfumers.

units.la: 12. Fasciculus myrrhæ. Id est, fertum ex myrrhæ ramis frondosis & floridis compaƈtum. Cùm myrrhæ arbor stillare soleat odoratiffimum liquorem (quæ myrrha solet nuncupari) ut advertunt historiæ naturalis scriptores, procul dubio instar cæterarum arborum resinam odoratam proferentium, eundem quoquo paƈto retinet odorem in caudice, ramis, foliis, & floribus.
units.tr: 12. "A bundle of myrrh." That is, a garland compacted of leafy and flowering branches of myrrh. Since the myrrh tree is accustomed to exude a most fragrant liquid, which is commonly called myrrh, as the writers of natural history point out, it undoubtedly, like the other trees that yield fragrant resin, retains the same fragrance in its trunk, branches, leaves and flowers.

units.la: Inter ubera &c. Alludit sponsa ad muliebrem consuetudinem gestandi ad pectus ferta odorifera & visu pulchra.
units.tr: "Between the breasts, etc." The bride alludes to the custom of women of wearing on the breast garlands that are fragrant and pleasing to the eye.

units.la: 13. Botrus Cypri. Cyprus in Ægypto est arbor ziziphi foliis, femine coriandri, flore candido, odorato. Coquitur hic in oleo, premiturque postea, quod Cyprus vocatur. Optimum habetur è Canopica in ripis Nili nata, fecundum Afcalone Judææ, tertium Cypro infula suavitatis odore. Quidam hanc esse dicunt, quæ in Italia Ligustrum vocatur. Hæc Plinius. lib. 12. hift.nat. cap.24. Cùm autem ligustri flores instar uvarum, in botros coeant, non incongrue botri nomine significantur à sponsa.
units.tr: 13. "Cluster of Cyprus." Cyprus in Egypt is a tree with the leaves of the jujube, the seed of coriander, and a white, fragrant flower. Here it is boiled in oil and then pressed, and the oil is called cyprus. The best is held to be that which grows in Canopus on the banks of the Nile; second, that from Ascalon in Judea; third, that from the island of Cyprus, with its sweet odour. Some say this is what in Italy is called privet. These are the words of Pliny, Natural History, book 12, chapter 24. Since privet flowers gather in clusters like grapes, the bride not unsuitably signifies them by the word "cluster."

units.la: In vineis Engaddi. Id est, prope Balfameta Engaddi.
units.tr: "In the vineyards of En-gedi." That is, near the balsam groves of En-gedi.

units.la: Particulam in fumi passim pro particula prope ostendimus in commentario nostro in Mat. 8. v. 2: multis scripturæ exemplis. Jam vineas Engaddi esse balfameta volunt plerique interpretes. Hieronymus in locis: Vocatur usque hodie vicus pragrandis Judæorum Engaddi juxta mare mortuum, unde & opobalsamum venit, quas vineas Engaddi Salomon nuncupat. Aponius in Cantica lib. 3. Vineæ Engaddi non vinum, sed balsamum gignunt. Et in eundem librum ante annos quingentos Robertus Foliot Londinensis Episcopus: Engaddi planities est juxta Jericho, in qua consistunt arbores in modum vineæ consitæ, ex quibus, dum vulnerantur, fluit balsamum. Recte in modum vineæ consitæ, ita enim veteres tradunt. Juftinus lib. 36. Arbores opobalsami formam similem piceis arboribus habent, nisi quod sunt humiles magis, & in vinearum morem excoluntur. Plinius lib. 12. cap. 25. Viti similior est balsami arbuscula, quam myrto. Malleolis feri dicitur, nuper vincta ut vitis, & implet collos vinearum modo, quæ fine adminiculis fe ipsæ sustinent. Tondetur similiter fruticans, ac rostris nitescit. Et è recentioribus Marinus Sanutus lib. 3. cap. 14. arbuscula illa est sicut vitis trium annorum. Quod autem cyprus nascatur prope balsameta Engaddi patet ex Josepho & ex suppositicio Egesippo; hic enim lib. 4. de excidio Jerosolymitano cap. 17. ait cyprum & balsamum nasci circa fontem ab Elisæo sanatum in agro Jerichuntino, cujus pars erat Engaddi. Josephus vero eandem regionem Jerichuntinam describens lib. 5. de Bello Judaico cap.4. earnait esse feracem opobalsami, cypri & myrobolani.
units.tr: We have shown, in our commentary on Matthew 8:2, with many examples from Scripture, that the particle "in" is often used for "near." Now most interpreters hold that the vineyards of En-gedi are balsam groves. Jerome, in his Book of Places: "Even today the great village of the Jews, En-gedi, lies beside the Dead Sea, whence also comes opobalsam; these Solomon calls the vineyards of En-gedi." Apponius, on the Canticles, book 3: "The vineyards of En-gedi produce not wine but balsam." And on the same book, some five hundred years ago, Robert Foliot, Bishop of London: "The plain of En-gedi is near Jericho, in which stand trees planted in the manner of a vineyard, from which, when they are wounded, balsam flows." Rightly "planted in the manner of a vineyard," for so the ancients report. Justin, book 36: "The opobalsam trees have a form similar to pitch-pines, except that they are lower and are cultivated in the manner of vines." Pliny, book 12, chapter 25: "The little balsam shrub is more like a vine than a myrtle. It is said to be tended by layering, and, bound like a vine, it fills the rows of vineyards, supporting itself without props. It is similarly pruned as a shrub, and it shines with cuttings." And among more recent writers, Marino Sanudo, book 3, chapter 14: "That little shrub is like a vine of three years." That cyprus grows near the balsam groves of En-gedi is clear from Josephus and from the spurious Hegesippus; for the latter, in book 4 of his account of the destruction of Jerusalem, chapter 17, says that cyprus and balsam grow around the spring healed by Elisha, in the field of Jericho, of which En-gedi was a part. Josephus, describing the same Jericho district in book 5 of the Jewish War, chapter 4, says that it is rich in opobalsam, cyprus and myrobalanum.

units.la: Engaddi. Vicus est in agro Jerichuntino, qui Plinio Engadda, Ptolomæo & Stephano Engada, sed Hebræis En-gedi dicitur, id est, fons capri, ut in libro Nominum rectè interpretatur Hieronymus. Hoc nomen à situ videtur adeptus: est enim in celsis rupibus, quæ in valles subjectas casum minari videntur, & terrorem transeuntibus incutiunt. Itaque fons inde promanans ideo fons hœdi seu capri videtur dictus, quasi solis capris esset pervius. Et pagus ibi conditus fontis nomen sibi retinuit, quamvis & à tuguriis, quæ Arabicè dicuntur, Chafac, in palmeto sitis, appelletur 2. Paral. 20. v. 2. Chafason-thamar, seu ut pronuntiat Vulgat. Asasonthamar. Circa pagum illum scilicet palmetum fuit nobilissimum & longè palmeto præstantior hortus opobalsami. Proinde Josephus lib. 9. Antiq. cap. 1. de Moabitis & Ammonitis: Bello oppugnabant Engadde, oppidum Asphaltiti Lacui vicinum, stadiis tresdecim distatum à Jerosolymis. In eo nascuntur egregiæ palmæ & opobalsamum. In Engaddi, inquit B. Greg. in Cantic. 1. balsamum gignitur, quo cum oleo pontificali benedictione, chrisma efficitur. Quod autem balsamum nusquam extra agrum Jerichuntinum nascatur, passim testantur veteres. Strab. lib. 16. Diodorus lib. 19. Justinus lib. 35. Josephus lib. 4. Antiq. cap. 3. & lib. 5. de bello Judaico cap. 4. Josephus bengorion lib. 4. cap. 20. RR. Levi & Kimchi in 4. Reg. 20. v. 13. &c. Nunc tamen præter balsamum Jerichuntinum visitur Americum, quod licet à Jerichuntino differat colore, censetur tamen verum balsamum a Romanensibus, unde validè ex illo confici chrisma declaraverunt Paulus III. & Pius IV. Hæc sufficiant dicta de littera, videamus jam spiritum sub litteræ cortice latentem. Ecclesia dicit, Etsi fervidæ ac humilis orationis meæ odor nubes penetraverit, & Dominus exauditor in ea delectatus fuerit, longè tamen major est fragrantia sponsi, cujus bonus odor myrrhâ, cypro, & balsamo fragrantior multòq; suavior; atque hinc est quod tantoperè concupiscam ut citò compleris in ejus ortu, vita, dictis, passionibus, morte, resurrectione, ascensione omnibus Legalibus umbris & Prophetarum præconiis, ipse solus per amoris sui incendium mihi vivat in corde. Præclarè B. Petrus Damiani in Serm. de SS. Flora & Lucilla: Nemo dubitat inter ubera pectoris esse locum cordis. Dilectus ergo inter sponsæ ubera commorabitur, quia indeficiindeficiens ejus amor ac desiderium ex ejus memoria non delétur.
units.tr: "En-gedi." It is a village in the field of Jericho, called by Pliny "Engadda," by Ptolemy and Stephanus "Engada," but by the Hebrews "En-gedi," that is, "spring of the goat," as Jerome rightly interprets in his Book of Names. It seems to have taken this name from its situation: it lies on high cliffs which seem to threaten to fall into the valleys below and strike terror into those who pass by. Accordingly the spring that rises there seems to have been called "spring of the kid" or "of the goat," as if it were accessible only to goats. And the village founded there kept the name of the spring, although it is also called Hazezon-tamar, from the booths, which in Arabic are called Chafac, set in a palm grove (2 Chronicles 20:2), or, as the Vulgate pronounces it, Asasonthamar. Around that village, namely, there was a palm grove, and a balsam garden far more excellent than the palm grove. Accordingly Josephus, book 9 of the Antiquities, chapter 1, speaks of the Moabites and Ammonites: "They attacked En-gedi by war, a town near the Asphaltite Lake, thirteen stadia distant from Jerusalem. In it grow excellent palms and opobalsam." "In En-gedi," says St. Gregory on the Canticles, book 1, "balsam is produced, with which, together with the pontifical oil and blessing, chrism is made." That balsam grows nowhere outside the field of Jericho is attested everywhere by the ancients: Strabo, book 16; Diodorus, book 19; Justin, book 35; Josephus, Antiquities book 4, chapter 3, and Jewish War book 5, chapter 4; Josephus ben Gorion, book 4, chapter 20; the rabbis Levi and Kimchi on 2 Kings 20:13, etc. Yet now, besides the balsam of Jericho, the American balsam is seen, which, although it differs from the Jericho balsam in colour, is nevertheless considered by the Papists to be true balsam; whence Paul III and Pius IV declared that chrism is validly made from it. Let these things suffice concerning the letter. Let us now see the spirit lying hidden beneath the bark of the letter. The Church says: Although the odour of my fervent and humble prayer has penetrated the clouds, and the Lord, who hears prayer, has been pleased with it, yet the fragrance of the bridegroom is far greater, whose good odour is more fragrant than myrrh, cyprus and balsam, and much sweeter. Hence it is that I so earnestly desire that he may quickly live in my heart, through the burning of his love, by means of his birth, life, words, sufferings, death, resurrection and ascension, and all the Legal shadows and the proclamations of the Prophets. Blessed Peter Damian excellently says in his sermon on Saints Flora and Lucilla: "No one doubts that the place of the heart lies between the breasts. The beloved therefore will dwell between the bride's breasts, because his love and desire, which never fails, is not erased from her memory."

units.la: Sponsus.
units.tr: The Bridegroom.

units.la: 14. ECce tu pulchra es amica mea, Ecce tu pulchra es, oculi tui columbarum.
units.tr: 14. Behold, thou art fair, my love; behold, thou art fair; thine eyes are doves' eyes.

units.la: EXPLICATIO.
units.tr: EXPLANATION.

units.la: 14. Ecce, &c. Congratulatur sponsus sponsæ tam casto & fervido amore sibi uni adhærenti; quod quàm optimè quadrat in Deum Ecclesiæ sub lege sibi desponsatæ congratulantem quòd unicè diligat adventum ipsius, ipsúmque amore continuo in cordis sui arcano complectatur.
units.tr: 14. Behold, etc. The bridegroom rejoices in the bride who clings to him alone with such chaste and fervent love. This fits very well the Church under the law, betrothed to God, who rejoices that she loves his coming alone and embraces him with constant love in the secret place of her heart.

units.la: Oculi tui columbarum. Hebraismus, id est, ut columbarum. Tribuuntur hic sponsæ, & infrà cap. 5. v. 12. oculi columbarum, id est, puri, venusti, simplices, casti denique, quod potissimùm Hebraei hîc intelligunt; quia columba solum conjugem respicit, neque oculos in ullum alium conjicit. Postquam (inquit Rabbi Salomon) compari suo desponsata est, alteri sociari non gaudet. & Aben Ezra, columbæ non solent ulli alteri, quàm compari suo consociari. quod idem de palumbe postquam docuit Ælian lib. 3. hist. cap. 44. addit Ἐὰν δὲ ἐπορθυμίαν ἰτέρους, Si autem libidinosos oculos in alios conjiciant, eos reliqui circumsidentes, marem quidem mares, fœminam verò fœminæ discerpunt. Ubi nota verbum ἐπιτροπεύω de libidinoso aspectu usurpari, quia oculi sunt in amore duces, & ab ὁράω, fit ἐπᾶν. Unde 1. Joan 2. v. 6. concupiscentia oculorum, & 2 Pet. 2. v. 14. oculos habentes plenos adulterii. Quod malo suo expertus David, à Deo obnixè petiit Ps. 118. Heb. 119. v. 37. oculos suos averteret ne viderent vanitatem, & Job c. 31. v. 1. cum iis fœdus pepigit ne virginem aspicerent.
units.tr: Thine eyes are doves' eyes. This is a Hebraism, that is, as the eyes of doves. Here, and below in chapter 5 verse 12, the eyes of doves are attributed to the bride, that is, pure, lovely, simple, and above all chaste. The Hebrews especially understand it this way, because the dove looks only to its mate and casts its eyes on no one else. After she has been betrothed to her mate (says Rabbi Solomon), she does not rejoice to be joined to another. And Aben Ezra: doves are not wont to be joined to anyone but their mate. Aelian, having taught the same about the wood pigeon (lib. 3. hist. cap. 44), adds: But if they cast lustful eyes on others [Ἐὰν δὲ ἐπιθυμίαν ἑτέρους], the others around them tear them apart: the males attack the males, and the females the females. Note that the verb ἐπιτροπεύω [epitropeuō] is used of a lustful glance, because the eyes are the leaders in love, and ἐπᾶν [epan] comes from ὁράω [horaō]. Hence 1 John 2:6, the lust of the eyes, and 2 Pet. 2:14, having eyes full of adultery. David, who learned this to his cost, earnestly asked God (Ps. 118, Heb. 119:37) to turn away his eyes so that they would not see vanity; and Job (chap. 31 verse 1) made a covenant with his eyes not to look upon a virgin.

units.la: Sponsa.
units.tr: The Bride.

units.la: 15. ECce tu pulcher es, dilecte mi, & decorus Lectulus noster floridus.
units.tr: 15. Behold, thou art fair, my beloved, and comely; our bed is flowery.

units.la: 16. Tigna domorum nostrarum cedrina, laquearia nostra cypressina.
units.tr: 16. The beams of our houses are cedar, and our rafters cypress.

units.la: EXPLICATIO.
units.tr: EXPLANATION.

units.la: EXPLICATIO.
units.tr: EXPLANATION.

units.la: ECce tu pulcher es, &c. Q. d. O sponse dilectissime, quanta quanta sit mea, quamdepraedicas, pulchritudo, nulla est si tua cum venustate & pulchritudine omnibus numeri absoluta conferatur. Atque haec verba optime competunt Synagogae Verbum aeternum alloquenti; summa quippe ejus pulchritudo non erat nisi figura adumbrans eum, qui cum esset ab aeterno splendor paternae gloriae, ubi venit plenitudo temporum, ut eos qui sub Lege erant redimeret, homo factus est & tanquam sponsus procedens de thalamo suo apparuit nitidus, decorus & speciosus forma prae filiis hominum.
units.tr: Behold, thou art fair, etc. That is to say: O most beloved bridegroom, however great my beauty may be, of which you speak so highly, it is nothing when compared with your loveliness and beauty, which is perfect in every respect. These words suit very well the Synagogue addressing the eternal Word. For her highest beauty was only a figure foreshadowing him who, though from eternity the brightness of the Father's glory, when the fullness of time came, to redeem those who were under the law, was made man and appeared like a bridegroom coming out of his chamber, bright, comely, and beautiful in form above the sons of men.

units.la: Lectulus, &c. Eleganter sponsa magnifico Regis palatio non inferiorem praedicat thorum pastoralem, quem ipsi recubanti patularam sub tegmine arborum herbae & flores. Sensus est ergo idem ac si diceret, o desideratissime sponse adesdum, veni & noli tardare, consumma cito matrimonium promissum casto connubio, thorum quam jucundissimum & magnificentissimum ad te excipiendum habeo paratum. Haec sponsae verba quam fieri potest perfectissime adumbrant vota Ecclesiae sub Lege invitantis Verbum Patris ut cito promissum in carne adventum exhibeat nec dedignetur per mysticum matrimonium una fieri caro cum ea, quae exemplis & institutis Patriarcharum & Prophetarum, tanquam quibusdam bene olentibus respersa floribus refulget, & quasi fortissimis trabibus innixa, pulcherrimisque laquearibus exornata domus nitescit, & incorrupta perseverat in veris Israelitis.
units.tr: Bed, etc. Elegantly, the bride declares that the pastoral bed, on which flowers and grass lie spread out under the shade of trees for him as he reclines, is no less fine than the king's magnificent palace. The sense is therefore the same as if she said: O most longed-for bridegroom, come now, do not delay, complete quickly the marriage promised by a chaste union. I have prepared a bed for you to receive, as pleasant and magnificent as possible. These words of the bride most perfectly portray the prayers of the Church under the law, inviting the Word of the Father to bring forth quickly the promised coming in the flesh, and not to disdain to become one flesh with her through a mystical marriage. She shines, sprinkled with the examples and institutions of the Patriarchs and Prophets like sweet-smelling flowers, and she stands like a house supported by very strong beams and adorned with most beautiful ceilings, and remains uncorrupted among the true Israelites.

units.la: Cypressina. Heb. בְּרוֹשִׁים, quam vocem alii volunt esse synonymam cum בְּרוֹשׁ Abietes; alii vero volunt significare arbores, quae vocabulo ab hac voce Hebraea derivato dicuntur a Plinio lib. 12. cap. 17. brutae. Ait autem brutam rrborem cupresso fusae similem, exalbidis ramis, jucundi odoris accensam, adoremque esse proximum cedro.
units.tr: Cypress. The Hebrew word [בְּרוֹשִׁים] some take to be synonymous with [בְּרוֹשׁ] fir trees; others wish it to mean trees which, from a word derived from this Hebrew term, Pliny (lib. 12, cap. 17) calls brutae. He says that the brutae tree is like the cypress with whitish branches, has a pleasant fragrance, and is next to the cedar in quality.

units.la: CAPUT SECUNDUM.
units.tr: CHAPTER 2.

units.la: Sponsus.
units.tr: The Bridegroom.

units.la: 1. EGo flos campi, & lilium convallium.
units.tr: 1. I am the flower of the field, and the lily of the valleys.

units.la: 2. Sicut lilium inter Ipinas sic amica mea inter filias.
units.tr: 2. As the lily among thorns, so is my love among the daughters.

units.la: EXPLICATIO.
units.tr: EXPLANATION.

units.la: 1. EGo, &c. Ad literam sensus est idem ac si diceret, Dilectissima sponsa, ecce venio citò; herbaceus enim & floridus ille lectulus tuus me in primis delectat, utpote qui sum flos campi & lilium convallium. Similiter Deus Verbum his verbis exhibetur ut promittens se propediem in carne adventurum & cum hominibus conversaturum; ut autem persTet in metaphora ab Ecclesia mox usurpata de lectulo florido, se cognominat florem campi & lilium convallium, q. d. Lectulus meus floridus non potest esse injucundus ei qui flos est & lilium. Variae autem à SS. PP. afferuntur rationes cur Christus dicatur flos campi & lilium convallium; communior tamen est, Christum se dicere florem campi, quia est flos de radice Jesse, qui absque virili opere è B. Virgine ortus est mundo, non secus ac flos campi ex inarata terra nascitur. Lilium vero convallium, quia humilibus se revelat, & amoris sui copiam largitur per praesentiam.
units.tr: 1. "I am," etc. Literally, the sense is the same as if he said, "My most beloved bride, behold, I come quickly; for that grassy and flowery couch of yours delights me greatly, since I am the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys." Likewise, God the Word is here presented as promising that he will shortly come in the flesh and dwell among men. To keep to the metaphor of the flowery couch, which the Church has just used, he names himself the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys, as if to say: "A flowery couch cannot fail to be pleasing to one who is a flower and a lily." The Fathers offer various reasons why Christ is called the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys; the most common, however, is that Christ calls himself the flower of the field because he is the flower from the root of Jesse, who was born to the world from the blessed Virgin without human labour, just as a flower of the field springs from unploughed ground. He is the lily of the valleys because he reveals himself to the humble and bestows the abundance of his love by his presence.

units.la: Flos. Heb. חבצלת, quod ab aliis redditur lilium, ab aliis narcissus, ab aliis rosa. Intelligendus est ergo flos antonomasticè dictus.
units.tr: Flower. Heb. [חבצלת], which some render lily, others narcissus, others rose. It is to be understood, then, as the flower spoken of par excellence.

units.la: Campi. Heb. השרון. Vox Saron est ambigua, significat enim campum, ut patet tum ex Esai. 35. v. 2. ubi vox Saron sic redditur à Symmacho, tum ex praesenti loco, ubi Vulgatus & Hellenistae eandem vocem Saron in eadem significatione accipiunt, sicut & Esai. 65. v. 10. Praeterea Saron omnis juxta Joppen, Lyddamque appellatur regio, in qua latissimi campi fertilesque tenduntur, ut observat B. Hier. in Esai. 33. unde Act. 9. v. 35. Et viderunt eum omnes, qui habitabant Lyddae & Saronae. & 1 Par. 27. v. 29. Armentis, quae pascebantur in Saron, praepositus fuit Setrai. trai Saronites. Hinc apud Talmudicos tractatu de Sabbato cap. 7. & de menstruata cap. 2. vinum Saroniticum inter generosa censetur, in quibus miscebantur duæ partes aquæ. Verum quem admodum in locis Esaiæ laudatis adjuncta omnino docent Saron ibi esse loci nomen, sic & hic comma sequens, & lilium convallium, docet Saron pro campo esse fumendum, quia sic textus melius cohæret.
units.tr: Of the field. Heb. [השרון]. The word Sharon is ambiguous, for it means a plain, as is clear both from Isaiah 35:2, where the word Sharon is so rendered by Symmachus, and from the present passage, where the Vulgate and the Hellenists take the same word Sharon in the same sense, as also at Isaiah 65:10. Moreover, as the blessed Jerome observes on Isaiah 33, the whole region near Joppa and Lydda is called Sharon, in which the widest plains and fertile fields stretch out; hence Acts 9:35, And all who dwelt at Lydda and Sharon saw him, and 1 Chronicles 27:29, Over the herds that were pastured in Sharon was Shitrai the Sharonite. Hence among the Talmudists, in the tractate on the Sabbath, chapter 7, and on the menstruating woman, chapter 2, Sharonite wine is counted among the choice wines, in which two parts of water were mixed. But just as the adjuncts in the passages of Isaiah cited show that Sharon there is the name of a place, so the following clause here, and the lily of the valleys, shows that Sharon must be taken for a plain, because the text coheres better in this way.

units.la: 2. Sicut lilium, &c. Non dicit lilium crescere inter spinas, sed lilium florem pulcherrimum confert cum spinis asperrimis, & affirmat, quale inter hujusmodi spinas ipsis collatum lilium, talem esse inter ceteras filias ipsis collatam sponsam. Hæc autem comparatio egregie commendat Ecclesiæ præstantiam, quia sicut lilium inter spinas eminet, ita super omnes Conventus Ecclesiæ Dei refulget, ut loquitur B. Ambr. in Ps. 118. in Oston. 5. cum autem vox שושנה Schoschana omne genus florum significet Hebraicè, multi hic rosam significare volunt.
units.tr: 2. As the lily, etc. He does not say that the lily grows among thorns; rather he compares the most beautiful flower with the sharpest thorns, and affirms that the lily, as compared with such thorns, is such as the bride, as compared with the other daughters, is. This comparison splendidly commends the excellence of the Church, for as the lily stands out among thorns, so the assembly of God's Church shines above all others, as the blessed Ambrose says on Psalm 118, Octonary 5, on Hosea 5. Since the Hebrew word [שושנה] Shoshanah signifies every kind of flower, many here want it to mean the rose.

units.la: Sponsa.
units.tr: The Bride.

units.la: 3. Sicut malus inter ligna sylvarum, sic dilectus meus inter filios. Sub umbra illius, quem desideraveram, sedi: & fructus ejus dulcis gutturi meo.
units.tr: 3. As the apple tree among the trees of the forest, so is my beloved among the sons. I sat under the shadow of him whom I had desired, and his fruit was sweet to my throat.

units.la: 4. Introduxit me in cellam vinariam, ordinavit in me charitatem.
units.tr: 4. He brought me into the wine cellar, and set love in order over me.

units.la: 5. Fulcite me floribus, stipate me malis: quia amore langueo.
units.tr: 5. Support me with flowers, surround me with apples, for I languish with love.

units.la: 6. Læva ejus sub capite meo, & dextera illius amplexabitur me.
units.tr: 6. His left hand is under my head, and his right hand shall embrace me.

units.la: EXPLICATIO.
units.tr: EXPLANATION.

units.la: 3. Sicut malus, &c. Sponsa largius cum fœnore sponsum laudat. q. d. Tu, dilectissime sponse, me tantùm ceteris puellis pulchriorem dixisti, quantùm lilium excellit spinis; ast ego te non solâ pulchritudine, sed & sermonum & morum suavitate omnibus hominibus longè superiorem agnosco, atque hinc est quòd vel umbra tua, in qua hactenus sedi, me tantoperè recreet. Ecclesia dicit Deo, tu, ô Rex gentium & desideratus earum me ceteris rationum coetibus compositam ab iis tantùm distare dicis, quantum spinis praestat lilium; at ego longe potiori jure nihil in gestis cujusvis sancti elucere agnosco, quod comparari posset tecum, cujus vel ipsa eloquia, utpote verba vitae aeternae, sunt praemelle suavia. Hinc Lex, quae umbra est futurorum gestorum, & eloquiorum tuorum, me incredibili hactenus laetitia affecit. Praeclare itaque B. Ambros. in Ps. 118. Octon. 8. de Ecclesia sub Lege: Legem acceperat, hanc sequebatur, hanc currebat viam. In Lege itaque requiescens in umbra Christi requiescebat.
units.tr: 3. As the apple tree, etc. The bride praises the bridegroom more lavishly, with interest. As if to say: "You, most beloved bridegroom, have called me more beautiful than the other girls, as the lily surpasses the thorns; but I acknowledge that you, not only in beauty but also in the sweetness of your words and manners, far surpass all men; and hence it is that even your shadow, under which I have sat until now, so greatly refreshes me." The Church says to God: "You, O King of the nations and their Desire, say that I, composed of the assemblies of the rest of the nations, differ from them as much as the lily excels the thorns; but I recognise with far greater right that nothing shining in the deeds of any saint can be compared with you, whose very utterances, as words of eternal life, are sweeter than honey." Hence the Law, which is the shadow of future things, and of your utterances, has until now affected me with incredible joy. Thus the blessed Ambrose admirably says on Psalm 118, Octonary 8, concerning the Church under the Law: She had received the Law, she followed it, she ran this way. Resting therefore in the Law, she was resting in the shadow of Christ.

units.la: 4. Introduxit me, &c. Q. d. Experiri me fecit dilectus meus, quam suavis sit.
units.tr: 4. He brought me, etc. As if to say: "My beloved has made me experience how sweet he is."

units.la: In Cellam vinariam. Quemadmodum, ut supra diximus, vinum phrasi Hebraica dicitur quidquid deliciosum, & voluptarium est, ita hic cellae vinariae nomine appellat sponsa mirificam suavitatem, qua sponsi beneficio potita est & exhilarata.
units.tr: Into the wine cellar. As we said above, in Hebrew idiom whatever is delightful and pleasurable is called wine; so here the bride calls by the name of wine cellar the wonderful sweetness which she has obtained and by which she has been gladdened through the kindness of the bridegroom.

units.la: Ordinavit in me charitatem. Non tam litteram, quam litterae sensum reddidit Vulgatus interpres. Ad verbum enim habetur Hebraice, & vexillum ejus super me charitas. q. d. Et sub vexillo amoris me sibi totam subjecit. Itaque ordinavit in me charitatem, idem est atque, constituit supra me charitatem, seu dilectionem sui mihi propositum, cujus in omnibus sequerer imperium, non secus ac vexillum sequuntur milites. Quod autem verbum ordinare hic sumatur pro constituere, patet ex Ambrosio in Ps. 118. in Octon. 5. Sic Rom. 13. v. 1. Omnis anima potestatibus sublimioribus subdita sit: non est enim potestas nisi a Deo: quae autem sunt, supple ex textu Graeco, potestates, a Deo ordinatae, id est, constitutae, τεταγμέναι sunt. Ecclesia dicit vinum Legis sibi datum a Deo, ne amplius vinacea uvarum diligeret, respiciens ad deos alienos, quorum objectu & cultu tempore illius diutinae in Aegypto morae pascebatur. Quinimo effecisse Deum dicit, ut prosus abjectis diis alienis, ipsi soli dilectione adhaereret.
units.tr: Set love in order over me. The Vulgate translator has rendered the sense of the letter rather than the letter itself. For in Hebrew the text reads, word for word, and his banner over me is love. As if to say: "And under the banner of love he has wholly subjected me to himself." Thus set love in order over me is the same as appointed love over me, or his love and intention towards me, whose command I would follow in all things, just as soldiers follow a banner. That the verb to set in order is here taken in the sense of to appoint is clear from Ambrose on Psalm 118, Octonary 5. So Romans 13:1, Let every soul be subject to the higher powers, for there is no power but of God; but those that are, supply from the Greek text, powers, are ordained of God, that is, appointed [τεταγμέναι]. The Church says that the wine of the Law was given to her by God so that she would no longer love the dregs of grapes, looking back to strange gods, by whose presence and worship she had been fed during that long stay in Egypt. Indeed, she says God has brought it about that, with strange gods wholly cast aside, she should cling to him alone in love.

units.la: 5. Fulcite, &c. Sensus est, Hei languenti ex amore opem festinate, & iis, quae vobis praesto sunt, remediis aegram sustentate. Hic idem sensus est sive vocem Hebraicam בַּאֲשִׁישׁוֹת Baaschifchoth cum Symmacho & Vulgato interpreteris in flore, seu, floribus; sive cum Hellenistis vertas, in unguentis. Petit Ecclesia sub Lege ut sibi prae amore Christi venturi languenti, quod eum nondum pro desiderio praesentem videat, cito per consolationem Scripturarum subveniatur.
units.tr: 5. Support, etc. The sense is: "Hasten to bring help to me, who am faint with love, and sustain me, sick as I am, with those remedies that are at hand for you." This sense is the same whether the Hebrew word [בַּאֲשִׁישׁוֹת] Baashishoth is rendered with Symmachus and the Vulgate translator as in flower, or with flowers, or whether with the Hellenists you render it with ointments. The Church under the Law asks that, since she languishes for love of Christ who is to come, and since she does not yet see him present as she desires, she be quickly helped by the comfort of the Scriptures.

units.la: 6. Laeva ejus, &c. Q. d. Utinam ille, cujus absentis amore langueo, jam praesens adsit, meque dextera complexus, sinistra mihi languidum fulciat caput. Imo, inquit Ecclesia, languori meo nec ipsum Scripturarum solatium mederi poterit, nisi ipse Christus trai Saronites. Hinc apud Talmudicos tractatu de Sabbato cap. 7. & de menstruata cap. 2. vinum Saroniticum inter generosa censetur, in quibus miscebantur duæ partes aquæ.Verùm quemadmodum in locis Esaïæ laudatis adjuncta omnino docent Saron ibi esse loci nomen, sic & hîc comma sequens, & lilium convallium, docet Saron pro campo esse sumendum, quia sic textus melius cohæret.
units.tr: 6. His left hand, etc. As if to say: "Would that he, in whose absent love I languish, were now present, embracing me with his right hand and supporting my faint head with his left. Indeed," says the Church, "not even the very comfort of the Scriptures will be able to heal my languor, unless Christ himself Setrai the Saronite. Hence among the Talmudists, in the tractate on the Sabbath, chapter 7, and on the menstruating woman, chapter 2, Sharonite wine is counted among the choice wines, in which two parts of water were mixed. But just as the adjuncts in the passages of Isaiah cited show that Sharon there is the name of a place, so the following clause here, and the lily of the valleys, shows that Sharon must be taken for a plain, because the text coheres better in this way.

This comparison splendidly commends the excellence of the Church, for as the lily stands out among thorns, so the assembly of God's Church shines above all others, as the blessed Ambrose says on Psalm 118, Octonary 5. Since [שושנה] Shoshanah signifies every kind of flower in Hebrew, many here want it to mean the rose.

units.tr: The Bride.

units.la: 3. Sicut malus inter ligna sylvarum, sic dilectus meus inter filios. Sub umbra illius, quem desideraveram, sedi: & fructus ejus dulcis gutturi meo.
