units.tr: 3. As the apple tree among the trees of the forest, so is my beloved among the sons. I sat down under his shadow, whom I had desired, and his fruit was sweet to my throat.

units.la: 4. Introduxit me in cellam vinariam, ordinavit in me charitatem.
units.tr: 4. He brought me into the cellar of wine, and set love in order within me.

units.la: 5. Fulcite me floribus, stipate me malis: quia amore langueo.
units.tr: 5. Stay me with flowers, compass me about with apples: for I am sick with love.

units.la: 6. Læva ejus sub capite meo, & dextera illius amplexabitur me.
units.tr: 6. His left hand is under my head, and his right hand shall embrace me.

units.la: EXPLICATIO.
units.tr: EXPLANATION.

units.la: 3. Sicut malus, &c. Sponsa largius cum fœnore sponsum laudat. q. d. Tu, dilectissime sponse, me tantùm ceteris puellis pulchriorem dixisti, quantùm lilium excellit spinis; ast ego te non solâ pulchritudine, sed & sermonum & morum suavitate omnibus hominibus longè superiorem agnosco, atque hinc est quòd vel umbra tua, in qua hactenus sedi, me tantoperè recreet. Ecclesia dicit Deo, tu, ô Rex gentium & desideratus earum me ceteris rationum coetibus compositam ab iis tantùm distare dicis, quantum spinis praestat lilium; ast ego longe potiori jure nihil in gestis cujusvis sancti elucere agnosco, quod comparari possit tecum, cujus vel ipsa eloquia, utpote verba vitae aeternae, sunt praemelle suavia. Hinc Lex, quae umbra est futurorum gestorum, & eloquiorum tuorum, me incredibili hactenus laetitia affecit. Praeclare itaque B. Ambros. in Ps. 118. Octon. 8. de Ecclesia sub Lege: Legem acceperat, hanc sequebatur, hanc currebat viam. In Lege itaque requiescens in umbra Christi requiescebat.
units.tr: 3. As the bramble, etc. The bride praises the bridegroom more lavishly than she praises herself. The sense is: You, most beloved bridegroom, have called me more beautiful than the other maidens only as much as the lily surpasses the thorns. But I acknowledge that you surpass all men far more, not only in beauty but also in the sweetness of your words and conduct. For this reason even your shade, under which I have so far sat, refreshes me so greatly. The Church says to God: You, O King of the nations and their desire, say that I, composed of the assemblies of other peoples, differ from them only as much as the lily excels the thorns. But with far greater right I acknowledge that nothing shines forth in the deeds of any saint that can be compared with you, whose very utterances, as words of eternal life, are exceedingly sweet. Hence the Law, which is the shadow of future events and of your sayings, has so far filled me with incredible joy. Accordingly B. Ambrose rightly says, in his commentary on Psalm 118, Octonary 8, concerning the Church under the Law: She had received the Law, she followed it, she ran this way. Resting therefore in the Law, she was resting in the shadow of Christ.

units.la: 4. Introduxit me, &c. Q. d. Experiri me fecit dilectus meus, quam suavis sit.
units.tr: 4. He brought me in, etc. That is: My beloved has made me experience how sweet he is.

units.la: In Cellam vinariam. Quemadmodum, ut supra diximus, vinum phrasi Hebraica dicitur quidquid delicioum, & voluptarium est, ita hic cellae vinariae nomine appellat sponsa mirificam suavitatem, qua sponsi beneficio potita est & exhilarata.
units.tr: Into the wine cellar. As we said above, in Hebrew idiom whatever is delightful and pleasurable is called wine. Likewise here the bride calls by the name of the wine cellar the wonderful sweetness which she has obtained and in which she has been gladdened by the kindness of the bridegroom.

units.la: Ordinavit in me charitatem. Non tam litteram, quam litterae sensum reddidit Vulgatus interpres. Ad verbum enim habetur Hebraice, & vexillum ejus super me charitas. q. d. Et sub vexillo amoris me sibi totam subjecit. Itaque ordinavit in me charitatem, idem est atque, constituit supra me charitatem, seu dilectionem sui mihi propositit, cujus in omnibus sequerer imperium, non secus ac vexillum sequuntur milites. Quod autem verbum ordinare hic sumatur pro constituere, patet ex Ambrosio in Ps. 118. in Octon. 5. Sic Rom. 13. v. 1. Omnis anima potestatibus sublimioribus subdita sit: non est enim potestas nisi a Deo: quae autem sunt, supple ex textu Graeco, potestates, a Deo ordinatae, id est, constitutae, τεταγμέναι sunt. Ecclesia dicit vinum Legis sibi datum a Deo, ne amplius vinacea uvarum diligeret, respiciens ad deos alienos, quorum objectu & cultu tempore illius diutinae in Aegypto morae pascebatur. Quinimo effecisse Deum dicit, ut prosus abjectis diis alienis, ipsi soli dilectione adhaereret.
units.tr: He ordered love in me. The Vulgate translator rendered the sense of the words rather than the words themselves. For literally in Hebrew it reads: and his banner over me is love. That is: under the banner of love he has made me wholly subject to himself. So "he ordered love in me" means the same as "he set love above me," or proposed to me his love, whose command I would follow in all things, just as soldiers follow a banner. That the word ordinare is taken here for constituere (to set up or establish) is clear from Ambrose on Psalm 118, Octonary 5. So too Romans 13:1: Let every soul be subject to the higher powers; for there is no power but of God; the powers that be, supply from the Greek text, are ordained of God, that is, are established [tetagmenai]. The Church says that God gave her the Law of wine so that she would no longer love the dregs of the grapes, that is, look to the strange gods, by whose presence and worship she had been fed during her long sojourn in Egypt. Indeed, she says that God has brought it about that, with the strange gods utterly cast aside, she should cleave to him alone in love.

units.la: 5. Fulcite, &c. Sensus est, Hei languenti ex amore opem festinate, & iis, quae vobis praesto sunt, remediis aegram sustentate. Hic idem sensus est sive vocem Hebraicam Baaschischoth cum Symmacho & Vulgato interpreteris in flore, seu, floribus; sive cum Hellenistis vertas, in unguentis. Petit Ecclesia sub Lege ut sibi prae amore Christi venturi languenti, quod eum nondum pro desiderio praesentem videat, cito per consolationem Scripturarum subveniatur.
units.tr: 5. Stay me, etc. The sense is: Hasten to bring help to me, faint with love, and sustain me, sick, with the remedies that are at hand. The sense is the same whether one renders the Hebrew word Baaschischoth with Symmachus and the Vulgate translator as in flower, or with flowers; or whether, with the Hellenists, one renders it in ointments. The Church under the Law asks that, since she is faint with love for the Christ who is to come, and since she does not yet see him present with the longing of her desire, she be quickly relieved by the comfort of the Scriptures.

units.la: 6. Laeva ejus, &c. Q. d. Utinam ille, cujus absentis amore langueo, jam praesens adsit, meque dextera complexus, sinistra mihi languidum fulciat caput. Imo, inquit Ecclesia, languori meo nec ipsum Scripturarum solatium mederi poterit, nisi ipse Christus jam jam adveniat, & mecum desponsata sibi uxore matrimonium consummet per Incarnationis mysterium.
units.tr: 6. His left hand, etc. The sense is: Would that he, whose absence I languish for in love, were now present, and embracing me with his right hand, support my faint head with his left. Indeed, says the Church, not even the very comfort of the Scriptures will be able to heal my languor, unless Christ himself come at once, and, his bride having been betrothed to him, consummate the marriage through the mystery of the Incarnation.

units.la: Sponsus alloquitur sponsæ comites.
units.tr: The bridegroom addresses the companions of the bride.

units.la: 7. ADjuro vos, filiæ Jerusalem, per capreas, cervósque camporum, ne suscitetis, neque evigilare faciatis dilectam, quoadusque ipsa velit.
units.tr: 7. I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, by the roes and the hinds of the field, that you stir not up, nor awaken my beloved, until she please.

units.la: EXPLICATIO.
units.tr: EXPLANATION.

units.la: 7. ADjuro, &c. In hoc sacro Dramate rustico, cùm sponsus sponsæ comites adjurat per capreas cervósque camporum, his valde delectari innuit eos, qui rusticum vitæ genus eligunt. Proinde apud summum Poëtam cervus fortuito saucius fuit prima occasio tumultûs inter Latii rusticos & Trojanos concitati. Et Macrobium, qui hanc belli causam deridet ut levem nimis Saturnalium lib. 5. cap. 17. Pontanus ex professo refellit. Solemus autem rogare & adjurare per ea quæ sunt charissima. Ita Dido lib. 4. Æneid.
units.tr: 7. I adjure, etc. In this sacred rustic drama, when the bridegroom adjures the companions of the bride by the roes and hinds of the field, he indicates that those who choose a rustic way of life take great delight in such things. Accordingly, among the chief poet, a stag wounded by chance was the first occasion of the uproar stirred up between the rustics of Latium and the Trojans. Pontanus expressly refutes Macrobius, who in the fifth book of the Saturnalia, chapter 17, mocks this cause of war as too trivial. We are accustomed, however, to ask and adjure by those things which are most dear to us. So Dido in the fourth book of the Aeneid:

units.la: Per ego has lacrymas, dexteramque tuam te, (Quando aliud mihi jam miseræ nihil ipsa reliqui) Per connubia nostra, per inceptos hymenæos; Si bene quid de te merui, fuit aut tibi quidquam Dulce meum, &c.
units.tr: By these tears of mine, and by your right hand, since I, wretched, have nothing else left to me, by our marriage, by the nuptials begun; if I have deserved well of you in any way, or if anything of mine was sweet to you, etc.

units.la: Ceterùm per cervos & capreas adjurare, nihil aliud est, quàm orare & deprecari. Quippe vox adjurandi, fi proprie fumatur, ut jurare non licet nisi per solum Deum, Deut. 6. v. 13. ita nec adjurare. Hinc Genef. 24. v. 3. Abraham adjurat servum suum per Dominum, Deum cæli & terræ.
units.tr: But to adjure by stags and roes is nothing other than to entreat and beseech. Indeed, the word to adjure, if taken properly, is like to swear: it is lawful to adjure only by God alone, Deut. 6:13. Hence in Genesis 24:3 Abraham adjures his servant by the Lord, the God of heaven and earth.

units.la: Filiæ Jerusalem, &c. Id est, Virgines Jerofolymitanæ.
units.tr: Daughters of Jerusalem, etc. That is, the virgins of Jerusalem.

units.la: Cervósque camporum. Id est, qui degunt in agris, ab urbe Jerusalem non multùm diftitis.
units.tr: And the hinds of the field. That is, those who dwell in the fields, not far distant from the city of Jerusalem.

units.la: Ne suscitetis, &c. Q. d. Parcite somnum sponsæ amore languentis abrumpere, neque evigilare faciatis invitam. Hæc sponsi adjuratio adumbrat Deum adjurantem animas fideles, per ea, quæ sibi sunt charissima, ne Ecclesiam dulcedine contemplationis & charismatum ipsius absorptam, perturbent, & ab hoc pio sopore invitam avocent ad alia.
units.tr: That you stir not up, etc. The sense is: Spare the bride, languishing in love, and do not break her sleep, nor make her awake against her will. This adjuration of the bridegroom foreshadows God adjuring faithful souls, by those things which are most dear to them, not to disturb the Church, absorbed in the sweetness of contemplation and of her own spiritual gifts, and not to call her away from this holy slumber against her will to other things.

units.la: Sponsa loquitur in somnis.
units.tr: The bride speaks in her sleep.

units.la: 8. VOx dilecti mei, Ecce iste venit saliens in montibus, transiliens colles.
units.tr: 8. The voice of my beloved! Behold, he comes leaping upon the mountains, skipping over the hills.

units.la: 9. Similis est dilectus meus capreæ, hinnuloque cervorum. En ipse stat post parietem nostrum, respiciens per fenestras, prospiciens per cancellos.
units.tr: 9. My beloved is like a roe or a young hart. Behold, he stands behind our wall, looking in through the windows, peering through the lattice.

units.la: 10. En dilectus meus loquitur mihi: Surge, propera amica mea, columba mea, formosa mea, & veni.
units.tr: 10. Behold, my beloved speaks to me: Arise, make haste, my love, my dove, my fair one, and come.

units.la: 11. Jam enim hyems transiit, imber abiit & recessit.
units.tr: 11. For now the winter is past; the rain is over and gone.

units.la: 12. Flores apparuerunt in terra nostra, tempus putationis advenit: vox turturis audita est in terra nostra.
units.tr: 12. The flowers have appeared in our land; the time of pruning has come; the voice of the turtledove is heard in our land.

units.la: 13. Ficus protulit grossos suos: vineæ florentes dederunt odorem suum. Surge amica mea, speciosa mea, & veni.
units.tr: 13. The fig tree has put forth its green figs, and the vines in blossom have given forth their scent. Arise, my love, my fair one, and come.

units.la: 14. Columba mea in foraminibus petræ, in caverna maceriæ, ostende mihi faciem tuam, sonet vox tua in auribus meis: vox enim tua dulcis, & facies tua decora.
units.tr: 14. My dove, in the clefts of the rock, in the hiding place of the wall, let me see your face; let your voice sound in my ears, for your voice is sweet and your face is comely.

units.la: 15. Capite nobis vulpes parvulas, quæ demoliuntur vineas: nam vinea nostra floruit.
units.tr: 15. Catch us the foxes, the little foxes that spoil the vineyards, for our vineyard has flowered.

units.la: EXPLICATIO.
units.tr: EXPLANATION.

units.la: 8. VOx dilecti mei, Q. d. Vocem sponsi adventantis mihi audire videor.
units.tr: 8. The voice of my beloved. That is, I seem to hear the voice of the bridegroom drawing near to me.

units.la: Ecce iste venit saliens, &c. Id est, properat quam velocissime dilectus meus ad me, nec ullis itineris difficultatibus ipsius cursus retardatur. Hæc verba optime quadrant in Ecclesiam sub Lege intra se cogitantem jamjam implendum esse magnum Incarnationis sacramentum, nec Dei Verbum propositis sibi in humanitate subeundis opprobriis & suppliciis ab ejusdem humanitatis assumtione posse deterreri.
units.tr: Behold, he comes leaping, etc. That is, my beloved hastens to me as swiftly as he can, and nothing in the difficulties of the journey slows his course. These words fit very well the Church under the Law, which thinks within itself that the great sacrament of the Incarnation is about to be fulfilled, and that the Word of God cannot be deterred by the reproaches and sufferings he must undergo in taking on humanity.

units.la: 9. Similis est, &c. Passim in hoc sacro Dramate sponsus capreæ comparatur & hinnulo cervorum, idque ob formæ decorem, ut multi volunt, quia hujus sponsi, qui dicitur Pf. 44. 3. Speciosus forma præ filiis hominum, forma fuse commendatur infrà cap. 5. Plerique veterum sponsum toties cum caprea conferri censent, quòd dorcas seu caprea fit animal perspicacissimum. Origenes in Cantica Hom. 3. Caprea habet in natura sua, ut non solum videat ipsa, & perspiciat acerrimè, sed & aliis visum præbeat. Afferunt namque hi, quibus medicinæ peritia est, inesse animali intra viscera humorem quendam, qui caliginem depellat oculorum, & obtusiores quoque visus exacuat. Merito ergo capreæ vel damulæ Christus comparatur, quia non solum videt Patrem, sed & videri ab aliis facit, quorum visus ipse curaverit. S. Greg. Nyss. Hom. 5. in Cant. Caprea significat visus acumen ejus, qui omnia perspicit. Philo Carpathius, Sponsus, scilicet Christus capreæ assimilatur, eo quod corda omnium subtilissimè rimetur, & inspiciat cogitationes omnes. Aponius in Cantica libro quarto, Caprea pro eo osinor similem dici, quia nostræ salutis illustratio cæcitatem cordis auferens, &c. Theodoretus de Christo hic, Eum cum caprea sponsa confert, propter visus acumen, & perspicaciam, & futurorum præcognitionem. Michael Pfellus in cantica, Caprea allegoricè videntem significat. Nam ipse Christus omnium corda intuetur. Quæ quidem vera & pie dicta, nescio an ad mentem Salomonis; quia hæ Allegoriæ Græci capreæ nominis Etymologiâ totæ nituntur. Neque enim in sacro textu quidquam est, unde pateat Salomonem id respexisse. Quin de sponsi saltibus, aut fuga aut reditu iis locis agitur, quibus in hoc sacro cantico sponsus confertur cum caprea & hinnulo cervorum. Itaque nihil puto respici, quàm capreæ & cervorum in cursu aut saltu agilitatem prope incredibilem: cui similis sponsi alacritas, & exequendi celeritas, ac facilitas, quidquid agat aut moliatur. Quod maximè quadrat in Christum Ecclesiæ sponsum, qui omnipotentissimâ facilitate omnia quæcunque vult facit, & cujus gratia nescit tarda molimina. Porro quia in præsenti, quo de agimus, versu sponsi saltus comparantur cum summa cervi & capreæ in saltu agilitate, operæ pretium est observare ex Gesnero prope Francofordiam extare locum à cervino saltu nominatum, in quo lapides duo visuntur erecti interstitio pedum fere sexaginta, quanto spatio ibi saliisse dicitur cervus, idque supra plaustrum oneratum, cùm venatores instarent. Refert quoque Varro lib. 2. Rust. cap. 3. capras feras salire è saxo pedes plus sexagenos.
units.tr: 9. He is like, etc. Throughout this sacred drama the bridegroom is compared to a roe or to a young hart of the deer, and many think this is for the beauty of his form. Of this bridegroom, who is said in Psalm 44:3 to be fairer in form than the sons of men, the form is praised at length below in chapter 5. Most of the ancients think the bridegroom is so often compared with the roe because the doe or roe is a most keen-sighted animal. Origen, in his third homily on the Song: The roe has by nature that it not only sees, and sees most sharply, but also gives sight to others. For those who have skill in medicine say that the animal has within its entrails a certain humour which dispels the mist from the eyes and sharpens even dull sight. Rightly, then, Christ is compared to the roe or the young hind, because he not only sees the Father but also makes himself seen by others, whose sight he has healed. Gregory of Nyssa, homily 5 on the Song: The roe signifies the keenness of sight of him who sees all things. Philo of Carpathus: The bridegroom, that is Christ, is likened to the roe because he searches the hearts of all most subtly and sees all their thoughts. Aponius in the fourth book on the Song: The roe is said to be like him because the illumination of our salvation takes away the blindness of the heart, etc. Theodoret on this passage: He compares him with the roe as a bride would, for the sharpness and keenness of sight and for foreknowledge of the future. Michael Psellus on the Song: The roe allegorically signifies one who sees, for Christ himself looks upon the hearts of all. These things are indeed true and piously said, but I do not know whether they agree with Solomon's mind, since these Greek allegories rest entirely on the etymology of the name for roe. For there is nothing in the sacred text that shows Solomon had this in view. Indeed, the leaping of the bridegroom, whether in flight or in return, is spoken of in those places where in this sacred Song the bridegroom is compared with the roe and the young hart. So I think nothing is meant except the almost incredible agility of the roe and the hart in running or leaping, to which the bridegroom's alacrity, and the speed and ease with which he carries out whatever he does or undertakes, is like. This fits especially Christ, the bridegroom of the Church, who does with almighty ease whatever he wills, and who by his grace knows no slow efforts. Further, since in the present verse, on which we are engaged, the bridegroom's leaps are compared with the great agility of the stag and the roe in leaping, it is worth noting, from Gesner, that near Frankfurt there is a place named from a stag's leap, where two stones stand upright at a distance of about sixty feet, which is said to be the distance a stag leapt there, over a loaded cart, while hunters pressed upon it. Varro also reports, in the second book of his Rustics, chapter 3, that wild goats leap from a rock more than sixty feet.

units.la: En ipse fiat, &c. Vehemens adventùs sponsi desiderium sponsæ somnianti suadet ipsum jamjam adventare, & sese videndum exhibere per cancellos, non secus ac rosa erumpens ex rimis folliculi modicum sese aperientis. Sic autem revera Christi Incarnatio per Legales umbras & Prophetarum ænigmata veteribus in Ecclesia sub Lege fidelibus apparuit, dum quasi sopiti ceterorum, suique prorsus immemores, ad unum Christi adventum omnium votis exoptatum vigiles erant, eúmque accelerari enixè rogabant.
units.tr: Behold, he stands, etc. The bride's vehement longing for the bridegroom's coming makes her, as in a dream, feel that he is already at hand and shows himself to be seen through the lattice, just as a rose bursts forth through the chinks of a bud that opens only a little. Indeed, in this way the Incarnation of Christ appeared through the legal shadows and the riddles of the Prophets to the faithful of the Church under the Law, who, as if lulled to sleep and quite forgetful of everything else, were watchful for the one coming of Christ, which was the desire of all, and earnestly begged that it might be hastened.

units.la: 10. En dilectus meus, &c. Jam videtur sponsæ à se audiri sponsum sibi loquentem blandis verbis, ut amore languentem soletur, & quam diuturnior sponsi mora & promissi conjugii futuri dilatio in deliquium incidere fecerat, instantes nuptiæ refocillent. Hæc itaque verba intellecta de Christo desponsatam sibi sub Lege Ecclesiam alloquente eundem sensum formant, atque illa ejusdem sponsi cælestis verba apud Esaïam cap. 40. Consolamini, consolamini populle meus, dicit Deus vester. Revelabitur gloria Domini, & videbit omnis caro pariter, quod os Domini locutum est. & ibidem cap. 52. Consurge, consurge, induere fortitudine tua Sion, induere vestimentis gloriæ tuæ Jerusalem civitas sancti: quia ego ipse qui loquebar in Lege & Prophetis multifariam, ecce adsum.
units.tr: 10. Behold, my beloved, etc. Now the bride seems to hear the bridegroom speaking to her in tender words, so as to comfort her in her love-sickness, and so that the impending wedding may revive her, for the longer delay of the bridegroom and the postponement of the promised future marriage had brought her to a swoon. Therefore, taking these words as spoken of Christ, the Church, betrothed to him under the Law, addressing him, expresses the same sense, and so does the heavenly bridegroom's own word in Isaiah 40: Comfort, comfort my people, says your God. The glory of the Lord shall be revealed, and all flesh shall see together that the mouth of the Lord has spoken. And in the same prophet, chapter 52: Awake, awake, put on your strength, O Zion; put on the garments of your glory, O Jerusalem, city of the holy one, for I myself, who spoke in the Law and the Prophets in many ways, behold, I am here.

units.la: Amica mea, &c. Blandis appellationibus sponsam ad se allicit sponsus. Cur autem cum columba conferatur sponsa supra dictum est.
units.tr: My friend, etc. The bridegroom draws the bride to himself with tender names. Why the bride is compared with the dove has been said above.

units.la: Et veni.Ad nuptias ab antiquo promissas & prophetatas. Heb. Et veni tibi, quia nimirum Ecclesia unita est cælesti sponso per Incarnationis mysterium non Dei sed suo commodo; neque enim Deus per hoc mysterium factus est beatior, sed Ecclesia inde beata. Christus enim Dominus non sibi, sed nobis incarnatus est. Hinc Ef. 9. v. 5. Parvulus natus est nobis, Filius datus est nobis. Et Angelus ad pastores ait Luc. 2. v. 11. Natus est vobis hodie Salvator, qui est Christus Dominus.
units.tr: And come. To the wedding promised and foretold from of old. The Hebrew reads and come to you, because the Church is united to the heavenly bridegroom through the mystery of the Incarnation not for God's advantage but for her own; for God was not made happier by this mystery, but the Church is made blessed by it. For Christ the Lord was made flesh not for himself but for us. Hence Isaiah 9:5: A little child is born to us, a son is given to us. And the angel says to the shepherds, Luke 2:11: To you is born this day a Saviour, who is Christ the Lord.

units.la: 11. Jam enim hyems transiit. Q. d. Invitat te ut properes ad meos amplexus velipsa veris tempestas, quæ jamjam hyemi successit. Vernum quippe tempus præ ceteris anni temporibus dicatum esse copulæ conjugali docent plantæ cunctæ & bruta animantia, quibus unica tunc prolificandi cura. Proponit autem cælestis sponsus ob oculos Ecclesiæ jam instare dies salutis & tempus acceptabile, quo Dei Filius reconciliandam authori suo naturam generis humani est assumturus. Hos autem dies salutis adumbrat ver, quod quàm elegantissimè hic describitur. Qui autem minutius scrutari velit quâ ratione singulæ verni temporis descriptionis particulæ quadrent in illos dies salutis, quibus Deus incarnatus & cum hominibus conversatus est, & pro hominibus passus resurrexit, consulat Greg. Nyss. hom. 5. in cantic. Bernardum ser. 58. in cantic. &c.
units.tr: 11. For now the winter is past. That is to say, the very storm of spring, which has now followed winter, invites you to hasten to my embraces. Indeed, all plants and the brute animals teach that the spring season is, above the other seasons of the year, dedicated to the marriage bond, since at that time their one care is to bring forth offspring. The heavenly bridegroom sets before the eyes of the Church that the days of salvation and the acceptable time are now at hand, on which the Son of God was to take on the nature of the human race, to reconcile it to its Author. Spring, which is described here most elegantly, foreshadows these days of salvation. Whoever wishes to examine more closely how each part of the description of spring fits those days of salvation, on which God was incarnate and lived among men, and suffered for men and rose again, should consult Gregory of Nyssa, homily 5 on the Song, and Bernard, sermon 58 on the Song, and others.

units.la: 12. Flores apparuerunt in terra nostra. Eleganter B. Bernardus Ser. 59. in Cantic. Adverte quanta suavitatis sit Deum caeli dicere, In terra nostra. Quisquis terrigenae & filii hominum audite, magnificavit Dominus facere nobiscum. Multum illi cum terra, multum cum sponsa, quam de terris sibi adscisci placuit. In terra, inquit, nostra. Non plane principatum sonat vox ista, sed consortium, sed familiaritatem. Tanquam sponsus hoc dicit, non tanquam Dominus. Quid? Conditor est, & consortem se reputat. Amor loquitur, qui dominium nescit. Carmen nimirum amoris est, nec aliis hoc, quam amatorijs fulciri oportuit. Amat & Deus, nec aliunde hoc habet, sed ipse est unde amat: & ideo vehementius, quia non amorem tam habet, quam hic est ipse. Verum quos amat, amicos habet, non servos. Denique amicus fit de magistro, nec enim amicos discipulos diceret, si non essent. Vides amori cedere etiam majestatem? Ita est, neminem suspicit amor, sed ne despicit quidem. Omnes ex aequo intuetur, qui perfecte se amat, & in se ipso celsos humilesque contemperat, nec modo pares, sed unum eos facit. Tu Deum forsitan adhuc ab hac amoris regula excipi putas: sed qui adhaeret Deo, unus spiritus est cum eo. Quid miraris hoc? Ipse factus est tanquam unus ex nobis. Minus dixi, non tanquam unus, sed unus. Parum est parem esse hominibus, homo est. Inde terram nostram vindicat sibi, sed quasi patriam, non quasi possessionem. Quidni vindicet? Inde illi sponsa, inde substantia corporis. Inde sponsus ipse, inde duo in carne una. Si caro una, cur non & patria una? Caelum caeli Domino, terram autem dedit filiis hominum. Ergo ut filius hominis haereditat terram, ut Dominus subjicit, ut conditor administrat, ut sponsus communicat. Dicendo nempe, in terra nostra, proprietatem professio abnuit, societatem non respuit. Haecenus B. Bernardus.
units.tr: 12. The flowers have appeared in our land. Bernard elegantly, in sermon 59 on the Song: Notice how sweet it is that the God of heaven says, "in our land." Whoever you are, sons of earth and sons of men, hear: the Lord has done great things with us. He has much to do with the land, much with the bride whom he was pleased to take to himself from the earth. "In our land," he says. This word does not plainly sound of lordship, but of fellowship and familiarity. He speaks as a bridegroom, not as a lord. What? He is the creator, yet counts himself a partner. Love speaks, which knows no dominion. Surely this is a song of love, and it ought to be supported by nothing but lovers' words. God too loves, and he has this from nowhere else, but he himself is the source from which he loves; and so he loves the more vehemently, because he does not so much have love as he is love. Yet those whom he loves he has as friends, not as servants. Finally, a friend comes from a master, for he would not call them friends if they were not. Do you see that majesty too yields to love? Thus it is: love looks up to no one, yet neither does it despise anyone. It regards all alike, who loves himself perfectly, and in himself tempers the high and the low, making them not merely equal but one. Perhaps you think God is still excepted from this rule of love; but whoever cleaves to God is one spirit with him. Why do you wonder at this? He himself has become as one of us. I have said too little: not "as one," but "one." It is not enough to be equal to men; he is man. Hence he claims the land for himself, but as a fatherland, not as a possession. Why should he not claim it? Hence he has a bride, hence the substance of a body. Hence the bridegroom himself, hence two in one flesh. If the flesh is one, why not the fatherland also one? The heavens of heaven belong to the Lord, but the earth he has given to the sons of men. So, as the son of man, he inherits the earth; as the Lord, he subjects it; as the creator, he administers it; as the bridegroom, he shares it. For in saying "in our land," his claim refuses to profess ownership, but does not reject partnership. Thus far Bernard.

units.la: Tempus putationis advenit. Praeclare B. Greg. Nyss. Hom. 5. in Canticum Canticorum: O quam eleganter nobis describit veris amoenitatem creator veris, cui dicit David, Aestatem & ver tu plasmasti ea. Solvit hyemis tristitiam, dicens transisse hybernam moestitiam, & imbrium molestiam. Ostendit prata scatentia & decorata floribus. Flores autem dicit esse in suo vigore, & jam idoneos qui amputentur, ita ut eos omnino legendorum florum studiosi homines, ad metendam corollam, aut ad unguenti compositionem tollere possint. Tempus autem laetius reddit oratio, avium quoque cantibus in sylvis resonantibus, suavi voci turturum sonante in auribus. Ficum autem dicit & vitem quoddam quasi proemium in iis quae apparent, fructuum futurorum ostentare: cum grossos quidem illa jam proferat, haec ita floreat, ut odoratus deliciis illius fragrantiae abunde perfruatur. Atque sic quidem luxuriat oratio in describendo verno tempore, & tristitiam repellens, & lubenter versans in jucundis narrationibus. Haec B. Greg. Nyss.
units.tr: The time of pruning has come. Gregory of Nyssa, admirably, in Homily 5 on the Song of Songs: O how elegantly the Creator describes to us the pleasantness of spring, of whom David says, "You have made summer and spring." He releases us from the sadness of winter, saying that the dreary winter has passed, and the trouble of the rains. He shows meadows bursting forth and adorned with flowers. He says the flowers are in their full vigour, and already fit to be cut, so that people eager to gather them can take them, whether to make a garland or to prepare perfume. The speech also makes the season more cheerful, with the songs of birds resounding in the woods and the sweet voice of the turtle-dove sounding in the ears. He speaks of the fig and the vine as a kind of foretaste, in what now appears, of the fruits to come: the fig already puts forth its large fruit, while the vine blossoms so that one may abundantly enjoy the delights of its fragrance. Thus the speech luxuriates in describing the spring season, driving away sadness and gladly dwelling on pleasant narratives. So Gregory of Nyssa.

units.la: Vox turturis audita est in terra nostra. Turturem esse avem migratoriam non ex hoc tantum loco, & ex Jerem.8.v.7.habetur sed & naturalis historiae scriptores produnt. Arist. lib. 8. hist. cap. 3. Palumbus & columba semper apparent, sed turtur æstate tantum. Nam hyeme non conspicitur. At ibidem. cap. 12. de palumbo id ipsum negat, quod hic affirmaverat, & solas columbas jugiter manere scribit. Decedunt, inquit, & palumbi, & liviæ, & hirundines, & turtures, neque hic hyemant, sed columbæ manent: & ibidem cap. 16. ait quod hyeme & ciconia latet, & merula, & turtur, & alauda. Sed de turture maxime omnium constat; nemo enim, prope dixerim, turturem per hyemem uspiam vidisse memoratur. Varro etiam lib. 3. de re rustica cap. 5. Turdi quotannis trans mare in Italiam advolant circiter æquinoctium autumnale, & eodem revolant ad æquinoctium vernum. Et alio tempore turtures ac coturnices immani numero. Et Cicero lib. 2. de finibus: Turtures cursu & peregrinatione lætantur. Et S.Greg. Nyssenus in cantic. Hom. 5. Hyeme fugit luscinia, torpet hirundo, à nido peregrinatur turtur. Sunt tamen qui turturem putant non tam abire, quam occultari. Plin. lib. 10. hist. nat. cap. 24. Virius turtur occultatur, pennáque amittit. Alii vere perperam legunt; neque enim turtur vere occultatur sed hyeme. Quin ipse Aristoteles Hist. anim. lib. 8. cap. 12. asserit nonnullos turtures remanere in locis apricis. Non possum hic non addere Hebræos in præsenti, quo de agimus, versu, turturis nomine, quæ est avis columbini generis, Spiritum-sanctum intelligere, unde verba sacri textûs; Vox turturis audita est in terra nostra, sic reddit Chaldæus Paraphrastes: Et vocem Spiritus-sancti, id est, liberationem, quam Abrahamo patri vestro prædixi, jam audivistis. Sed & Origenes in cantica Hom. 2. hæc sacri Cantici verba refert ad Spiritum-sanctum, dicens: Spiritus-Sanctus, quando de magnis & occultioribus Sacramentis, & quæ multi capere non possunt, loquitur, in turturis appellatione signatur, id est, ejus avis, quæ semper in montium jugis, & in arborum verticibus commoratur. In vallibus autem, & his quæ ad homines usque perveniunt, columba assumitur. Ceterum priusquam ulterius pergamus, operæ pretium est hic observare quod vox Hebræa Zamir זמיר quæ redditur à Vulgato, lxx. Aquila & Symmacho putatio in hoc versu, vertitur à recentioribus cantillatio, ut intelligatur de cantu avium, qui verno tempore exaudiri incipit. Porro putationem non vitis, sed florum cum supra laudato Gregorio Nysseno intelligendam evincit contextus sacri seriei, ni velis ante verbum advenit subintelligendam particulam postquam.
units.tr: The voice of the turtle-dove has been heard in our land. That the turtle-dove is a migratory bird is known not only from this place and from Jeremiah 8:7, but also from the writers of natural history. Aristotle, History of Animals, book 8, chapter 3: The wood-pigeon and the dove are always to be seen, but the turtle-dove only in summer, for it is not seen in winter. Yet in the same work, chapter 12, he denies the very same thing about the wood-pigeon that he had affirmed here, and writes that only the doves remain constantly. The wood-pigeons, he says, and the ring-doves, and swallows, and turtle-doves depart, and they do not winter here, but the doves remain. And in chapter 16 of the same work he says that in winter the stork hides, and the blackbird, and the turtle-dove, and the lark. But concerning the turtle-dove it is most certain of all; for, I might almost say, no one is recorded to have seen a turtle-dove anywhere during winter. Varro too, in book 3 of On Agriculture, chapter 5: Thrushes fly every year across the sea into Italy at about the autumn equinox, and fly back again at the spring equinox. And at other times turtle-doves and quails in immense numbers. And Cicero, book 2 of On Ends: Turtle-doves delight in running and in wandering abroad. And Gregory of Nyssa in his Homily 5 on the Song: In winter the nightingale flees, the swallow lies torpid, the turtle-dove wanders away from its nest. Yet there are those who think the turtle-dove does not so much depart as go into hiding. Pliny, book 10 of Natural History, chapter 24: The turtle-dove hides away and loses its feathers. Others read it wrongly as spring; for the turtle-dove is not hidden in spring but in winter. Indeed Aristotle himself, History of Animals, book 8, chapter 12, asserts that some turtle-doves remain in sunny places. I cannot help adding here that the Hebrews, in the present verse which we are discussing, understand by the name of the turtle-dove, a bird of the pigeon kind, the Holy Spirit; hence the Chaldee Paraphrast renders the words of the sacred text, The voice of the turtle-dove has been heard in our land, thus: And you have now heard the voice of the Holy Spirit, that is, the deliverance which I foretold to Abraham your father. But Origen too, in Homily 2 on the Song, refers these words of the sacred Song to the Holy Spirit, saying: When the Holy Spirit speaks of great and more hidden sacraments, which many cannot grasp, he is signified by the name of the turtle-dove, that is, of that bird which always dwells on the mountain ridges and in the tops of trees. In the valleys, however, and in places that reach as far as men, the dove is taken. But before we go further, it is worth noting here that the Hebrew word zamir זמיר, which the Vulgate, the Seventy, Aquila and Symmachus render as "pruning" in this verse, is rendered by more recent writers as "singing", so that it is understood of the song of birds, which begins to be heard in the spring season. Further, that pruning must be understood of flowers, not of the vine, the context of the sacred sequence proves together with the above-cited Gregory of Nyssa, unless you wish to supply the particle after before the word has come.

units.la: 13. Surge amica mea, &c. Hæc iterata sponsæ ad nuptias promissas invitatio & blanda compellatio vehementiam sponsi in sponsam amoris & benevolentiæ prodit. Vide B Bernard. Serm, 61. in cantica.
units.tr: 13. Arise, my love, etc. This repeated invitation of the bridegroom, promising marriage, and this tender address, reveal the bridegroom's ardour and goodwill of love towards the bride. See Bernard, Sermon 61 on the Song.

units.la: 14. Columba mea in foraminibus, &c. Aptè sponsam præ metu & verecundia latitantem vocat sponsus columbam in foraminibus seu fissuris petræ, & in caverna maceriæ, seu in latibulo præcipitii. Nam columbæ in columbariis habent ארובות arubboth, id est, foramina seu fenestras, in quibus latere & nidificare solent. Unde illud Esa. 60. v. 8. Qui sunt isti, qui ut nubes volant, & quasi columbæ ad fenestras suas? id est, ad columbaria sua, ut habet Chaldæus Paraphrastes. Sed in metu latent columbæ ubivis, in fossis, in petris, in montibus,&c. Hinc Jerem. 48. vers. 28. Moabitæ, qui præ metu hostium relictis urbibus suis in rupium antris delitescunt, dicuntur esse quasi columba nidificans in summo ore foraminis, seu ut alii vertunt, in lateribus oris fossæ, hoc est, ut patet ibidem ex Chaldæo Paraphraste, ut columba, quæ in simili metu præter naturam, relicto foramine columbarii, descendit ut habitet in ima fossa. Hinc & Hebraei præsentem sacri Cantici, quem explicamus, versum intelligunt de Synagoga Israelitica, quam in exitu ex Ægypto ab una parte persequebatur Pharao, ab altera concludebat desertum anguibus plenum. Hinc & illud Homeri Iliad φ. vers. 495. ——————Φύγεν ὣς τε πτήλεια, H′ ῥἀθ' ἱενχος Κοιλῳ ἐισέπλατο πέτρῳ.
units.tr: 14. My dove in the clefts of the rock, etc. Aptly the bridegroom calls the bride, who lies hidden through fear and shyness, a dove in the holes or fissures of the rock, and in the cave of the wall, or in the hiding-place of the precipice. For doves in their dovecotes have arubboth [ארובות], that is, holes or windows, in which they are accustomed to lie hidden and to nest. Hence that passage of Isaiah 60:8: Who are these who fly like clouds, and like doves to their windows? that is, to their dovecotes, as the Chaldee Paraphrast has it. But in fear doves hide everywhere, in ditches, in rocks, on mountains, and so on. Hence in Jeremiah 48:28 the Moabites, who through fear of the enemy leave their cities and hide in the caves of the cliffs, are said to be like a dove nesting at the top of the mouth of a hole, or, as others translate it, on the sides of the mouth of a ditch; that is, as is clear from the same place in the Chaldee Paraphrast, like a dove which in similar fear, contrary to its nature, leaves the hole of the dovecote and descends to dwell in the bottom of a ditch. Hence also the Hebrews understand the present verse of the Song which we are explaining as referring to the Israelite synagogue, which, when it went out of Egypt, was pursued by Pharaoh on one side and hemmed in on the other by the desert full of serpents. Hence also that line of Homer, Iliad 21, verse 495: "She fled like a dove, which into a hollow rock..."

units.la: Fugit ut columba, quæ ab accipitre volavit in petram cavam, in antrum. Etiam Ezec. 7. vers. 18. qui ex magna clade evaserunt oberrare leguntur in montibus quasi columbæ convallium, quæ nempe metu aucupis, aut accipitris, naturali sede desertâ, coguntur alio secedere ut vitæ suæ consulant. Epiphanius Hær. 59. num. 9. tegmen petræ interpretatur, Christi benignitatem, misericordiamque Domini. ἐν σκέπῃ πέτρας ἐν φιλανθρωπίᾳ Χεισῷ, χ̣ ἐνὶελεῖ κωφὶς, τῦτεστι σκέπη Πέτρας, σκέπη ἐλπίδος, χ̣ πίστεως, χ̣ ἀληθείας. Nempe fides & spes nobis divinâ benignitate data ex auditu veritatis prædicatæ nos unit Christo, qui est Petra salutis nostræ. Meritum proinde meum, inquit Bernardus Ser. 61. in Cantic. miseratio Domini: non plane sum meriti inops, quamdiu ille miserationum non fuerit. Quod si misericordiæ Domini multæ, multus nihilominus in meritis sum.Nunquid justitias meas cantabo? Domine memorabor justitiæ tuæ solius, ipsa est enim mea; nempe factus es mihi tu justitia à Deo. Idem Ser. 15. in Psal. 90. Hoc, inquit, est totum hominis meritum, si totam spem suam ponat in eum, qui totum hominem salvum fecit. Ostende mihi faciem tuam, &c. Facies Synagogæ seu Ecclesiæ sub Lege, in qua omnis ipsius decor relucebat, erat ipsius fides in Christum venturum; hæc fides & vox hanc fidem corde, ore & opere profitendam resonans semper placuit cœlesti sponso, antequam veniret & ut suum in carne adventum hominibus manifestaret, ea fecisset opera, quæ alius nemo fecit. Itaque Christus incarnandus in Ecclesia sub Lege sibi desponsata nondum nupta commendat fidem & prædicationem sui adventus mox futuri ad redemtionem generis humani.
units.tr: She flees as a dove which has flown from the hawk into a hollow rock, into a cave. Also in Ezekiel 7:18 those who escaped the great slaughter are read as wandering on the mountains like doves of the valleys, which, indeed, through fear of the fowler or the hawk, abandon their natural seat and are compelled to withdraw elsewhere to look after their lives. Epiphanius, Heresy 59, number 9, interprets the covering of the rock as the kindness of Christ and the mercy of the Lord: in the shelter of the rock, in the loving-kindness of Christ, and in the mercy of the Lord; that is, the shelter of the Rock, the shelter of hope, and of faith, and of truth [ἐν σκέπῃ πέτρας, ἐν φιλανθρωπίᾳ Χριστοῦ, καὶ ἐν ἐλέει Κυρίου, τουτέστι σκέπη Πέτρας, σκέπη ἐλπίδος, καὶ πίστεως, καὶ ἀληθείας]. Indeed faith and hope, given to us by divine kindness through the hearing of the preached truth, unite us to Christ, who is the Rock of our salvation. My merit, therefore, says Bernard in Sermon 61 on the Song, is the mercy of the Lord. I am by no means lacking in merit, as long as he has not withdrawn his mercies. But if the mercies of the Lord are many, I am nonetheless rich in merits. Shall I sing of my own righteousness? Lord, I will be mindful of your righteousness alone, for that is my own; you are made to me righteousness from God. The same, in Sermon 15 on Psalm 90: This, he says, is the whole merit of man, if he places all his hope in him who has made the whole man safe. Show me your face, etc. The face of the Synagogue, or of the Church under the Law, in which all its beauty shone forth, was its faith in the Christ who was to come; this faith, and the voice resounding to profess this faith in heart, mouth and deed, has always pleased the heavenly bridegroom, before he came, and in order to make his coming in the flesh manifest to men, he did those works which no other has done. Thus Christ, about to be incarnate, commends to the Church under the Law, which he had betrothed to himself but not yet married, the faith and the proclamation of his coming, which was soon to take place for the redemption of the human race.

units.la: 15. Capite, &c. Inducitur à sponsa sponsus hortans sodales ut, interea dum ipsa dormit, capiant noxias vineis bestiolas, ne vineam florentem demoliantur, antequam illæ bestiolæ viribus augescant; vetus enim adagium est, veteranam vulpem laqueo non capi. Sponsus autem cælestis veros doctores hortatur ut falsos erroris revincant, & eorum strophas & vulpinas versutias, quibus credulæ plebi facile imponunt transfigurantes se in Apostolos Christi, cùm sint pseudo-apostoli & operarii dolosi, in apertam traditæ semel sanctis fidei lucem proferant. Has autem vulpes vult divinus ille sponsus capi parvulas, id est, in ipso ortu, & priusquam eorum sermo, ut cancer, late serpserit, quomodo loquitur Apost. 2 Tim. 2. v. 17. & florentem sincerà religione plebem perverterint.
units.tr: 15. Take us, &c. The bride introduces the bridegroom urging his companions that, while she herself sleeps, they should catch the harmful little foxes in the vineyards, so that they do not lay waste the flourishing vine before those little beasts grow stronger. For there is an old saying, an old fox is not caught in a snare. The heavenly bridegroom, however, urges true teachers to refute the false teachers of error, and to bring out into the open light of the faith once delivered to the saints their wiles and foxlike cunning, by which they easily deceive the credulous common people, disguising themselves as apostles of Christ when they are really false apostles and deceitful workers. That divine bridegroom wants these foxes caught while they are still small, that is, at their very birth, and before their speech, like a cancer, has spread far, as the Apostle puts it (2 Tim. 2:17), and has corrupted the people who flourished in sincere religion.

units.la: Principiis obsta: Sero medicina paratur, Cùm mala per longas invaluere moras.
units.tr: Resist beginnings: the remedy is prepared too late when evils have grown strong through long delays.

units.la: Hinc & illud Psal. 136. Filia Babylonis, Beatus qui tenebit & allidet parvulos tuos ad petram. Illas itaque vulpes à veris doctoribus, quibus id muneris incumbit, ut colant vineam Domini Sabaoth, quæ est domus Israël, vult cælestis sponsus capi, de quibus vulpibus conqueritur per Jeremiam Prophetam cap. 11. verf. 10. dicens: Pastores multi demoliti sunt vineam meam, conculcaverunt partem meam: dederunt portionem meam desiderabilem in desertum solitudinis. De hoc eodem vulpium genere dicitur Ezech. 13. verf. 4. Quasi vulpes in desertis, Prophetæ tui Israël erant. quæ scilicet per cuniculos subjectam terram excavant & suffodiunt. Quod faciebant illi Prophetæ, cùm Jerosolymorum ruinas reparare & sepem obducere debuissent, ut imminenti malo occurrerent. Eo enim respectu conferri cum vulpibus suadent statim sequentia: Non ascendistis ex adverso, neque opposuistis murum pro domo Israel, ut staretis in prælio in die Domini.
units.tr: Hence also that saying in Psalm 136: Daughter of Babylon, happy is he who seizes and dashes your little ones against the rock. The heavenly bridegroom wants those foxes caught by true teachers, to whom this duty falls, that they may tend the vineyard of the Lord of hosts, which is the house of Israel. He complains of these foxes through the prophet Jeremiah, chapter 11, verse 10, saying: Many ministers have destroyed my vineyard, they have trampled my portion; they have made my pleasant portion a desolate wilderness. Of this same kind of fox Ezekiel 13:4 says: Your prophets, O Israel, were like foxes in the deserts, which of course dig and burrow under the ground through tunnels. The prophets did this when they ought to have repaired the ruins of Jerusalem and built up the hedge, so as to meet the impending evil. That is the point of the comparison with foxes, which the following words make clear: You have not gone up against the breach, nor set up a wall for the house of Israel, to stand in battle in the day of the Lord.

units.la: Nobis. Sibi ait sponsus & sponsæ capiendos esse eos, qui divinant mendacium dicentes: Ait Dominus, cùm Dominus non miserit eos. Nam qui hæreticum convicit, etsi ipsum non converterit, vulpem tamen cepit, sponso & sponsæ; sponsæ quidem, dem, quia confirmatur inde in fide; sponso verò, quia fortitudo sponsæ est gaudium sponsi. Vide B. Bernard. Serm.64. in Cantic.
units.tr: For us. The bridegroom says to himself and the bride that those are to be caught who divine lies, saying, "The Lord says," when the Lord has not sent them. For whoever refutes a heretic, even if he does not convert him, has nevertheless caught a fox for the bridegroom and the bride: for the bride, because she is thereby strengthened in faith; for the bridegroom, because the strength of the bride is the joy of the bridegroom. See St Bernard, Sermon 64 on the Song.

units.la: Vulpes. Multas esse in Palæstina vulpes non solùm præsens hujus Dramatis, cujus Scena est in montibus & campis Jerosolymitanis, testatur locus, sed & factum Samsonis Judic. 15. verf. 4. & quod multa Palæstinæ loca aut circa Palæstinam à vulpibus nomen habuerunt, ut terra Sual, id est terra Vulpis 1 Sam. seu Reg.13.v.17.Et urbs Judæ Josue 15. v.28. Similiter & urbs Simeonis Josue 19. verf. 6. & 2 Esd. 11. verf. 27. dicitur Hafarfual, & eadem Simeonis urbs dicitur 1 Paral. 4. verf. 28. Hafarfuhal, quod est, castrum vulpis. Danitarum urbs Selebin Jof. 19. verf. 42. seu Salebim ut vocatur Judic. 1. verf. 35. ubi Amorrhæi dicuntur eam occupasse, & 3 Reg. 4. verf. 9. Loco laudato Judicum à Græcorum aliis redditur Thalabin, ab aliis Vulpes, & hodie utrumque legitur in nostris exemplaribus Jos. 19. verf. 11. Locus maritimus Merala Zabulonitarum à Syro interprete vocatur collis vulpis. Eandem vulpium in Palæstina abundantiam testatur & illud Threm. 5. verf. 18. Propter montem Sion quia periit, vulpes ambulaverunt in eo. Similiter & illud David de hostibus suis Psal. 62. verf. 11. Tradentur in manus gladii, pars vulpium erunt, seu ut vertunt Syrus & Arabs, Vulpibus erunt pro cibo. Ubi Rex sanctissimus è carnivoris feris pro toto genere unam ponit speciem, eámque despectissimam, quasi sit magis probrosum à vulpe discerpi & devorari, quàm à nobiliore fera. Vulpes autem esse carnivoras patet ex eo quod Pausanias, Polyænus & Plinius lib. 11. hist. nat. cap.37. narrat Aristomenem conjectum in illud barathrum prope Lacedæmonem, in quod capite damnati præcipites ex alto demittebantur, & triduum ibi commoratum per sublustres tenebras vulpem vidisse cadavera appetentem, eámque caudâ arreptam secutum per opaca viarum, & cadaverum ibi jacentium osse confracto, quo montis angustias amovebat atque excindebat, tandem ex specu illo evasisse dias in luminis oras. Et barathrum illud ex quo evasit Aristomenes dicebatur Cæadas; nempe Cæadas Lacedæmoniis idipsum fuit, quod Græcorum aliis κα΄ιατον vel κα΄ιετο΄ς, id est, locus effossus, vel terræ dehiscentis ruptura, quam efficiunt terræ-motus, atque inde etiam carcer dictus est κα΄ιαδ΄ας, ut testatur Strabo lib. 8. Hujusmodi ruptura cum frequentes fuerint in agro Laconico, sunt qui Spartam inde ab Homero Iliad B. versu. 581. & Odyss.D. versu 1. dici statuunt κα΄ιετάεσταν, ubi mendosè legitur vulgò κατωέσσαν. Verùm ut ad textum Scripturæ redeamus, operæ pretium est observare ex B. Ambr. lib. 7. in Luc. 9. Quàm apte sponsus caelestis falsos doctores seu haereticos per vulpes designarit. Fallax, inquit, vulpes est, animal, & insidiis semper intentum, rapinae fraudem exercet. Nihil tutum, nihil otiosum, nihil patitur esse securum, quod inter ipsa hospitia hominum praedam requirat. Haereticis vulpes comparat. Vulpes enim plenum fraudis est animal foveam parans, & in fovea semper latere desiderans. Ita sunt haeretici, qui domum sibi parare non norunt, sed circumscriptionibus suis alios decipere conantur. Jacob enim domum habitat, haereticus in fovea est, ut fraudulenta vulpes gallinae illi Evangelicae dolum semper intendens, de qua scriptum est, Quoties volui congregare filios tuos sicut gallina pullos suos, & noluisti? ecce relinquetur vobis domus vestra deserta. Merito ergo foveas habent, qui domum, quam habuerant, perdiderunt. Hoc animal neque mansuescit unquam; unde & Apostolus ait: Haereticum hominem post unam correptionem devita. Neque ulli est aut cibo utile: non enim de hoc dixit Christus: Meus cibus est ut faciam voluntatem Patris mei, qui in caelis est. Quin etiam a fructibus suis relegat, dicens: Capite nobis vulpes pusillas exterminantes vineas, hoc est, quae minorem vineam, non majorem exterminant. (Ubi observa a sancto Ambrosio adjectivum pusillas non ad vulpes, sed ad vineas referri. Quod idem S. Doctor in Ps. 118. octon. 11, in fine quoque facit. Verba ipsius sunt ibi: Merito scriptum est in Canticis Canticorum: Prehendite nobis vulpes pusillas exterminantes vineas, ut vineae nostrae floreant. Quo ostenditur quod vel Dominus Jesus, vel Ecclesia fraudulentorum dolos a vineis suis exterminandos esse praecipiant, ne pauxillulis vineis noceant, quia adultis jam viribus nocere non possunt. Haereticus enim imperfectum tentare potest, non perfectum.) Et ideo Samson ad caudas eorum faces ligavit, & in messes alienigenarum dimisit, eo quod haeretici fructus incendere conantur alienos, latratibus magis sonori, quam vocibus; qui enim Verbum negant, nec vocem habent: ad praesens ore liberi, sed in futurum finem jam vincti, caudae facibus significantes sui finis incendium. Haec Ambrosius. Magistro praestantissimo succinit praestantissimus discipulus Ecclesiarum magister Augustinus enarrans Psalmum octogesimum. Quamvis, ait, opinionum varietate discordent, simili tamen vanitate colligantur. In pejus isti consentiunt, quamvis a se invicem dissentire videantur. Ideo Samson caudas vulpium colligavit. Vulpes autem significant insidiosos, maximeque haereticos dolosos, fraudulentos, cavernosis anfractibus latentes, odore etiam retro putentes. Haec inibi Augustinus interpretans haec verba Ps. 61. v. 10. Ut decipiant ipsi de vanitate in idipsum. Sic & sub Innocentio III. celebrata Synodus Lateranensis cap. 3. Facies quidem, inquit, diversas habent, sed caudas caudas adinvicem colligatas, quia de vanitate conveniunt in idip–sum. Nempe ut optime advertit B. Isidorus Hispalensis in fine cap 5. lib. 8. Etymol. Haereses dum inter se multis erroribus divisae invicem sibi dissentiunt, communi tamen nomine adversus Ecclesiam Dei conspirant. Sed vanum est hoc omnium haereticorum consilium, cum portae inferi non sint contra Dei Ecclesiam praevalituras. Vide Commentarium nostrum in Mat. 16. v. 18. Potest etiam dici quod quia haereticus violat foedus cum Deo initum & juratam illi fidem frangit, assimilatur vulpi, quae, ut observat Rabbi David Kimchi in Jud. 15. ex Talmudicis, retrocedere & in adversum ire solet, id est, ut R. Salomon in glossa interpretatur,
units.tr: Foxes. That there were many foxes in Palestine is attested not only by the present drama, whose scene is set in the mountains and fields around Jerusalem, but also by the deed of Samson (Judg. 15:4), and by the fact that many places in Palestine, or near Palestine, took their name from foxes, such as the land of Shual, that is, the land of the fox (1 Sam. or 1 Kings 13:17). There is also a town of Judah (Josh. 15:28), and a town of Simeon (Josh. 19:6), which is called Hazar-shual in Nehemiah 11:27, and the same town of Simeon is called Hazar-shual in 1 Chronicles 4:28, that is, the fortress of the fox. The town of the Danites, Selebin (Josh. 19:42), or Shaalbim as it is called in Judges 1:35, where the Amorites are said to have occupied it, and 1 Kings 4:9. In the passage of Judges just cited, some of the Greek versions render it Thalabin, others Foxes, and today both readings are found in our copies (Josh. 19:11). The maritime place Merala of the Zebulunites is called by the Syriac translator the hill of the fox. The same abundance of foxes in Palestine is attested by Lamentations 5:18: Because of Mount Zion, which lies desolate, foxes walk upon it. Similarly David's words about his enemies, Psalm 62:11: They shall be delivered into the hand of the sword; they shall be a portion for foxes, or, as the Syriac and the Arabic render it, they shall be food for foxes. Here that most holy King takes one species from among the carnivorous beasts to stand for the whole genus, and that the most despised one, as if it were more shameful to be torn apart and devoured by a fox than by a nobler beast. That foxes are carnivorous is clear from the fact that Pausanias, Polyaenus and Pliny (Nat. Hist. 11, ch. 37) relate that Aristomenes was thrown into that pit near Sparta, into which condemned men were cast headlong from a height, and that after staying there three days in the dim light he saw a fox going after the corpses, and, seizing its tail, followed it through the dark passages, breaking the bones of the corpses lying there, by which he widened and cut through the narrow passages, and at last escaped from that cave into the light of day. The pit from which Aristomenes escaped was called Caeadas; indeed Caeadas among the Lacedaemonians was the same thing that others of the Greeks called [κάιατον] or [κάιετος], that is, a hollow dug out, or a rupture of the gaping earth, which earthquakes produce; and from this the prison too was called [καιάδας], as Strabo attests (Bk. 8). Since such ruptures were frequent in the Laconian country, some hold that Sparta was called [καιετάεσταν] from Homer, Iliad B, line 581, and Odyssey D, line 1, where the vulgar text wrongly reads [κατωέσσαν]. But to return to the text of Scripture, it is worth observing from St Ambrose, Book 7 on Luke 9, how aptly the heavenly bridegroom has designated false teachers, or heretics, by foxes. The fox, he says, is a deceitful animal, always intent on snares, and it practises fraud in its plunder. Nothing is safe, nothing is idle, nothing is left secure, since it seeks prey even among the dwellings of men. He compares it to heretics. For the fox is a creature full of fraud, digging a pit and always wishing to lie hidden in the pit. So are the heretics, who do not know how to make a home for themselves, but try to deceive others by their cunning. Jacob dwells in a house; the heretic is in a pit, like the crafty fox, always plotting against that Gospel hen, of whom it is written: How often would I have gathered your children together, as a hen gathers her chicks, and you would not? Behold, your house is left to you desolate. Rightly, then, do those who have lost the house they once had have pits. This animal never becomes tame; hence the Apostle also says: Avoid a heretical man after one warning. Nor is it of any use for food; for Christ did not say of this animal: My food is to do the will of my Father who is in heaven. Indeed He also drives it away from its fruits, saying: Catch us the little foxes that destroy the vineyards, that is, the ones that destroy the smaller vineyard, not the greater. (Here observe that St Ambrose refers the adjective little not to the foxes but to the vineyards. The same holy Doctor does the same at the end of his exposition of Psalm 118, octave 11. His words there are: Rightly it is written in the Song of Songs: Catch us the little foxes that destroy the vineyards, so that our vineyards may flourish. By this is shown that either the Lord Jesus or the Church commands that the deceits of the fraudulent be rooted out of their vineyards, lest they harm the little vineyards, since they can no longer harm them when they have grown to full strength. For the heretic can attack the imperfect, not the perfect.) And so Samson tied firebrands to their tails and let them loose into the cornfields of the foreigners, because heretics try to set fire to other people's fruits, barking more loudly than they speak; for those who deny the Word have no real voice: free in mouth for the present, but already bound to an end in the future, and with their tails signifying by the firebrands the burning of their end. So Ambrose. The most excellent disciple, Augustine, teacher of the Churches, echoes his excellent master in expounding Psalm 80. Although, he says, they disagree with one another in the variety of their opinions, they are nevertheless bound together by a similar vanity. Those men agree in worse things, though they seem to differ from one another. So Samson tied together the tails of the foxes. Now the foxes signify the insidious, and above all the deceitful and fraudulent heretics, who lurk in cavernous windings and who even stink behind. Augustine says this in interpreting Psalm 61:10, that they may deceive, they themselves, out of vanity into the same thing. So too the Lateran Synod celebrated under Innocent III, chapter 3: They have indeed diverse faces, it says, but their tails are tied together, because they agree out of vanity into the same thing. Indeed, as St Isidore of Seville rightly observes at the end of chapter 5 of Book 8 of the Etymologies: Heresies, although they are divided among themselves by many errors and disagree with one another, nevertheless conspire together under a common name against the Church of God. But this counsel of all heretics is vain, since the gates of hell shall not prevail against the Church of God. See our commentary on Matthew 16:18. It may also be said that, because the heretic violates the covenant made with God and breaks the faith sworn to Him, he is likened to the fox, which, as Rabbi David Kimchi observes on Judges 15 from the Talmudic writers, is wont to go backwards and turn against the way, that is, as Rabbi Solomon interprets it in his gloss,

units.la: Cum venatores insectantur vulpem, non ea fugiendo recta procurrit; sed per multos et varios anfractus discurfat. Cui non absimile est quod ait B. Isidorus lib. 12. orig. cap. 2. Vulpes dicta quasi volupes; est enim volubilis pedibus, & nunquam rectis itineribus, sed tortuosis anfractibus currit. Hinc & Nonnius, Vulpinari dictum est fraudibus & mendaciis vetera pervertere, vel effingere. Dictum ab inrecto, seu intorto vulpium cursu. Aristoteles lib. 1. Hist. Anim. cap. 1. vulpes recenset inter animalia callida & malefica. Aelianus lib. 4. Hist. cap. 39. ait eas attigisse summum malitiae & fraudis fastigium. Hinc Horatius de arte Poetica, Nunquam te fallunt animi sub vulpe latentes,
units.tr: When hunters chase a fox, it does not flee in a straight line but runs off through many and varied twists and turns. Not unlike this is what St. Isidore says in Origines 12, chapter 2: The fox (vulpes) is so called as if it were "volupes," for it is nimble of foot and never runs by straight paths but by winding detours. Nonnius too: To play the fox (vulpinari) means to pervert or counterfeit old things by frauds and lies. The word comes from the fox's crooked, twisting course. Aristotle, in Historia Animalium 1, chapter 1, lists the fox among the cunning and harmful animals. Aelian, in book 4 of his Natural History, chapter 39, says that foxes have reached the highest pitch of malice and trickery. Hence Horace in the Ars Poetica: Never do the minds that lurk beneath the fox's skin escape you.

units.la: Et Persius satyra quinta, Astutam rapido servas sub pectore vulpem.
units.tr: And Persius in the fifth satire: You keep a cunning fox beneath your breast.

units.la: Demoliuntur vineas. Vulpes uvis maxime delectantur, unde illud Nicandri in Alexipharmacis versu 185. Cum pingui nocuit vulpes versuta racemo.
units.tr: They tear down the vineyards. Foxes take especial delight in grapes, whence the line of Nicander in the Alexipharmaca, verse 185: The crafty fox has harmed the rich cluster.

units.la: Et illud Theocriti Idyll. 10. in caprarii populo secundum elegantem versionem Heinsii. Area purpureis pulchrè circumdatur uvis, Quam puer exiguus residens custodit in horti Sepibus. Nunc circum vulpecula bina racemos, Altera percurrens depascitur, &c.
units.tr: And this line of Theocritus, Idyll 10, in the elegant version of Heinsius, on the goatherd's people: The enclosure is beautifully ringed with purple grapes, which a small boy, sitting, guards within the garden hedges. Now two little foxes run about the clusters, and the other one, running through, feeds on them, etc.

units.la: Idem videre est apud eundem Theocritum Idyll. 5. Varronem lib. 1. Rustic. cap. 8. Galenum lib. 3. de alimentorum facultatibus cap. 2. Hinc orta fabula omnibus nota de vulpe & uva, quam Phaedrus sic expressit, Fame coacta vulpes alta in vinea Uvam adpetebat, summis saliens viribus, Quam tangere ut non potuit, discedens ait Nondum matura est, nolo acerbam sumere.
units.tr: The same may be seen in Theocritus again, Idyll 5, in Varro, Rustic Matters 1, chapter 8, and in Galen, On the Powers of Foods, book 3, chapter 2. Hence arose the fable known to all, of the fox and the grape, which Phaedrus expressed thus: A fox, driven by hunger, leaped high within a vineyard, straining every nerve to reach the grapes above; when it could not touch them, it went off, saying: "They are not yet ripe; I do not want to take up sour ones."

units.la: בשצרק אותו אצו מרחיק לברוח אלאחוער על קלות
units.tr: When they pursue it, it hastens to flee backwards, and turns against the one who pursues it, with ease [בשצרק אותו אצו מרחיק לברוח אלאחוער על קלות] ## The bride's second dream.

units.la: Alterum sponsæ somnium.
16. Dilectus meus mihi, & ego illi, qui pascitur inter lilia;
units.tr: 16. My beloved is mine, and I am his, who feeds among the lilies;

units.la: 17. Donec aspiret dies, & inclinentur umbræ. Revertere : similis esto, dilecte mi, capreæ, hinnulóque cervorum super montes Bether.
units.tr: 17. Until the day breathes and the shadows lean away. Turn back: be like, my beloved, a roe or a young hart upon the mountains of Bether.

units.la: EXPLICATIO.
units.tr: EXPLANATION.

units.la: 16. Dilectus meus mihi. Id est, sponsus meus mira dignatione me amando prævenit.
units.tr: 16. My beloved is mine. That is, my bridegroom has anticipated me by loving me with wonderful condescension.

units.la: Et ego illi. Id est, & ego dilecta vicem rependo, adeò diligens eum, qui totus dignatur esse meus, mihíque intentus, ut tota sim illius contemnens omnia prospera & adversa mundi pro ipso, nec mori formidem pro dilectione ejus. Hæc sponsæ verba veram continent Ecclesiæ Christo desponsatæ vocem, quæ dum sollicita satagit & anxia est ut placeat Christo, nec ullâ rerum difficultate ab hoc propositò potest deterreri, ipsum Christum ad se convertit ut sit Deus ejus. ut enim præclarè B. Basilius pro more suo in id Pf. 29. Domine Deus noster clamavi ad te & sanasti me. ὐ πάντων Θεὸς ὁ Θεὸς, ἀλλὰ τῶν οἰκείωθέντων αὐτῷ διὰ τῆς ἀγάπης, &c. Non omnium Deus est Deus, sed eorum proprie qui charitate sunt ei conjuncti, ut Deus Abraham, Deus Isaac, Deus Jacob. Si enim omnium esset Deus, non utique sejunctum illis testimonium reddidisset, quasi aliquid eximium. Et Jacob dicebat: Auxiliatus est tibi Deus meus. Et Thomas rursus, ubi certò didicit resurrectionem, Dominum complexus ait: Dominus meus, Deus meus. Est itaque vox ista, Domine Deus meus, plena affectu fiduciæ, & conveniens statui prophetico. Mutuum autem Christi & Ecclesiæ amorem luculenter sanè Sermone in Synodo expressit Arnulphus Lexoviensis aureis his verbis: Dilecta dicitur Ecclesia, quia diligit & ipsa; neque enim diligeretur, nisi diligeret: ipse enim nisi diligentes se non diligit. Ego, inquit, diligentes me diligo. Prævenit tamen diligendo, quoniam ipse prior dilexit nos, sed ad hoc diligit, ut diligentes faciat. Nisi enim qui diligitur mutuâ ei dilectione respondeat, divinæ revocatur dilectionis affectus. Verum quanta inter ipsum & diligentem se discurrat alternæ charitatis affectio, difficile nobis, imò impossibile est explicare, quoniam nec ipsius Salomonis monis sapientia id perfectè nobis enarrare potuit; licèt diligentissime fuerit prosecutus inter eos modò complexus & oscula, modò aromata & unguenta, modò languorem spiritûs, modò animæ defectum, modò ferventem curiosæ æmulationis zelum; modò delicatum teneræ compassionis affectum.
units.tr: And I am his. That is, I, the beloved, repay him in turn, loving so intently him who deigns to be wholly mine and wholly attentive to me, that I am entirely his, despising all the prosperity and adversity of the world for his sake, and not fearing to die for love of him. These are the words of the bride, and they contain the true voice of the Church betrothed to Christ. While she anxiously and earnestly strives to please Christ, and cannot be turned from this purpose by any difficulty of circumstance, she turns Christ himself towards her, so that he may be her God. For as the blessed Basil admirably says, in his manner, on Ps. 29: Lord our God, I cried to you and you healed me. [οὐ πάντων Θεὸς ὁ Θεὸς, ἀλλὰ τῶν οἰκειωθέντων αὐτῷ διὰ τῆς ἀγάπης] &c. God is not the God of all, but of those who have been made his own through love; as the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, the God of Jacob. For if he were the God of all, he would not have given a separate testimony to them, as if they were something exceptional. And Jacob said: My God has helped me. And Thomas again, when he had surely learned of the resurrection, embracing the Lord said: My Lord and my God. That phrase, Lord my God, is therefore full of the emotion of trust, and suits the prophetic state. Arnulphus of Lisieux expressed the mutual love of Christ and the Church brilliantly in his sermon at the synod, in these golden words: The Church is called beloved because she also loves; for she would not be loved unless she loved, since he does not love unless those who love him. I love, he says, those who love me. Yet he anticipates her by loving, since he first loved us; but he loves in order to make them loving. For unless the one who is loved answers with mutual love, the affection of divine love is called back. But how great is the reciprocal affection of charity that runs between him and the one who loves him, it is difficult for us, indeed impossible, to explain; since not even the wisdom of Solomon himself could narrate it perfectly to us, although he pursued it most diligently among them: now embraces and kisses, now aromas and ointments, now languor of spirit, now failing of the soul, now the fervent zeal of a curious rivalry, now the delicate feeling of tender compassion.

units.la: Qui pascitur inter lilia. Sponsa videt in somnis sponsum inter lilia pernoctantem; seu Ecclesia sub Lege contemplatur desponsatum sibi Deum regnantem inter agmina beatorum mentium virtutibus & gloriâ candida, dum plerique ipsiusmet Ecclesiæ filii detinentur in profunda ignorantiæ nocte & obscurissima vitiorum caligine.
units.tr: Who feeds among the lilies. The bride sees in her dreams the bridegroom spending the night among lilies; or the Church under the Law contemplates God, betrothed to her, reigning among the companies of blessed minds, bright with virtues and glory, while many of the very sons of the Church are held in the deep night of ignorance and the darkest mist of vices.

units.la: 17. Donec aspiret dies & inclinentur umbræ. Eleganti periphrasi exprimit sponsa, quod simplicibus verbis dicere potuisset, donec diescat; quod in ore Ecclesiæ sub Lege significat, donec oriatur lux Evangelii, cujus incrementis usus umbrarum, seu Legalium ceremoniarum abrogetur, & opera tenebrarum abjiciantur, ut ambuletur honestè sicut in die.
units.tr: 17. Until the day breathes and the shadows lean away. By an elegant periphrasis the bride expresses what she could have said in plain words, until the day dawns. In the mouth of the Church under the Law this means until the light of the Gospel rises, with whose increase the use of shadows, that is, of the legal ceremonies, is abolished, and the works of darkness are cast off, so that we may walk honestly as in the day.

units.la: Revertere, &c. Sponsa seu Ecclesia sub Lege, quæ primò somniabat sponsum sibi præsentem, seque post parietem per cancellos aspicientem, in altero somnio ipsum videt à se recessisse ut inter lilia commoraretur; unde illum enixè rogat ut ad se non ingratam summi illius beneficii, quo ipsam sibi desponsavit, & confortem suarum divitiarum benignè & misericorditer facere promisit, quàm velocissimè revertatur.
units.tr: Return, &c. The bride, or the Church under the Law, who at first dreamed of the bridegroom present to her, and saw herself behind the wall, looking through the lattice, in another dream sees him having withdrawn from her to dwell among the lilies. Whence she earnestly asks him to return to her as quickly as possible, since he promised to make her, not ungrateful for that supreme benefit by which he betrothed her to himself, and the partner of his riches, kindly and mercifully.

units.la: Revertere, similis esto, &c. Id est, revertere tantâ celeritate, ut similis videaris capreæ & hinnulo cervorum supra montes Bether currentibus, quibus nullum animal est pernicius, ut expresse habet Xenophon in Cynegetico de cervi hinnulo.
units.tr: Return, be like, &c. That is, return with such speed that you may seem like a roe and a young hart running upon the mountains of Bether, than which no animal is swifter, as Xenophon expressly says of the young stag in his Cynegeticus.

units.la: Montes Bether. Hi montes ut & montes besamim, aromatum, qui in hoc sacro Dramate hinnulo pro statione assignantur, fuerunt Judeæ loca hodie nobis ignota. Est autem mons Bether, mons scissionis, & videtur ita dictus propter scissuras terræ, quæ fiunt imbrium violentiâ, hócque voluisse Græci, qui reddunt διχη κοιλωμάτων, id est, montes cavitatum. Sunt, qui malunt κυκλωμάτων, quæ lectio si potior esset, dicerem illos in textu Hebraeo legisse montes בתר Cether, non Bether, quia בתר Cether corona est κυκλοειδής; & montes coronæ vocari potuisse montes, quibus Jerusalem tanquam corona, cincta erat circumquaque, Ps. 124. Heb. 125. v. 2.
units.tr: Mountains of Bether. These mountains, like the mountains of besamim, of spices, which in this sacred drama are assigned to the hind as her station, were places in Judea now unknown to us. Now the mountain Bether is the mountain of division, and it seems to be so named because of the clefts in the earth made by the violence of rains. This is what the Greeks meant, who render it διχῆ κοιλωμάτων [dichē koilōmatōn], that is, mountains of hollows. Some prefer κυκλωμάτων [kyklōmatōn]. If that reading were the better one, I would say that they read in the Hebrew text the mountains Cether [בתר], not Bether, because Cether [בתר] means crown and is κυκλοειδής [kykloeidēs], circular. The mountains could then have been called mountains of the crown, since Jerusalem was encircled on all sides as by a crown, Ps. 124. Heb. 125. v. 2.

units.la: CAPUT TERTIUM.
units.tr: CHAPTER III.

units.la: Sponsa expergiscitur à somno & comites alloquitur.
units.tr: The bride awakes from sleep and addresses her companions.

units.la: 1. IN lectulo meo per noctes quaesivi quem diligit anima mea : quaesivi illum, & non inveni
units.tr: 1. ON my bed by night I sought him whom my soul loves; I sought him, and did not find him.

units.la: 2. Surgam, & circuibo civitatem : per vicos & plateas quaeram quem diligit anima mea : quaesivi illum, & non inveni.
units.tr: 2. I will rise and go about the city; through its lanes and squares I will seek him whom my soul loves. I sought him, and did not find him.

units.la: 3. Invenerunt me vigiles, qui custodiunt civitatem : Num quem diligit anima mea, vidistis ?
units.tr: 3. The watchmen who guard the city found me: Have you seen him whom my soul loves?

units.la: 4. Paululum cum pertransissem eos, inveni quem diligit anima mea : tenui eum, nec dimittam, donec introducam illum in domum matris meae, & in cubiculum genitricis meae.
units.tr: 4. Scarcely had I passed them when I found him whom my soul loves. I held him and will not let him go until I bring him into the house of my mother, and into the chamber of her who bore me.

units.la: EXPLICATIO.
units.tr: EXPLANATION.

units.la: 1. IN lectulo, &c. Narrat sponsa comitibus suis quomodo per noctem somniarit sponsum praesentem, seque alloquentem, & frustra per thorum huc illuc manus contulerit, & brachia ultro citroque moverit, ut ipsum sibi in primis earum amplexti hiteretur. Sic frustra dicit Ecclesia a se in litera Legis quiescente omnes adhibitos fuisse conatus ad sponsi dilectissimi amplexus sibi conciliandos per Legales ceremonias & umbrabilem Dei cultum. Contigit sponsae, quod amore captis contingere solet. Amores absentes animo pertinaciter illis obversantur; colloquia, vigiliae, insomnia, offendicula queque inveterati doloris suavissimam memoriam refricant; lumina sua errabundi quaeritant, obvios quosque an eis occurrerint, scicitantur, ut apud Ovidium conjux castissima,
units.tr: 1. On my bed, etc. The bride tells her companions how, in the night, she dreamed that the bridegroom was present and speaking to her, and how in vain she stretched her hands across the bed, here and there, and moved her arms back and forth, so that she might first of all clasp him in their embrace. So the Church says in vain that, while the letter of the Law lay at rest, every effort was made to win for herself the embraces of her most beloved bridegroom through the legal ceremonies and the shadowy worship of God. What happened to the bride is what usually happens to those captured by love. Absent loves stubbornly present themselves to the mind; conversations, wakefulness, sleeplessness, and all the stings of an old pain renew the sweetest memory. Wandering, they seek with their eyes, questioning each person they meet whether he has encountered the beloved, as the most chaste wife does in Ovid:

units.la: Quisquis ad haec vertit peregrinam littora puppim,
units.tr: Whoever turns his ship toward these foreign shores,

units.la: Ille mihi de te multa rogatus abit.
units.tr: Goes away after being asked by me many things about you.

units.la: 2. Surgam, &c. Q. d. cum viderem frustra a me quaesitum hoftu per cubile, quem diligit anima mea, decrevi surgere, stattimque me proripui è thalamo, ut dilectum sollicitè quæsitura per totam urbem vagarer ; nec tamen tam sollicitè quæsitus à me est inventus. Sic Ecclesia videns se in litera Legis nihil proficere ad accelerandum sponsi sui adventum, à litera occidente erigere se coepit ad spiritum vivificantem, (qui aptè dicitur civitas, quia in eo convenit Legis & Evangelii civium unitas) & sic percurrens obscurissima, & planissima quæque sacræ Scripturæ loca multùm quidem profecit, nec tamen sic statim, quem quærebat Christum invenit, ut non inventus ardentius quæreretur, & sponsa tarditate suâ capacior reddita multipliciùs quandoque inveniret quod quærebat, Vide B. Greg.Mag. 5. Moral. cap. 4.
units.tr: 2. I will rise, etc. That is to say: when I saw that he whom my soul loves was sought in vain by me on the bed, I resolved to rise, and at once I hurried out of the bedchamber, to wander through the whole city in anxious search for the beloved.
