Yet he was not found by me as quickly as he was anxiously sought. So the Church, seeing that she accomplished nothing in the letter of the Law toward hastening the coming of her bridegroom, began to raise herself from the killing letter to the life-giving Spirit (which is aptly called the city, because in it the Law and the Gospel are united as one body of citizens). Thus running through the most obscure and the plainest passages of Holy Scripture, she made much progress, yet she did not find Christ whom she sought so quickly that, once found, he was not sought more ardently; and the bride, made more capacious by her delay, would at some time find in many ways what she sought. See Blessed Gregory the Great, Moral. 5, chap. 4.

units.la: 3. Invenerunt me vigiles, &c. Hinc conjici potest quòd cùm Salomon hoc sacrum Drama conscriberet, non omnimodâ pace frueretur ; vix enim fit verisimile toto regno in pace compo-sito custodes urbem lustrasse per noctem eâ diligentiâ, quâ lustrarent si bellum ferveret. Salomon autem profundâ pace non est potitus, nisi subjugatis reliquiis gentium Israëlitis vicinarum, quibus ipsi Israëlitæ pepercerant. Ecclesia itaque dicit in hoc versiculo se in scrutandis Scripturis inventam ab habentibus clavem Scientiæ doctoribus, petiisse num Sponsum dilectum inter ejusdem lectionem deprehenderint, ut sibi earum sponsi amore velut oestro percitæ latibula ipsius omnia lustratur nuntiarent, quandónam nuptias promissas esset celebratius per magnum & ineffabile Incarnationis sacramentum.
units.tr: 3. The watchmen found me, etc. From this it can be conjectured that when Solomon wrote this sacred drama he did not enjoy entire peace. For it is hardly likely that, with the whole kingdom settled in peace, the guards would have patrolled the city by night with the diligence they would use if war were raging. Solomon, however, did not gain deep peace until the remnants of the neighboring peoples, whom the Israelites themselves had spared, had been subdued. The Church therefore says in this verse that, having been found while searching the Scriptures by the teachers who hold the key of knowledge, she asked whether they had discovered her beloved bridegroom in their reading, so that they might tell her all his hiding places, stirred as she was, like a gadfly, by love for him, and when the promised nuptials would be celebrated more solemnly through the great and ineffable sacrament of the Incarnation.

units.la: 4. Paululum cùm pertransissem, &c. Hæc secundum literæ so-num facilia sunt intellectu. De Ecclesia verò sic exponuntur à sancto Greg. Magno 18 Moral. cap. 27. Cùm Redemtorem suum Ecclesia quæreret, in antiquis prædicatoribus spem figere noluit, quæ dicit, Paululùm cùm pertransissem eos, inveni quem diligit anima mea ; illum quippe invenire non posset, si istos transire noluisset.
units.tr: 4. Scarcely had I passed them, etc. These words are easy to understand according to the sound of the letter. Concerning the Church, however, they are explained thus by St. Gregory the Great, Moral. 18, chap. 27: When the Church sought her Redeemer, she was unwilling to fix her hope in the ancient preachers; this is what she says: Scarcely had I passed them when I found him whom my soul loves; for she could not have found him if she had been unwilling to pass by them.

units.la: Tenui eum. Brachiis charitatis, & quibusdam fidei & devotionis lacertis, ut loquitur B. Ambr. in Ps. 47.
units.tr: I held him. With the arms of charity, and with certain sinews of faith and devotion, as Blessed Ambrose speaks in Ps. 47.

units.la: Nec dimittam. Omnis enim qui quærit invenit, & qui invenit adhærere debet, ne possit amittere, ut loquitur idem S. Doctor. in lib. de Isaac & anima cap. 5. Tenetur autem sponsus cordis custodiâ, orationis instantiâ, & nunquam interrupto devotionis fervore.
units.tr: And I will not let him go. For everyone who seeks finds, and whoever has found ought to cling fast, lest he lose him, as the same Holy Doctor says in the book On Isaac and the Soul, chap. 5. The bridegroom, however, is held fast by the guarding of the heart, by the persistence of prayer, and by a devotional fervor never interrupted.

units.la: Donec introducam eum in domum, &c. Id est, donec eum introduxerim in locum ad mutuos exhibendos amores maximè commodum, in quo concepta sac genita sum. His verbis negat Ecclesia se sponsum inventum dimissuram priùs, quàm simul ingredientur grediantur in cœlestem Jerusalem, quam Apostolus Gal. 4. v. 26. appellat matrem omnium nostrûm. Ita B. Theodoretus.
units.tr: Until I bring him into the house, etc. That is, until I have brought him into the place most suitable for the exchange of mutual loves, in which I was conceived and born. By these words the Church declares that she will not let go the bridegroom once found until they enter together into the heavenly Jerusalem, which the Apostle in Gal. 4, v. 26 calls the mother of us all. So Blessed Theodoret.

units.la: Sponsâ præ nimio gaudio de inventione & fruitione sponsi omni studio quæsiti in extasim incidente dicit Sponsus :
units.tr: Because of excessive joy at the finding and enjoyment of the bridegroom, which she sought with all her zeal, the bride falls into ecstasy, and the Bridegroom says:

units.la: 5. ADjuro vos filiæ Jerusalem per capreas cervosque camporum ne suscitetis, neque evigilare faciatis dilectam, donec ipsa velit.
units.tr: 5. I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, by the roes and the hinds of the field, that you neither stir up nor awaken my beloved until she herself wishes.

units.la: EXPLICATIO.
units.tr: EXPLANATION.

units.la: DE sensu hujus versiculi vide quæ diximus supra cap. 2. vers. 7.
units.tr: For the meaning of this verse, see what we said above on chapter 2, verse 7.

units.la: Chorus Pastorum.
units.tr: The Chorus of Shepherds.

units.la: 6. QUæ est ista, quæ ascendit per desertum sicut virgula fumi ex aromatibus myrrhæ, & thuris, & universi pulveris pigmentarii ?
units.tr: 6. Who is this that comes up out of the wilderness like a column of smoke from myrrh and frankincense and every powder of the perfumer?

units.la: 7. En lectulum Salomonis sexaginta fortes ambiunt ex fortissimis Israël :
units.tr: 7. Behold the bed of Solomon: sixty valiant men surround it, of the most valiant of Israel.

units.la: 8. Omnes tenentes gladios, & ad bella doctissimi : uniuscujusque ensis super femur suum propter timores nocturnos.
units.tr: 8. All of them hold swords and are most skilled in war; each man's sword is upon his thigh because of the terrors of the night.

units.la: 9. Ferculum fecit sibi Rex Salomon de lignis Libani :
units.tr: 9. King Solomon made himself a litter of the wood of Lebanon.

units.la: 10. Columnas ejus fecit argenteas, reclinatorium aureum, ascensum purpureum : media charitate confstravit propter filias Jerusalem.
units.tr: 10. He made its pillars of silver, its back of gold, its covering of purple, and its middle was paved with love for the daughters of Jerusalem.

units.la: 11. Egredimini & videte filiæ Sion Regem Salomonem in diademate, quo coronavit illum mater sua in die desponsationis illius, & in die lætitiæ cordis ejus.
units.tr: 11. Go forth, daughters of Zion, and see King Solomon in the diadem with which his mother crowned him on the day of his espousal, and on the day of the gladness of his heart.

units.la: EXPLICATIO.
units.tr: EXPLANATION.

units.la: 6. Quæ est ista, &c. Q. d. Unde Virgo ruri nata educata que tam speciosam corporis staturam, támque suavem nacta est odorem, ut haud absimilis videatur sumeæ columnæ rectà ascendenti ex suffitu myrrhæ, thuris, aliorúmque omnium id genus aromatum? Hac pastorum admiratione adumbrantur Angeli demirantes Ecclesiam, quæ per quotidianum prosectum instar fumi ex virtutibus erumpentem ad perfectiora,sublimioráque sursum contendit; nec vago quodam & erratico hac & illac fluxu dispergitur, sed colleētis viribus virgulæ seu columnæ instar ad Deum ascendit; unde B. Greg. 1 Moral.cap30. Sancta, inquit, Ecclesia sicut fumi virgula ex aromatibus ascendit, quia ex vitæ suæ virtutibus in interni quotidie incensi rectitudinem proficit, nec sparsa per cogitationes defluit, sed sese intra arcana cordis in rigoris virga constringit. Visibilia omnia fastidit, mentem in cœlestia attollit, nihilque aliud optat ac studet, quàm sponso suo sese per intimos cordis affectus adjungere, in eóque solo delectari ac pasci.
units.tr: 6. Who is this, etc. That is to say: whence is this virgin, reared and brought up in the country, who has gained so splendid a bodily stature and so sweet a fragrance that she seems not unlike a column of smoke rising straight up from the incense of myrrh, frankincense and all the other spices of that kind? By this admiration of the shepherds the angels are figured, wondering at the Church, which, rising upward like smoke from her virtues day by day, strives toward things more perfect and more sublime. She is not scattered by any wandering and erratic flow this way and that, but with her powers gathered together she ascends to God like a column or a staff. Whence blessed Gregory, in the first book of the Moralia, chapter 30: "The holy Church, he says, ascends like a staff of smoke from spices, because from the virtues of her life she advances daily toward the uprightness of the inner fire that is kindled, and she is not dispersed and does not flow away through scattered thoughts, but binds herself within the secret places of the heart like a rod of straightness." She despises all visible things, lifts her mind to heavenly things, and wishes and strives for nothing else than to join herself to her bridegroom through the innermost affections of the heart, and to delight and feed on him alone.

units.la: Per desertum. Lxx. è deserto. Donant autem Hebræi rus deserti nomine per respectum ad oppida & civitates populosas.
units.tr: Through the wilderness. The Septuagint: out of the wilderness. The Hebrews, however, give the name of wilderness to the open country in relation to towns and populous cities.

units.la: Virgula fumi. Thymiama olim apud Judæos ex præscripto Legis in honorem Dei conflagratum igne emittebat fumum, qui ad superiora rectus ferebatur & immutatus, idcirco virgulæ, aliàs columnæ æquiparatus. Quapropter inter miracula Templi decem, quæ numerantur in Pirké Avoth. c. 5. recensetur quòd quantàcumque ventorum vi agitaretur atque turbaretur aër, non impediebat quin illi columnæ & virgulæ fumi recta iter ad cælum esset.
units.tr: Column of smoke. Among the Jews, the incense offered by the prescription of the Law in honour of God, when it was burned with fire, sent up a smoke which rose straight upward and was not turned aside; for this reason it was likened to a staff, or otherwise to a column. Therefore among the ten miracles of the Temple, which are enumerated in Pirke Avot chapter 5, it is recorded that however violently the winds might stir and trouble the air, they did not prevent that column and staff of smoke from going straight up to heaven.

units.la: Universi pulveris pigmentarii. Thymiamatis compositionem ingredientia aromata singula in pulverem tenuissimum contusa oportebat, & postea ubi thymiama confectum erat, non integra solidáque adolebatur confectio, sed redacta subtilissimum in pulverem, ut videre est Exod. 30. Observat autem Philo Carpathius ad hunc sacri Cantici locum, quòd pigmenta sunt virtutes in corde collectæ, quæ quidem tunc pulvis pigmentarius fiunt, cùm diligenti judicio sigillatim recensentur, & mentis acrimonia quasi pistillo conteruntur, ne qua rudis adhuc ac crassa incultáque omnino affectio, sub virtutis nomine vitium revera fiat ac scelus.
units.tr: Of every powder of the perfumer. The spices that entered into the composition of the incense had each to be pounded into the finest powder, and afterwards, when the incense was made up, the compound was not burned whole and solid, but reduced to the finest powder, as can be seen in Exodus 30. Philo of Carpathus, however, observes on this place of the sacred Song that spices are virtues gathered in the heart, which indeed become a powder of spices when they are examined one by one with careful judgment, and are ground down, as it were in a mortar, by the sharpness of the mind, lest any affection still crude and thick and wholly uncultivated should in fact become a vice and a crime under the name of virtue.

units.la: 7. En lectulum Salomonis, &c. Q. d. Sponsa ista est magnificentissimi sponsi thalamus genialis, quem ipse adeò magnificavit cavit, ut in eo mirifice delectetur, & eum custodia prorsus regali stipare dignetur. Lectulus ille, quo Rex pacificus super omnes Reges universæ terræ magnificatus per Salomonem adumbratus incredibiliter delectatur, est Ecclesia sancta, quæ utpote donata & ornata donis & gratiis coelestibus, dicitur lectulus floridus; hanc contra pericula, quæ à principibus tenebrarum excitantur, circumvallavit precibus & exemplis, vigiliis & exhortationibus virorum quamplurimorum sanctitate & eruditione præstantissimorum.
units.tr: 7. Behold the bed of Solomon, etc. That is to say: this bride is the nuptial bed-chamber of the most magnificent bridegroom, which he himself has so greatly honoured that he delights in it marvellously, and deigns to surround it with a guard altogether royal. That couch on which the Peaceful King, magnified above all the kings of the whole earth, is figured through Solomon, and in which he takes incredible delight, is the holy Church, which, since she is endowed and adorned with heavenly gifts and graces, is called a flowering couch. Against the dangers stirred up by the princes of darkness, he has surrounded her with prayers and examples, with the vigils and exhortations of very many men, most outstanding in holiness and learning.

units.la: Sexaginta. Id est, quamplurimi; ponitur enim numerus definitus pro indefinito.
units.tr: Sixty. That is, very many; for a definite number is put for an indefinite one.

units.la: 8. Omnes tenentes gladios. Id est, omnes sunt idoneis armis instructi.
units.tr: 8. All holding swords. That is, all are equipped with suitable arms.

units.la: Doctissimi. Id est, exercitatissimi.
units.tr: Most skilled. That is, most practised.

units.la: Uniuscujusque ensis, &c. Id est, unicuique in promtu sunt arma, queis tuentur Salomonis lectulum contra maxima quæque pericula.
units.tr: Each man's sword, etc. That is, to each one are ready at hand the arms with which they guard Solomon's couch against all the greatest dangers.

units.la: Propter timores nocturnos. Id est, propter ingentia, quæ imminent pericula. Timores vocantur pericula, quia timenda sunt; nocturni vero dicuntur, quia noctu crebriora & majora sunt pericula, quam interdiu. Salutis autem pericula cum à rectoribus tenebrarum excitentur, merito timores nocturni nuncupantur. Hac metonymia, qua res expavescenda & timenda dicitur timor, Deus ipse Genes. 31. v 42. & in precibus Judæorum appellatur timor Isaac.
units.tr: Because of the terrors of the night. That is, because of the great dangers that threaten. Dangers are called terrors because they are to be feared; and they are called nocturnal because dangers are more frequent and greater by night than by day. But since the dangers to salvation are stirred up by the rulers of darkness, they are rightly called terrors of the night. By this metonymy, in which the thing to be dreaded and feared is called the fear, God himself in Genesis 31:42 is called in the prayers of the Jews the fear of Isaac.

units.la: 9. Ferculum, &c. Pro ferculo Hebraice est ? a verbo ?, fructificare, q. d. fœcundum sponsæ thalamum, lecticam, gestamen, carrucam, quâ deferuntur sponsæ, ut scribit Rabbi David, & merito; scimus enim apud veteres in usu suisse ut nova nupta curru equitans traduceretur, quod in Scuto Herculis describit Hesiodus. Eo autem curru nuptiali tres tantum vectari solitos scribit Pausanias; nimirum sponsam, quæ sederet in medio, sponsum, & paranymphum, qui annulum maritalem tradit. Hujusmodi carrucam dicitur fecisse Salomon, hoc est, ad laudem nominis sui Christus, ut scilicet ea traduceret sponsas sibi charissimas ad thalamum coelestium gaudiorum. Tota hæc carruca structa est ex lignis Libani, cedris videlicet incorruptibilibus, id est, sanctis undique flantibus incorruptibilitatem, & vivificantibus animas, ut exposuit S. Irenæus lib. 3. adversus hæreses cap. 11.
units.tr: 9. A litter, etc. For "litter" the Hebrew has a word derived from the verb meaning to be fruitful, that is, a fruitful bridal chamber, a litter, a carriage, a wagon, in which brides are carried, as Rabbi David writes, and rightly so; for we know that among the ancients it was the custom for a new bride to be conveyed riding in a chariot, which Hesiod describes in the Shield of Hercules. Pausanias writes that only three were accustomed to be carried in that nuptial chariot: namely the bride, who sat in the middle, the bridegroom, and the bridesman who hands over the wedding ring. Solomon is said to have made such a carriage, that is, Christ made it for the praise of his own name, so that he might convey to the heavenly bridal chamber of joys those brides most dear to him. This whole carriage was constructed of the wood of Lebanon, namely of incorruptible cedars, that is, of holy winds blowing from every side that bring incorruptibility, and giving life to souls, as Saint Irenaeus expounded in book 3 of Against Heresies, chapter 11.

units.la: 10. Columnas, &c. Argentum est puritas, vel claritas verbi, quo fulgent Ecclesiæ columnæ, seu Doctores.
units.tr: 10. Its pillars, etc. Silver is the purity or clarity of the Word, by which the pillars of the Church, or teachers, shine.

units.la: Reclinatorium. Id est, lectulum in quo recumbant, ex auro struxit. Aurum charitas est Christi. Ascensum purpureum. Id est, ephippium, stragulum, aulæum, operimentum lecti, est sanguis Christi splendescens quasi purpura, quâ nobilitatur & accenditur Ecclesia in amorem sponsi.
units.tr: The back. That is, the couch on which they recline he made of gold. Gold is the charity of Christ. Its purple covering. That is, the saddle-cloth, the coverlet, the hanging, the covering of the couch, is the blood of Christ shining like purple, by which the Church is ennobled and kindled to love of the bridegroom.

units.la: Media. Id est, interiora ferculi spatia.
units.tr: The middle. That is, the inner spaces of the litter.

units.la: Charitate constravit. Id est, ornavit rebus per fe amabilibus, scilicet, donis Spiritus-sancti.
units.tr: Paved with love. That is, adorned with things lovable in themselves, namely the gifts of the Holy Spirit.

units.la: Propter filias Jerusalem. Id est, ut sponsas sibi charissimas alliceret, & magnetis instar traheret.
units.tr: For the daughters of Jerusalem. That is, so that he might attract the brides most dear to him, and draw them as a magnet does.

units.la: II. Egredimini, &c. Q.d. Prodite filiæ Sion e gynecæis vestris visuræ Salomonem matris sollicitudine coruscantem nuptiali coronâ. Antiquissimi autem esse moris quòd sponsæ coronantur, ut alia taceam, docet corona Ariadnes, ex auro & Indicis gemmis ipso die nuptiarum illi à Venere indulta, & deinceps in cœlum translata. Vide Aratum, & Germanicum, & Festum Avienum in phænomenis, & Hyginum lib. 2. & Tert. de corona militis cap. 7. & 13. & Claudianum lib. 2. de raptu, ubi agens de Proferpina quæ caput floribus redimiebat paulo ante raptum, ad hunc morem ita alludit.
units.tr: 11. Go forth, etc. That is: come forth, daughters of Zion, from your women's chambers, to see Solomon shining with a mother's care in the nuptial crown. That it was a very ancient custom for brides to be crowned, to say nothing of other examples, is shown by the crown of Ariadne, of gold and Indian gems, granted to her by Venus on the very day of her wedding, and afterwards translated into heaven. See Aratus, Germanicus, and Festus Avienus in the Phaenomena, Hyginus book 2, Tertullian On the Soldier's Crown chapters 7 and 13, and Claudian book 2 On the Rape of Proserpina, where, speaking of Proserpina, who was wreathing her head with flowers shortly before her abduction, he alludes to this custom thus:

units.la: ——— feréque ignara coronat,
units.tr: …and, almost unknowing, she crowns herself,

units.la: Augurium fatale thori.
units.tr: an ominous omen of the marriage bed.

units.la: Ad hunc pariter morem alludere videtur Ezechiel cap. 16. v. 12. & hic Regum sapientissimus, ubi Angelos inducit hortantes Judæos, ut egressi de umbris Legis speculentur in Lege adumbratum Christum undique lapidibus vivis circumdandum ex quo lætus sibi Ecclesiam conjugem fecerit. Hac autem fidelium corona dicitur Christus redimitus sollicitudine matris, id est, eorum qui voluntati & nutui Divino in salute animarum curanda sunt obsecuti. Ut enim ait B. Greg. hom. 3. in Evang. Qui Christi soror & frater est credendo, mater efficitur prædicando. Quasi enim parit Dominum, quem cordi audientis infuderit, & mater ejus prædicando efficitur, fi per ejus vocem amor Domini in proximi mente generatur.
units.tr: Ezekiel in chapter 16, verse 12, and this wisest of kings seem likewise to allude to this custom, where he brings in the angels exhorting the Jews that, coming out of the shadows of the Law, they should behold Christ, foreshadowed in the Law, to be surrounded on every side with living stones, from whom he has made the Church his joyful wife. This crown of the faithful is said to be Christ crowned with the care of a mother, that is, with the care of those who have yielded obedience to the will and nod of God in the care of souls. For as blessed Gregory says in homily 3 on the Gospel: "He who is the sister and brother of Christ by believing becomes a mother by preaching. For he, as it were, gives birth to the Lord, whom he has poured into the heart of the hearer; and he becomes his mother by preaching, if through his voice the love of the Lord is begotten in the mind of his neighbour."

units.la: CAPUT QUARTUM.
units.tr: CHAPTER IV.

units.la: Sponsus adveniens sponsam alloquitur.
units.tr: The bridegroom, coming, addresses the bride.

units.la: 1. QUàm pulchra es amica mea, quàm pulchra es! Oculi tui columbarum, absque eo quod intrinsecùs latet. Capilli tui sicut greges caprarum, quæ ascenderunt de monte Galaad.
units.tr: 1. How beautiful you are, my love, how beautiful you are! Your eyes are doves', apart from what lies hidden within. Your hair is like a flock of goats that have come up from Mount Gilead.

units.la: 2. Dentes tui sicut greges tonsarum, quæ ascenderunt de lavacro, omnes gemellis fœtibus, & sterilis non est inter eas.
units.tr: 2. Your teeth are like a flock of shorn sheep that have come up from the washing, all bearing twins, and none is barren among them.

units.la: 3. Sicut vitta coccinea labia tua, & eloquium tuum dulce. Sicut fragmen mali punici, ita genæ tuæ, absque eo quod intrinsecùs latet.
units.tr: 3. Your lips are like a scarlet thread, and your speech is sweet. Your cheeks are like a piece of pomegranate, apart from what lies hidden within.

units.la: 4. Sicut turris David collum tuum, quæ ædificata est cum propugnaculis: mille clypei pendent ex ea, omnis armatura fortium.
units.tr: 4. Your neck is like the tower of David, built with bulwarks: a thousand shields hang from it, all the armour of the brave.

units.la: 5. Duo ubera tua sicut duo hinnuli capreæ gemelli, qui pascuntur in liliis.
units.tr: 5. Your two breasts are like two young roes, twins of a gazelle, that feed among the lilies.

units.la: 6. Donec aspiret dies & inclinentur umbræ, vadam ad montem myrrhæ & ad collem thuris.
units.tr: 6. Until the day breathes and the shadows decline, I will go to the mountain of myrrh and the hill of frankincense.

units.la: 7. Tota pulchra es amica mea, & macula non est in te.
units.tr: 7. You are wholly beautiful, my love, and there is no blemish in you.

units.la: 8. Veni de Libano sponsa mea, veni de Libano, veni: coronaberis de capite Amana, de vertice Sanir & Hermon, de cubilibus leonum, de montibus pardorum.
units.tr: 8. Come from Lebanon, my bride, come from Lebanon, come: you shall be crowned from the top of Amana, from the summit of Senir and Hermon, from the dens of lions, from the mountains of leopards.

units.la: 9. Vulnerasti cor meum soror mea sponsa, vulnerasti cor meum in uno oculorum tuorum, & in uno crine colli tui.
units.tr: 9. You have ravished my heart, my sister, my bride; you have ravished my heart with one of your eyes, and with one lock of your neck.

units.la: 10. Quàm pulchræ sunt mammæ tuæ soror mea sponsa! Pulchriora sunt ubera tua vino, & odor unguentorum tuorum super omnia aromata.
units.tr: 10. How beautiful are your breasts, my sister, my bride! Your breasts are better than wine, and the scent of your ointments surpasses all spices.

units.la: 11. Favus distillans labia tua sponsa, mel & lac sub lingua tua : & odor vestimentorum tuorum sicut odor thuris.
units.tr: 11. Your lips drip honeycomb, bride; honey and milk are under your tongue, and the scent of your garments is like the scent of incense.

units.la: 12. Hortus conclusus, soror mea sponsa, hortus conclusus, fons signatus.
units.tr: 12. A garden enclosed is my sister, my bride, a garden enclosed, a sealed fountain.

units.la: 13. Emissiones tuæ paradisus malorum punicorum cum pomorum fructibus : cypri cum nardo.
units.tr: 13. Your shoots are a paradise of pomegranates with the fruit of apple trees: cypress with nard.

units.la: 14. Nardus & crocus, fistula & cinnamomum cum universis lignis Libani, myrrha & aloë cum omnibus primis unguentis.
units.tr: 14. Nard and saffron, calamus and cinnamon, with all the trees of Lebanon, myrrh and aloes, with all the finest ointments.

units.la: 15. Fons hortorum, puteus aquarum viventium, quæ fluunt impetu de Libano.
units.tr: 15. A fountain of gardens, a well of living waters, which flow with force from Lebanon.

units.la: EXPLIC- ATIO.
units.tr: EXPLANATION.

units.la: I. QUàm pulchra es, &c, Quatenus sponso placet sponsa, seu Christo Ecclesia, sic ille omnia & singula laudat ejus bona.
units.tr: I. How beautiful you are, etc. Inasmuch as the bride pleases the bridegroom, that is, the Church pleases Christ, he praises each and every one of her good qualities.

units.la: Oculi tui columbarum. Vide quæ diximus supra cap. I. verf. 15.
units.tr: Your eyes are doves'. See what we said above, chap. I, verse 15.

units.la: Absque eo, quod intrinsecus latet. Sensum per paraphrasin reddit Vulgatus interpres, non verba, quæ Hebraicè sonant ex sententia Rabbinorum Jarchi & Jonæ, intra vittam seu velum. Has itaque sponsi voces sic intellexit Vulgatus interpres, ac si diceret Iponsus : Omitto eximium illud gratiæ, quod in ipsis oculis latenter emicat intra velum, quo operta facie incedis. Verè autem dicitur de Ecclesia Christi sponsa dum laudatur, plus esse id quod intrinsecus latet soli Deo notum, quàm quod extrinsecus hominum oculis apparet. In eundem sensum cum Vulgata versione incidunt versiones Græcæ, extra silentium tuum seu taciturnitatem tuam.
units.tr: Apart from what lies hidden within. The Vulgate translator renders the sense by paraphrase rather than the words; the Hebrew words, according to the rabbis Jarchi and Jonah, mean within the band or veil. The Vulgate translator therefore understood these words of the bridegroom as if he said: "I pass over that outstanding grace which shines hidden within the veil with which you go about with your face covered." And it is truly said of the bride of Christ, the Church, when she is praised, that what lies hidden within, known to God alone, is greater than what appears outwardly to the eyes of men. The Greek versions agree with the Vulgate in this sense: beyond your silence, or your taciturnity.

units.la: Capilli tui sicut greges caprarum. Sponsæ capilli non capris in genere, sed caprarum pilis assimilantur. Valdè autem frequens est in Scriptura, cùm de capris agitur, ellipsis vocis pili, ut videre est in textu Hebræo Exod. 25. v. 4. 26. v. 7. 35. v. 26. quibus in locis Vulgatus interpres vocem pili Hebraicè subauditam sua in versione expressit. Caprini autem in Oriente pili humanis non sunt prorsus absimiles, unde est quòd in Apuleii Asino aureo lib. 3. Photis, cùm non potuisset Bœorii juvenis capillos apud tonsorem surripere, prout à domina jussa fuerat, quia tonsor prohibuerat id scelus: Cum tristis, inquit, inde discederem, ne prorsus vacuis manibus, conspicio quendam forficulis tondentem caprinos utres; quos cum probè constrictos, inflatosque, & jam pendentes cernerem, capillos eorum humi jacentes, flavos, ac per hoc illi Boeotio juveni consimiles, aufero, eosque dominæ meæ dissimulatâ veritate, trado. Tale est quod Ælianus hist. lib. 15. cap. 30. ex Callisthene Olynthio refert, in Lycia capras esse hirsutissimas, & egregiis villis, ita ut ab iis cincinni, & quasi quidam comarum cirri dependere videantur. Proinde galericuli ex hœdina pelle confecti ad dissimulandam calvitiem ita meminit Martialis lib. 12. Epigram. 45.
units.tr: Your hair is like a flock of goats. The bride's hair is compared not to goats in general but to the hair of goats. In Scripture, when goats are spoken of, the word hair is very often understood though not stated, as can be seen in the Hebrew text of Exod. 25. v. 4, 26. v. 7, 35. v. 26; in these places the Vulgate translator has expressed in his version the word hair, which is understood in Hebrew. Goats' hair in the East is by no means unlike human hair, and so in Apuleius' Golden Ass, book 3, when Photis, the young man from Boeotia, could not steal the hair at the barber's shop as her mistress had ordered, because the barber had forbidden that crime, the narrator says: "As I was leaving there sad, lest I should go away with my hands entirely empty, I saw a man cutting goatskin bags with small shears; when I saw them tightly tied, swollen, and now hanging, I took the hair lying on the ground, yellow, and therefore like that Boeotian youth, and handed it to my mistress, concealing the truth." Similar is what Aelian reports in his Historia, book 15, chap. 30, from Callisthenes of Olynthus: "In Lycia the goats are very shaggy, with splendid fleeces, so that curls and, as it were, locks of hair seem to hang from them." Accordingly Martial, book 12, epigram 45, also mentions small caps made of kidskin used to hide baldness:

units.la: Hœdinâ tibi pelle contegentiNudæ tempora verticesque calvæ.
units.tr: Covering your temples and bald crown, which were bare, with kidskin.

units.la: Et Rebecca hœdinis pellibus texit Jacobi collum & manus Gen. 27. v. 16. ut haberetur pro fratre Esaü, qui hirsutus erat toto corpore. Sic & Michol 1 Sam. seu Reg. 19 v. 13. viri sui caesariem quomodocunque imitari conata est mollioribus illis & tenuioribus caprarum pilis, quos posuit ad caput statuæ à se pro viro suo Davide elapso in lecto positæ. Nihil autem mirum quòd Michol in promtu habuerit hujusmodi caprarum villos, cùm illorum temporum matronæ inter cetera nere discerent pilos caprarum, ut patet ex Exodo cap. 35. v. 25. & 26. Merito itaque B. Greg. Nyssen. Hom. 15. in Cantic. pilos in presenti sacri Dramatis loco, quo de agimus, in capra respici animadvertit, Caprinum, inquit, animal ad capillorum laudationem ideò fortasse sumtum est, quòd hujus natura idoneè ad pilorum laudationem comparata sit: ita ut ornamenti, quod in capillis situm est, imago quædam sit hoc animal, cùm densis pilis sit naturaliter hirsutum.
units.tr: And Rebecca covered the neck and hands of Jacob with kidskins, Gen. 27. v. 16, so that he might be taken for Esau his brother, who was hairy over his whole body. So too Michal, 1 Sam. or 1 Kings 19 v. 13, tried in some way to imitate the hair of her husband with the softer and finer hair of goats, which she placed at the head of a statue that she had laid in bed in place of her husband David, who had escaped. Nor is it surprising that Michal had such goat-hair ready to hand, since the matrons of those times learned among other things to spin goats' hair, as is clear from Exodus chap. 35, v. 25 and 26. Rightly, then, St Gregory of Nyssa, in Homily 15 on the Song of Songs, observes that in the present passage of this sacred drama, which we are discussing, the hair of the goat is regarded: "The goat," he says, "was perhaps chosen for the praise of hair because its nature is well suited to the praise of hair, so that the animal is a certain image of the adornment that lies in the hair, since it is naturally shaggy with thick hair."

units.la: Quæ ascenderunt de monte Galaad. Hanc versionem præter Græcos, & Syrum & Vulgatum interpretem, Arabica insuper & Chaldaica lingua confirmant. Neque vero frustrà dicuntur sponsæ capilli similes esse caprarum villis, cùm ascendunt, non cùm descendunt, quia caprae cùm ascendunt, longiores illi villi sunt in naturali situ; at cùm descendunt, iidem reflectuntur, & invertuntur, quod minùs decorum est. Unum est, quod possit opponi, nimirùm, id non quadrare, ut caprae dicantur ascendere è monte Galaad; etenim, ut ait Aponius hic hærens lib. 6. in Cantic. De monte descendere dicitur, & in montem ascendere. Sed duo sunt, quæ respondeam; primò etiam de monte ascendi, nempe è monte inferiore ad alterum superiorem, vel ex ejusdem montis partibus inferioribus ad alias superiores. Sic qui ex Alpium, Pyrenaeorúmve media parte ad cacumen enititur, dici potest è monte ascendere. Itaque ut verum fit, quod à Brocardo asseritur, montem Galaad vicinorum omnium esse altissimum, & ut reliquorum caput ob sui eminentiam, tamen ex illo monte capras ascendere dixeris, cùm illius partem emensæ nituntur ad fastigium. Secundò potest hîc esse verborum trajectio, ita ut illa intelligas quasi hoc ordine sita sint, Capilli tui sicut greges caprarum de monte Galaad, quæ ascenderunt, nempe, ad illum montem. Hujus trajectionis exempla non infrequentia sunt in Scripturis sacris, ut Psal. 67. v. 25. Ut intingatur pes tuus in sanguine, lingua canum tuorum ex inimicis, ordo est, ut intingatur pes tuus in sanguine ex inimicis & lingua canum tuorum. Et recte dicitur caprarum de monte Galaad, quia regio fuit pascuis abundans, unde Galaad dicitur Num. 22. v. 1. Apta animalibus alendis terra. Et Mich. 7. v. 14. Pascentur Basan & Galaad juxta dies antiquos. Et Jerem. 50. v. 19. Pascetur Carmelum & Basan, & in monte Ephraim & Galaad saturabitur anima ejus. Quin ut terra Basan ovibus, ita terra Galaad est capris aptior; quia montosa & sylvosa est. Dioscorides lib. 2. in capite de lacte, capras pasci dicit, quercu, lentisco, oleâ, & terebintho; ejusmodi arboribus scatent montana Galaad. Resiniferas saltem arbores, quales sunt lentiscus, & terebinthus, in his locis non defuisse docent sacri Scriptores, qui resinæ de terra Galaad non semel meminerunt. Vide Gen. 38. v. 25. & Jerem. 8. v. 22. & 46. v. 11. Præclarè autem hæc à sponso facta capillorum sponsæ commendatio quadrat in Ecclesiam Christi sponsam; ut enim ait B. Theodoretus: Capilli ea quodam modo significant, quæ sponsæ haud ita sunt necessaria, quæque ad corpus pertinent; vitâ enim ac sensibus capilli carent: quasi dicat: In negotiis etiam humanis, in quibus non possumus, non implicari, te laudabiliter, decoréque geris, caprarum gregi videris, similis, qui pascitur in Galaad, & propter altitudinem insignis.
units.tr: Which have come up from Mount Gilead. The Greeks, and the Syriac and Vulgate translators, confirm this version, and so do the Arabic and Chaldee languages. Nor is it in vain that the bride's hair is said to be like the fleece of goats as they climb, not as they descend, because when goats climb their fleece lies in its natural position and is longer, but when they descend the same fleece is turned back and inverted, which is less becoming. One objection might be raised, namely that it does not fit that goats are said to ascend from Mount Gilead; for, as Aponius, who here sticks to the text, says in book 6 on the Song of Songs: "One is said to descend from a mountain and to ascend to a mountain." But I have two answers. First, one can also ascend from a mountain, namely from a lower mountain to a higher one, or from the lower parts of the same mountain to higher parts. So one who strives from the middle part of the Alps or the Pyrenees to the peak can be said to ascend from the mountain. Thus, even if it is true, as Brocardus asserts, that Mount Gilead is the highest of all the neighbouring mountains and, because of its eminence, the head of the rest, you may still say that goats ascend from that mountain, since they climb through part of it to its summit. Second, there may be a transposition of words here, so that you understand them as if they stood in this order: "Your hair is like a flock of goats from Mount Gilead, which have come up," namely, to that mountain. Examples of such transposition are not rare in the sacred Scriptures, such as Psalm 67, v. 25: "That your foot may be dipped in blood, the tongue of your dogs from your enemies," the order being: "that your foot may be dipped in blood from your enemies and the tongue of your dogs." And it is rightly said "of the goats of Mount Gilead", because that region was abundant in pasture; hence Gilead is called in Num. 22. v. 1 "a land fit for feeding animals". And Mic. 7. v. 14: "Let Bashan and Gilead be fed as in the days of old." And Jer. 50. v. 19: "Carmel and Bashan shall feed, and on the mount of Ephraim and Gilead his soul shall be satisfied." Indeed, as the land of Bashan is more suited to sheep, so the land of Gilead is more suited to goats, because it is mountainous and wooded. Dioscorides, book 2, in the chapter on milk, says that goats are fed on oak, mastic, olive and terebinth; such trees abound in the mountains of Gilead. The sacred writers show that resin-bearing trees, such as the mastic and the terebinth, were not lacking in these places, since they mention resin from the land of Gilead more than once; see Gen. 38. v. 25, Jer. 8. v. 22 and 46. v. 11. This commendation of the bride's hair, made by the bridegroom, fits the Church, the bride of Christ, very well. As St Theodoret says: "Hair in a certain way signifies those things which are not so necessary for the bride and which pertain to the body; for hair lacks life and sensation. It is as if he said: 'Even in human affairs, in which we cannot avoid being entangled, you conduct yourself laudably and becomingly; you seem like a flock of goats that feeds in Gilead and is remarkable for its height.'"

units.la: 2. Dentes tui, Scilicet albi, æquales, & inter se coaptati. Sicut grex tonsarum. Heb. succisarum seu dedolatarum. Q. d. Dentes tui candore, proportione & symmetriâ non sunt absimiles gregi ovium tam similium, quàm si ex ligno aut ære ad eundem typum effictæ fuissent & succisæ, seu fabrefactæ. Hinc Pagninus optimè vertit ex textu Hebræo, Dentes tui ut grex ovium æqualium. Porro in dentibus maximè laudatur munditiēs seu candor & proportio. Hinc in Imaginibus Lucianus: At subridendo, Polystrate, dentes ostendebat. Quomodo dixerim tibi quàm albos, quàm æquales, & inter se coaptatos? Sicubi monile pulcherrimum vidisti ex nitidissimis, & magnitudine paribus margaritis: adeò concinnâ serie erant nati.
units.tr: 2. Your teeth: that is, white, even, and fitted closely together. Like a flock of shorn sheep. The Hebrew has shorn or trimmed. The sense is: your teeth, in their whiteness, proportion and symmetry, are not unlike a flock of sheep so alike that they might have been carved from wood or cast in bronze to one pattern, then shorn or shaped. Hence Pagninus translates the Hebrew well: Your teeth are like a flock of even sheep. Moreover, in teeth, cleanness or whiteness and proportion are especially praised. Hence Lucian in the Images: But when he smiled, Polystratus, he showed his teeth. How can I tell you how white they were, how even, and how well fitted together? If you have ever seen a most beautiful necklace of the purest pearls, equal in size, they were arranged in such an elegant row.

units.la: Quæ ascenderunt de lavacro. Comparat sponsus sponsæ suæ dentes eleganti symmetriâ inter se coaptatos non modò gregi ovium staturâ & mensurâ æqualium, ac si unaquæque cæsa suisset ad instar sociæ suæ, ut loquitur Aben-Ezra, verùm etiam eosdem dentes ratione nitoris & candoris omnis immunditiæ expertes assimilat earundem ovium gregi recens lauto.
units.tr: Which have come up from the washing. The bridegroom compares the bride's teeth, fitted together in an elegant symmetry, not only to a flock of sheep equal in height and size, as if each had been cut to be like its companion, as Aben Ezra puts it, but also, in their brightness and whiteness, free of all dirt, to a flock of the same sheep freshly washed.

units.la: Omnes gemellis fœtibus, &c. Quasi diceret, dentes tui, ô pulcherrima sponsa, omnis immunditiæ expertes tam æquales sunt, æqualiterque perutiles, ut eos intuens intueri mihi videor gregem ovium tam perfectè inter se æqualium, & æqualiter perutilium, ac si æqualiter juissent succisæ, ut loquitur in Lexico Kimchius. Extare oves gemelliparas expressè testatur Aristoteles Hist. Anim. lib. 6. cap. 19. & qui in Mirabilibus tradit Illyricanas oves non modò esse gemelliparas, sed & biferas, id est, bis in anno parere. Oves gemelliparas Græci Δίκυμα, prisci Romani ambegnas vocant. Fulgentius in libello de prisco Sermone ad Chalcidium cap. 6. Bebius macer, qui Fastos diês scripsit, ait Junonicas, quæ geminos parerent, æves sacrificari cum duobus agnis altrinsecùs alligatis; quas oves ambegnas vocari, quasi ex utraque parte agnos habentes. Hanc ovium fœcunditatem Græci ad Apollinem Nomium referebant. Proinde Callimachus Hymno in Apollinem petit, ut ejus beneficio, quæ unipara erat, gemellipara repente fiat.
units.tr: All bear twins, &c. As if he said: your teeth, O most beautiful bride, free of all dirt, are so even and equally useful that, looking at them, I seem to see a flock of sheep so perfectly equal to one another and equally productive, as if they had been cut to the same measure, as Kimchi says in his Lexicon. That there are twin-bearing ewes Aristotle clearly attests in History of Animals book 6, chapter 19. And the author of the Mirabilia records that Illyrian sheep are not only twin-bearing but bearing twice a year, that is, they lamb twice in a year. The Greeks call twin-bearing sheep dikyma [Δίκυμα], and the early Romans called them ambegnae. Fulgentius, in his little book on the old sermon to Chalcidius, chapter 6: Bebius Macer, who wrote the Fasti, says that ewes were sacrificed to Juno, who bore twins, with two lambs tied on either side; these sheep are called ambegnae, as if they had lambs on both sides. The Greeks referred this fruitfulness of sheep to Apollo Nomius. Accordingly Callimachus, in his Hymn to Apollo, asks that by his favour a ewe that bore one lamb should suddenly bear twins.

units.la: Sterilis non est inter eas. Hebraicè ad verbum, quæ abortiat non est in iis. Quasi diceret, Nulla est in universo illo ovium grege, cui dentes candidulos ex omni parte decoras & perutiles assimilavi, quæ non sit utilissima. Eleganter autem per dentes sponsæ adumbrantur Ecclesiæ Doctores,qui, ut ait S. Greg. Nyss. Hom. 7. in Cantic. in Ecclesia usum dentium in comminuendo dogmatum difficultates exercent; Dum enim, ut loquitur S. Greg. Magnus, sacram Scripturam exponendo minoribus fratribus dilucidant, quasi panem parvulis, tanquam matres filiis commasticant, quo infirmi ad fortia convalescant. Hi deposito veteri homine Jesum Christum induti unitate fidei, spei, charitatis & doctrinæ sic sunt undecunque æquales, ut merito comparentur gregi ovium divinâ quadam arte ad perfectam ex omni parte æqualitatem efformatarum. Nullus horum Doctorum Ecclesiæ inutilis est, cùm omnes pro virili geminam Dei & proximi dilectionem in cordibus fidelium parturiant.
units.tr: There is none barren among them. In the Hebrew, word for word: none that miscarries is among them. As if he said: there is none in that whole flock of sheep, whose teeth I have likened to these, pretty in every part and useful, that is not most useful. Now the bride's teeth elegantly shadow the teachers of the Church, who, as St Gregory of Nyssa says in Homily 7 on the Song, in the Church exercise the use of their teeth in grinding down the difficulties of doctrines; for while, as St Gregory the Great says, they make sacred Scripture clear to the younger brethren by expounding it, they chew it for them as mothers chew bread for their little children, so that the weak may grow strong. These, having put off the old man and put on Jesus Christ, are equal on every side in the unity of faith, hope, love and doctrine, so that they are rightly compared to a flock of sheep shaped by a certain divine art into perfect equality in every part. None of these teachers of the Church is useless, since all of them, each to the best of his power, bring forth the twofold love of God and neighbour in the hearts of the faithful.

units.la: 3. Sicut vitta, &c. Q. d. Labia tua jugi purpurâ flagrant adinstar vittæ coccineæ, sermóque tuus apprimè urbanus ac venustus est. Assimilantur autem labia Ecclesiæ vittæ coccineæ, quia Dominici sanguinis pretium, quo redemta est, prædicare non cessat, hæcque prædicatio omni acceptione digna auditores in ardentissimam Dei dilectionem suaviter, fortiterque simul abripit.
units.tr: 3. Like a thread of scarlet, &c. As if he said: your lips glow with a constant purple like a scarlet thread, and your speech is most courteous and charming. Now the Church's lips are likened to a scarlet thread because she never ceases to proclaim the price of the Lord's blood by which she was redeemed, and this proclamation, worthy of every welcome, sweetly and strongly carries the hearers away into the most burning love of God.

units.la: Sicut fragmen, &c. Sensus est, in genis tuis non minus elucet venustatis, quàm in fragmine mali punici, quod rubentium granorum splendore mirè decoratur. Commendatur autem hic verecundus ille rubor, quo, qui genarum instar in Ecclesiæ facie manifesti apparent, ne iram Dei provocent elati, salubriter de propria infirmitate erubescunt.
units.tr: Like a slice of pomegranate, &c. The sense is: in your cheeks there shines no less beauty than in a slice of pomegranate, which is wonderfully adorned with the brightness of its reddening seeds. Here is commended that modest blush by which those who appear as cheeks on the face of the Church, being proud, blush wholesomely at their own weakness, lest they provoke the anger of God.

units.la: Absque eo quod intrinsecus latet. Vide superius dicta v. 1. Solent amantes à pulchris manifestis membra tecta pulchriora judicare. Sic Apollo apud Ovid. 1. Metam. Daphnidis feminuda ad lacertos brachia videns, latentem illorum partem pulchriorem reputabat.
units.tr: Apart from what lies hidden within. See what was said above at verse 1. Lovers are wont to judge the parts that are covered more beautiful than those that are openly seen. So Apollo in Ovid, Metamorphoses book 1, seeing the bare arms of Daphnis, judged the part hidden from him more beautiful.

units.la: Spectat inornatos collo pendere capillos: Et quid si comantur? ait. Videt igne micantes Sideribus similes oculos, videt oscula quæ non Est vidisse satis. Laudat digitosque, manusque; Brachiaque, & nudos media plus parte lacertos. Siqua latent, meliora putat.
units.tr: He sees her hair hanging unadorned about her neck; and what if it is dressed? he says. He sees eyes gleaming like stars, he sees kisses, which it is not enough to have seen. He praises her fingers and hands, her arms and her bare forearms for more than half their length. Whatever is hidden, he thinks, is more beautiful.

units.la: 4. Sicut turris David &c. Turris David dicitur Templi Jerosolymitani turris; ædificium quippe Templi potiùs est Davidis, qui partis de-hostibus victoriis, effusóque sanguine opes acquisivit; ingenti solertiâ ligna & lapides præparavit, ac tandem Dei manu ac beneficio singulari descriptiones ejus ac leges accepit, & filio cuncta opera exequenda distribuit: quàm ipsius Salomonis, qui jussa paterna executus est.
units.tr: 4. Like the tower of David, &c. The tower of David is called the tower of the Jerusalem Temple. For the building of the Temple is more truly David's, since he gained wealth by victories over enemies and by shedding blood; with immense skill he prepared the timber and stones, and at last by the hand and singular benefit of God he received its plans and laws, and he assigned to his son all the work to be carried out, more than Solomon himself, who carried out his father's commands.

units.la: Collum tuum. Sc. rectum, rotundum, congruenti proportione procerum, & monilibus baccatis circumdatum. Collum Ecclesiæ dicuntur ipsius pastores, quorum præcipuum munus est verbi Dei praedicatio; unde S. Greg. Naz. orat. 1. αὐτῷ τῷ λόγου διανομὴν λέγω τὸ πρῶτον τῆς ἡμετέρας. Ipsam verbi distributionem dico nostrum omnium primum officium. Et Zonaras ad Canonem Apostolicum inter probatos à Græcis 38. ait Χρὴ ἀπαραίτητον πάντῃ ἐπισκόπῳ τὸ διδάσκειν. Docere est officium cuius Episcopo irrecusabile. Unde Synodus vulgò Reiaticina, seu in urbe Regia Ticino congregata anno DCCC. L. sub Leone IV, Ut Episcopi Canonicas Scripturas & sancta dogmata jugi meditatione discutiant, & Presbyteris ac Clericis suis subtilius tractando & differendo, occultos sacrarum literarum thesauros aperiant, populis verò juxta ipsorum capacitatem Dominicis & festis diebus verbum prædicationis impendere non negligant. Quòd si quis se deinceps ab hac observatione, & ab his quæ superius sunt statuta, subtraxerit: tanquam proprii defertor officii divinis legibus subjacebit. Pastores itaque collo designantur, primo quia in corpus Christi mysticum cibum verbi Dei transmittunt. Secundò quia vocem divinæ voluntatis enuntiativam ovibus suis proferunt. Tertiò quia mediatores sunt inter summum Pastorem & Episcopum animarum Jesum, & commissas sibi animas, & quasi Christum caput, cujus Vicarii sunt, corpori suo, id est, Ecclesiæ conjungunt. Hi ergo propter fortitudinem & excelsam cœlestium gaudiorum contemplationem turri assimulantur, quæ turris, ut loquitur B. Greg. Magnus, David esse dicitur, quia David manu fortis interpretatur, per quod Christus significatur, cujus est quicquid forte, & excelsum operantur. Cum propugnaculis turris Davidi ædificata dicitur: quia sancti prædicatores contra adversarios homines, si necesse est, miraculum armantur: Contra autem vitia clypeis se muniunt: quia ne spiritualibus hostibus succumbant, virtutibus se defendunt. In quibus omnis armatura fortium pendet, quia quisquis hostium cuneis fortiter resistere vult, in eis exempla videt, quibus armatus hostes strenue superare valeat. Mille autem hic pro perfectione ponitur, quia in millenario numero omnes numeri persecte complentur. Non possum hic prætermittere Gregorii Nazianzeni monitum pro pastoribus animarum. Nόμον, inquit, Orat. 32. πίθηματι πάσι τ' ψυχῶν εἰκονόμοις, ἢ τὰ λόγια ταμίαις μήτε τῷ σκληρῷ τεχνίῳ, μήτε τῷ ὑπεσταλμένῳ κατεπαίρειν, ἀλλ' ἀλόγως εἶναι ἀεὶ τὸν λόγον, μηδ' ἑτέρῳ τὸ μέτριον ὑπερ-ξαίνοντας. Quæ sic vertit doctissimus Billius. Cunctis animarum dispensatoribus, rectæ doctrinæ arbitris legem statuo, ut nec per duritiam hominum animos exasperent, nec per summissionem elatos & insolentes efficiant; sed prudenter & consulte in fidei causa se gerant, nec in alterutro horum mediocritatem excedant. Synodus Lateranensis quinta sub Leone decimo notat in sessione undecima quòd diversi concionatores officii sui immemores, cùm ipsis incumbat populum ædificare, virtutes inserere, vitia evellere, Deúmque, & non se ipsos prædicare, & Christi gloriam promovere, prædicant tamen in primis ad propriam ostensionem. Secundò errores contra sacram Doctrinam ferunt. Tertiò Scripturas depravant & distorquent ad vanas interpretationes à sanctis Patribus & probata Ecclesiæ intelligentia alienas, aut etiam iisdem prorsus contrarias. Quartò mala propediem eventura vel comminiscuntur, vel ab aliis accepta populo prænunciant ad vanos terrores excitandos: qui mox vertuntur in scandalum & derisum, verbíque Dei contemtum. Quintò conficta miracula enuntiant. Sextò in sacros Pontifices & Ecclesiarum Prælatos audacter & temerè invehuntur. Hos omnes defectus Leo X. approbante Concilio districte prohibet & contravenientes subjicit excommunicationi, cujus absolutio extra periculum mortis uni reservatur Romano Pontifici.
units.tr: Your neck. That is, straight, round, of fitting proportion and length, and encircled with necklaces of pearls. The neck of the Church is said to be her ministers, whose chief office is the preaching of the Word of God. Hence St Gregory Nazianzen, Oration 1: αὐτῷ τῷ λόγου διανομὴν λέγω τὸ πρῶτον τῆς ἡμετέρας [the very distribution of the word I call the first of our duties]. And Zonaras, on the Apostolic Canon 38, which the Greeks accept, says: Χρὴ ἀπαραίτητον πάντῃ ἐπισκόπῳ τὸ διδάσκειν [teaching is a duty that a bishop may by no means refuse]. Hence the synod commonly called Reiaticina, or gathered in the royal city of Ticino in the year 850 under Leo IV: That bishops should examine the canonical Scriptures and holy doctrines by constant meditation, and by treating them more carefully and discussing them with their presbyters and clergy, should open the hidden treasures of the sacred letters; and that they should not neglect to bestow on the people, on Sundays and feast days, the preaching of the Word according to the people's capacity. But if anyone henceforth withdraws himself from this observance and from what has been laid down above, he shall be subject to the divine laws as a deserter of his own office. The ministers, then, are designated by the neck, first because they pass on the food of the Word of God to the mystical body of Christ; second, because they utter to their sheep the voice declaring the divine will; third, because they are mediators between the supreme Shepherd and Bishop of souls, Jesus, and the souls committed to them, and they join Christ, the head, whose vicars they are, to his body, that is, the Church. These therefore are likened to a tower, on account of their strength and their lofty contemplation of heavenly joys; which tower, as St Gregory the Great says, is said to be David's, because David is interpreted as strong of hand, which signifies Christ, whose is whatever strong and lofty thing they do. It is said to be built with bulwarks of David, because the holy preachers arm themselves against hostile men, if need be, with the weapon of miracles; but against vices they fortify themselves with shields, because, lest they succumb to spiritual enemies, they defend themselves by virtues. On these depends all the armour of the brave, because whoever wants to resist strongly the wedges of enemies sees in them examples by which, armed, he may be able to overcome the enemies vigorously. A thousand here stands for perfection, because in the number one thousand all numbers are perfectly completed. I cannot pass over here the warning of Gregory Nazianzen to the shepherds of souls. In Oration 32 he says: νόμον ... [I lay down a rule for all dispensers of souls and stewards of right doctrine: that they should not exasperate men's minds by harshness, nor make the proud and insolent prouder by condescension, but that they should conduct themselves wisely and prudently in the cause of the faith, and not exceed the mean in either direction]. This is translated thus by the most learned Billius: To all dispensers of souls and arbiters of sound doctrine I lay down the rule that they neither exasperate men's minds by harshness, nor make the elated and insolent more so by submissiveness; but that they conduct themselves prudently and deliberately in the cause of the faith, and in neither of these exceed the mean. The Fifth Lateran Council under Leo X notes in its eleventh session that various preachers, forgetful of their office, though it is incumbent on them to edify the people, to plant virtues and root out vices, and to preach God and not themselves, and to promote the glory of Christ, nevertheless preach chiefly for their own display. Secondly, they bring forth errors against sacred doctrine. Thirdly, they corrupt and distort Scripture into vain interpretations alien to the holy Fathers and to the approved understanding of the Church, or even wholly contrary to them. Fourthly, they either invent evils about to happen soon, or announce to the people evils received from others, to stir up empty terrors, which soon turn into scandal and mockery and contempt for the Word of God. Fifthly, they report fabricated miracles. Sixthly, they rashly attack the holy Pontiffs and the prelates of the Churches. Leo X, with the approval of the Council, strictly forbids all these defects and subjects those who transgress to excommunication, the absolution of which, outside danger of death, is reserved to the Roman Pontiff alone.

units.la: Omnis armatura fortium. Quâ nempe hostes devicerant, & praeclara facinora gesserant. Usitatum enim erat Palaeftinis & Phoenicibus arma, quibus hostes devicerant, in locis publicis asservare quasi victoriae trophaea,quae pietatem colentes Deo suo in templis offerebant : sicut de gladio, quo David percusserat Philiftaeum,scriptum legimus 1 Sam.seu Reg.12.& Jos. 15.Antiq. cap. 14. ait : Circum Templum affixa erant spolia barbarica, quae omnia Herodes denuo dedicavit, additis etiam recentibus Arabicis. Quod quidem trophaeum non in Templo, sed in monte fecifle scribitur Saül repulsus à Deo 2 Sam.seu Reg. 15. v. 12.
units.tr: All the armour of the mighty. That is, the arms with which they had conquered their enemies and performed notable exploits. For it was customary among the Palestinians and Phoenicians to keep in public places, as trophies of victory, the weapons with which they had defeated enemies, and those who worshipped their God offered them in the temples. So we read that the sword with which David struck down the Philistine is written of in 1 Sam. or Reg. 12, and Josephus, Antiq. ch. 14, says: Around the Temple were fixed barbarian spoils, all of which Herod dedicated anew, adding also recent Arabian ones. It is written that this trophy was set up not in the Temple but on a mountain, when Saul was rejected by God, 2 Sam. or Reg. 15 v. 12.

units.la: 5. Duo ubera tua, &c. Ut capreae domesticae, ita etiam ferae, capreae putà, rupicaprae, &c. quandoque sunt gemelliparae. Quod etiam de cerva testatur Philosophus Hist. lib. 6. cap.29. Neque frustrà est, quòd sponsæ ubera non cum hinnulis modò, sed & cum geminis hinnulis conferuntur. Nam ut duo ubera sunt simillima, ita similes fere sunt, qui gemini nascuntur. Hinc Plautus in Menaechmorum prologo, Ei nati sunt filii duo gemini, Ita forma simili pueri, uti mater sua Nec internosse posset, quae mammam dabat, Neque adeo mater ipsa, quae illos pepererat.
units.tr: 5. Your two breasts, etc. As domestic goats, so also wild ones, such as wild goats and rock goats, are sometimes twin-bearing. The Philosopher also testifies this of the doe, Hist. book 6 ch. 29. It is not without reason that the bride's breasts are compared not only with young deer but with twin young deer. For as two breasts are very alike, so those born as twins are nearly alike. Hence Plautus in the prologue to the Menaechmi: He had two sons, twins, so alike in form that the mother herself, who gave the breast, could not tell them apart, nor even the mother who had borne them.

units.la: Et Cyclops Galateae metamorphofeos lib. 13. fab. 8. Inveni geminos, qui tecum ludere possint, Interse similes, vix ut dignoscere possis. Villosae catulos in summis montibus ursae.
units.tr: And the Cyclops in Ovid's Metamorphoses book 13, fable 8: I have found twins who can play with you, so alike that you can scarcely tell them apart. Cubs of a shaggy bear on the high mountains.

units.la: Proinde dixit Homerus Iliad. Π'. ut refert Plutarchus in consolatione ad Apollonium, Somno & morti geminis, ita eorum similitudinem quasi ob oculos ponens. Nam in iis, quae gemina sunt, maximè se prodit similitudo. Itaque Latinè geminum & gemellum pro simili recte dixeris, ita enim veteres passim usurpant. Pacuvius in Hermiona apud Nonnium, Par fortitudo, gemina confidentia.
units.tr: Accordingly Homer, Iliad Π', as Plutarch reports in his Consolation to Apollonius, says of Sleep and Death as twins, setting their likeness before the eyes: For in things that are twins, likeness shows itself most of all. So in Latin one may rightly say geminum and gemellum for similar, for the ancients use them everywhere. Pacuvius in Hermiona, quoted by Nonnius: Equal courage, twin confidence.

units.la: Catullus in Mamurram & Caesarem. Morbosi pariter, gemelli utrique.
units.tr: Catullus, on Mamurra and Caesar: Equally diseased, both of them twins.

units.la: Horatius Sat. 3. lib. 2. ——par nobile fratrum Nequitiâ, & nugis, pravorum & amore gemellum.
units.tr: Horace, Satires book 2, ch. 3: —a noble pair of brothers, twins in wickedness and in trifles, and in their love of the depraved.

units.la: Et lib. 1. Epist. 10. ——hac in re scilicet una Multùm dissimiles, ad cetera pene gemelli.
units.tr: And Epistles book 1, ch. 10: —very unlike in this one respect, yet almost twins in everything else.

units.la: Cicero partit. Oratoriarum secst 32. Memoriam: quae est gemina literaturae quodammodo, & in dissimili genere persimilis. Et in Orat. pro Sexto Roscio, Par est avaritia, eadem impudentia, gemina audacia. Et pro quinto Roscio fere in fine, Simillima & maxime gemina societas hereditatis. Et Verrina tertia ad Epistolam Timarchidis, Gemino & simillimo nequitia, improbitate, audacia. Et in Pisonem, Illud vero geminum consilium Catilinae & Lentuli. In quibus locis qui pro gemina & geminum, volunt germana & germanum rescribi, toto coelo aberrant, ut jam ab aliis est observatum. Patet igitur sponsae mammae quorsum cum geminis hinnulis conferantur; nempe quia non nisi geminae protuberant, unde in Frivolaria a Plauto nominantur fororiantes; & tam sunt inter se similes, quam esse solent hinnuli duo gemini. Quanquam, ut dicam quod res est, non tota ubera, sed papillas solum cum hinnulis conferri putem. Neque enim hinnulis absolute comparantur ubera, sed hinnulis duobus geminis, qui pascuntur inter lilia. Nempe in rustico Dramate a rebus quae ruri sunt, similitudines sumi oportuit, & in his areolae aut agri partes liliis consitae mammas virginum utcunque exprimunt, candore scilicet, & tumore suo. Lilium enim his duobus a Plinio commendatur, quod candor ejus eximius est, nec ulli florum excelsitas major; unde Poëta.
units.tr: Cicero, Partitiones Oratoriae, section 32: Memory, which is in a way twin to literature, and in a different kind very similar. And in the speech for Sextus Roscius: Avarice is equal, impudence the same, audacity twin. And near the end of the speech for Roscius: A most similar and most twin partnership of inheritance. And in the third Verrine, on the letter of Timarchides: Twin and most similar wickedness, dishonesty, audacity. And against Piso: That twin plan of Catiline and Lentulus. In these passages, those who want germana and germanum written in place of gemina and geminum are wholly mistaken, as others have already observed. It is clear, then, why the bride's breasts are compared with twin young deer: namely, because only twins protrude in pairs, whence Plautus in the Frivolaria calls them fororiantes; and they are as alike to each other as two twin young deer usually are. Yet, to say what is the case, I think that not the whole breasts but only the nipples are compared with the young deer. For breasts are not compared absolutely with young deer, but with two twin young deer that feed among lilies. Indeed, in a rustic drama the comparisons must be drawn from rural things, and in these, beds or portions of fields planted with lilies somehow express the breasts of maidens, namely by their whiteness and their swelling. For the lily is commended by Pliny for these two qualities: its whiteness is outstanding, and no flower is taller. Whence the poet:

units.la: Et grandia lilia quassans.
units.tr: And shaking the tall lilies.

units.la: Et candoris quidem ratione ex Junonis lacte fingitur ortum. Atque ut hic candor uberum candorem refert, ita cum in horti areola, aut in agri portione aliquot numero lilia supra planum solum eminent, mammas imitari videntur, quae pari ratione supra pectus assurgunt & protuberant. Rursus in illis liliis si pascantur rufi hinnuli duo gemini, & prorsus similes, eminus aspicientibus tanquam papillae in uberibus apparebunt. Neque novum videri debet, quod vel hic hinnuli, vel supra cap. 2. v. 16. & infra cap. 6. v. 3. greges pascuntur inter lilia; cum in Judaea & Syria liiia non colantur in hortis, ut apud nos, sed in agris passim occurrant. Unde Mat. 6. v. 28. a Christo vocantur lilia agri, seu, ut habet Syra versio, (quo idiomate Christus inter Judaeos concionabatur) lilia deserti, id est, quae sponte proveniunt, etiam in desertis locis, & a nullo excultis. Hinc Calphurnius in Litigio, Eclog. 6.
units.tr: And indeed, from the reason of its whiteness, the lily is fabled to have arisen from Juno's milk. And as this whiteness recalls the whiteness of breasts, so when some lilies stand above the level ground in a garden bed or a portion of a field, they seem to imitate breasts, which in like manner rise and protrude above the chest. Again, if two twin reddish young deer, quite alike, feed among those lilies, they will appear from a distance like nipples on breasts. Nor should it seem strange that here, or above in ch. 2 v. 16, and below in ch. 6 v. 3, flocks feed among lilies; for in Judaea and Syria lilies are not cultivated in gardens as they are with us, but occur everywhere in the fields. Hence in Matt. 6 v. 28 they are called by Christ "lilies of the field", or, as the Syriac version has it (the language in which Christ preached among the Jews), "lilies of the desert", that is, those which grow of their own accord, even in deserted places, and are tended by no one. Hence Calpurnius in the Litigium, Eclogue 6.

units.la: En! aspicis illum,
units.tr: Look! Do you see him,

units.la: Candida, qui medius cubat inter lilia cervum?
units.tr: O fair one, who lies in the midst of the lilies, the stag?

units.la: Jam per duo sponsae ubera putamus designari duas Decalogi tabulas, quae sunt duo Ecclesiae ubera coaptata duobus suavissimis hinnulis capreae gemellis, id est, duobus charitatis praeceptis consimilibus, ad quae praecepta Decalogi referuntur; pascuntur in liliis, donec aspiret dies & inclinentur umbrae, dum magis ac magis ad charitatis fervorem accenduntur fideles sanctorum exemplis, & doctrinis, donec absorbeatur, quod mortale est, seu usque ad consummationem seculi.
units.tr: Now through the two breasts of the bride we think are signified the two tables of the Decalogue, which are the two breasts of the Church, fitted to two most sweet fawns of a roe, that is, to two like precepts of charity, to which the precepts of the Decalogue are referred. They feed among the lilies until the day breathes and the shadows lean, while the faithful are kindled more and more to the fervour of charity by the examples and teachings of the saints, until what is mortal is swallowed up, that is, until the consummation of the age.

units.la: 6. Donec aspiret dies & inclinentur umbrae. Id est, donec diescat, & noctis tenebrae recedant. Hoc autem plerique Interpretes referunt ad versum praecedentem, ad haec scilicet verba, qui pascuntur, etsi non desint qui id referant ad verbum mox sequens, vadam.
units.tr: 6. Until the day breathes and the shadows lean. That is, until it grows light and the darkness of night recedes. Most interpreters refer this to the preceding verse, namely to these words, who feed, although there are not lacking those who refer it to the word immediately following, I will go.

units.la: Vadam ad montem myrrhae, & ad collem thuris. Per montem myrrhae, & collem thuris, videntur significari montes aromatum, qui infra cap. 8. v. 14. hinnulis pro statione assignantur; hi autem Judaeae montes hodie nobis sunt ignoti. Eleganter vero sponsa designatur per loca pascua hinnulorum, cujus duo ubera hinnulis assimilantur. Atque ita promittit sponsus se jamjam ad dilectissimam sibi sponsam venturum, ipsique indivulse & indissolubiliter adhaesurum. Haec optime quadrant in Christum spondentem se jamjam impleturum magnum Incarnationis sacramentum, ut ipse & Ecclesia sibi olim desponsata jam sint duo in carne una, imo jam essent esse duo, sed fiant caro una in aeternum.
units.tr: I will go to the mountain of myrrh, and to the hill of frankincense. By the mountain of myrrh and the hill of frankincense seem to be meant the mountains of spices, which below (ch. 8, v. 14) are assigned to the young harts as their pasture. These mountains of Judea are now unknown to us. The bride is elegantly portrayed by the pastures of the harts, whose two breasts are compared to young harts. The bridegroom thus promises that he will soon come to his most beloved bride and cleave to her inseparably and indissolubly. These words fit Christ excellently, as he promises that he will soon fulfil the great sacrament of the Incarnation, so that he and the Church, once betrothed to him, may be two in one flesh. Indeed they already are two, but they will become one flesh forever.

units.la: 7. Tota pulchra es, &c. Pergit sponsus laudare sponsam, & eximium in ea commendat decorem sine macula & sine ruga fulgentem. Hoc non de Ecclesia duntaxat triumphante, sed & de militante intelligi potest, quantum ad professionem sanctitatis & fidei, ut loquitur doctissimus Eftius. Nihil enim in fide falsum, nihil in moribus pravum, Ecclesia praescribit, sed omnia pura, sancta, incoinquinata, macula & ruga carentia, nec quidquam tale invenitur apud quascunque sectas. Non desunt inter SS. PP. qui putant militantem Ecclesiam totam denominari pulchram a parte, quia scilicet in ea sunt multi perfecti, qui immaculati dicuntur, utpote qui sunt sine macula peccati mortalis; ut enim praeclare Aug. Serm. 3. de Verbis Apostoli, non quia non possumus hic esse sine peccato, homicidia facere debemus, aut adulteria, vel cetera mortifera peccata, quae uno ictu perimunt. Talia non facit bonae fidei & bonae spei Christianus, sed illa sola, quae quotidiano orationis penicillo tergantur. Hinc quod statuit Nicaena Synodus prima oecumenica Can. 2. excludendum de Clero (qui ceteris fidelibus praelucere debet verbo & opere) eum, qui duobus aut tribus testibus fit convictus reus ψυχικὸς ἁμαρτήματος, id est, peccati animalis, haud improbabiliter Theodorus Balsamon Antiochenus Patriarcha intelligit de quacunque culpa incompatibili cum divina gratia. Balsamoni favere videntur haec B. Hier. verba in c.
units.tr: 7. You are wholly fair, etc. The bridegroom goes on to praise the bride, and commends in her an outstanding beauty shining without spot or wrinkle. This can be understood not only of the Church triumphant but also of the Church militant, as regards the profession of holiness and faith, as the most learned Estius says: For the Church prescribes nothing false in faith and nothing depraved in morals, but all things pure, holy, undefiled, free from spot and wrinkle; and nothing of the kind is found among any sects whatever. Among the holy Fathers there are not lacking those who think that the Church militant is called wholly fair in part, because in it there are many perfect people, who are called unblemished, inasmuch as they are without the spot of mortal sin. For as Augustine splendidly says in Sermon 3 on the Words of the Apostle: Although we cannot be here without sin, we ought not to commit murders, or adulteries, or other deadly sins which kill with a single blow. A Christian of good faith and good hope does not commit such things, but only those which are wiped away by the daily brush of prayer. Hence, the first ecumenical Synod of Nicaea, in canon 2, decreed that a member of the clergy (who ought to shine before the other faithful in word and deed) who is convicted by two or three witnesses of being guilty of psychikos hamartematos [ψυχικὸς ἁμαρτήματος], that is, animal sin, is to be excluded. Theodore Balsamon, patriarch of Antioch, not improbably understands this as any fault incompatible with divine grace. These words of St Jerome on Titus 1 seem to favour Balsamon's view.

units.la: 1. Ep. ad Titum : Sine crimine jubetur esse Episcopus, quod puto uto alio verbo irreprehensibilem nominatum. Non quod eo tanpùm tempore, quo ordinandus est, sine ullo sit crimine, & præteritas maculas nova conversatione diluerit : sed quòd ex eo tempore, quo in Christo renatus est, nullâ peccati conscientiâ remordeatur. Quomodo enim potest præses Ecclesiæ auferre malum de medio ejus, qui in-delicto simili corruit ? Aut quâ libertate corripere peccantem potest, cùm tacitus sibi ipse respondeat eadem admisisse, quæ corripit ? Sic & B. Isidorus lib. 2. de Officiis Ecclesiasticis cap. 5. Quod, inquit, is qui post baptismum aliquo mortali peccato corruptus ad Sacerdotium non promoveatur, Lex ipsa testatur. Moyses enim in Lege præcepit Sacerdotibus ne aliquod pecus vitiatum ad aram Deo offerant; Unde & in Numeris vitula rufa, cujus cinis expiatio est populi, non aliter jubetur offerri ad altare Domini, nisi quæ terrena opera non fecerit, jugúmque delicti non traxerit, nec vinculis peccatorum fuerit alligata. Sed quid plura objiciamus? Si enim is qui in Episcopatu mortale aliquod peccatum admiserit, non debet offerre panes Domino, quanto magis ante Ordinationem peccator inventus, repudiari debet ut non ordinetur ? Idipsum testatur S. Greg. Magnus, plurimis, iisque luculentissimis epistolarum suarum locis lib. 3. Ep. 26. Pervenit ad nos quosdam de sacris Ordinibus lapsos vel post pœnitentiam, vel ante, ad Officii sui ministerium revocari : quod omninò prohibemus, & in hac re sacratissimi quoque Canones contradicunt. Et lib. 4. Ep. 17. Si lapsis ad suum Ordinem licentia concedatur, vigor Canonicæ procul dubio frangitur disciplinæ, dum pro reversionis spe, pravæ actionis desideria quis concipere non formidat. Et. lib. 6. Ep. 39. criminaliter abscedentem, in locum de quo lapsus est, nulla permittit ratio revocari. S. Martinus primus in epistola ad Amandum Trajectensem Episcopum de Presbyteris & Diaconis lapsis post ordinationes suas ait : Nullatenus in hujusmodi peccato delinquentibus ad destructionem Canonum compassionem exhibeas. Nam quì semel post Ordinationem suam in lapsum cecidesit, jam depositus erit, nullùmque gradum Sacerdotii poterit adipisci : Sed sufficiat ei lamentationibus, fletibúsque assiduis quonisque advixerit, in eadem pœnitentia addurare, ut commissum delictum Divinâ gratiâ extinguere valeat. Si enim tales quærimus ad sacros Ordines promovendos, quibus nulla ruga, nullumque vitæ contagium præpediat; quanto magis si post Ordinationem suam, quispiam in lapsum ceciderit, & prævaricationis peccato deprehendatur obnoxius, omninò prohibendus est cum manibus lutulentis atque pollutis Mysterium nostræ salutis tractare ? Sitque hujusmodi semper juxta sacrorum Canonum instituta in hac vita depositus; at ab illo qui, mentis interiora scrutatur, nullùmque de ovibus errare congaudet, dum aspexerit sinceraм pœnitentiam ejus, in terribili terribili iudicio habeat reconciliatum, id est, reconciliationem. Concilium Valentinum in Gallia sub S. Damaso Papa Can. 4. Statuit, Quicunque sub Ordinatione vel Diaconatus, vel Presbyterii, vel Episcopatus mortali crimine dixerint se esse pollutos, a sua pradicta Ordinationibus submovendos reos, scilicet vel veri confessione, vel mendacio falsitatis, &c. Similiter Concilium Toletanum quartum Can. 52. Qui ita poenitentiam accipiunt, ut aliquod mortale peccatum se perpetrasse publice fateantur, ad Clerum vel honores Ecclesiasticos pervenire nullatenus poterunt. Quia tamen in praefatis & similibus authoritatibus nonnulli intelligi volunt tantum peccata ab antiquis capitalia & mortalia per antonomasiam dicta, cujusmodi erant apostasia circa fidem, homicidium & fornicatio, aliaque peraeque gravia delicta, quorum expiationi Ecclesiae leges publicam injungebant poenitentiam; sunt quoque nonnulli qui animale peccatum in laudato Canone secundo Nicaeno restringant ad ea duntaxat peccata, quae ex mortalibus antonomastice dicuntur mortalia, & praeterea sunt gravia. Sunt denique qui per animale peccatum putant a Nicaena Synodo significari completam per actum externum luxuriam post Baptismum vel Ordinem susceptum; Dicque Canon Nicaenus secundus est conformis Canonibus 9. & 10. Concilii Neocaesareensis, & Eliberino Canoni 30. vel ipsi S. Gregorii Magni oraculo lib. 3. Ep. 26. Qui post acceptum sacrum Ordinem lapsus in peccatum carnis fuerit, sacro Ordine ita carebit, ut ultra ad ministerium non accedat.
units.tr: 1. Ep. ad Titum: He is commanded to be without crime, a bishop, which I think is called by another word "irreproachable". Not because he is without any crime only at the time when he is to be ordained, and has washed away past stains by a new way of life; but because from the time when he was reborn in Christ he is not troubled by any consciousness of sin. For how can the president of the Church remove evil from its midst from one who has fallen into a similar fault? Or with what freedom can he rebuke a sinner, when he silently answers himself that he has committed the very things he rebukes? So too St Isidore, in book 2 of On the Ecclesiastical Offices, chapter 5: That a man who has fallen into some mortal sin after baptism should not be promoted to the priesthood, the law itself bears witness. For Moses commanded in the Law that the priests should not offer any blemished animal to God on the altar. Hence also in Numbers the red heifer, whose ashes are the expiation of the people, is commanded to be offered on the altar of the Lord only if it has not done earthly works, has not borne the yoke of sin, and has not been bound with the chains of sins. But why should we raise more objections? For if one who has committed any mortal sin in the episcopate ought not to offer bread to the Lord, how much more should a sinner found before ordination be rejected so that he is not ordained? St Gregory the Great attests the same thing in very many, and very clear, passages of his letters. Book 3, letter 26: It has come to us that some who have fallen from holy orders are to be restored to the ministry of their office, either after repentance or before it. This we absolutely forbid, and in this matter the most sacred canons also speak against it. And book 4, letter 17: If permission were granted to the fallen to return to their order, the force of canonical discipline would undoubtedly be broken, since, on the hope of return, someone will not fear to conceive desires for wicked action. And book 6, letter 39: No reason allows one who has departed through crime to be restored to the place from which he fell. St Martin I, in a letter to Amandus, bishop of Maastricht, concerning presbyters and deacons who have fallen after their ordinations, says: By no means show compassion to those who offend in this kind of sin, to the destruction of the canons. For whoever has once fallen into sin after his ordination is already deposed, and can never attain any degree of the priesthood. But it suffices for him, with lamentations and constant tears, to persist in the same repentance for as long as he lives, so that he may be able to extinguish the committed offence by divine grace. For if we seek such men to be promoted to holy orders, in whom no wrinkle and no contagion of life hinders them, how much more, if anyone after his ordination has fallen into sin and is found liable to the sin of prevarication, must he be absolutely forbidden to handle with muddy and polluted hands the mystery of our salvation?
