And let such a man always be deposed in this life according to the provisions of the sacred canons; but let him who searches the innermost thoughts, and rejoices over no sheep going astray, when he has seen his sincere repentance, hold him reconciled in the terrible terrible judgment, that is, reconciliation. The Council of Valence in Gaul, under Pope St Damasus, canon 4, decreed: Whoever have said under ordination to the diaconate, the presbyterate, or the episcopate that they are polluted by mortal crime, are to be removed from their said ordinations as guilty, either by true confession or by the lie of falsehood, etc. Likewise the Fourth Council of Toledo, canon 52: Those who receive repentance in such a way that they publicly confess that they have committed some mortal sin can by no means attain to the clergy or ecclesiastical honours. Yet since some wish that in the aforementioned and similar authorities only those sins are understood which the ancients called capital and mortal by pre-eminence, such as apostasy from the faith, murder, and fornication, and other equally grave offences, for the expiation of which the laws of the Church imposed public repentance; there are also some who, in the praised second canon of Nicaea, restrict animal sin to those sins which among mortal sins are called mortal by pre-eminence, and which are in addition grave. Finally, there are those who think that by animal sin the Synod of Nicaea signifies complete lust carried out by external act after baptism or after receiving orders. And so the second Nicene canon agrees with canons 9 and 10 of the Council of Neocaesarea, and with canon 30 of Elvira, and with the very oracle of St Gregory the Great, book 3, letter 26: Whoever, having received holy orders, falls into sin of the flesh, shall be so deprived of holy orders that he shall go no further to the ministry.

units.la: 8. Veni de Libano, &c. Hortatur sponsus sponsam, quam dilectione & nimia charitate sibi despondit, ut assueta vinearum & gregum cuslodia dimissa veniat suae coronae, seu beatitudinis particeps fieri. Hunc eundem sensum veritas Hebraica, versio Graeca & Vulgata Latina exprimit, licet aliis & aliis verbis. Haec autem optime adumbrant Christum vocantem ad se Ecclesiam laborantem sub jugo & maledicto Legis, ut relictis infirmis & egenis elementis edomandae humani generis superbiae necessariis hactenus oneribus, ipsum per haec figuratum agnoscat & recipiat Salvatorem; haec quippe est vita aeterna ut verum Deum cognoscamus, & quem misit Jesum Christum. Legalibus disciplinis, inquit Tert. 2. adverf. Marcion. Deus oneravit Judaeos, ut duritiem eorum edomaret, & operosis officiis dedolaret.
units.tr: Come from Lebanon, etc. The bridegroom exhorts the bride, whom he has betrothed to himself in love and exceeding charity, to put aside her accustomed keeping of vineyards and flocks and come to share his crown, or his blessedness. The Hebrew text, the Greek version and the Latin Vulgate express this same sense, though in different words. These words very well foreshadow Christ calling to himself the Church, labouring under the yoke and curse of the Law, so that, leaving behind the weak and needy elements, the burdens hitherto necessary for taming the pride of the human race, she may acknowledge and receive him, figured by these things, as Saviour. For this is eternal life, that we know the only true God and Jesus Christ whom he sent. "By the legal disciplines," says Tertullian in book 2 against Marcion, "God burdened the Jews, so that he might tame their hardness and smooth it away by laborious duties."

units.la: De Libano. Libanus est insignis Phoeniciae mons in sacris Litteris celebratissimus, qui Judaeae fines a septentrione claudit. Hujus montis vinum commendat Oseas, dum cap. 14. v. 8. de Israelitis a Deo sanatis & dilectis ait: Germinavit quasi vinea, memoriale ejus sicut vinum Libani. Ejusdem vero montis parcua celebrat Psaltes, dum ait Pf. 28. v. 5. Confringet Dominus cedros Libani, potentes, sublimes, gloriosos terræ, & confringet eos tanquam, non secus ac vitulum Libani, hoc est, divites, deliciosos, ac pingues, quasi vitulum assuetum pascuis montis Libani.
units.tr: From Lebanon. Lebanon is a famous mountain of Phoenicia, much celebrated in Holy Writ, which closes the borders of Judaea on the north. Hosea commends the wine of this mountain when, in chapter 14 verse 8, he says of the Israelites healed and loved by God: "He shall grow like a vine, his memorial shall be like the wine of Lebanon." The Psalmist celebrates the trees of the same mountain when he says in Psalm 28 verse 5: "The Lord shall break the cedars of Lebanon, the mighty, the lofty, the glorious ones of the earth, and he shall break them as a calf of Lebanon," that is, not otherwise than the rich, the delicate and the fat, like a calf accustomed to the pastures of the mountain of Lebanon.

units.la: Coronaberis. Heb. contemplaberis. Sensus est idem ac si diceret; experieris, dilectissima sponsa, te tibi summam comparasse felicitatem levi jactura, dum ut mihi vinculo matrimonii indissolubili adhæreas, feracissima quæque loca deseruerish.
units.tr: You shall be crowned. Hebrew: you shall behold. The sense is the same as if he said: you will find, most beloved bride, that you have gained the greatest happiness at a small loss, since, in order to cling to me in the indissoluble bond of marriage, you have left behind the most fertile places.

units.la: De capite Amana. Hæc referuntur ad verbum veni, non ad verbum coronaberis. Est autem Amana mons altissimus trans Jordanem juxta Libanum situs in finibus terræ Israel ad septentrionem. Alii volunt hic designari montem præcelsum ejusdem nominis, qui Ciliciam à Syria dirimit, de quo Plinius lib. 5. Nat. Hist. cap. 22.
units.tr: From the top of Amana. These words refer to the word come, not to the word you shall be crowned. Amana is a very high mountain beyond the Jordan, situated near Lebanon, on the northern borders of the land of Israel. Others want the very lofty mountain of the same name to be meant here, which separates Cilicia from Syria, of which Pliny speaks in book 5 of the Natural History, chapter 22.

units.la: De vertice Sanir & Hermon. Montem Hermon Amorrhæi Sanir seu Senir vocant, ut patet ex Deut. 3. v. 9. 1. Paralip. 5. v. 25. Ezech. 27. v. 5. quasi felinum dixeris, fortasse à felibus ibi diversari solitis. Felis scilicet ut Arabice Sinaur vel Sinar קנור, ita Chaldaice שנור Schunar vel שנורא Schunera vocatur. Hinc Talmudici onirocritici in Beracoth cap. 9. sol. 56. B. Qui חתול Chatul, id est, felem videt in somnis in loco, in quo felis vocatur שנורא Schunera, fiet illi שירה Schira Naa, id est, Canticum pulchrum. At si videat in loco, in quo vocatur שנרא Schinara, quomodo apud Arabes fiet illi שינוירא Schinuira, id est, mutatio mala. Hæ sunt frigidæ vocum allusiones; quale est quod Satyrus ab Alexandro visus in somnis dum Tyrum obsideret, significavit Tyrum ab illo propediem capiendam, quia Σάτυρος divulsâ voce est σὺ τύρος, tua est Tyrus. Et cum alius vidisset Thessalonicen, hoc omnem victoriæ spem illi ademit, quia nomen ipsum urbis significabat θὲς ἄλλῳ νίκλω, alii relinque victoriam. Porro mons Hermon hodieque ab Arabibus vocatur Senir. Illum definit Alcamus Lexicographus Arabs montem inter Emesam & Baalbech, quæ olim Heliopolis. Ibidem felis Sinar vel Sinaur dicitur à naturæ malignitate. Nam Arabice Sener est prava indoles.
units.tr: From the peak of Sanir and Hermon. The Amorites call Mount Hermon Sanir or Senir, as is clear from Deut. 3 verse 9, 1 Paralip. 5 verse 25, and Ezek. 27 verse 5. You might call it "feline", perhaps from the cats that used to make their home there. The cat is called in Arabic Sinaur or Sinar [קנור], and in Chaldee likewise Schunar or Schunera [שנור, שנורא]. Hence the Talmudic dream interpreters, in Berachoth chapter 9, folio 56 B: "He who sees a cat [חתול, Chatul] in a dream, in a place where the cat is called Schunera [שנורא], there shall come to him Schira Naa [שירה], that is, a beautiful song. But if he sees it in a place where it is called Schinara [שנרא], there shall come to him, as among the Arabs, Schinuira [שינוירא], that is, an evil change." These are cold plays on words, like what Satyrus, seen by Alexander in a dream while he was besieging Tyre, signified: that Tyre would soon be taken by him, because Satyros [Σάτυρος], with the word divided, is sy tyros [σὺ τύρος], "Tyre is yours." And when another man saw Thessalonica, this took away all hope of victory from him, because the name of the city itself signified thes allo nikle [θὲς ἄλλῳ νίκλω], "leave the victory to another." Moreover, Mount Hermon is still today called Senir by the Arabs. The Arab lexicographer Alcamus defines it as the mountain between Emesa and Baalbek, which was once Heliopolis. There a cat is called Sinar or Sinaur because of the malignity of its nature, for in Arabic sener means a wicked disposition.

units.la: De cubilibus Leonum, de montibus Pardorum. In sacris & prophanis libris Leo & Pardus sæpe junguntur, tanquam animalia aliquo modo homogenea; secundum enim in feris à Leone locum Pardo tribuunt Arabes, & cum naturale Pardo fit odium in Leonem, alternam inter eos victoriam esse asserunt in Damire in cap. de Pardo. Incertum est autem utrum à Salomone montes Pardorum appellentur quilibet montes Pardis frequentes, præcipuè Libanus, Amana, Sanir & Hermon, quorum hîc est mentio : an verò aliqui fuerint tum circa Libanum montes peculiariter sic nominati, ut is de quo Brocardus, A Tripoli per duas leucas est mons Leopardorum, rotundus & altus, una leucâ à Libano distans.
units.tr: Of the dens of lions, of the mountains of leopards. In sacred and profane books the lion and the leopard are often joined together, as animals somehow of one kind. For the Arabs give the leopard second place among the wild beasts after the lion, and since the leopard has a natural hatred of the lion, they assert that victory passes back and forth between them, in Damiri in the chapter on the leopard. It is uncertain, however, whether by Solomon the mountains of the leopards are called any mountains frequented by leopards, especially Lebanon, Amana, Sanir and Hermon, which are mentioned here, or whether there were then around Lebanon mountains peculiarly so named, like the one of which Brocardus writes: "Two leagues from Tripoli is the mountain of the leopards, round and high, one league distant from Lebanon."

units.la: Pardorum. B. Hier. lib. 1. In Jovinianum cap. 17. & B. Gaudentius tract. 2. legunt Leopardorum. Hoc mirum non est, quia quamvis Leopardi vox præcisè sumta animal significet ex Leæna & Pardo natum, tamen Catachrefticῶς pro Pardo jam olim usurpata est, ut in his Fl. Vopisci. Editi deinde centum Leopardi Lybici, centum deinde Syriaci. Nam in Syria Leopardi ex mixto semine nulli sunt, sed solùm in Africa, nec in Africa ipsa tam numerosi occurrunt, ut Romæ potuerint edi per centurias. Neque aliud voluit Symmachus lib. 4. Epist. 12. cùm Romanam caveam scripsit Leopardorum cursus implevisse. Itaque in his Lampridii in Heliogabali vita, Ebrios amicos plerumque claudebat, & subito nocte Leones, & Leopardos, & ursos exarmatos immittebat, ita ut expergefacti in cubiculo eodem Leones, ursos, Pardos cum luce, vel, quod est gravius, nocte, invenirent, vocantur Pardi, qui paulò ante Leopardi, Hinc in veteri Glossario Latino-Græco in capite de Bestiis, Leopardus est παρδάλεις. Quæ catachresis nostris seculis ita invaluit, ut plebs hodie Leopardi nomine nihil quàm Pardum intelligat.
units.tr: Of the leopards. Blessed Jerome in book 1 against Jovinian, chapter 17, and Blessed Gaudentius, tract 2, read Leopardorum. This is not surprising, because although the word leopardus, taken strictly, signifies an animal born of a lioness and a leopard, it was long ago used catachrestically for the pard, as in this passage of Flavius Vopiscus: "Then a hundred Libyan leopards were displayed, then a hundred Syrian." For in Syria there are no leopards from mixed seed, only in Africa, and even in Africa they do not occur so numerously that they could be shown at Rome by hundreds. Nor did Symmachus mean anything else in book 4, letter 12, when he wrote that "the Roman cage had filled the course of leopards." So too in this passage from Lampridius in the life of Heliogabalus: "He used to shut up his drunken friends, and suddenly at night he would send in unarmed lions, leopards and bears, so that when they woke they found in the same bedroom lions, bears, pards by daylight, or, what is worse, at night," the animals are called pards, which a little before were called leopards. Hence in the old Latin-Greek glossary, under the chapter on beasts, leopardus is pardaleis [παρδάλεις]. This catachresis has taken such hold in our own centuries that the common people today understand by the name of leopard nothing but the pard.

units.la: 9. Vulnerasti cor meum, &c. Postquam sponsus in superiori sententia vocavit dilectam, illam intuitus, ejúsque pulchritudine mirum in modum recreatus, in hæc prorupit, quibus sui in sponsam amoris vehementiam ἐμφατικῶς reddit contestatam. Sensus est idem ac si Christus diceret Ecclesiæ : hoc est, quod me ad te amandam vehementius, mirificè præ cæteris allicit, atque accendit, quòd unitatem ejusdem fidei ac dilectionis ab orbe condito ad consummationem usque seculi, & in Doctoribus, & in plebe, in pastoribus & in ovibus constanter & immobiliter serves.
units.tr: 9. You have ravished my heart, etc. After the bridegroom, in the sentence above, had called his beloved and looked upon her, and was marvellously refreshed by her beauty, he broke out into these words, by which he expresses emphatically the vehemence of his love for the bride. The sense is the same as if Christ said to the Church: this is what draws and kindles me more strongly and wonderfully than others to love you, that you constantly and immovably keep the unity of the same faith and love from the creation of the world to the end of the age, both in the teachers and in the common people, in the ministers and in the sheep.

units.la: Soror mea. B. Hier. lib. 1. contra Jovin. putat ideo sponsam vocari sororem, ut tolleretur suspicio fœdi amoris. Alii non minùs probabiliter putant ut sponsæ testaretur sponsus quàm ardenter ipsam diligat, ipsum sororis appellatione usum ; est quippe hæc appellatio blandientis, & intimæ amicitiæ ac familiaritatis. Sic Esther 15. v. 12. dicebat Estheræ conjugi suæ Rex Assuerus frater tuus sum.
units.tr: My sister. Blessed Jerome, in book 1 against Jovinian, thinks the bride is called sister so that suspicion of foul love might be removed. Others think, no less plausibly, that the bridegroom used the name of sister so as to attest to the bride how ardently he loves her; for this title belongs to one who caresses, and to intimate friendship and familiarity. Thus in Esther 15 verse 12, King Ahasuerus said to his wife Esther: "I am your brother."

units.la: In uno oculorum tuorum. Per unum oculum significatur unitas sanctorum Doctorum plebem Dei doctrinâ & præceptis ad cœlestia ducentium.
units.tr: In one of your eyes. By one eye is signified the unity of the holy teachers, who lead the people of God to heavenly things by doctrine and precepts.

units.la: In uno crine. Heb. ad verbum, per unum torquem, seu sertum, tum, scilicet, ex crine contorto. Significatur autem per unum crinem, seu torquem ex crine contorto, multitudo plebis fidelis unitae in eadem fide, qua, veluti collo, Ecclesia capiti suo, quod est Christus Jesus, jungitur. Ita fere S. Greg. Magnus.
units.tr: In one hair. Hebrew, word for word: by one chain, or garland, that is, of twisted hair. By one hair, or chain of twisted hair, is signified the multitude of the faithful people united in the same faith, by which the Church is joined, as by a neck, to her head, which is Christ Jesus. So almost Saint Gregory the Great.

units.la: 10. Quàm pulchrae, &c. Q. d. Quis non admiretur speciem, pulchritudinemque mammarum tuarum? De Ecclesiae mammis seu uberibus diximus supra v. 5.
units.tr: 10. How beautiful, etc. That is: who would not admire the beauty and comeliness of your breasts? We spoke above, at verse 5, of the breasts or udders of the Church.

units.la: Pulchriora sunt ubera tua vino. Id est, meliora (ut dicitur supra cap. 1.) sunt ubera tua vino. Pulchrum quippe & bonum promiscue usurpantur. Hoc nempe vult sponsus longè delectabilius esse ubera sponsae veluti fugere, atque iis inhaerere, quàm lagunculam, aut utrem vini generosissimi exhaurire. Simile est illud Salomonis dictum in Proverbiis cap. 5. v. 19. quum commendat viris amorem conjugum suarum ferventissimum, Ubera ejus inebrient te omni tempore. Praeclare Aug. tract. 3. in Ep. 1. B. Joannis: Quisquis novit natum esse se Spiritu, avidè inhiet uberibus matris, & citò crescit. Est autem mater Ecclesia, & ubera ejus duo testamenta Scripturarum Divinarum. Hinc sugatur lac omnium Sacramentorum, temporaliter pro aeterna salute nostra gestorum: ut nutritus atque roboratus perveniat ad manducandum cibum, quod est, in principio erat Verbum, & Verbum erat apud Deum, & Deus erat Verbum. Lac nostrum Christus humilis est: Cibus noster, idem ipse Christus aequalis Patri.
units.tr: Your breasts are more beautiful than wine. That is, your breasts are better than wine, as is said above in chapter 1. For beautiful and good are used interchangeably. The bridegroom wishes to say that it is far more delightful to cling to the bride's breasts, as it were, and to be fastened to them, than to drain a flask or a skin of the finest wine. Similar is that saying of Solomon in Proverbs chapter 5 verse 19, where he commends to husbands the most fervent love of their wives: "Let her breasts inebriate you at all times." Augustine says splendidly, in tract 3 on the First Epistle of John: "Whoever knows that he has been born of the Spirit eagerly gapes at his mother's breasts and grows quickly. The mother is the Church, and her breasts are the two Testaments of the Divine Scriptures. Hence is sucked the milk of all the sacraments, performed in time for our eternal salvation, so that, nourished and strengthened, he may come to eat the food, which is: In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and God was the Word. Our milk is Christ humble; our food is the same Christ, equal to the Father."

units.la: Et odor unguentorum, &c. Per unguenta sponsae designari Spiritus sancti charismata Justus Orgelitanus, Aponius, atque Anselmus afferunt. Per odorem istorum charismatum in Divinis naribus sine cessatione redolentium aiunt Ecclesiam sanctam universis rebus hujus seculi, quae per aromata designantur, praeferri.
units.tr: And the smell of the ointments, etc. Justus of Urgel, Aponius and Anselm report that the ointments of the bride designate the charisms of the Holy Spirit. They say that by the odour of these charisms, which ever exhale before the divine nostrils, the holy Church is preferred to all the things of this age, which are designated by the spices.

units.la: 11. Favus distillans, &c. Quia mel non solum dulce est, sed & initium dulcoris habet, ut loquitur Ecclesiasticus cap. 11. v. 9. id est, summè dulce est, inde est quod quaecunque vel sunt gustui dulcia, vel animo grata & jucunda, cum melle conferuntur tum à sacris, tum à prophanis Scriptoribus. Rectè, inquit B. Greg. Magnus, labia sponsae favus vocantur, quia dum in carnis fragilitate sapientia magna habetur, quasi mel in cera abscondituri. Quando verò electus quisque praedicat, quando coelestia gaudia revelat nescientibus, tunc favus distillat; quia quanta dulcedo sapientiae in corde lateat, per oris fragilitatem audientibus manifestat.
units.tr: 11. The honeycomb drips, etc. Because honey is not only sweet but also has the beginning of sweetness, as Ecclesiasticus says in chapter 11, verse 9, that is, it is supremely sweet. Hence whatever things are either pleasant to the taste or agreeable and delightful to the mind are compared with honey, both by sacred and by secular writers. Rightly, says St Gregory the Great, the lips of the bride are called a honeycomb, because while great wisdom is held in the frailty of the flesh, it is as if the honey were hidden in the wax. But when any chosen one preaches, when he reveals heavenly joys to those who do not know them, then the honeycomb drips; because through the frailty of his mouth he makes manifest to the hearers how great a sweetness of wisdom lies hidden in the heart.

units.la: Mel & lac sub lingua tua: Sancta Ecclesia mel in lingua praetendit, quia sapientiae dulcedinem loquendo, quam veraciter praedicans tanquam mellis dulcedine reficit: lac gerit, quia congruenti sibi doctrinâ parvulos quosque nutrit : sub lingua autem hæc omnia sibi reservat, quia internam dulcedinem assiduè secum portat. B. Greg. Mag.
units.tr: Honey and milk are under your tongue. The holy Church holds out honey on her tongue, because by speaking she refreshes with the sweetness of wisdom, which she truly preaches, as with the sweetness of honey; she bears milk, because she nourishes each of the little ones with teaching suited to them. But she keeps all these things under her tongue, because she constantly carries the inner sweetness with her. St Gregory the Great.

units.la: Odor vestimentorum, &c. Suavitates odorum, qui afflantur e sponsæ vestimentis, designant ferventissimos illos charitatis afsectus, thuris instar recta cœlum petentes in ipsis externis sanctæ Ecclesiæ bonis operibus.
units.tr: The smell of your garments, etc. The sweetnesses of the odours that breathe from the bride's garments designate those most fervent affections of charity, rising straight to heaven like incense, in the very external good works of the holy Church.

units.la: 12. Hortus conclusus, &c. Hoc est, tu, ô sponsa dilectissima, hortus, seu fons vallo aut muro septus, & circummunitus, & aliis omnibus illibatus, tanquam Domino charus, ne cuipiam in eum ingredi, aut fructus decerpere, seu aquam præterquam Domino haurire liceret. Pulchre autem incorruptæ sponsæ pudicitia nullum præter sponsum amatorem admittens adumbrat sanctam Dei Ecclesiam, quæ, ut loquitur Vincentius Lirinensis in Commonitorio cap. 32. Sedula & cauta depositorum apud se dogmatum custos, nihil in his unquam permutat, nihil minuit, nihil addit. Eadem Christi Ecclesia circumvallata protectione Christi, qui pollicitus est ipsi se semper affuturum, dicitur fons signatus, quia doctrinæ cœlestis manat fluentis, quibus credentes à peccatis lavat, & veritatis scientiâ potat ; hæcque Ecclesiæ doctrina sic veritatis munita est signaculo, ut neque hæretici, neque maligni spiritus fidem Catholicam violare, aut in eam irrumpere valeant. Ita ferè Casliodorus & venerabilis Beda explicant cur Ecclesia Christi dicatur fons signatus. Quàm aptè verò virgo caute virginitatem servans cum horto concluso conferatur, mirificè Catullus in suo Epithalamio illustrat his versibus. Ut flos in septis secretus nascitur hortis, Ignotus pecori, nullo contusus aratro, Quam mulcent aurae, firmat sol, educat imber, Multi illum pueri, multae optavere puellae. Idem cum tenui carptus defloruit ungue, Nulli illum pueri, nullae optavere puellae. Sic virgo dum intacta manet, tunc chara suis, sed Cum captum amisit polluto corpore florem, Nec pueris jucunda manet, nec grata puellis.
units.tr: 12. A garden enclosed, etc. That is: you, O most beloved bride, are a garden, or a fountain, fenced and walled round and kept unharmed from all others, as dear to the Lord, so that no one is allowed to enter it, to pick its fruits, or to draw water from it except the Lord. Moreover, the chastity of the uncorrupted bride, admitting no lover but her spouse, beautifully prefigures the holy Church of God, which, as Vincent of Lérins says in his Commonitorium, chapter 32, is a careful and watchful guardian of the doctrines entrusted to her, never changing anything in them, diminishing nothing, adding nothing. The same Church of Christ, walled about by the protection of Christ, who promised that he would always be present with her, is called a sealed fountain, because it flows with streams of heavenly doctrine, with which it washes believers from their sins and gives them to drink the knowledge of truth; and this doctrine of the Church is so fortified with the seal of truth that neither heretics nor evil spirits can violate the Catholic faith or break into it. Cassiodorus and the venerable Bede explain in much the same way why the Church of Christ is called a sealed fountain. How aptly a virgin who guards her virginity carefully is compared with an enclosed garden, Catullus illustrates wonderfully in his Epithalamium with these verses: As a flower born secretly in a fenced garden, unknown to the flock, bruised by no plough, which the breezes caress, the sun strengthens, the rain nourishes; many boys, many girls have desired it. The same flower, when plucked by a tender nail and lost its bloom, no boy, no girl has desired. So the virgin, while she remains untouched, is dear to her own; but when she has lost the flower she has been taken of, with her body defiled, she remains pleasing neither to boys nor pleasant to girls.

units.la: 11. Emissiones tuae, &c. Ne quis putaret sponsam cum horto concluso semel atque iterum collatam, minùs Domino aliisque omnibus utilem, quòd sit hortus ab aliorum consortio divisus atque separatus, in eadem similitudine perstiltens præsenti & sequenti versiculo asserit quòd quemadmodum paradisus, quamvis conclusus & septus, suavissimos tamen ex se odores fundit, dulcissimos fructus, salubberrima poma, ac longè prospicientibus jucundissimum præbet spectaculum; sic & sponsa tota licèt sponso suo dedita, jucundissima tamen exhibet intuentium oculis exempla pudoris & modestiæ, suavissimos boni nominis odores spirat virtutúmque omnium mira edit in omnes documenta. Hæc quàm aptissimè quadrant in sanctam Dei Ecclesiam, quæ præventa à Deo amatore suo, ipsi inviolatam servat fidem, filiósque suis præclaris charitatis, humilitatis, patientiæ, modestiæ, virtutum denique omnium documentis verbo & opere quàm suavissimè reficit & recreat.
units.tr: 11. Your outgoings, etc. Lest anyone think that the bride, compared once and again with an enclosed garden, is less useful to the Lord and to all others because the garden is divided and separated from the company of others, the verse in the present and following line, persisting in the same likeness, asserts that just as a paradise, though enclosed and fenced, nevertheless pours forth most sweet odours from itself, the sweetest fruits and most wholesome apples, and offers a most delightful spectacle to those who look from afar; so also the bride, though wholly devoted to her spouse, nevertheless presents to the eyes of onlookers most delightful examples of modesty and decorum, breathes the sweetest odours of good name, and displays wonderful instruction in all virtues to all. How very aptly these things fit the holy Church of God, which, anticipated by God her lover, keeps its faith inviolate towards him, and most sweetly refreshes and restores its sons, by word and deed, with the splendid examples of charity, humility, patience, modesty, and finally of all virtues!

units.la: 14. Cum universis lignis Libani. Id est, cum cunctis odoriferis arbustis & odoribus Libani.
units.tr: 14. With all the trees of Lebanon. That is, with all the fragrant shrubs and spices of Lebanon.

units.la: Primis. Id est, præstantissimis.
units.tr: Chief. That is, most excellent.

units.la: 15. Fons hortorum, &c. Hæc est singularitas sponsæ, quæ sic more putei altum & immanentem bonorum ad se uberrimè ex perenni fonte profluentium cumulum spatioso receptaculo continet, ut tamen more fluvii eadem bona quàm liberalissimè profundat & communicet. Eleganter itaque B. Greg. Nyss. Hom. 9. in Cantic. Hoc est omnium maximè admirabile; nam cùm omnes putei aquam simul habeant consistentem, sola sponsa aquam in se habet permanentem; adeo ut putei profundum habeat, & fluvii perennem motionem. Hæc est singularis Ecclesiæ laus, quòd communicet sibi Divinitùs infusos gratiarum latices, largiterque cœlestia dona dispenset, nec tamen unquam data ipsa cœlitùs plenitudo exhauriatur, aut minuatur.
units.tr: 15. The fountain of gardens, etc. This is the singularity of the bride, who, like a well, holds in her spacious receptacle the high and abundant store of good things flowing most richly to her from a perpetual spring, and yet, like a river, pours out and shares these same good things most generously. Therefore St Gregory of Nyssa, Homily 9 on the Canticles, elegantly says: This is the most admirable of all; for while all wells hold their water standing still, the bride alone holds water that remains flowing within her; so that she has the depth of a well and the perpetual motion of a river. This is the singular praise of the Church, that it shares among its members the streams of grace poured into it by God, and dispenses heavenly gifts abundantly, and yet the fullness given from heaven is never exhausted or diminished.

units.la: Fluunt impetu de Libano. Q. d. ex præcelsissimo monte largissimorum imbrium instar continuo impetu defluunt. Jacobus Vitriacus Historiæ Jerofolymitanæ cap. 33. Ad pedes autem Libani montis in partibus illis oritur fons amœnissimus, aquas habens limpidissimas, quæ per quosdam subterraneos meatus fluunt impetu de Libano, omnes hortos regionis copiosè irrigantes. Hunc dicunt esse fontem hortorum, de quo in Canticis Salomon facit mentionem. & cap. 43. In Tyri territorio in loco aliquantulum edito est fons sive puteus, supra quem fessus in itinere dicitur quievisse Dominus, cùm transiret per fines Sidonis, & Tyri. Habet autem aquas limpidissimas intrinsecùs, ita copiosè scaturientes, quòd omnia pomaria, & hortos olerum, & universam irrigat regionem. Hunc Salomon in Canticis, puteum aquarum viventium appellat. Brocardus : Distat ab hac urbe Tripoli Libanus tribus leucis, ad cujus pedem oritur fons hortorum, fluens impetu de Libano, ut in Cantico Salomonis dicitur, habens quidem scatebram humilem, sed illico tumescens fit fluvius magnus, irrigans & fœcundans omnes hortos, & totam regionem, quæ est inter Libanum & Tripolim. Eadem tradunt posteriores alii sacri Topographi. Sed ante omnes Gulielmus Tyrius lib. 7. belli sacri cap. 22. Tyrum pervenerunt, runt, ubi circa illum egregium & seculis admirabilem fontem hortorum, & puteum aquarum viventium castrametati in pomœriis late patentibus, & multâ commoditate refertis, nocte quieverunt una.
units.tr: They flow with force from Lebanon. That is, they stream down in a continuous rush from the most lofty mountain, like very heavy rains. Jacques de Vitry, in his History of Jerusalem, chapter 33: At the foot of Mount Lebanon, in those parts, there rises a most pleasant spring, having the clearest waters, which flow with force from Lebanon through certain underground channels, copiously watering all the gardens of the region. They say this is the fountain of gardens, of which Solomon makes mention in the Canticles. And in chapter 43: In the territory of Tyre, in a somewhat raised place, there is a fountain or well, above which the Lord is said to have rested wearied on his journey, when he passed through the borders of Sidon and Tyre. It has within it the clearest waters, gushing so abundantly that they water all the orchards, the vegetable gardens and the whole region. Solomon in the Canticles calls this the well of living waters. Brocardus: Lebanon is three leagues distant from this city of Tripoli, at whose foot rises the fountain of gardens, flowing with force from Lebanon, as is said in Solomon's Canticle; it has indeed a humble spring, but at once it swells into a great river, watering and making fruitful all the gardens and the whole region which lies between Lebanon and Tripoli. Other later sacred topographers hand down the same things. But before all, William of Tyre, book 7 of the Holy War, chapter 22: They came to Tyre, where, encamped near that remarkable fountain of gardens, admired through the ages, and the well of living waters, in spacious meadows well supplied with every convenience, they rested together for one night.

units.la: Sponsa.
units.tr: The Bride.

units.la: 16. SUrge aquilo, & veni auster, & perfla hortum meum, & fluent aromata illius.
units.tr: 16. Arise, O north wind, and come, O south wind, blow upon my garden, that its spices may flow out.

units.la: EXPLICATIO.
units.tr: EXPLANATION.

units.la: SPonsa comparata horto plantis aromaticis undique confito ventos duos præcipuos obtestatur, ut simul perflantes longè lateque diffundant eam, quâ perfusa est, odoris suavitatem. In Aquilone, inquit Glossa, mundi adversa; in Austro blandimenta intellige. Unde Ecclesia non solum Austrum ad perflandum hortum suum, sed etiam Aquilonem ad surgendum, seu insurgendum, hoc est, ad eundem hortum impugnandum provocat, ut hac gemina impugnatione probata & pulsata mirum suæ in castissimo Dei amore constantiæ, quam nec tristia frangere, nec mollia detinere possunt, odorem undique diffundat.
units.tr: The Bride, comparing herself to a garden planted on every side with aromatic herbs, calls upon the two chief winds, that by blowing together they may spread far and wide the sweetness of the fragrance with which she has been perfumed. "The north," says the Gloss, "understand as the adversities of the world; the south as its flatteries." Hence the Church calls not only the south wind to blow upon her garden, but also the north wind to rise up, that is, to assail that same garden; so that, being tested and buffeted by this twofold assault, she may diffuse on every side the wonderful fragrance of her constancy in the most chaste love of God, which neither sorrows can break nor pleasures detain.

units.la: CAPUT QUINTUM.
units.tr: CHAPTER FIVE.

units.la: Prosequitur Sponsa Votum suum.
units.tr: The bride pursues her wish.

units.la: 1. VEniat dilectus meus in hortum suum, & comedat fructus pomorum suorum.
units.tr: 1. Let my beloved come into his garden, and eat the fruit of his pleasant fruits.

units.la: EXPLICATIO.
units.tr: EXPLICATION.

units.la: 1. VEniat, &c. Optat sponsa ut sponsus effusâ odoris fragrantiâ illectus invisat hortum suum conclusum, & gaudeat matura dulcissimorum ejusdem horti fructuum suavitate. Optat Ecclesia ut Christus se invisat, &, iis, quæ sibi ab ipso bonorum omnium largitore insunt, pascatur, & delectetur gratiis & virtutibus.
units.tr: 1. Let him come, etc. The bride wishes that the bridegroom, drawn by the fragrance of the spreading odour, would visit his enclosed garden and rejoice in the ripe sweetness of its most delightful fruits. The Church wishes that Christ would visit himself, and be fed and delighted by the graces and virtues that are in her by the gift of him who is the giver of all good things.

units.la: Sponsus.
units.tr: The Bridegroom.

units.la: VEni in hortum meum soror mea sponsa, messui myrrham meam cum aromatibus meis: comedi favum cum melle meo, bibi vinum meum cum lacte meo: comedite amici, & bibite, & inebriamini charissimi.
units.tr: I have come into my garden, my sister, my bride: I have gathered my myrrh with my spices; I have eaten my honeycomb with my honey; I have drunk my wine with my milk: eat, friends, and drink; be drunk, beloved.

units.la: EXPLICATIO.
units.tr: EXPLANATION.

units.la: SE jam hoc functum munere respondet sponsus, ac hortum sponsae ingressum afflatam ex confitis ibi aromatibus suavitatem odoratione percepisse, & ibidem opiparè hilarem inmodum esse epulatum; jamque hoc unum superesse, ut amici quoque adsint epulo magnificentissimo, & famem & sitim dulciculis cibis, potionibusque largiter expleant. Hoc sponsi responsum praeclarè Christum exprimit annuentem votis Ecclesiae sub Lege supplicitèr deprecantis, ut citò adesset sponsus. Quasi diceret, Ecce, quem expectabas, Salvator adveni, valdeque recreatus fumo odore quàm suavissimo virtutum & bonorum operum, quem Patriarchae, Prophetae, caeterique justi tui in me credentes exhalarunt. Quid enim myrrhae, aromatumque nomine, nisi, ut alicubi loquitur B. Greg. Mag. virtutum suavitas, seu bene redolens electorum vita designatur? Addit Christus adagiali locutione se in adventu suo opiparè epulatum, dum videlicet propositio sibi gaudio sustinuit crucem, & implevit quae praedicta erant de ipso in Divinis eloquiis quovis melle dulcioribus; Meus cibus est, inquit Joan. 4. v. 34. ut faciam voluntatem ejus, qui misit me, ut perficiam opus ejus. Vinum lacte dilutum bibit Christus, dum pascitur & delectatur prudentia senili cum innocentia & simplicitate parvulorum in electis suis conjuncta; ut enim eleganter pro more B. Isidorus Pelusiota lib. 3. Epist. 175. Prudentia simplicitate temperata divinam quamdam rem, hoc est, numeris omnibus absolutam virtutem parit. At si altera sejungatur, illa in perversitatem incidit, haec verò in stultitiam definit. Itaque lacte significatur innocentia parvulorum; vinum verò, quod moderatè potatum acuit ingenium, dicitúrque vulgò lac senum, designat virilem prudentiam. Bibit sponsus vinum cum lacte, quia delectatur iis, qui malitiâ parvuli sunt, sensibus autem perfecti, ut loquitur Apostolus 1. Cor. 14. v. 20. Hinc forte olim renatis in Christo vinum lácq; tribuebatur, qui mos ac typus in Occidentis Ecclesiis etiamnum tempore B. Hieronymi, servabatur, ut ipse testis est in Commentariis suis in Esa. cap. 55. Si tamen nobis constaret vinum olim neophytis propinari solitum, fuisse ubique vinum dulce, quomodo id nobis constat de quibusdam Belgarum Ecclesiis ex Panoplia Guillelmi Lindani Episcopi Ruremondensis, per lac vino mixtum intelligi homines fragiles fide salutari imbutos, (cum quibus esse delicias sunt Christi) constanter asseveraremus, inducti hac authoritate S. Clementis Presbyteri Alexandrini lib. 1. Pedagogi cap. 6. Miscetur lac vino dulci : est autem utilis mixtio, veluti contemperata affectione ad incorruptionem : lac enim a vino serescit, & finditur, & quidquid est ejus adulterinum, id tanquam per aquae ductum educitur. Eodem autem modo spiritualis fidei societas se habet in hominem patibilem ; ferescere enim faciens carnales concupiscentias, hominem ad aeternitatem contrahit, Divinis immortalem efficiens.
units.tr: The bridegroom now answers that, this duty being done, he has entered the bride's garden and perceived there the sweet fragrance of the spices mingled together, and has feasted there with great joy and abundance. All that remains is for his friends also to join the most splendid banquet and to satisfy their hunger and thirst fully with sweet food and drink. This reply of the bridegroom clearly portrays Christ, granting the prayers of the Church, which under the Law had humbly begged that the bridegroom might come soon. It is as if he said: "Behold, the Saviour whom you were waiting for has come, and he is refreshed by the most sweet-smelling incense of virtues and good works, which your Patriarchs, Prophets and other righteous men breathed out in faith in me. For what is meant by the name of myrrh and spices, if not, as St Gregory the Great says somewhere, the sweetness of virtues, or the life of the elect that gives off a good fragrance?" Christ adds, in a proverbial manner, that on his coming he feasted richly, since he gladly undertook the cross and fulfilled what had been foretold of him in the Divine oracles, sweeter than any honey: My meat is, he says in John 4:34, to do the will of him that sent me, and to finish his work. Christ drinks wine mixed with milk when he feeds on and delights in the wise judgement of age joined with the innocence and simplicity of little children in his elect. For, as St Isidore of Pelusium elegantly says in his third book, letter 175: Prudence tempered by simplicity brings forth a certain divine thing, that is, a virtue perfect in all its parts. But if the one is separated from the other, the former falls into perversity, and the latter ends in foolishness. Thus milk signifies the innocence of little children, while wine, which when drunk in moderation sharpens the mind, and which is commonly called the milk of the old, signifies manly prudence. The bridegroom drinks wine with milk because he delights in those who are children in malice, but perfect in understanding, as the Apostle says in 1 Cor. 14:20. Hence perhaps wine mixed with milk was once given to those newly reborn in Christ, a custom and type which was still observed in the Churches of the West in the time of St Jerome, as he himself bears witness in his commentary on Isaiah, chapter 55. Yet if we could be sure that the neophytes were once customarily given sweet wine everywhere, as we are sure of this for some Churches of the Belgians from the Panoplia of William Lindanus, Bishop of Roermond, we would firmly affirm that by milk mixed with wine are meant frail men imbued with saving faith (with whom are Christ's delights), being moved by this authority of St Clement, Presbyter of Alexandria, in the first book of the Paedagogus, chapter 6: Milk is mixed with sweet wine. The mixture is useful, as an affection tempered towards incorruption: for milk is made sharp by wine, and is split, and whatever is adulterated in it is drawn off as through a channel of water. In the same way, the fellowship of spiritual faith stands towards the suffering man; for by making the carnal lusts ferment, it draws man to eternity, making him immortal by divine means.

units.la: Comedite amici, &c. Non solum Christus verâ fidelium fide, seu prudentiâ per simplicitatem temperata delectatur, sed etiam hortatur ipsos fideles ad congaudendum tali convivio, ut loquitur Glossa.
units.tr: Eat, O friends, etc. Not only does Christ delight in the true faith of the faithful, that is, in prudence tempered by simplicity, but he also urges the faithful themselves to rejoice together at such a banquet, as the Gloss says.

units.la: Inebriamini. Praeclare Ambrosius lib. 1. de Cain & Abel cap. 5. Haec ebrietas sobrios facit; haec ebrietas gratiae, non temulentiae; laetitiam generat, non titubantiam. Sobria illa ebrietas, vero, non mero ingurgitans; Non madens vino, sed ardens Deo, inquit Bernardus in tract de diligendo Deo, ad finem. Ebrietas haec, Summa sobrietas est; mundi memoriam obliterat, & Deum praesentem animo semper inculcat. Amadeus Laufaniaepiscopus.
units.tr: Be drunken. Ambrose admirably says in the first book of On Cain and Abel, chapter 5: This drunkenness makes men sober; this is the drunkenness of grace, not of intoxication; it produces joy, not staggering. That sober drunkenness is not gulping down wine, but not being soaked in wine; it is burning with God. Bernard says, in his treatise On Loving God, near the end: This drunkenness is the highest sobriety; it wipes out the memory of the world and keeps God present in the mind always. Amadeus, bishop of Lausanne.

units.la: Sponsa nocturnum suum somnium suis narrat comitibus.
units.tr: The bride tells her companions of her dream at night.

units.la: 2. EGo dormio & cor meum vigilat: vox dilecti mei pulsantis: Aperi mihi soror mea, amica mea, columba mea, immaculata mea; quia caput meum plenum est rore, & cincinni mei guttis noctium.
units.tr: 2. I sleep, but my heart waketh: it is the voice of my beloved that knocketh, saying, Open to me, my sister, my love, my dove, my undefiled: for my head is filled with dew, and my locks with the drops of the night.

units.la: 3. Expoliavi me tunicâ meâ, quomodo induar illâ? lâ? Lavi pedes meos, quomodo inquinabo illos ?
units.tr: 3. I have put off my coat; how shall I put it on? I have washed my feet; how shall I defile them?

units.la: 4. Dilectus meus misit manum suam per foramen, & venter meus intremuit ad tactum ejus.
units.tr: 4. My beloved put in his hand by the hole of the door, and my bowels were moved for him.

units.la: 5. Surrexi, ut aperirem dilecto meo : manus meae stillaverunt myrrham, & digiti mei pleni myrrhâ probatissimâ.
units.tr: 5. I rose up to open to my beloved; and my hands dropped with myrrh, and my fingers with sweet smelling myrrh upon the handles of the lock.

units.la: 6. Pessulum ostii mei aperui dilecto meo: at ille declinaverat, atque transierat. Anima mea liquefacta est, ut locutus est : quaesivi, & non inveni illum: vocavi & non respondit mihi.
units.tr: 6. I opened to my beloved; but my beloved had withdrawn himself, and was gone: my soul failed when he spake: I sought him, but I could not find him; I called him, but he gave me no answer.

units.la: 7. Invenerunt me custodes qui circumeunt civitatem: percusserunt me, & vulneraverunt me : tulerunt pallium meum mihi custodes murorum.
units.tr: 7. The watchmen that went about the city found me, they smote me, they wounded me; the keepers of the walls took away my veil from me.

units.la: 8. Adjuro vos, filiae Jerusalem, si inveneritis dilectum, ut nuntietis ei, quia amore langueo.
units.tr: 8. I charge you, O daughters of Jerusalem, if you find my beloved, that you tell him that I am sick of love.

units.la: EXPLICATIO.
units.tr: EXPLANATION.

units.la: 2. EGo dormio, &c. Q. d. Somni necessitas contrahit palpebras, at vehemens sponsi amor oculos mentis meae excitat, atque saepenumero per somnum mihi blandam pulsantis vocem audire videor hunc in modum, Aperi mihi, &c. Etenim consuevit anima, quae interdiu cogitat, eadem in somniis per phantasiam cernere, ut loquitur Chrysost. Hom. 10. de Poenit. Hoc de Ecclesia dictum sic exponit Aug. tract. 57. in Joan. Otium meum non impenditur nutrienda desidia, sed percipienda sapientia. Ego requiesco a negotiis actibus, & animus meus Divinis se intendit affectibus. Hinc B. Ambrosius in Epistola 60. ad Anysium ait: Est Sanctorum etiam somnus operarius.
units.tr: 2. I sleep, etc. That is to say: the need for sleep closes my eyelids, but the strong love of the bridegroom wakes the eyes of my mind, and often in sleep I seem to hear his gentle voice knocking in this way: Open to me, etc. For the soul that thinks during the day is accustomed to see the same things in dreams through the imagination, as Chrysostom says in Homily 10 on Repentance. Augustine, Tractate 57 on John, explains this as said of the Church: My leisure is not spent on nourishing idleness, but on acquiring wisdom. I rest from business and activities, and my mind is given over to divine affections. Hence St Ambrose, in Epistle 60 to Anysius, says: The sleep of the saints is also busy.

units.la: Vox dilecti, &c. Enarrat sponsa sibi in somnis visum sponsum non tam manu fores ostii, quam blanda voce intima pectoris sui pulsantem, ne diutius patiatur ipsum frigido noctis tempore sub dio extra fores manere. Pulsat dilectus, cum fideles suos provocat Christus, aut ad suarum incrementa virtutum, aut certe ad lucrandas animas proximorum. B. Petrus Damiani in serm. de Ss. Flora & Lucilla.
units.tr: The voice of my beloved, etc. The bride relates that in her sleep she saw the bridegroom knocking, not so much with his hand on the doors as with a gentle voice at the innermost part of her breast, so that she would not let him stand outside the doors any longer in the cold of the night, under the open sky. The beloved knocks when Christ summons his faithful, either to the growth of their virtues or certainly to winning the souls of their neighbours. St Peter Damian, in the sermon on Saints Flora and Lucilla.

units.la: Soror mea. Soror utique, inquit idem ibid. quia regni mei mihi cohaeres effecta, & in necessitudinem mihi fraternae adoptionis adscita. Vide dicta supra cap. 4. v. 9. cur sponsa vocetur Soror. Amica mea. Quia de jugo servitutis erepta, cognovisti meae veritatis arcana. Idem ibid.
units.tr: My sister. "Sister, certainly," says the same author in the same place, because she has been made a co-heir of my kingdom and admitted into the kinship of my fraternal adoption. See above on chapter 4, verse 9, for why the bride is called sister. My friend. Because she has been snatched from the yoke of servitude and has come to know the secrets of my truth. The same, ibid.

units.la: Columba mea. Sponsam toties Columbae suae nomine indigitat sponsus, significari volens hanc à se unicè diligi, seque illi vicissim unicè charum esse, quomodo in columbis mirus est amor inter conjuges, & conjugii lex firmissima. Neque enim pluribus copulari volunt, neque mutuum consortium unquam deserunt, nisi per viduitatem, inquit Arist. hist. lib. 9. cap. 7. ita & Plin. hist. nat. lib. 10. cap. 34. Propertius lib. 2. eleg. 12. &c. Sic Ecclesia Christum solum pro sponso agnoscit, & illeunam habet Ecclesiam, quam sibi in æternum desponsavit in justitia, judicio, misericordia & miserationibus, ut dicitur Osee 2. verf. 19. hinc Apostolus 2. Cor. 11. verf. 2. Despondi vos uni viro virginem castam exhibere Christo.
units.tr: My dove. The bridegroom addresses the bride by the name of his dove so often, wishing to signify that he loves her alone and that he is in turn dear to her alone, just as among doves there is a remarkable love between spouses and a most firm law of marriage. For they do not wish to pair with several, nor ever leave their mutual partnership, except through widowhood, says Aristotle, History of Animals, book 9, chapter 7; so too Pliny, Natural History, book 10, chapter 34, and Propertius, book 2, elegy 12, etc. So the Church acknowledges Christ alone as her bridegroom, and he has one Church, which he has betrothed to himself for ever in righteousness, judgement, mercy and compassion, as is said in Hosea 2, verse 19. Hence the Apostle, 2 Cor. 11, verse 2: I have betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a chaste virgin to Christ.

units.la: Immaculata mea. Sic denominatur Ecclesia militans ab iis,quos completitur, justis, qui sine crimine sunt. S. Aug. tract. 58. in Joan. & lib. de Perfectione justitiae : Non ideo sine peccato est aliquis, quoniam non habet maculam criminis. Unde & Apostolus cum ministros eligeret Ordinandos, non ait : Siquis sine peccato, quod invenire non posset : sed ait, Siquis sine crimine, quod utique posset. Synesius de sua Episcopatus recusatione ad fratrem scribens Epist. 105. ait . Palam ac liberè dico Sacerdotem debere esse omnis maculæ expertem, multum ut ei superfit, tanquam qui aliorum labes eluat. Ut enim præclare Terentius, Nonne id flagitium est, te aliis consilium dare, Foris sapere, tibi non posse auxiliarier ?
units.tr: My undefiled. The Church militant is called this by those whom she embraces, the righteous, who are without crime. St Augustine, Tractate 58 on John, and in the book On the Perfection of Righteousness: Someone is not without sin merely because he has no stain of crime. Hence also the Apostle, when choosing ministers to be ordained, did not say: "If anyone is without sin", which no one could find; but he said: "If anyone is without crime", which indeed anyone could be. Synesius, writing to his brother about refusing the bishopric, Epistle 105, says: I say openly and freely that a priest ought to be free of every stain, all the more so since he is to cleanse the defilements of others. As Terence puts it so well: Is it not a disgrace that you give advice to others, yet are not able to help yourself in your own affairs?

units.la: Omnia, inquit Cicero actione quintâ in Verrem, quæ vindicaris in alio, tibi ipsi vehementer fugienda sunt. Etenim non modo accusator, sed ne objurgator quidem ferendus est, qui, quod in alio vitium reprehendit, in eo ipso deprehenditur. Vide quæ diximus supra cap. 4. v. 7. Huc facit & illud Talmudicum adagium, quod extat in tractatu Sanhedrin capite 2. ואחר קשטעצמך Orna teipsum , & postea ornato alios. Vide & Mat. 7. v. 5. & Commentarium nostrum ibidem.
units.tr: Everything, says Cicero in the fifth speech against Verres, which you condemn in another must be most strongly avoided by yourself. For not only the accuser, but not even the censurer ought to be tolerated, who reproves in another a fault that is found in himself. See what we said above on chapter 4, verse 7. The Talmudic proverb also bears on this, found in the tractate Sanhedrin, chapter 2: [ואחר קשטעצמך] Adorn yourself, and afterwards adorn others. See also Matt. 7, verse 5, and our commentary there.

units.la: Aperi mihi. Hoc est, de quiete & otio dilectæ tibi contemplationis egredere, & ad perhibendum veritati meæ testimonium ferventissimè te, & constanter, impende. B. Petrus Damiani loco mox laudato.
units.tr: Open to me. That is, come out of the quiet and leisure of the contemplation dear to you, and devote yourself most fervently and constantly to bearing witness to my truth. St Peter Damian, in the passage just cited.

units.la: Guttis noctium. Ros alius mane,pluit, alius ipsa nocte. Ille vocatur Of. 6. verf. 4. טל משכים Ros matutinus, vulgat, Ros mane pertransiens, & 13. verf. 3. Ros matutinus præteriens, & Sap. 11. v. 23. Gutta roris antelucani, Græce ψακὰς δρόσου ὀρθρινή, Gutta roris matutina. Hunc Salomon vocat guttas noctium. Arabes hæc distinguunt propriis nominibus; illis enim æque ac Hebræis tal rorem in genere sonat, & redan matutinum, ut sedan nocturnum rorem sonat. Utroque tempore pluebat manna, aut ros illi prævius, de quo dicitur Exod. 16. verf. 13. Mane quoque ros jacuit per circuitum castrorum. & Num. 11. verf. 9. Cumque descenderet nocte super castra ros. Caput Christi, inquit B. Petrus Damiani loco laudato, Deus est, ut dicit Apostolus. Cincinni vero intimæ sanctorum cogitationes sunt, quæ non laxæ fluunt, & dissolutæ, sed timoris & amoris Dei sunt vinculo colligatæ. Enimvero, quid per rorem, & guttas noctium, nisi tenebrosas, & frigidas quorumdam reproborum mentes accipimus? Caput ergo Sponsi in reprobis plenum est rore, cum seculares quique à Dei charitate torpescunt, & per voluptatum suarum lasciviam defluunt, juxta id quod Dominus dicit; Abundavit iniquitas, & refrigescet Charitas multorum. Matth. 24. Hujusmodi plane cum sanctos Dei persequuntur & odiunt, in illorum cordibus quasi cincinni sponsi guttis noctium pleni sunt. Cumque tales multiplicantur, & Ecclesiam persecutionibus aggravant, tunc sponsus sponsam exhortatur, ut surgat, & studio prædicationis valenter insistat.
units.tr: Drops of the nights. One dew falls in the morning, another in the night itself. The former is called in Hosea 6, verse 4, [טל משכים] morning dew, which the Vulgate renders the dew passing by in the morning, and in 13, verse 3, the passing morning dew; and in Wisdom 11, verse 23, a drop of dew before dawn, in Greek [ψακὰς δρόσου ὀρθρινή], the morning drop of dew. Solomon calls this the drops of the nights. The Arabs distinguish these by proper names: for tal, like the Hebrew, signifies dew in general, and redan the morning dew, as sedan signifies the night dew. In both periods the manna fell, or the dew that went before it, of which Exodus 16, verse 13 says: In the morning also the dew lay round about the camp; and Numbers 11, verse 9: And when the dew fell on the camp in the night. The head of Christ, says St Peter Damian in the passage praised above, is God, as the Apostle says. The locks are the innermost thoughts of the saints, which do not flow loose and dissolved, but are bound together by the chain of the fear and love of God. Indeed, what do we understand by the dew and the drops of the night, if not the dark and cold minds of certain reprobate people? The head of the Bridegroom is therefore full of dew among the reprobate, when worldly people grow cold in the love of God and drip away in the wantonness of their pleasures, according to what the Lord says: Iniquity has abounded, and the love of many will grow cold, Matt. 24. When such people persecute and hate the saints of God, the locks of the bridegroom are, as it were, full of the drops of the night in their hearts. And when such people multiply and weigh down the Church with persecutions, then the bridegroom urges the bride to rise and to devote herself vigorously to the zeal of preaching.

units.la: 3. Expoliavi me &c. Sensus est, ut ego lectum petii, tunicam exutam reliqui; nunc vero quis modus resumendi eam, & pedes meos tam accurate ablutos rursus inquinandi? Pulchre hæc de Ecclesia exponit loco laudato B. Petrus Damiani, quasi Ecclesia diceret: Exui me curis, & occupationibus seculi, & in solo me tuæ contemplationis amore constrinxi. Quomodo itaque nunc discursionis iter arripiam? Quomodo strepitus, & luctamen obloquentium feram? Quod autem per tunicas curas, sollicitudinesque significet, ostendit Dominus, cum dicit: Qui in tecto est, non descendat tollere tunicam suam. Matth. 24. Quod est aperte dicere, qui sublimi contemplationis arce subnititur, nequaquam descendat, ut iterum seculari negotii occupationibus implicetur. Lavi pedes meos, quomodo inquinabo illos? Id est, gressus mei operis ab aspersione terreni pulveris dignis pœnitentiæ fletibus ablui. Quo pacto jam potero, nisi quibus assueta sum, cœlestia meditari?
units.tr: 3. I have put off my garment, etc. The sense is: as I have sought my bed, so I have left my tunic off; but now what way is there to put it on again, and to soil my feet so carefully washed? St Peter Damian, in the passage praised above, expounds these words well concerning the Church, as if the Church were saying: I have put off the cares and occupations of the world, and I have bound myself in the sole love of your contemplation. How then shall I now take up the course of running about? How shall I endure the noise and the struggle of those who contradict me? That the tunic signifies cares and anxieties is shown by the Lord when he says: He who is on the roof, let him not come down to take up his garment, Matt. 24. That is to say plainly: he who rests on the lofty height of contemplation must by no means come down, lest he be entangled again in the occupations of worldly business. I have washed my feet; how shall I defile them? That is, let the steps of my work be cleansed from the sprinkling of earthly dust by tears worthy of repentance. How can I now, unless to the things I am accustomed to, meditate on heavenly things?

units.la: 4. Dilectus meus, &c. Q. d. Dum sic surgere refugerem, & excusarem difficultatem, dilectus fores pulsans per foramen serræ, cui clavis immittitur, digitum manus immisit, ad cujus tactum commota sunt viscera mea. Dilectus, inquit B. Petrus Damiani loco mox laudato, manum per foramen mittit, & ventrem tangit, cum occulta conditor inspiratione cor visitat, atque ad agonem certaminis, & sancti laboris inflammat. Nam quod venter cor significet, ostendit Propheta, cum dicit (Jerem. 4.) Ventrem meum doleo; quod profecto quid effet, aperit, cum subjungit: Sensus cordis mei dissipati sunt.
units.tr: 4. My beloved, etc. That is to say: while I shrank from rising and made excuses for the difficulty, my beloved, knocking at the door, put his finger in through the hole of the lock where the key is inserted, and at his touch my bowels were moved. The beloved, says St Peter Damian in the passage praised just above, puts his hand through the hole and touches the belly, when the hidden Creator visits the heart with secret inspiration and inflames it to the struggle of the contest and of holy labour. For that the belly signifies the heart, the Prophet shows when he says (Jer. 4): My bowels, my bowels! I am pained; and he makes plain what this is when he adds: The senses of my heart are troubled.

units.la: 5. Surrexi, &c. Sensus est : Itaque misericordia commota surgens intempestâ nocte accessi prope, ut dilecto meo pulsanti aperirem. Ecclesia postponit contemplationis requiem, ut loquitur mox laudatus B. Petrus Damiani loco citato, & ad fervorem obedientiæ intrinsecus accensa surgit, ut aperiat : quia promptissimo animo humiliter obediens, calcat propriam, ut totis viribus voluntatem impleat Divinam.
units.tr: 5. I rose, etc. The sense is: therefore, moved by pity, I rose in the dead of night and came near, so that I might open to my beloved who was knocking. The Church sets aside the rest of contemplation, as the same St Peter Damian, cited just above in the same place, puts it, and, kindled inwardly with the fervour of obedience, she rises to open; because, with a most ready mind, humbly obedient, she tramples on her own will, so that she may fulfil the Divine will with all her strength.

units.la: Manus meæ, &c. Sponsa sponso pulsanti januam apertura sui vi se perfudit unguento ; solebant quippe Orientales fœminæ lotæ variis unguentis, vel saltem unguento aliquo se perfundere ; sic de Judith legimus, Judith. 10. v. 3. Et lavit corpus suum, & unxit se myrto optimo. Sic Dan. 13. v. 17. Susannah cum lavaretur in pomario puellis dixisse legimus : Afferte mihi oleum, & smigmata, & ostia pomarii claudite, ut laver. Sic Ruth. 3. v. 3. Noëmi præcepit Ruth, Lavare & ungere. Sic ergo & sponsa jam lota, ut significavit dicens, Lavi pedes meos, inunxisse se innuit pariter dicens: Manus meæ distillaverunt myrrham, &c.
units.tr: My hands, &c. The bride, about to open the door to the bridegroom who was knocking, anointed herself with perfume. Eastern women were accustomed to bathe and to anoint themselves with various ointments, or at least to sprinkle themselves with some ointment. So we read of Judith: "And she washed her body and anointed herself with the best myrrh" (Judith 10:3). So too Dan. 13:17: when Susanna was bathing in the garden, we read that she said to the maidens, "Bring me oil and ointments, and shut the doors of the garden, that I may wash." So Ruth 3:3: Naomi instructed Ruth, "Wash and anoint yourself." So the bride, already washed, as she showed by saying "I have washed my feet," likewise indicated that she had anointed herself, saying: "My hands dripped with myrrh, &c."

units.la: Digiti mei, &c. Repetit more Scripturæ familiari altero hemistichio, quod in præcedenti dixerat.
units.tr: My fingers, &c. In the familiar manner of Scripture, she repeats the second half-verse of what she had said before.

units.la: Myrrha probatissima. Sensum non verba reddidit ex Hebræo Vulgatus Interpres ; Hebraice enim ad verbum habetur, myrrha transeunte ad manubria pessuli : Quasi diceret, myrrhâ tam fragranti, ut ejus odor transierit ad manubria pessuli, quæ manibus myrrhâ delibutis contrectaveram, ut sponso pulsanti aperirem. Designat Ecclesia his verbis prædicatores suos, qui, ut Christo ad Evangelii prædicationem vocanti obediant, postponunt contemplationis studium, verbo & exemplo sic se gerere, ut in omnibus eorum sermonibus & operibus ea eluceat gratia & veritas, quæ pios fulciat, atque ab omni vitiorum corruptela conservet ; impios vero amaritudine imbuat, atque illos vel conficiat, vel ad pœnitentiam impellat. Metaphora sumitur à myrrha, quæ tametsi mire odorata sit, insigniter tamen est amara.
units.tr: Very choice myrrh. The Vulgate translator rendered the sense rather than the words from the Hebrew. In Hebrew the phrase literally reads "myrrh passing over onto the handles of the bolt." As if she said: with myrrh so fragrant that its odour passed onto the handles of the bolt, which I touched with my myrrh-smeared hands, in order to open to the knocking bridegroom. By these words the Church designates her preachers, who, in order to obey Christ calling them to the preaching of the Gospel, put aside the pursuit of contemplation, and who so conduct themselves in word and example that in all their sermons and works there shines that grace and truth which sustains the pious and preserves them from every corruption of vice; but which imbues the impious with bitterness, and either destroys them or drives them to repentance. The metaphor is taken from myrrh, which, although wonderfully fragrant, is nonetheless remarkably bitter.

units.la: 6. Pessulum, &c. Id est, ostio aperto, dilectus meus transgressus jam abierat. Egressa est Ecclesia è quiete & otio dilectæ sibi contemplationis, ut ferventissima veritatis prædicatione removeret ex hominibus ignorantiam, cæcitatem, & amorem seculi, quibus veluti pessulis cor humanum clauditur Deo; verùm ut in hoc suscepto propter necessitatem charitatis negotio cœlestis sponsus desponsatæ sibi Ecclesiæ probet dilectionem, permittit eam tribulationibus conflictari. Ut enim præclarè Richardus Victorinus in Cantic. cap. 35. Sponsa cùm se magis dignam susceptioni (cœlestis sc. sponsi) exhibuerit, non illi se præbet, sicut desiderat, sed ab ea declinat, ut in humilitate eam conservet, & desiderium ejus amplius excitet, & perfectius impleat. Tunc autem declinare dicitur, quando præsentiam suam jenti-re non dat, cùm ei tamen præsens sit.
units.tr: 6. The bolt, &c. That is, with the door opened, my beloved had already passed by and gone away. The Church went out from the rest and leisure of the contemplation dear to her, so that by the most fervent preaching of the truth she might remove from men ignorance, blindness, and love of the world, by which the human heart is shut against God as with bolts. But so that the heavenly bridegroom might prove his love for the Church betrothed to him in this undertaking, which she had taken up out of the necessity of charity, he allows her to be struck by tribulations. For, as Richard of St Victor excellently says on the Song, ch. 35: "When the bride has shown herself more worthy of receiving him (the heavenly bridegroom), he does not give himself to her as she desires, but turns away from her, so as to keep her in humility, and to stir up her desire further and fulfil it more perfectly. Then he is said to turn away when he does not give his presence to be felt, although he is present to her."

units.la: Anima mea, &c. Mentem, non sonum verborum Hebraici textus, ut & alibi passim, expressit Vulgatus Interpres. Quasi diceret sponsa: Ego ut audivi vocem sponsi expectatissimi, hæsi attonita & quasi propemodum exanimata. Hoc optime quadrat in Ecclesiam voce sponsi fui in ipsius amorem extra se raptam. Ut enim ait B. Dionys. de Div. Nom. cap. 4. Est extaticus Divinus amor, quo scilicet Deus amatur; qui non permittit ut sui sint qui amant, sed eorum quos amant; unde divinus Paulus hoc amore divino captus, & extaticæ virtutis consors atque particeps factus, ore divino ait ad Gal. 2. Vivo ego, jam non ego, vivit verò in me Christus: tanquam verus amator, ac extra se in Deum raptus, & non jam vitam suam, sed amati tanquam vehementer dilectam vitam vivens.
units.tr: My soul, &c. The Vulgate translator expressed the meaning, not the sound of the words of the Hebrew text, as he does in many other places. As if the bride said: when I heard the voice of the longed-for bridegroom, I stood astonished and almost lifeless. This fits the Church very well, who was carried out of herself into his love by the voice of the bridegroom. For, as St Dionysius says in On the Divine Names, ch. 4: "There is an ecstatic divine love, by which God is loved; which does not permit those who love to belong to themselves, but to those whom they love. Whence divine Paul, seized by this divine love and made a partner and sharer in ecstatic virtue, says with divine mouth in Gal. 2: 'I live, yet not I, but Christ lives in me'; as a true lover, carried out of himself into God, living not his own life, but the life of the one loved, as one greatly beloved."

units.la: Quæsivi, &c. Sponsa rapta in amorem sponsi nec ardenter quæsitum invenit sponsum, nec enixè roganti ostendit faciem suam sponsus; & in hoc quoque sponsa Ecclesiam adumbrat. Nam ut verbis Richardi nostri loco mox cit.: utar, nec ad omnia quæ petit Ecclesia, vel desiderat, Deus, respondet ei, sed cùm non exaudit ad voluntatem, tamen exaudit melius ad utilitatem: concedit enim quod magis expedire novit.
units.tr: I sought, &c. The bride, carried into love of the bridegroom, did not find the bridegroom though she sought him ardently, nor did the bridegroom show his face to her though she prayed earnestly; and in this too the bride foreshadows the Church. For, to use the words of our Richard cited just above: "God does not answer her in all things that the Church asks or desires; but when he does not hear according to her will, he nonetheless hears better for her benefit, for he grants what he knows to be more expedient."

units.la: 7. Invenerunt, &c. Sponsæ, dum quaquaversùm quærit sponsum, occurrunt murorum custodes, civitatem perlustrantes; hi sponsam percutiunt, vulnerant, & peplum ejus abreptum auferunt, quòd scilicet sponsa sponsi absentiam sicut acerbissimam rem mœrens, lugubri lamentatione turbaret nocturnam quietem. Custodes, inquit Menochius, sunt tyranni hæresibus imbuti, qui Ecclesiam per concionatores & doctores clamare prohibebant, & clamantem plagis male accipiebant. Hi pallium sponsæ non solum tulerunt, sed per schismata & hæreses etiam scidërunt.
units.tr: 7. They found, &c. While the bride seeks the bridegroom everywhere, the guards of the walls, who patrol the city, meet her. These strike and wound the bride and carry off her cloak, namely because she, grieving over the bridegroom's absence as a most bitter thing, was disturbing the nocturnal quiet with mournful lamentation. "The guards," says Menochius, "are tyrants imbued with heresies, who forbade the Church to cry out through preachers and teachers, and who treated with blows the one crying out. These not only took away the bride's cloak, but through schisms and heresies also tore it."

units.la: Pallium. Heb. Peplum seu velamen, quo mulieres æstate operiuntur in Arabia & Mesopotamia. Apud Judæos tam solemne est fœminis velamen capitis, ut inde noscantur, inquit Tertullianus de corona militis cap. 4.
units.tr: Cloak. Hebrew: a peplum, or veil, with which women cover themselves in summer in Arabia and Mesopotamia. Among the Jews a head-veil is so customary for women that they are known by it, says Tertullian, On the Soldier's Crown, ch. 4.

units.la: 8. Adjuro vos, &c. Q.d. Audistis, charissimæ sociæ, quanta passa sim in somnis propter dilectum, jam hoc unum vos oro & obtestor, ut ipsi dilecto nuntietis, si vobis occurrat, me præ nimio ejus amore deficere. Sancta Dei Ecclesia obtestatur fideles, deles, ut orantes coelesti sponso suum offerant desiderium, quo ipsa ad ejusdem sponsi fruitionem medullitus suspirat, fervet, anhelat, anxiatur. Cum præsto est, inquit Bernardus Serm. 51. in Cantic. quod amatur, viget amor; languet cum abest: quod non est aliud quàm tædium quoddam impatientis desiderii, quo necesse est affici mentem vehementer amantis, eo absente, quem amat, dum totus in expectatione quantamlibet festinationem reputat tarditatem.
units.tr: 8. I adjure you, &c. That is: You have heard, dearest companions, how much I suffered in my dreams on account of the beloved. Now this one thing only I beg and entreat you: if you meet him, tell my beloved that I am fainting from excess of love for him. The holy Church of God entreats the faithful that, in praying, they offer to the heavenly bridegroom the desire with which she herself sighs, burns, pants, and is troubled in her innermost being for the enjoyment of that same bridegroom. "When what is loved is present," says Bernard, Sermon 51 on the Song, "love flourishes; it languishes when it is absent. This is nothing other than a certain weariness of impatient desire, with which the mind of one who loves must be strongly affected when the beloved is absent, since, wholly in expectation, it counts any delay as slowness."

units.la: Chorus Puellarum Ferosolymitanarum.
units.tr: The Chorus of the Maidens of Jerusalem.

units.la: 9. Qualis est dilectus tuus ex dilecto, ô pulcherrima mulierum; Qualis est dilectus tuus ex dilecto, quia sic adjurasti nos?
units.tr: 9. What kind of man is your beloved above other men, O most beautiful of women? What kind of man is your beloved above other men, that you have so solemnly adjured us?

units.la: EXPLICATIO.
units.tr: EXPLANATION.

units.la: 9. Qualis, &c. Supplicibus sponsæ verbis excitatæ adolescentulæ, pulchritudinem ejusdem sponsæ demirantes, obnixè eam rogant, ut quoniam tam graviter ipsas adjuravit, edisseret, qualis tandem sit ille sponsus, quem tam fortiter amat, & præ aliis amabilem prædicat. Sanctæ animæ Ecclesiam matrem qualis fit quem tantopere videre concupiscit non ignorantes interrogant, sed quia cælestis illius sponsi laudum commemoratione jucunditatem captant.
units.tr: 9. What kind, etc. The young maidens, roused by the earnest words of the bride, admire her beauty and urgently ask her, since she has adjured them so earnestly, to describe what sort of bridegroom he is whom she loves so intensely and proclaims lovelier than all others. The holy soul does not ask because she is ignorant of what kind of bridegroom the mother Church longs so greatly to see, but because she takes delight in recounting the praises of that heavenly bridegroom.

units.la: Dilectus ex dilecto. Hebraismus, id est, præ cæteris dilectus.
units.tr: Beloved above beloved. A Hebraism, that is, beloved above all others.

units.la: Sponsa.
units.tr: The Bride.

units.la: 10. Dilectus meus candidus & rubicundus, electus ex millibus.
units.tr: 10. My beloved is white and ruddy, chosen out of thousands.

units.la: 11. Caput ejus aurum optimum: comæ ejus sicut elatæ palmarum, nigræ quasi corvus.
units.tr: 11. His head is the finest gold; his locks are like the high palm fronds, black as a raven.

units.la: 12. Oculi ejus sicut columbæ super rivulos aquarum, quæ lacte sunt lotæ, & resident juxta fluenta plenissima.
units.tr: 12. His eyes are like doves beside streams of water, bathed in milk and sitting by very full brooks.

units.la: 13. Genæ illius sicut areolæ aromatum consitæ à pigmentis pigmentariis : labia ejus lilia distillantia myrrham primam.
units.tr: 13. His cheeks are like beds of spices planted by perfumers; his lips are lilies dripping with the finest myrrh.

units.la: 14. Manus illius tornatiles aureæ, plenæ hyacinthis, venter ejus eburneus distinctus sapphiris.
units.tr: 14. His hands are rounded and golden, full of hyacinths; his belly is of ivory, decked with sapphires.

units.la: 15. Crura illius columnæ marmoreæ, quæ fundatæ sunt super bases aureas. Species ejus ut Libani, electus ut cedri.
units.tr: 15. His legs are marble columns set upon golden bases. His appearance is like Lebanon, chosen as the cedars.

units.la: 16. Guttur illius suavissimum, & totus desiderabilis : talis est dilectus meus, & ipse est amicus meus, filiæ Jerusalem.
units.tr: 16. His throat is most sweet, and he is wholly desirable. Such is my beloved, and he is my friend, O daughters of Jerusalem.

units.la: EXPLICATIO.
units.tr: EXPLANATION.

units.la: 10. Dilectus meus, candidus & rubicundus. Hebraismus, Q. d. sponsus meus est candidus & lucidus, id est, summo candore nitens ἐν λιὰ λυσίν. Quemadmodum enim, quamvis nihil videatur remotius, quàm ut purpureus color idem credatur esse cum summè candido, tamen purpureum à Latinis sic usurpari constat, quia purpureos olores Horatius ad Venerem lib. 4. Oda prima, & Albinovanus in Mœcenatis obitum dixit purpuream nivem, quia utrique colori, candido, inquam, & purpureo, hoc commune est, ut admixti luminis multum habeant; Sic Hebræi ruborem iis tribuunt, quæ sunt maximè candida, & ipsi Latini rutila & rutilare dicunt, quæ summè candent, nitent, lucent, & splendent. Hinc lepræ macula, cujus albor Exod. 4. v. 6. Num. 12. v. 10. & 4. Reg. 5. v. 27. cum nivis candore confertur, dicitur Levit. 13. v. 19. לבנה, אדמדמת id est, alba impensè rubra, quod est, summè candida, atque ideò lucens, qui verus lepræ color est; unde lepræ macula dicitur Hebraicè בהרת id est, lucida. Nam Arabicè bahara est lucere, Chaldaicè בהיר est lucidus, Hebraicè quoque Job. 37. v. 21. אור בהיר est lumen lucidum, seu lux nitida. Cæterum lepræ epithetum adamdemeth, Levit. 13. v. 19. minùs benè à multis vertitur, fubrubra, seu, subrufa, cùm in vocibus Hebræis geminatæ radicales literæ significationem non minuant, sed intendant. Itaque si אדום rufum seu rubrum fonat, אדמדם valdè rufum, seu summè rubrum significat. Hæ autem voces cùm opponuntur albo, ad ruborem pertinent; at cùm conjunguntur albo, ut in præsenti, quo de agimus, sacri Dramatis loco, & Levitic. 13. v. 19. non significant colorem ab albo diversum, sed alborem in intenso gradu. Hinc & Jeremias Thren. 4. v. 7. rubicundos dicit illos, quos lacte & nive candidiores dixerat. Hinc & eadem vox quæ Hebræis est rubere, in Arabica lingua, quæ Hebraicæ dialectus est, significat candere, & cius derivata candorem eximium importante secundum Lexicographos.
units.tr: 10. My beloved, white and ruddy. A Hebraism: the sense is, my bridegroom is white and bright, that is, shining with the highest whiteness [en lia lysin]. For although nothing seems further removed than that purple should be taken to be the same as the purest white, yet it is established that the Latins use purple in this way: Horace in the first ode of the fourth book speaks of purple swans, and Albinovanus, on the death of Maecenas, spoke of purple snow, because both colours, white and purple, I mean, share this trait, that when mixed they contain much light. So the Hebrews attribute redness to things that are most white, and the Latins themselves say rutila and rutilare of things that gleam most brightly, shine, glow and sparkle. Hence the spot of leprosy, whose whiteness is compared with the whiteness of snow in Exodus 4:6, Numbers 12:10 and 4 Kings 5:27, is called in Leviticus 13:19 [lavanah adamdemeth], that is, white, exceedingly red, which means most white and therefore shining, which is the true colour of leprosy; whence the spot of leprosy is called in Hebrew [baheret], that is, bright. For in Arabic bahara means to shine; in Chaldee [bahir] means bright; and in Hebrew also, in Job 37:21, [or bahir] means bright light, or shining radiance. Moreover, the epithet of leprosy, [adamdemeth], in Leviticus 13:19, is rendered by many less well as somewhat red or somewhat ruddy, since in Hebrew words doubled radical letters do not diminish the meaning but intensify it. Thus if [adom] signifies ruddy or red, [adamdam] signifies very ruddy, or most red. But these words, when they are set against white, pertain to redness; yet when they are joined to white, as in the present passage of the sacred drama and in Leviticus 13:19, they do not signify a colour different from white but whiteness in its intense degree. Hence Jeremiah also in Lamentations 4:7 calls ruddy those whom he had called whiter than milk and snow. Hence too the same word which in Hebrew means to be red, in the Arabic language, which is a dialect of Hebrew, means to be white*, and its derived forms, according to the lexicographers, carry an extraordinary whiteness.

units.la: Electus ex millibus. Heb. ad verbum vexillatus, seu, insignitus ex decem millibus. Quasi diceret, coloris suavitate & nitore omnes facile superat dilectus meus. Hoc maximè quadrat in cœlestem Ecclesiæ sponsum, candor est enim lucis æternæ, ut dicitur Sap. 7. v. 26. Et si candori nomen est à luce igneâ,nam candere proprium est ignis, longè potiori jure candoris nomen sibi vindicat, Christus splendor gloriæ, & figura substantiæ ejus, qui lux est, & in quo tenebræ non sunt ullæ, quíque ignis conjumens dicitur Deut. 4. v. 24. Hic sponsus cœlestis merito dicitur electus ex millibus, seu insignis inter decem millia,quia, inquit B. Petrus Damiani in Serm. 2. de Ss. Flora & Lucilla, ex omni Sanctorum multitudine solus est, qui fuit dignus audire: Hic est Filius meus dilectus in quo mihi bene complacui. Ille est, de quo, ut ait idem instituit. Monial. ad Blancam cap. 4. Salomon, Virum, inquit, de mille unum reperi. Millenarius quippe numerus totius humani generis est intelligenda perfectio, in quo Salvator tanquam passer est unicus in ædificio.
units.tr: Chosen out of thousands. In Hebrew, word for word, standard-bearer, or marked out from ten thousand. As if to say: my beloved surpasses all others easily in the sweetness and brightness of his colour.
