This fits most of all the heavenly bridegroom of the Church, for it is the brightness of eternal light, as it is said in Wisdom 7:26. And if the name of whiteness comes from fiery light, for to shine is proper to fire, he claims the name of whiteness for himself by a far greater right, Christ, the brightness of glory and the express image of his substance, who is light, and in whom there is no darkness at all, and who is called a consuming fire in Deuteronomy 4:24. This heavenly bridegroom is rightly called chosen out of thousands, that is, outstanding among ten thousand, because, says Blessed Peter Damian in his second sermon on Saints Flora and Lucilla, out of the whole multitude of the saints he alone was found worthy to hear: This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased. He is the one of whom, as the same writer says in the Nun's Instruction to Blanca, chapter 4, Solomon says: I have found one man among a thousand. For the number one thousand is to be understood as the perfection of the whole human race, in which the Saviour, like a sparrow, is unique on the housetop.

units.la: II. Caput ejus aurum optimum. Agitur hic de Rege coronato sub persona pastoris, ut patet ex cap. 3. v. 11. hujus sacri Dramatis. Sensus itaque horum verborum est idem ac si diceretur : Caput dilecti fulget corona ex selectissimo & optimo, seu purissimo auro conflatâ. Per coronam auream, quâ fulget caput sponsi, ut B. Hier. per cidarim mundam super caput Jofuè filii Josedech Zach. 3. splendorem Divinitatis intellige. Certe, inquit Hier. in Mat. 9. fulgor ipse, & majestas Divinitatis occultæ, quæ etiam in humana Christi facie relucebat, ex primo ad se videntes trahere poterat aspectu. Auri nomine, ait B. Greg. Mag. 33. Moral. cap. 8. ipsa intima Divinitatis claritas designatur, sicut in Canticorum Canticis sponsi species describitur : Caput ejus aurum optimum ; quia vero caput Christi Deus, nil verò est in metallis auro fulgentius, sponsi caput aurum dicitur : quia ejus humanitas ex Divinitatis sua nobis claritate principatur.
units.tr: II. His head is the finest gold. Here the king is spoken of, crowned under the figure of a shepherd, as is clear from chapter 3, verse 11 of this sacred drama. The sense of these words is therefore the same as if it were said: the head of my beloved shines with a crown made of the most select and finest, that is, purest gold. By the golden crown with which the bridegroom's head shines, understand the splendour of the Godhead, as Blessed Jerome understood the clean mitre on the head of Joshua the son of Jehozadak in Zechariah 3. Surely, says Jerome on Matthew 9, the very brilliance and majesty of the hidden Godhead, which shone even in the human face of Christ, could draw to itself the gaze of those who saw it at first sight. By the name of gold, says Blessed Gregory the Great in the 33rd book of the Moralia, chapter 8, the innermost brightness of the Godhead is designated, just as the appearance of the bridegroom is described in the Song of Songs: His head is the finest gold; because Christ's head is God, and nothing among metals shines more than gold, the bridegroom's head is said to be gold, because his humanity takes its beginning from the brightness of his Godhead for us.

units.la: Comæ ejus. Heb. id est, antiæ ejus, ita enim interpretatur doctissimus Bochartus, quia Kuffa Arabicè est comæ portio quæ fronti imminet, aut ex anteriore capitis parte propendet. Hæc capillitii pars ferè sola apparet, cùm caput est corona cinctum. Hinc in præsenti descriptione sponsi coronati sponsa solum antiarum meminit.
units.tr: His locks. In Hebrew, that is, his forelocks; for thus the most learned Bochart interprets it, because kuffa in Arabic is the portion of the hair that hangs over the forehead, or falls down from the front part of the head. This part of the hair alone is almost always visible when the head is encircled by a crown. Hence in the present description of the crowned bridegroom the bride mentions only the forelocks.

units.la: Sicut elatæ palmarum. ἐλάτη, inquit Menochius, est nomen Graecum, significans germen palmae novellum, seu involucrum instar calicis, seu vaginulae fructuum palmae florentium. Porro vaginâ hac se pandente, prorumpunt flosculi numerosi modicè densi, & longis villis appensi, botri magni instar coacervati. Potuerunt autem antiae spondi sic fuisse concinnatae, ut elatarum palmae se se diffundentium figuram oculis exhibuerint; capilli enim in quamlibet figuram flecti possunt. Textus Hebraeus, handquam hanc habet elatarum similitudinem, sed loco illius habet tantum vocem [Hebrew], quae communiter vertitur à recentioribus, acervi, cumuli, seu tumuli, & volunt capillorum crispitudinem, seu densitatem laudari; nos vero cum doctissimo Bocharto vocem taltalim interpretamur pendulas, tanquam geminatum à verbo [Hebrew] pendere, Sic ex [Hebrew] geminato factum [Hebrew] pulcher es Psal. 45. v. 3. De illis igitur antiis loquitur sponsa, quae in sponsi frontem, aures & genas pendulae sunt.
units.tr: Like high palm fronds. [elate], says Menochius, is a Greek name, meaning the young shoot of the palm, or the sheath like a cup, or little case of the fruits of the flowering palm. Moreover, when this sheath opens, there burst forth numerous small flowers, moderately dense, hung on long fine threads, gathered together like a great cluster of grapes. The forelocks of the bridegroom could have been arranged in such a way that they presented to the eyes the shape of spreading high palm fronds; for hair can be bent into any shape. The Hebrew text does not have this comparison to high palms at all, but in place of it has only the word [Hebrew word], which is commonly rendered by more recent writers heaps, piles, or mounds, and they wish the crispness or thickness of the hair to be praised. But we, with the most learned Bochart, interpret the word taltalim as hanging down, as a doubled form of the verb [Hebrew word], to hang, just as the doubled form [Hebrew word] in Psalm 45:3, you are fair, is made from it. So the bride speaks of those forelocks which hang down over the bridegroom's forehead, ears and cheeks.

units.la: Nigrae quasi corvus. Id est, sunt coracini coloris, qui à doctis definitur, color cum aliquo splendore nigerrimus, qualis est gagatis, & nostri serici villosi, cùm color pullus nihil habeat luminis & nitoris. Hinc Vitruvius distertis verbis lib. 8. cap. 3. coracinum colorem à pullo distinguit. Color coracinus placet in capillis, unde Apuleii libro secundo laudatur capillus corvinâ nigredine caerulus, ubi caerulus est idem ac niger, ut Graece κυάνεος. Itaque cum corvo confertur Martialis lib. 3. Epigr. 43. etiam qui arte nigrum habet capillitium, Mentiris juvenem tinctis, Lentine, capillis, Tam subito corvus, qui modo cygnus eras.
units.tr: Black as a raven. That is, they are of the colour of a raven, which learned writers define as a very deep black with some lustre, such as jet or our shot silk, whereas the colour dun has no brightness or sheen. Hence Vitruvius, in plain words in book 8, chapter 3, distinguishes the raven colour from dun. The raven colour pleases in hair, and so Apuleius in book 2 praises hair blue with a raven's blackness, where blue means the same as black, as the Greek κυάνεος [kyaneos] does. Martial too compares with a raven a man who has artificially black hair, in book 3, epigram 43: You pass yourself off as young, Lentinus, with dyed hair; how suddenly a raven, when a moment ago you were a swan!

units.la: Et de Theoro balbutiens Alcibiades, apud Aristophanem in Vespis, Ὀλὰς Θεωλον τὴν κεφαλὴν κόλακα ἔχ̱ς, κόλακα, id est, adulatoris, caput illi tribuens pro κεφαλὴ, id est, corvi capite, quia, R. non poterat aliter efferre quam per L. Sed sequitur Ὁ ῥᾳδῶς γε τὰΤ' Ἀλκιβιάδης ἐβδελύλιξεν,
units.tr: Alcibiades, stammering about Theorus in Aristophanes' Wasps, says: "Ὀλὰς Θεωλον τὴν κεφαλὴν κόλακα ἔχ̱ς" [You have the head of Theorus, a flatterer]. He gives the word kolax, flatterer, in place of korax, raven, because he could not pronounce R and could only say L. But there follows: "Ὁ ῥᾳδῶς γε τὰΤ' Ἀλκιβιάδης ἐβδελύλιξεν" [Alcibiades indeed lisped it rightly].

units.la: Hoc recte balbutiit Alcibiades, quia revera Theorus adulator erat insignis. Porro quia ad formae decus pertinet, ut coracino colore crines fulgeant, à nonnullis summo studio affectantur, atque ab ipso corvo remedia à curiosis expetuntur, quibus hoc consequantur. Hinc Plinius Hist. lib. 29. cap. 5. Corvi quum in aereo vase permixtum, illitumque, deraso capite, nigritiam capillis affert, &c. Alii sanguine & cerebro ejus utuntur cum vino nigro. Alii excoquunt ipsum, & nocte concubia in plumbeum vas condunt. Et Ælianus lib. primi cap. 48. hist. Corvi ova audio nigros esse re pilos. Eadem præscribunt Sextus, Marcellus, & Rasis, & Arabum non pauci alii. Quamadmodum igitur ut Christi seniem gravitatem & sapientiam adumbret Scriptura, cum describit Dan. 7. verf. 9. & Apoc. 1. v. 14. ut senem & canis capillis, ita ut & ipsius juvenilis vigor nunquam senescens comminuendetur, cum nobis exhibet sub specie hominis habentis comam coracini coloris. Comæ capitis sponsi secundum communiorem SS. PP. sententiam & Literæ magis consentaneam sunt symbolum Divinarum cogitationum & consiliorum Dei; Nigror vero comarum est symbolum incomprehensibilitatis eorundem consiliorum & cogitationum Dei.
units.tr: Alcibiades lisped this correctly, because Theorus was in fact a notorious flatterer. Moreover, since it belongs to the grace of appearance that the hair shine with a raven colour, some people eagerly pursue it, and curious persons seek from the raven itself remedies by which they may achieve it. Hence Pliny, Natural History, book 29, chapter 5: When a raven is mixed in a bronze vessel and smeared on a shaven head, it gives the hair blackness, etc. Others use its blood and brain with black wine. Others boil the bird itself and bury it in a leaden vessel on a moonless night. Aelian, Natural History, book 1, chapter 48, says: I hear that the eggs of the raven have black hairs. Sextus, Marcellus, Rhazes and not a few other Arab writers prescribe the same things. Just as Scripture, when it describes Christ in Daniel 7:9 and Revelation 1:14 as an old man with white hair, shows his venerable gravity and wisdom, so here it presents to us, under the form of a man, one whose hair is of raven colour, to signify the never-aging vigour of his youth. According to the more common opinion of the holy Fathers, and the one more in agreement with the letter, the locks of the bridegroom's head are a symbol of the divine thoughts and counsels of God; the blackness of the locks, however, is a symbol of the incomprehensibility of those same counsels and thoughts of God.

units.la: Priusquam ad frequentis versiculi difcuffionem progrediamur, non abs re visum est hic advertere præsentem, quo de agimus, versum à B. Paulino ep. 4. ad Severum laudari his verbis: Caput ejus ut aurum cephas, crines ejus albetes nigræ, sint corax.
units.tr: Before we proceed to the discussion of this frequently quoted verse, it has seemed not out of place to note here that the verse under discussion is cited by the blessed Paulinus, in his fourth letter to Severus, in these words: His head is like gold, cephas; his locks are black, like a raven's.

units.la: Quod spectat ad prius hemistichium, sciendum quòd Hebraice legitur רֹאשׁוֹ כֶּתֶם פָּז rosfcho kethem paz, caput ejus aurum obrizum, ut verrit Sanctes Pagninus, vel ut Arias Montanus, massa auri obrizi; nam & Aquila Græce extulit, λίθος χρυσίς, lapidea vel massa auri. Theodotio vero ἐπίσημον ἐν χρυσίῳ, insignes in auro. Male Kircherus in suo Indice Hebraico, χρυσίον κεφαλήν, aureum caput; nam lxx. scripserunt, χρυσοῦν κεφάς, aurum cephas, ut constat ex S. Gregorio Nyssneno in Canticum Hom. 13. qui κεφάς exponit, purum & quod omni-mi vtura careat, & sincerum. Sunt ergo qui putent ex duabus dictionibus Kethem & pas, five phas ut veteres Hebræi legebant, conflatam fuisse vocem κεφάς. Alii vero existimant lxx. scripsisse χρυσίον ἐκ Φάζ, id est, aurum ex regione Phas advectum, & degenerasse illas duas dictiones in hanc unam κεφάς. Hinc B. Paulinus loco supra laudato per aurum cephas, seu ut alii legunt, aurum paz putat probabilius aliquod & purius aurum significari, sicut illud de terra Evilath. Ef. 13. v. 12. pro Hebræo paz Græci reddidere aurum apyrum, hoc est B. Basilio interprete, quod nullam alienæ materiæ ambiguitatem in se habet, sed quamprimum apparet, solo aspectu fidem facit se probum esse, & ab omni ære, aut alterius cujuscunque metalli permissione purum. Similiter B. Theodoretus in eundem Esaiæ locum, Apyrum, inquit, aurum est, quod etiam sine igne probatum apparet, hoc est, incoctum, ἄπυρον. Nam Græci ἄπυρον nominant, ut ait Agatharchides, aurum quod e fodina tam purum eruitur, ut nulla coctione sit opus ad illud expurgandum. Hoc auri genus multi nunc vocant euryzum, ut advertit Theodoretus, five obryzum, sed perperam; neque enim obryzum pro Ophirizo rizo dicitur, quamvis nonnulli in hac allusione sibi placentes aurum Ophir sic vocent: sed ευρυζον vel οζευζον dicitur aurum, quod saepius despumavit & excoctum est. Nam ζρυειν, ζρυζειν, ευρυζειν de illis rebus dicuntur, quae effervescendo ipsum ejiciunt, unde & obrussa Latine est auri experimentum quod igne sumitur. Interpretes Hebraeum paz vertunt modo aurum, modo obryzum sine addito; subinde aurum obryzum, obryzum pretiosum, lapis pretiosus, topazion, aurum primum, & aurum optimum.
units.tr: As for the first half-verse, it should be noted that in Hebrew it reads רֹאשׁוֹ כֶּתֶם פָּז [rosfcho kethem paz], his head is pure gold, as Sanctes Pagninus renders it, or, as Arias Montanus has it, a mass of pure gold. Aquila rendered it in Greek as λίθος χρυσίς [lithos chrysis], a stone or mass of gold. Theodotion rendered it ἐπίσημον ἐν χρυσίῳ [episēmon en chrysiō], distinguished in gold. Kircher wrongly writes in his Hebrew index χρυσίον κεφαλήν [chrysion kephalēn], golden head; for the Seventy wrote χρυσοῦν κεφάς [chrysoun kephas], gold cephas, as is clear from Gregory of Nyssa in his thirteenth homily on the Song, who explains κεφάς [kephas] as pure, free from all alloy, and unmixed. Some therefore think that the word κεφάς was formed from the two words Kethem and pas, or phas, as the ancient Hebrews read it. Others think the Seventy wrote χρυσίον ἐκ Φάζ [chrysion ek Phaz], gold brought from the region of Phaz, and that these two words were corrupted into the single word κεφάς. Hence the blessed Paulinus, in the passage quoted above, takes gold cephas, or as others read it, gold paz, to mean more probably some especially pure gold, just as in the passage about the land of Evilath (Isaiah 13:12) the Greeks rendered the Hebrew paz as unfired gold (ἄπυρον χρυσίον [apyron chrysion]). This, according to the interpretation of St Basil, is gold that has no admixture of foreign matter in it, but at first sight proves itself genuine, and is pure from any copper or from the admixture of any other metal. Likewise the blessed Theodoret, on the same passage of Isaiah, says: Apyrum is gold which appears proved even without fire, that is, unfired (ἄπυρον [apyron]). For the Greeks call ἄπυρον, as Agatharchides says, gold which is dug out of the mine so pure that no refining is needed to cleanse it. Many now call this kind of gold euryzum, as Theodoret notes, or obryzum, but wrongly; for obryzum is not said of Ophir, although some, pleased with this allusion, call the gold of Ophir by that name. Rather, εὔρυζον [euryzon] or οὐρυζον [ouryzon] is said of gold that has often been skimmed and refined; for ζρυειν, ζρυζειν and εὐρυζειν are used of things that cast out the impurity by boiling, whence also obrussa is the Latin term for the test of gold by fire. The interpreters render the Hebrew paz sometimes simply as gold, sometimes as obryzum without addition, and sometimes as refined gold, precious stone, topaz, first gold, and best gold.

units.la: Jam quod attinet ad alterum praesentis versiculi hemistichium, quod B. Paulinus laudat his verbis, crines ejus abietes nigrae, sicut corax, & Vulgatus sic exprimit, comae ejus sicut elatae palmarum, nigrae sicut corvus, hoc LXX. dixerunt, Βοστρυχοι αυτης ελάται, μελανες ως κοράξ, cincinni ejus elatae, nigri sicut corvus. Significat autem hic vox elatae Graece & Latine palmae fructum, ut diximus, non vero genus palmae prae aliis procerae, ut quidam censent. Nam ελάτη Galeno est genus palmae germen; Dioscoridi, fructus palmarum adhuc florentium involucrum & calyx; Marcellus vocat corticosum palmae adhuc florentis operimentum. Hujus autem elatae cortex niger est, & aliquantum subfulvus. Graecam praeterea vocem ελάτινη fumi pro abiete patet ex LXX. qni eam hoc sensu usurparunt Gen. 21. v. 15. Esa. 41. v. 19. Ezech. 31. v. 8. Hinc viri doctissimi Ambrosius lib. 2. de Spiritu sancto, & in Oston. 15. Ps. 118. & B. Paulinus in laudata epistola quarta ad Severum in praesenti sacri Dramatis versiculo per elatas intellexere abietes. Plinius lib. 12. hist. nat. c. 24. videtur insuper exististimasse & arborem ipsam palmam dici elatam. Pagninus e Graeco LXX. hic vertit, comae ejus ductiles, sed male, cum omnes libri habeant ελάται, non ελάται, quod est ductiles, ut patet ex iisdem LXX. Num. 16. v. 3. neque dictio βοστρυχοι crines masculini generis cum foeminina voce ελάται jungi congrue possit, atque ita versio Pagnini eodem vitio laborat, quo Latina versio, quâ B. Paulinus est usus, crines abietes nigrae, cum Graece sit, Βοστρυχοι ελάται μελανες ως κοράξ. Ergo crines nigri dici possunt, non abietes: sed receptam versionem sollicitandam non censuit B. Paulinus, ut neque S. Ambrosius.
units.tr: Now as to the second half of the present verse, which the blessed Paulinus quotes in these words, his locks are black as a raven's, like the abietes, and which the Vulgate renders thus, his locks are like the palm's elatae, black as a raven: the Seventy said this, Βοστρυχοι αυτης ελάται, μελανες ως κοράξ [Bostrychoi autēs elatai, melanes hōs korax], his curls are elatae, black as a raven. Now the word elatae, in both Greek and Latin, signifies the fruit of the palm, as we have said, and not a kind of palm which is taller than others, as some think. For ἐλάτη [elatē] is for Galen the sprout of the palm-kind; for Dioscorides it is the sheath and calyx of palm-fruit still in flower; Marcellus calls it the bark-like covering of the palm still in flower. The bark of this elate is black and somewhat tawny. That the Greek word ἐλάτινη [elatinē] is used for fir is clear from the Seventy, who employ it in this sense at Genesis 21:15, Isaiah 41:19 and Ezekiel 31:8. Hence the most learned men Ambrose, in book 2 on the Holy Spirit and in his exposition of Psalm 118, and the blessed Paulinus in the fourth letter to Severus already cited, understood by elatae firs in this verse of the present sacred drama. Pliny in Natural History, book 12, chapter 24, seems moreover to have thought that the palm tree itself is called elata. Pagninus, translating from the Greek of the Seventy, renders here his locks are pliable, but wrongly, since all the books have ἐλάται [elatai], not ἐλάται [elatai] meaning pliable, as is clear from the same Seventy at Numbers 16:3. Nor can the word βοστρυχοι [bostrychoi], locks, of masculine gender congruently be joined with the feminine ἐλάται [elatai]; and so Pagnini's version suffers from the same fault as the Latin version used by the blessed Paulinus, locks, firs, black, whereas the Greek is Βοστρυχοι ελάται μελανες ως κοράξ. Therefore the locks may be called black, not firs; but the blessed Paulinus, like St Ambrose, did not think the accepted version should be disturbed.

units.la: 12. Oculi ejus, &c. Ut supra cap. 1. v. 15. & 4. v. 1. sponsae, ita hic sponso tribuuntur oculi columbarum, id est, puri, venusti, simplices, & casti. Describuntur autem hic columbae ad aquas, quod columbae ad aquas oculos habent excitatiores, quia ad eas libentius degunt. Proinde Varro lib. 3. de re Rustica cap. 7. in descriptione πτεισεσθηρισσεια, id est, columbarii ait: Aquam purum esse oportet quae influat, unde & bibere, & ubi se lavare possint; permanda sunt enim hae volucres. Itaque florem columbaria quotquot mensibus oportet crebro everrere.
units.tr: 12. His eyes, etc. As in chapter 1, verse 15, and chapter 4, verse 1, the bride's eyes are compared to doves' eyes, so here the bridegroom is given the eyes of doves, that is, pure, lovely, simple and chaste. Doves are described here as being by the waters, because doves that dwell by the waters have keener eyes, since they live there more willingly. Accordingly Varro, in book 3 of On Agriculture, chapter 7, in describing the dovecote (in Greek [πτεισεσθηρισσεια]), says: The water that flows in must be clean, from which they can both drink and bathe, for these birds must be bathed. And the floor of the dovecote must be swept as often as the months require.

units.la: Quae lacte sunt lota. Id est, quae sunt candidissimae: ac si alba fierent, quae lacte lavantur; ut nigra, quae atramento. Tale est illud Job. 9. v. 30. Si lotus fuero quasi aquis nivis, & fulserint velut mundissimae manus meae. Heb. ad verbum, Si lavero me aquis nivalibus, & mundavero smegmate manus meas.
units.tr: Which have been washed in milk. That is, which are most white: as if they were made white by being washed in milk, as black things are made black by ink. Such is that in Job 9:30: If I wash myself in waters of snow, and make my hands clean as with soap. The Hebrew, word for word, is: If I wash myself with snowy waters, and cleanse my hands with lye.

units.la: Residentes juxta fluenta plenissima. Optime textus Hebraei mentem assecutus est Vulgatus interpres; dicuntur enim hic columbae Hebraice ad verbum, sedentes ad plenitudinem, supple, aquarum (quemadmodum Scriptura passim agit de maris plenitudine, ut videre est. 1 Par. 16. v. 32. Ps. 95. v. 12. & 97. v. 9. &c.) id est, ad loca ubi aquae scatent, & ad riparum altitudinem propè accedunt, ita ut sint potu faciles. Remotum est, quod Philo Carpathius, E. Greg. Mag. Beda, Philippus Abbas, &c. (quod legitur nusquam apud historiae naturalis Scriptores, quod quidem sciam,) columbas ideo dicunt juxta fluenta residere, ut vel intuentes aquam umbram in aqua videant, super quam se projiciant, ungues rapacium sic effugiant. Sed videtur id ex parte sumtum ex historia cujusdam avis, quae Arabice vocatur Chatipho-dhiuibi, quasi dicas raptorem umbrae suae, quia cum umbram suam in aqua videt, accedit ad eam ut rapiat eam. Ita Alcamus Lexicographus Arabs. Haec avis a Damire vocatur Koralia voce Cerica, & Riphraph a motitatione alarum, & Mulaibo dhillibi, ludens cum umbra sua, & asseritur esse in genere passerum, seu avicularum. Itaque haec avis diversa est a graculis, de quibus dicit Tzetzes Chiliad. 4. Hist. 119. quod si in parva pelve oculum fontis, ad umbram suam graculos detinebis, ac si effent Narcissii Lacones, ex iis qui propriam umbram amant. Obiter nota Narcissum non fuisse Laconem, sed Boeotum, ut testantur Ovidius lib. 3. Metam. Fab. 5. Conon Hist. 24. Strabo lib. 9. Hyginus Fab. 271. atque alii sine numero. Tamen Laconem facit Tzetzes loco laudato, & Chil. 1. Hist. 9. quasi fuerit Hyacinthi popularis, quem illi confert Hist. 11. Hic memoriae lapsus ferendus non est in Tzetze, qui eo in loco ita se jactat, Neque enim magis memorem Tzetzae ullum alium Deus in vitam produxit, eorum qui fuerunt, aut nunc sunt. Et paulo ante dixerat se omnes libros scire. Sed ut eo redeamus, unde digressi sumus, Hebraei Scripturae interpretes, quae nos ad columbas, ut ad columbarum oculos referant, sacra verba sic reddunt: Oculi ejus ut columbarum (oculi) ad decursus aquarum, lacte loti, insiti in plenitudine, id est, locum suum implentes, ut gemma palam, quod Hebraice dicitur כליהימ, involutio seu plenitudo lapidis Exod. 28. v. 17. Ita Aben-Ezra, & R. Salomon, qui vult designari oculos columbarum pulchros esse, quia sicut gemmæ palis inclusæ, nec prominent, nec deprestì sunt, sed ita siti ut fossam suam impleant. Hanc interpretationem sequuntur multi recentiores. Verùm hæc interpretatio displicet, primò quòd sic color lacteus oculis tribui videtur, quorum præcipua pars, id est, pupilla, nigra est, aut cærulea, &c. Secundò quòd, quamvis gemmæ palis inclusæ Hebraicè dicantur lapides impletionum, id est, qui palas implent, & insitio gemmæ in palam impletio lapidis, tamen gemma in palam insita nuspiam dicitur יושבת על הלאי manens, seu residens ad plenitudinem. Neque etiam, id aptè dici poterit; quis enim pecuniam ad sacci, aut vinum ad dolii plenitudinem manere vel stare dixerit, cùm saccus pecuniâ, aut vino dolium plenum est? Et hæc quidem de litera. Jam oculi sponsi designant constitutos à Christo Ecclesiæ Pastores & Doctores, qui priùs columbæ dicuntur, quàm ad rivulos aquarum residere memorentur. Nam ut bene Philo Carpathius in præclarum sacri Dramatis locum, Omni labe puri, & defæcati, simplices, planeque prudentes esse debent omnes hi, qui sacra cæterosque, atque cœlestia docituri sunt & monituri, ob idque, postquam ipsi à fluentis Spiritus sancti mundati sunt, & candore virtutis illustrati, juxta plenitudines aquarum residere dicuntur, ut Scripturæ sacræ profana, arcanâque rimantes, ea Christiano populo ad salutem summâ charitate impartiantur.
units.tr: Sitting beside the very full streams. The Vulgate translator has grasped the meaning of the Hebrew text well. For the Hebrew, word for word, says that the doves are sitting at the fullness, understood "of the waters" (just as Scripture often speaks of the fullness of the sea, as one may see in 1 Chron. 16:32, Ps. 96:12 and 98:7, etc.), that is, at places where the waters bubble up and come close to the high banks, so that they are easy to drink from. It is far-fetched when Philo of Carpathus, Gregory the Great, Bede, Philip the Abbot, and others say (a thing which, as far as I know, is read nowhere in the writers on natural history) that doves sit beside the streams so that, by looking at the water, they may see their shadow in it, onto which they throw themselves, and so escape the talons of birds of prey. But this seems to have been taken in part from the account of a certain bird which is called in Arabic Chatipho-dhiuibi, as if you should say the robber of its own shadow, because when it sees its shadow in the water it approaches it in order to seize it. So the Arabic lexicographer Alcamus. Damir calls this bird Koralia, by a Cerican word, and Riphraph from the flapping of its wings, and Mulaibo dhillibi, playing with its shadow; and it is said to belong to the class of sparrows, or small birds. This bird, therefore, is different from the jackdaws of which Tzetzes speaks (Chiliad. 4, Hist. 119), who says that if you put the eye of a spring into a small basin, you will keep jackdaws fixed on their own shadow, as if they were Narcissus the Laconian, one of those who love their own shadow. In passing, note that Narcissus was not a Laconian but a Boeotian, as Ovid attests (Metam. 3, fab. 5), and Conon (Hist. 24), Strabo (book 9), Hyginus (Fab. 271) and countless others. Yet Tzetzes, in the passage cited and in Chil. 1, Hist. 9, makes him a Laconian, as if he were a countryman of Hyacinthus, whom he compares to him in Hist. 11. This lapse of memory in Tzetzes should not be excused, for in that place he boasts in such terms: For God has brought into life no other man more mindful than Tzetzes, of those who have been or are now. And a little before he had said that he knew all books. But to return to where we departed from: the Hebrew interpreters of Scripture, who refer us to doves as if to the eyes of doves, render the sacred words thus: His eyes are like doves' (eyes) beside the water-courses, washed in milk, set in fullness, that is, filling their place, like a jewel set in its socket, which in Hebrew is called kelioth-male, the setting or fullness of a stone (Exod. 28:17). So Aben Ezra and Rabbi Solomon, who holds that the eyes of doves are meant to be beautiful because, just as gems set in sockets neither protrude nor sink, but are so placed that they fill their hollow. Many recent writers follow this interpretation. But this interpretation displeases me, first because it seems to attribute a milky colour to the eyes, whose chief part, the pupil, is black or blue, and so on. Secondly, although gems set in sockets are called in Hebrew stones of fullnesses, that is, which fill the sockets, and the setting of a gem in a socket is called the fullness of a stone, yet nowhere is a gem set in a socket said to remain or sit at the fullness. Nor could this be aptly said: for who would say that money remains or stands at the fullness of a sack, or wine at the fullness of a cask, when the sack is full of money or the cask full of wine? So much for the letter. Now, the eyes of the bridegroom designate the ministers and teachers of the Church, appointed by Christ, who are called doves before they are said to sit by the rivulets of waters. For, as Philo of Carpathus rightly says on the notable passage of the sacred drama: All those who are going to teach and admonish concerning sacred and other, even heavenly, things ought to be pure of all stain, and purged, simple, and plainly prudent; and therefore, after they themselves have been cleansed by the streams of the Holy Spirit and illuminated by the brightness of virtue, they are said to sit beside the fullnesses of the waters, so that, searching out the profane and hidden things of Holy Scripture, they may impart them to the Christian people with the greatest love for their salvation.

units.la: 13. Genæ illius, Hoc est, perpulchræ sponsi genæ concinnâ sui formâ & odoris suavitate similes sunt areolis aromatum, in quibus sedulo artificio, topiarióque opere à pigmentariis confectæ sunt odoriferæ plantationes. Porro pro eo quod habemus, consitæ à pigmentariis,Hebraicè habetur, מגדלות מרקחים, quod est ad verbum, turriculæ aromatum, nempe in quibus pretiosa aromata asservantur, ut illæ turriculæ id sint, quod hodie Gallicè vocamus cassolettes. Genæ, inquit Philo Carpathius, Christi sunt sacræ Scripturæ, quæ unguentum suavissimum spirant ad omnem animi languorem sanandum. Ut enim ex genis cognoscitur homo, itâ plane ex sacris Scripturis apertissima Christi Domini cognitio comparatur; nam ut cecinit quidam de Prophetarum oraculis,
units.tr: 13. His cheeks, that is, the cheeks of the most beautiful bridegroom, are like beds of spices, in their neat form and sweetness of smell, in which fragrant plants have been planted by the perfumers with careful craft and topiary work. Further, for what we have, planted by the perfumers, the Hebrew has migdelot merqachim, which is, word for word, little towers of spices, namely those in which precious spices are kept, so that these towers are what we today in French call cassolettes. The cheeks, says Philo of Carpathus, of Christ are the sacred Scriptures, which breathe the sweetest ointment to heal every weariness of the soul. For just as a man is recognised by his cheeks, so from the sacred Scriptures the most manifest knowledge of Christ the Lord is gained; for, as someone has sung of the oracles of the prophets,

units.la: Omnia de Christo : per Christum cuncta loquuntur.
units.tr: All things are of Christ: through Christ all things speak.

units.la: Labia illius lilia. Id est, liliorum instar (quæ ex Dioscori lib. 3. cap. 99. & Plin. Hist. lib. 21. cap. 5. in Syria sunt laudatissima) purpurea.
units.tr: His lips are lilies. That is, purple, like lilies (which, according to Dioscorides, book 3, chapter 99, and Pliny, Natural History, book 21, chapter 5, are most praised in Syria).

units.la: Distillantia myrrham primùm.Heb. ad verbum, myrrham transeuntem, id est, maximè venalem, utpote quæ præstantissima est. His verbis adumbrat sponsa quàm suavis sit fermocinatio sponsi, in cujus labiis diffusa est gratia. Hæc autem commendant amantissima amabilissimáque Christi verba, & divinam ipsius, sive per se, sive in ministris suis loquatur, eloquentiam, & dicendi vim maximam, gratia & veritate plenam.
units.tr: Dripping myrrh, first of all. The Hebrew, word for word, is passing myrrh, that is, the myrrh most in demand for sale, as being the most excellent. By these words the bride shadows how sweet the bridegroom's speech is, in whose lips grace is poured out. These words, moreover, commend the most loving and lovable words of Christ, and his divine eloquence, whether he speaks in himself or through his ministers, and the greatest power of speaking, full of grace and truth.

units.la: 14. Manus illius tornatiles &c. Id est, manus illius circumdantur annulis aureis, in quorum palis inclusi praefulgent hyacinthi. Sunt autem Christi manus veluti sphaerae quaedam aureae, quae in orbem continuo per beneficentiam, suarumque gratiarum, in quibus ipsius munificentia mirifice resplendet, lucem & influxum communicant mortalibus. Porro Christi manus dicuntur plenae hyacinthis, quia omnis ejus operatio ad spem & desiderium rerum caelestium nos excitat; hyacinthus enim ad caelestia repraesentanda adhibetur, quia hyacinthus tam gemma, quam flos coloris est caelestis.
units.tr: 14. His hands are rounded, etc. That is, his hands are encircled with golden rings, in whose sockets hyacinths shine forth. Christ's hands are indeed like golden spheres which, turning continually in a circle through his beneficence and his graces, in which his munificence shines wonderfully, communicate light and influence to mortals. Moreover, Christ's hands are said to be full of hyacinths, because all his working stirs us up to the hope and desire of heavenly things; for the hyacinth is used to represent heavenly things, since the hyacinth, both as a gem and as a flower, is of a heavenly colour.

units.la: Venter ejus eburneus, distinctus sapphiris. Heb. ad verbum, venter, seu viscera ejus polities eboris operta sapphiris. Sensus est, venter sponsi candore & laevore non absimilis ebori, (cujus scilicet tam insignis est candor, ut illum certatim celebrent, tum sacri, tum prophani scriptores,) operitur sapphiris quam fulgentissimis; atque ita ut capitis, sic sponsa & nativam & adscititiam ventris pulchritudinem laudat. Per ventrem autem intelligit totum corpus quod a collo ad imum ventrem interjacet, B. Petrus Damiani in serm. de S. Joanne Evangelista putat praesenti hemistichio designari in Christo diversitatem humanitatis, a Divinitate inconfuse ipsi unita. In membris, inquit, humani corporis vix aliquid ventre fragilius, sive tenerius invenitur, ideoque per ventrem recte fragilitas in Christo assumtae humanitatis accipitur; ebur autem os est elephantis, quod videlicet animal fortur esse calidissimum, frigidissimaeque naturae. Venter ergo sponsi eburneus est, quia suscepta redemtoris humanitas ab omni peccatorum contagio casta prorsus, & inviolata permansit; Siquidem peccatum non fecit, nec dolus inventus in ore ejus. Sapphirus autem lapis est, serveni coeli colorem habens: unde Exod. 24. in visione Domini dicitur. Erat sub pedibus ejus quasi opus lapidis sapphirini, & quasi coelum cum serenum est. Per sapphiros ergo opera Divinitatis intelliguntur, quae in carne Dominus ostendebat. Venter ergo sponsi distinctus erat sapphiris, quia Christi humanitas divinis virtutibus refulgebat. Nec plenus sapphiris esse dicitur, sed distinctus, ita videlicet, ut inter sapphiros candor eboris appareret; quia sic Dominus ex parte hominis assumti operabatur humana, ut aliquando nihilominus ex parte Deitatis ostenderet & Divina. Nam esurire, sitire, postremo crucifigi, & mori, humanitatis erant opera; miracula vero facere, & non solum alios, sed semetipsum etiam a mortuis suscitare, evidentissima erant Divinitatis indicia.
units.tr: His belly is of ivory, inlaid with sapphires. The Hebrew, word for word, is: his belly, or his bowels, are polished ivory, covered with sapphires. The meaning is that the bridegroom's belly, not unlike ivory in whiteness and smoothness (whose whiteness is so remarkable that both sacred and profane writers vie in praising it), is covered with the most brilliant sapphires; and so the bride praises both the natural and the acquired beauty of his belly, just as she did of his head. By belly, moreover, she means the whole body which lies between the neck and the lower belly. Blessed Peter Damian, in his sermon on St John the Evangelist, thinks that this half-verse designates in Christ the difference between his humanity and his Divinity, which is united to it without confusion. Among the members of the human body, he says, scarcely anything is found more fragile or tender than the belly; and therefore, rightly, by the belly is understood the frailty of the humanity assumed by Christ. Ivory, however, is the bone of the elephant, an animal which is said to be exceedingly hot and of a very cold nature. The bridegroom's belly is therefore of ivory, because the humanity assumed by the Redeemer remained wholly chaste and inviolate from every contagion of sin; for he did no sin, neither was guile found in his mouth. A sapphire, however, is a stone having the colour of the clear sky; whence, in Exodus 24, in the vision of the Lord, it is said: Under his feet was as it were a paved work of sapphire stone, and as it were the heaven in its clearness. By sapphires, therefore, are understood the works of the Divinity, which the Lord showed forth in the flesh. The bridegroom's belly was therefore inlaid with sapphires, because the humanity of Christ shone with divine powers. Nor is it said to be full of sapphires, but inlaid, so that the whiteness of the ivory appeared among the sapphires; because in this way the Lord, on the side of the assumed man, worked human works, so that at times he nevertheless showed forth also the divine works on the side of the Deity. For to hunger, to thirst, and finally to be crucified and to die, were works of the humanity; but to work miracles, and to raise not only others but even himself from the dead, were most evident signs of the Divinity.

units.la: 15. Crura ejus columnæ marmoreæ. Heb. ווו עמודי שיש id est, Aquila & Theodotione interpretibus, columnæ Parinæ. Passim autem à veteribus Hebraeum שׁשׁ vel שׁשׁ vertitur Parinus, seu Parius lapis, seu Parium marmor, ut videre est in Vulgat. & versione lxx. 1. Par. 29. v. 2. Esther. 1. v. 6. Marmor autem, quod ab insula Maris Ægei, (quæ dicitur Paros) Parium nominatur, est candidissimum. Itaque crurum nomine sponsa complectens tibias & femora, unica columnarum marmorearum similitudine quinque in eis commendat dotes, rectitudinis videlicet, candoris, roboris, soliditatis, & debitæ proportionatæque pinguedinis.
units.tr: 15. Her legs are columns of marble. In Hebrew, columns of marble [עמודי שיש], which Aquila and Theodotion rendered columns of Parian stone. Throughout the ancient versions the Hebrew shesh [שׁשׁ] is commonly rendered Parian, or Parian stone, or Parian marble, as can be seen in the Vulgate and the Septuagint at 1 Chron. 29.2 and Esth. 1.6. Marble, which is named Parian after the island of the Aegean Sea called Paros, is very white. So by the word legs, the bride, in describing the shins and thighs with the single image of marble columns, commends five qualities in them: straightness, whiteness, strength, solidity, and a fitting and proportionate fullness.

units.la: Quæ fundatæ sunt, &c. His verbis designat sponsa tam elegantem esse & concinnam crurum sponsi connexionem cum ipsius pedibus aureo calceamento ornatis, quàm eleganter & concinnè super bases aureas fundantur marmoreæ columnæ. Per Christi crura intelligimus quæ fecit & docuit; nam in omnem terram exivit sonus eorum. Doctrina autem & Christi merita assimilantur columnis marmoris Parii, quia veritatis candore, gratiæ pinguedine, rectitudine præceptorum, robore exemplorum, & soliditate promissorum Ecclesiam fulciunt & inflexibiliter sustentant. Hæ autem columnæ marmoreæ dicuntur fundatæ super bases aureas, quia vita & doctrina universa Christi super duplicem amoris basim, Dei videlicet & proximi sustinentur; quidquid enim Christus fecit & docuit, ad hunc retulit finem, ut Deo & hominibus vehementissimum suum testaretur amorem, sicque à Deo impetraret Ecclesiæ duplicem hanc, Dei scilicet ipsius & proximi dilectionem, & homines suo excitaret exemplo, ut juxta ipsius præceptum diligerent invicem, sicut ipse dilexerat eos propter Deum.
units.tr: Which are set upon sockets of gold, etc. By these words the bride signifies that the joining of the bridegroom's legs to his feet, adorned with golden sandals, is as elegant and well-fitted as marble columns are elegantly and neatly set upon golden bases. By Christ's legs we understand what he did and taught, for their sound has gone out into all the earth. His teaching and his merits are likened to columns of Parian marble, because by the whiteness of truth, the fullness of grace, the straightness of his precepts, the strength of his examples and the solidity of his promises, they support the Church and hold it up unbending. These marble columns are said to be set upon golden bases because the whole life and teaching of Christ rests upon a twofold foundation of love, namely of God and of neighbour. For whatever Christ did and taught he referred to this end: that he might bear witness to his most ardent love for God and for men, and so obtain from God for the Church this twofold love, of God himself and of neighbour, and by his own example stir men up to love one another, as he according to his command had loved them for God's sake.

units.la: Species ejus ut Libani. Id est, aspectus ejus, seu quicquid in illo conspicitur, ut vultus decor, oris lepor, habitus totius corporis, non minus plenum est jucunditatis, quàm aspectus Libani herbarum, florum, atque arborum varietate amœnissimi. Christus Libano similis est, quia virtutibus viret, floret, vernat, & ut Libanus amœnus est. Nam cùm in cæteris hominibus divisio gratiarum reperiatur, ita ut hic præditus sit aliquo dono gratiæ, quo alter careat, in Christo omnia gratiæ dona, & in summo quidem gradu concurrunt, quia, ut loquitur Apostolus, in ipso complacuit omnem plenitudinem Divinitatis inhabitare Col. 1. verf. 19.
units.tr: His appearance is like Lebanon. That is, his aspect, or whatever is seen in him, such as the beauty of his face, the grace of his mouth, and the bearing of his whole body, is no less full of delight than the view of Lebanon, most pleasant with its variety of herbs, flowers and trees. Christ is like Lebanon because he flourishes, blooms and grows green with virtues, and is pleasant as Lebanon is. For while in other men a division of gifts is found, so that one has some gift of grace that another lacks, in Christ all the gifts of grace meet together, and in the highest degree, because, as the Apostle says, in him it pleased all the fullness of the Godhead to dwell (Col. 1.19).

units.la: Electus ut cedri. Tantùm cæteros homines proceritate superat, quantum cedri reliquis eminent arboribus. Nam Hebraeis electus significat procerum, sicut bonus pulchrum, Sic. 1. Reg. 9. v. 2. Saül electus & bonus dicitur, & additur ratio, quia ab humero sursum eminebat super omnem populum, & non erat in Israël eo melior, id est, pulchrior ; nam certè animo tunc melior Saüle erat Samuel, fortassis & alii. Hoc optimè quadrat in sponsum Ecclesiæ Christum, qui est caput omnis principatus, & potestatis, ut dicitur Col. 2. v. 10. tantò melior Angelis effectus, quanto differentius præ illis nomen hæreditavit. Heb. 1. v. 4.
units.tr: Chosen as the cedars. He surpasses other men in stature just as cedars tower above the other trees. For among the Hebrews chosen signifies tall, as good signifies handsome. In 1 Sam. 9.2 Saul is called chosen and good, and the reason is added: because he stood higher than all the people from the shoulder upward, and there was none in Israel better than he, that is, more handsome. For certainly in spirit Samuel was then better than Saul, and perhaps others too. This fits very well Christ, the bridegroom of the Church, who is the head of every principality and power, as it is said in Col. 2.10, made so much better than the angels, as he has obtained a more excellent name than they (Heb. 1.4).

units.la: 16. Guttur illius suavissimum. Hebraicè ad verbum, palatum ejus dulcedines, id est, Chaldæo Paraphrasté interprete, verba palati ejus sunt dulcia sicut mel. Sensus est idem ac si diceret sponsa, non solum in sponso est apta figura membrorum cum coloris quadam suavitate,& inter se omnes partes cum quodam lepore consentiunt, ita ut ipsius pulchritudine species nulla vel excogitari possit ornatior ; verùm etiam tanta est suavitas sermonis ejus, ut vox suavior audiri non possit. Hæc in Christum præ filiis hominum formâ speciosum quadrare aptè videntur, de quo vaticinatus est Esaias cap. 42. Non clamabit, nec audietur vox ejus foris, & de quo dictum est Joan. 7. v. 46. Nunquam sic locutus est homo. Et ad quem Apostolorum coryphæus dicit Joan. 6. v. 69. Verba vitæ æternæ habes.
units.tr: 16. His mouth is most sweet. In Hebrew, literally, his palate is sweetness; that is, according to the Chaldee paraphrast Onkelos, the words of his palate are sweet as honey. The sense is the same as if the bride said: in the bridegroom there is not only a fitting arrangement of limbs with a certain pleasantness of colour, and all the parts agree together with a certain charm, so that no more adorned beauty of form can be thought of; but also his speech is so sweet that a voice more pleasant cannot be heard. These things seem fitly to apply to Christ, who is fairer than the sons of men, of whom Isaiah prophesied in chapter 42: He shall not cry out, nor shall his voice be heard abroad; and of whom it is said in John 7.46: Never has a man spoken like this. And to whom the leader of the Apostles says in John 6.69: You have the words of eternal life.

units.la: Totus desiderabilis. Græcè ὅλος ἐπιθυμία, id est, totus desiderium. Hæc verba sic expendit B. Theodoret. Dubitans, inquit, sponsa quibus sponsum laudibus præterea cumularet, uno verbo se expedit, & cuncta complectitur : quid, inquiens, in singulis ejus partibus pulchritudinis explicandis moror ? Totus est desiderium, omnes ad se amandum trahit. B. Hier. lib. 1. contra Jovin. hunc versum his verbis laudat : gutta ejus dulcedines, & totus concupiscentia. B. autem Ambrosius de Christo agens lib. 3. de fide cap. 5. De quo alio, inquit, potuit Ecclesia dicere, Fauces ejus dulcedines, & totus desiderium ?
units.tr: Altogether desirable. In Greek, holos epithymia, that is, wholly desire. The blessed Theodoret weighed these words thus: The bride, doubting with what further praises she should heap up the bridegroom, frees herself with one word and embraces everything: "Why," she says, "should I linger in explaining the beauty of each of his parts? He is wholly desire; he draws all to love him." Saint Jerome, in book 1 against Jovinian, praises this verse with the words: his mouth is sweetness, and he is wholly desire. And Saint Ambrose, speaking of Christ in book 3 of On the Faith, chapter 5, asks: Of whom else could the Church have said, his mouth is sweetness, and he is wholly desire?

units.la: Talis est, &c. Id est, talis tantúsque est ille, quem tam ardenter diligo : & ipse cùm talis ac tantus sit, ut hactenus recensui, me amat, mihíque suâ adhærere amicitiâ non dedignatur. Advertit autem Cassiodorus Christum quidem dici dilectum Ecclesiæ per fidem vivam ipsi inhærentis ; amicum verò quia ipsam de vinculo peccati redemtam, secretorum suorum conscium facere dignatus est.
units.tr: Such is he, etc. That is, such and so great is he whom I love so ardently; and since he is such and so great as I have hitherto recounted, he loves me, and does not disdain to cleave to me in friendship. Cassiodorus, moreover, observes that Christ is called the beloved of the Church because of the living faith by which she cleaves to him, but is called the friend because he has deigned to make her, redeemed from the bond of sin, a sharer in his secrets.

units.la: Chorus Puellarum Ierosolymitarum.
units.tr: The Chorus of the Daughters of Jerusalem.

units.la: 17. Quò abiit dilectus tuus, ò pulcherrima mulierum ? Quò declinavit dilectus tuus, & quæremus cum tecum ?
units.tr: 17. Whither has your beloved gone, O fairest of women? Whither has your beloved turned aside, that we may seek him with you?

units.la: EXPLICATIO.
units.tr: EXPLANATION.

units.la: 17. Quò abiit, &c. Verbis sponsæ de sponso adeò eleganter suavitérque colloquentis, ita captæ atque incensæ sunt sponsi amore sodales sponsæ, ut sollicitè quærant ex ea, ut edisserat, quónam ille diverterit; se enim aiunt sollicitudinis eum quærendi socias esse velle. Sic fideles animæ Ecclesiam de Christi laudibus sermocinantem audientes, totæ flagrant desiderio potiundi, fruendíque ipso cœlesti Ecclesiæ sponso. Unde viam, modum, & media quærunt ab Ecclesia, quibus inveniri possit Christus. Nam qui sine Ecclesia duce Christum quærit, ex filiabus non Jerusalem, sed Belial est, inquit venerabilis Beda, errare, currere, fatigari potest, procedere aut invenire non potest, aiunt Cassiodorus & Haymo.
units.tr: 17. Whither has he gone, etc. By the bride's words, spoken so elegantly and sweetly about the bridegroom, her companions are so captivated and inflamed with love for the bridegroom that they eagerly ask her, as she describes him, where he has turned aside; for they say they wish to be partners in the search for him. So faithful souls, hearing the Church speak of the praises of Christ, all burn with desire to possess and enjoy Christ himself, the heavenly bridegroom of the Church. Hence they ask the Church for the way, the manner, and the means by which Christ may be found. For he who seeks Christ without the Church as guide, who is of the daughters not of Jerusalem but of Belial, may run, wander and grow weary, but cannot advance or find him, say Cassiodorus and Haymo, following the venerable Bede.

units.la: CAPUT SEXTUM.
units.tr: CHAPTER SIX.

units.la: Sponsa.
units.tr: The Bride.

units.la: 1. Dilectus meus descendit in hortum suum ad areolam aromatum, ut pascatur in hortis, & lilia colligat.
units.tr: 1. My beloved is gone down into his garden, to the bed of spices, to feed in the gardens and to gather lilies.

units.la: 1. Ego dilecto meo, & dilectus meus mihi, qui pascitur inter lilia.
units.tr: 1. I am my beloved's, and my beloved is mine: he feedeth among the lilies.

units.la: EXPLICATIO.
units.tr: EXPLANATION.

units.la: 1. Dilectus, &c. Quasi dicat, non procul abiit, sed in vicinia descendit in hortum suum, quo solet se recipere, ut ibi pascat & lilia colligat. Ex mente S. Greg. Nyss. Hom.15. descensus sponsi in hortum suum, descensus est Dei in animam, seu in humanam naturam, quam pulcherrimum plantarat hortum ac paradisum. Per areolam, seu ut lxx. vertunt phialam aromatum, intelligimus verarum virtutum fragrantiam. Pascitur Christus in hortis dum piis Sanctorum, vel naturæ à se assumtæ laboribus delectatur. Lilia colligit dum bonorum defideriorum & operum famâ, ut liliorum odore recreatur.
units.tr: 1. "My beloved, etc." It is as if she said: he has not gone far away, but has come down into the neighbourhood, into his own garden, where he is accustomed to withdraw, to feed there and gather lilies. According to the mind of St Gregory of Nyssa, Homily 15, the bridegroom's descent into his garden is God's descent into the soul, or into human nature, which he planted as a most beautiful garden and paradise. By the little area, or, as the Seventy translate it, "a phial of spices" [φιάλην ἀρωμάτων], we understand the fragrance of true virtues. Christ feeds in the gardens when he takes delight in the labours of the pious saints, or of the nature he has assumed. He gathers lilies when he is refreshed by the good report of holy desires and works, as by the scent of lilies.

units.la: 2. Ego dilecto, &c. Vide quæ diximus supra cap. 2. v. 16. In hæc autem verba erumpit sponsa, dum sodalium interrogationi respondens subito comparere videt dilectum.
units.tr: 2. "I am my beloved's, etc." See what we said above on chapter 2, verse 16. The bride breaks out into these words when, answering the question of her companions, she suddenly sees the beloved appear.

units.la: Sponsus.
units.tr: The Bridegroom.

units.la: 3. Pulchra es, amica, suavis & decora sicut Jerusalem, terribilis ut castrorum acies ordinata.
units.tr: 3. Thou art beautiful, my love, sweet and comely as Jerusalem, terrible as an army set in array.

units.la: 4. Averte oculos tuos à me, quia ipsi me avolare fecerunt. Capilli tui sicut grex caprarum, quæ apparuerunt de Galaad.
units.tr: 4. Turn away thine eyes from me, for they have made me fly away. Thy hair is like a flock of goats that have appeared from Gilead.

units.la: 5. Dentes tui sicut grex ovium, quæ ascenderunt de lavacro, omnes gemellis fœtibus, & sterilis non est in eis.
units.tr: 5. Thy teeth are like a flock of ewes that have come up from the washing, all of them bearing twins, and none of them is barren.

units.la: 6. Sicut cortex mali punici, sic genæ tuæ absque occultis tuis.
units.tr: 6. As a piece of a pomegranate, so are thy cheeks, beyond what is hidden by thy veil.

units.la: 7. Sexaginta sunt Reginæ, & octoginta concubinæ, & adolescentularum non est numerus.
units.tr: 7. There are threescore queens and fourscore concubines, and virgins without number.

units.la: 8. Una est columba mea, perfecta mea, una est matri suæ, electa genitrici suæ. Viderunt eam filiæ, & beatissimam prædicaverunt, Reginæ & concubinæ, & laudaverunt eam.
units.tr: 8. My dove, my perfect one, is only one; she is the only one of her mother, the chosen one of her who bore her. The daughters saw her and called her blessed; the queens and the concubines saw her and praised her.

units.la: EXPLICATIO.
units.tr: EXPLANATION.

units.la: 3. Pulchra es, &c. Alii ex Hebræo reddunt: pulchra es amica mea, sicut Thirsa, decora sicut Jerusalem, terribilis sicut castra cum vexillis. Quibus symbolis quis non videat ingentem, atque optimè cœlestibus armis instructam Christi fidelium multitudinem; uni capiti Christo copulatam, ejus sanguine, tanquam purpurâ fulgentem, ejus augustissimâ cruce tanquam vexillo conspicuam, sub ejus quasi Imperatoris auspiciis, in hoc sæculo felici ausu, felicioríque spe militantem, in futuro vero, æternâ pace omnium bonorum accretione cumulatâ fruentem indicari? Est Ecclesia Christi terribilis, ut castrorum acies ordinata, contra quam portæ inferi non prævalebunt, universa nimirum mirum spirituum infernorum potestas, exercitatissimæ, inquam copiæ, veterani milites, & ad omne audax facinus perpetrandum paratissimi : quales ad portas munitissimarum urbium tuendas solent deputari. Ad literam sponsus dicit sponsam æquè pulchram nobilemque esse, ac Thirsa civitas (cujus nomen Latinè redditur hic Suavis à Vulgat. ) situ & amœnitate loci spectatissima 3. Reg. 14. v. 17. & Jerusalem Urbs perfecti Doctoris, ut dicitur Thren. 2. v. 15. ejusdémque sponsæ oculorum conjectum adeo vehementem esse atque violentum, dicit sponsus, ut oculorum acies æquè formidabiliš fit, atque acies militum ad dimicandum instructa.
units.tr: 3. Thou art beautiful, etc. Others render it from the Hebrew: you are beautiful, my friend, like Tirzah, comely as Jerusalem, terrible as an army with banners. What reader would not see in these emblems an immense multitude of Christ's faithful, most excellently armed with heavenly weapons, joined to the one head Christ, shining with his blood as with purple, conspicuous by his most august cross as by a banner, fighting in this age under the auspices of their Commander, as it were, with a happy daring and a happier hope, and in the future enjoying eternal peace, their every good heaped up and increased? The Church of Christ is terrible as an ordered array of armies, against which the gates of hell shall not prevail; that is, the whole power of the infernal spirits, very well-trained forces, I say, veteran soldiers, and most ready for every bold deed, such as are usually posted to guard the gates of the strongest cities. Literally, the bridegroom says that the bride is as beautiful and noble as the city Tirzah (whose name the Vulgate renders here as Suavis), most admired for the situation and pleasantness of its site, 1 Kings 14:17, and as Jerusalem, the city of the perfect teacher, as is said in Lamentations 2:15. And the bridegroom says that the glance of his bride's eyes is so vehement and violent that the sharpness of her eyes is as formidable as an army drawn up for battle.

units.la: 4. Averte oculos, &c. Hoc est, dejice paululum oculos tuos à me ; eorum enim vim acerrimam ferre non valens, à te, in cujus vultu alioquin acquiesco, invitus oculos abstinere compellor, dum tantisper respiro. Magna hic energia exprimit cœlestis sponsus quanta sit efficacia & virtus orationis & contemplationis, quarum symbolum sunt oculi sponsæ, seu Ecclesiæ ; ipsi enim Deo, si dicere licet, robur ac dominium auferunt ; Sententia enim Dei sanctorum precibus frangitur, inquit B. Hier. in Ezech. 13. Itaque quem admodum Deus Exod. 32. v. 10. non mutabilitate animi, sed ut Mosi deprecandi ausum præbéret, dicebat illi, Dimitte me ut irascatur furor meus ; ita hic divinus Ecclesiæ sponsus, ut ipsam magis atque magis ad sui contemplationem instimulet, dicit ei, Averte oculos, &c. sic ostendens ei, quanti ipse faciat sanctos suos & preces eorum.
units.tr: 4. Turn away your eyes, etc. That is: lower your eyes a little from me; for I, unable to bear their most keen force, am compelled, though unwillingly, to abstain from your gaze, in whose face I otherwise find rest, while I take breath for a little while. Here the heavenly bridegroom expresses with great energy how great is the efficacy and power of prayer and contemplation, whose symbols are the eyes of the bride, or Church; for they take from God himself, if it is lawful to say so, his strength and dominion: for the sentence of God is broken by the prayers of the saints, says St Jerome on Ezekiel 13. So just as God, in Exodus 32:10, not from any change of mind but to give Moses the boldness to pray, said to him, Let me alone, that my wrath may burn, so here the divine bridegroom of the Church, in order to stir her more and more to contemplate him, says to her, Turn away your eyes, etc., thereby showing her how highly he values his saints and their prayers.

units.la: Capilli tui, &c. Quæ sequuntur usque ad versum septimum exclusive, vide exposita supra cap. 4. vers. v. 1. 2. & 3.
units.tr: Your hair, etc. For what follows up to the seventh verse, exclusive, see what was explained above, chapter 4, verses 1, 2 and 3.

units.la: Quæ apparuerunt, Heb. שגלשו pro quo Vulgatus Interpres hic & Ixx. tum hic, tum supra cap. 4. v. 1. legisse videtur גלש, extrito Schin, id est, quæ apparuerunt ; nam גלה est revelari, apparere, videri. Verùm quia verbum שגל nuspiam occurrit, præterquam in duobus locis parallelis, in præsenti videlicet versu, & supra cap. 14. vers. 1. variam varii significationem ipsi tribuunt. Nam Aben-Ezra explicat שגל quæ apparent, & videntur, aut deteguntur ab oculo. Rabbi Jonas, השכיום mane surrexerunt, tanquam ex lingua Arabica, quâ שגל auroram vocari asserit. Alii observant vocem גבה, quæ calvastrum significat, ab onkelo reddi שגל, & à Jonathane שגלשו Levit. 13. v. 41. unde inferunt שגלשו reddendum esse, quæ depilantur ; nempe inter dumeta, & spinas montis Galaad, in quibus hærere solent longiores caprarum villi. In qua sententia sunt præter Rabbi Salomonem Jarchi, Pomarius & Aquinas. Sed quia id videtur incommodum, ut sponsæ crines conferantur, cum capris calvis & depilibus ; Capræ, inquiunt, unt, in illo monte non plane depilantur, sed poliuntur, & comuntur inter arbusta fylvæ, atque ita decoræ fiunt, ac fi pectine pecterentur. Quæ res est fine exemplo, ut pili dumis hærentes sic digerantur, ac fi cum arte & industria pexi fuissent. Nec fi fieret, voce שגלש id significaretur, fi גלש est depilari; aliud enim est comi, aliud depilari & deglabrari; & pecten ad glabrum & calvum nihil attinet; unde in Apophoretis Martialis,
units.tr: Which have appeared: Hebrew shegalshu [שגלשו], for which the Vulgate translator, here and above in chapter 4, verse 1, seems to have read galash with the shin removed, that is, which have appeared; for galah means to be revealed, to appear, to be seen. But because the word shegal occurs nowhere except in the two parallel places, namely the present verse and chapter 14, verse 1, various interpreters assign it various meanings. Ibn Ezra explains shegal as which appear, and are seen, or are uncovered by the eye. Rabbi Jonah renders it they rose early in the morning, as if from the Arabic language, in which he asserts that shegal means the dawn. Others observe that the word gabah, which means a bald head, is rendered by Onkelos as shegal, and by Jonathan as shegalshu in Leviticus 13:41; hence they infer that shegalshu should be rendered which are depilated, namely among the brambles and thorns of Mount Gilead, in which the longer hairs of goats are wont to cling. In this opinion are, besides Rabbi Solomon Jarchi, Pomarius and Aquinas. But since this seems unsuitable, that the bride's hair should be compared with bald and hairless goats, others say: the goats on that mountain are not really depilated, but are polished and combed among the bushes of the wood, and thus become beautiful, as if they had been combed with a comb. But this is an unprecedented thing, that hairs caught in brambles should be arranged as if they had been combed with skill and industry. Nor, even if it were so, would the word shegalsh signify this, if galash means to be depilated; for it is one thing to be combed and another to be depilated and made bald; and a comb has nothing to do with the bald and smooth head; whence in the Apophoreta of Martial:

units.la: Quid faciet nullos hic inventura capillos, Multifido buxus quæ tibi dente datur?
units.tr: What will the box-comb with its many teeth, given to you, do here, where it will find no hairs?

units.la: Et Phædrus, fabulâ 87.
units.tr: And Phaedrus, fable 87:

units.la: Invenit calvus forte in trivio pectinem, Accessit alter æque defectus pilis. Heia, inquit, commune, quodcunque est lucri, Ostendit ille prædam, & adjecit simul, Superum voluntas favit, sed fato invido: Carbonem, ut aiunt, pro thesauro invenimus.
units.tr: A bald man by chance found a comb at the crossroads; another, equally lacking hair, came up. "Hey," said he, "whatever gain there is, let us share it." The first showed his prize, and at the same time added: "The will of the gods favours us, but by an envious fate we have found, as they say, a lump of charcoal instead of a treasure."

units.la: Inter recentiores alii vocem שגלשוך reddunt, quæ nitescunt; alii, quæ emicant: alii, quæ detondent; supple, dumeta; alii, quæ detondentur; alii, quæ fe depilarunt; alii, quæ aspiciunt seu prospectant. Verùm optimè redditur à Vulgato Interprete suprà cap. 4. v. 1. quæ ascenderunt; ita enim & Græci interpretes reddunt in hoc versu quarto præfentis capitis sexti, & Syrus tum hic, tum suprà cap. 4. v. 1. vertit, ut grex caprarum, qui ascendit. Quod sumtum ex Arabica lingua, quâ Gialofa non solùm sedere, sed & ascendere significat, ut testatur Golius ex Giavhari, & Gels, est terra elatior, mons excelsus. Quò eódem facit quòd auroram vocari Arabicè גילש ait Rabbi Jonas; aurora enim nihil quidquam est, quàm ascensus solis. Præterea Chaldæis גלשושיתא vox palàm inde deducta significat collem & eminentiam. Nam Chaldæus in paraphrasi locorum sacri Dramatis, in quibus modò versamur, per capras Galaaditicas intelligit filios Jacob Patriarchæ, & vocem שגלש interpretatur שעברו גלשושיתא כטורא גלעד, qui collectis lapidibus eminentiam (id est, acervum) fecerunt in monte Galaad. Eadem vox גלשושיתא in editione Antuerpiana & Parifiensi habetur in Chaldaica paraphrasi Eccles. 12. v. 8. pro eminentia, seu colle; ibi tamen in editione Buxtorfii legitur גבשיתא per Beth.
units.tr: Among more recent writers some render the word shegalshu as which gleam; others as which shine forth; others as which are shorn, supplying brambles; others as which are being shorn; others as which have depilated themselves; others as which look out or look forth. But it is best rendered, as the Vulgate translator does above in chapter 4, verse 1, which have ascended; for so the Greek interpreters also render it in this fourth verse of the present sixth chapter, and the Syriac, both here and above in chapter 4, verse 1, translates it as a flock of goats which ascends. This is taken from the Arabic language, in which jalasa means not only to sit but also to ascend, as Golius attests from al-Jawhari; and gels is a higher land, a lofty mountain. To which also agrees what Rabbi Jonah says, that the dawn is called gilsh in Arabic; for the dawn is nothing other than the ascent of the sun. Moreover, among the Chaldeans the word galshoshita, plainly derived from this, signifies a hill and an eminence. For the Chaldee paraphrast, in his paraphrase of the passages of this sacred drama with which we are now occupied, understands by the Gileadite goats the sons of the patriarch Jacob, and interprets the word shegalsh as they who, having gathered stones, made an eminence (that is, a heap) on Mount Gilead. The same word galshoshita is found in the Antwerp and Paris editions of the Chaldee paraphrase of Ecclesiastes 12:8 for eminence or hill; there, however, in the edition of Buxtorf it is read gabshita with a Beth.

units.la: Galaad. Hunc montem scatere refinifer arboribus, quales sunt lentiscus, & terebinthus, proindeque aptum esse capris alendis diximus suprà cap. 4. v. 1.
units.tr: Gilead. We have said above, chapter 4, verse 1, that this mountain abounds with trees such as the mastic and the terebinth, and is therefore suitable for feeding goats.

units.la: 5. Dentes tui, &c. Vide dicta suprà cap. 4. verf. 2.
units.tr: 5. Your teeth, etc. See what was said above, chapter 4, verse 2.

units.la: 6. Sicut cortex, &c. Vide quæ diximus cap. 4. verf. 3.
units.tr: 6. Like a cut, etc. See what we said in chapter 4, verse 3.

units.la: 7. Sexaginta sunt Reginæ, &c. Sensus est, habeo quàm plurimas Reginas, & longè plures concubinas, & insuper innumeras in gynæceo, e quo Reginæ vel concubinæ desumuntur, adolescentulas. Reginæ autem dicuntur uxores primariæ, non solius thori Regii, sed & regiminis domûs & bonorum mariti participes; concubinæ autem, uxores secundariæ, solius thori coniortes. S. Epiphanius in Compendio fidei Christianæ docet per sexaginta Reginas intelligendas esse sexaginta duas generationes ab Adam ad Christum usque, quæ compendio sexaginta vocantur, ut Septuaginta Interpretes pro Septuaginta duobus; per octoginta pallacas, hæreses octoginta; per adolescentulas, quarum non est numerus, Philosophorum sectas & gentium varias Religiones.
units.tr: 7. There are sixty queens, etc. The sense is: I have very many queens, and far more concubines, and besides countless young maidens in the harem, from which queens or concubines are taken. Queens are called principal wives, sharers not only in the royal bed but also in the governance of the house and in the husband's goods; concubines, secondary wives, are companions of the bed alone. St Epiphanius, in his Compendium of the Christian Faith, teaches that by the sixty queens are to be understood the sixty-two generations from Adam to Christ, which in summary are called sixty, as the Seventy translators are called for the seventy-two; by the eighty concubines, the eighty heresies; by the young maidens, who are without number, the sects of the philosophers and the various religions of the gentiles.

units.la: 8. Una est mea columba, &c. Quasi diceret, verumtamen hæc sponsa à me unicè diligitur, ipsique vicissim unicè iam charus; quomodo in columbis mirus est amor inter conjuges, & conjugii est lex firmissima. Mutua est inter nos dilectio, & tanta quidem, quanta est inter unicam filiam & ipsius amantissimam pariterque amantissimam matrem. Allusit huc Tertul. de Monogamia cap. 8. ad simplicitatem columbæ provocat, avis non tantùm innocuæ, verùm & pudicæ, quam unam unus masculus novit. Porrò amatoriam hanc dicendi formulam illustrat Tibullus lib. 4. Tu mihi sola places, nec jam te præter in urbe Formosa est oculis ulla puella meis.
units.tr: 8. My dove is one, etc. As if he were to say: nevertheless this bride is loved by me alone, and in turn is most dear to me alone; just as among doves there is a wonderful love between mates, and the law of marriage is most firm. Our mutual love is such, and indeed as great as that between an only daughter and her most loving and equally loving mother. Tertullian alludes to this in On Monogamy, chapter 8: he calls us to the simplicity of the dove, a bird not only harmless but also chaste, which knows only one mate. Moreover, Tibullus, book 4, illustrates this amatory mode of speech: You alone please me, nor is there any girl in the city fair in my eyes apart from you.

units.la: Jam per unicam columbam esse sanctam Dei Ecclesiam intelligendam communis est SS. PP. sententia. Quia nimirum solus Christus diligitur ab Ecclesia, in solum ea credit, solum reveretur.
units.tr: That the holy Church of God is to be understood as the one dove is the common opinion of the holy Fathers. For Christ alone is loved by the Church, she believes in Him alone, and she reveres Him alone.

units.la: B. Greg. Magnus. Mater nostra, inquit, est regeneratrix gratia, apud quam una columba eligitur, quia illos solos colligit, qui in simplicitate permanent, & ab unitate non scinduntur. Multi quippe fideles, cùm in id ipsum intendunt, dum uno desiderio Christi se invicem nutriunt, dum habentes cor unum, & animam unam, in charitate se uniunt, ex multis membris unum corpus efficiunt, omnesque in unitatis simplicitate & unitate viventes, una columba existunt; quæ sola perfecta, & electa genitrici suæ dicitur: quia extra hanc, quam diximus Ecclesiam, nemo ad perfectionem, nemo ad vitam, nisi per hanc solam, gratia fovente, nutritur.
units.tr: Blessed Gregory the Great says: "Our mother is the grace that regenerates, and in her the one dove is chosen, because she gathers only those who remain in simplicity and are not torn from unity. For many believers, when they strive towards this very thing, and while they nourish one another with one desire for Christ, while they have one heart and one soul and are united in charity, form one body out of many members, and all of them, living in the simplicity and unity of unity, are one dove. She alone is called perfect and chosen by her mother, because outside this Church which we have described, no one is nourished to perfection or to life, except through her alone, grace cherishing her."

units.la: Viderunt eam, &c. Id est, omnes illæ Reginæ, concubinæ, & puellæ simul atque tam speciosam, tam ornatam, tam sponsam charam, & omnibus ab ipso prætiatam sponsam intentis oculis contemplantur, immensis laudibus & encomiis eam in cælum efferunt. Porro hæc quàm optimè quadrare in sanctam & Catholicam Ecclesiam nemo diffitebitur, qui serio expenderit quot & quantis encomiis fuerit celebrata à Patriarchis & Prophetis, qui eam ut futuram sponsam in sponso nascituro aliquando prospexerunt. Hanc Philosophi beatam pronunciaverunt, dum deposito erroris magisterio discipuli facti sunt veritatis, cujus ipsa est columna & firmamentum. Hanc & ipsi quoque haeritici celebrare convincuntur, dum ut incautos ad suam sectam alliciant, ementiuntur apud se solos esse Ecclesiam Catholicam. Verum non humanis documentis, sed divinis oraculis Sancta Ecclesia demonstranda est, ut praeclare ait Aug. lib. De unitate Ecclesiae cap. 3.
units.tr: They saw her, etc. That is, all those queens, concubines and maidens, as soon as they see the bride so beautiful, so adorned, so dear a spouse and one prized above all by the bridegroom, gaze upon her with fixed eyes and extol her to heaven with immense praises and eulogies. Moreover, that this fits the holy and Catholic Church very well, no one will deny who weighs seriously how many and how great the praises with which she has been celebrated by the Patriarchs and Prophets, who foresaw her at some time as the bride in the bridegroom yet to be born. The philosophers pronounced her blessed, when, having put aside the teaching of error, they became disciples of the truth, of which she is the pillar and foundation. Heretics too are shown to praise her, when, in order to attract the unwary to their sect, they falsely claim that only they themselves are the Catholic Church. But the holy Church is to be demonstrated not by human proofs but by divine oracles, as Augustine finely says in his book On the Unity of the Church, chapter 3.

units.la: Puellarum Chorus.
units.tr: Chorus of the Maidens.

units.la: Quae est ista, quae progreditur quasi aurora consurgens, pulchra ut luna, electa ut sol, terribilis ut castrorum acies ordinata?
units.tr: Who is she that looks forth as the morning, fair as the moon, clear as the sun, and terrible as an army with banners?

units.la: EXPLICATIO.
units.tr: EXPLICATIO.

units.la: Quae est ista, &c. Sensus est, quae est ista, cujus insignis decor & pulchritudo sicut aurorae stella inter alias stellas emicat, lunae instar coruscat, rutilat ut sol, & in modum aciei instructae est ad aspectum pulcherrima & cum quodam stupore admirabilis? Haec optime quadrant in Philosophos obstupescentes & demirantes sincerissimam sapientiam, qua prae aliis cujusvis sectae hominibus fulget Ecclesia Catholica sole justitiae illustrata; ita ut cuncta & singula ipsius de fide & moribus dogmata non modo erroris & vitii macula careant, sed & maximo sanctitatis & veritatis fulgore splendeant & colluceant, cum Graeciae scholae, ut loquitur B. Prosper adversus Collatorem, cap. 26. Romana eloquentia, & totius mundi inquisitio circa inveniendum summum bonum, acerrimis studiis, excellentissimis ingeniis laborando nihil egerint, nisi ut evanescerent in cogitationibus suis, & obscuraretur cor insipiens eorum, qui ad noscendam veritatem semetipsis ducibus utebantur.
units.tr: Who is she, etc. The sense is: who is she, whose remarkable beauty and loveliness shines among others as a star at dawn, gleams like the moon, glows like the sun, and is arrayed like an army in battle order, most lovely to behold and wondrously admirable? This fits very well the philosophers who stood amazed and wondered at the most sincere wisdom by which the Catholic Church shines above the people of every other sect, illumined by the sun of righteousness; so that all and each of her doctrines concerning faith and morals not only lack any stain of error and vice, but also gleam and glow with the greatest brilliance of holiness and truth. As Blessed Prosper says against Collator, chapter 26: The schools of Greece, the Roman eloquence, and the whole world's inquiry into finding the highest good, labouring with the keenest zeal and the most excellent talents, have accomplished nothing except to vanish away in their own thoughts, and the foolish heart of those was darkened, who used themselves as guides in coming to know the truth.

units.la: Sponsam abeuntem revocat accurrens quàm velocissimè sponsus.
units.tr: The bridegroom hastens swiftly to call back the bride as she departs.

units.la: 10. DEscendi in hortum nucum, ut viderem poma convallium, & 'inspicerem si floruissει vinea, & germinassent mala punica.
units.tr: 10. I went down into the garden of nuts, to see the fruits of the valleys, and to look whether the vine had flourished and the pomegranates had budded.

units.la: 11. Nescivi: anima mea conturbavit me propter quadrigas Aminadab.
units.tr: 11. I knew not: my soul troubled me because of the chariots of Amminadib.

units.la: 12. Revertere, Revertere Sulamitis : revertere, revertere, ut intueamur te.
units.tr: 12. Return, return, O Shulamite; return, return, that we may gaze upon you.

units.la: EXPLICATIO.
units.tr: EXPLANATION.

units.la: 10. UT viderem poma convallium. Hebraei ferè omnes reddunt convallis, quos imitatus est Pagninus. Lxx. vertunt, descendi in hortum nucis videre genimina torrentis. Symmachus vertit, ad considerandos fructus convallis ; alius verò interpres Græcus, ad videndum fructum torrentium. Vatablus Græcos sequutus, ut spectarem, inquit, virentes plantas ad torrentem. Quæ omnes versiones ita cum Vulgata nostra lectione conspirant, ut locum hujus hortⁱ manifeste ostendant; nempe vallem Hennon, in quam, utpote humili loco sitam à Regia Salomonis descendendum omninò erat. Irrigabat autem vallem hanc, & Regium hortum torrens Cedron. Quare meritò descendit, ut videret pomifera ligna horti, quæ juxta torrentis fluenta, uberiores & pulchriores fructus afferebant; vel si malis juxta Vulgatam interpretari, descendit videre fructus, vel poma lignorum, quæ juxta diductos per declivia convallis plures rivulos plantata sunt. Quia enim plurium horti sui fructuum copiam commendet, non convallis sed convallium dixit, per quas decurrunt aquarum rivuli, proptereáque etiam citatus Græcus Interpres, torrentium dixit, non torrentis, cùm unus tantummodò Cedron torrens legatur, aut hodiernâ die conspiciatur propter Hierosolymam fluere. Mens verborum sponsi est eadem ac si diceret ad sponsam amabilissimam : Tandem ad te veluti ad hortum pretiosissimum, pariter & amœnissimum diverti deliciarum causâ & voluptatis. Jam autem supra c. 4. v. 12. sponsus sponsam comparaverat cum horto concluso, & ibid.v.15. cum fonte hortorum, qui scilicet, ut refert Schindlerus, oritur ad pedem Libani, rigans omnes hortos, & totam regionem quæ est inter Libanum & Tripolim. Porrò tam arbores quàm herbæ sepтo cinctæ & munitæ horti nomine significantur. Sic cœlestis sponsus hic inducitur quasi jamjam descendens è cœlis, quasi è sinu Patris ad desponsatam sibi Ecclesiam in perpetua charitate dilectam per Incarnationis mysterium animi gratiâ, veluti ad Paradisum voluptatis divertens, quia deliciæ ipsius, esse cum filiis hominum.
units.tr: 10. To see the fruits of the valleys. Almost all the Hebrews render this as of the valley, and Pagninus follows them. The Seventy translate, I went down into the walnut garden to see the produce of the torrent. Symmachus renders, to consider the fruits of the valley, and another Greek interpreter, to see the fruit of the torrents. Vatablus, following the Greeks, says, that I might look at the green plants by the torrent. All these versions agree with our Vulgate reading in showing the place of this garden clearly. It was the valley of Hinnom, into which the bridegroom had to go down, since it lay low, below the king's palace. A torrent, the Kidron, watered both this valley and the royal garden. He rightly went down to see the fruit-bearing trees of the garden, which, beside the streams of the torrent, bore richer and finer fruit. Or, if you prefer to interpret according to the Vulgate, he went down to see the fruits or the apple trees, which were planted beside the many little streams that run down the slopes of the valley. Since he means to commend the abundance of the fruits of his garden, he says not valley but valleys, through which the streams of water run. For the same reason the Greek interpreter cited also says torrents, not torrent, since only one torrent, the Kidron, is read of, or is seen today, flowing past Jerusalem. The meaning of the bridegroom's words is the same as if he said to his most lovely bride: "At last I have turned aside to you, as to a most precious and most pleasant garden, for the sake of delight and pleasure."
