Now already in chapter 4, verse 12, the bridegroom had compared the bride with a shut-up garden, and in verse 15 with a fountain of gardens, which, as Schindler reports, rises at the foot of Lebanon, watering all the gardens and the whole region between Lebanon and Tripoli. Moreover, both trees and herbs enclosed and protected by a hedge are signified by the name of garden. So the heavenly bridegroom is here introduced as if he were just now coming down from heaven, as if from the Father's bosom, to his betrothed Church, loved in perpetual charity; through the mystery of the Incarnation he turns aside in the grace of his soul, as to a paradise of delight, because his delights are to be with the sons of men.

units.la: II. Nescivi, &c. Sensus est, mei quasi oblitus de hoc uno fui foliicitus, ut quàm velocissimè ad sponsam venirem, nec ad eam occurrens velocitate vel à celerrimis quadrigis anteverterer. Idem est sensus textûs Hebræi, qui sic habet ad verbum, nescivi, anima mea posuit me currus Ammi nadib, id est, populi mei Principis. Nempe Principes, & aulici, qualis fortean ævo Salomonis fuit Aminadab, solent subvehi celerrimis in quadrigis. Et revera Christus Ecclesiæ sponsus, suæ quasi Divinitatis & majestatis oblitus, in plenitudine temporum exinanivit semetipsum formam servi accipiens, & ut quàm citissimè à summo cœlo ad desponsatam sibi in terris Ecclesiam adveniret, & matrimonio consummato una cum ipsa fieret caro, à Regalibus sedibus veniens exultavit ut gigas ad viam incomparabili velocitate currendam; ut enimvait B. Greg. 18. Moral. cap. 27. Nuntiante Angelo, & Spiritu sancto adveniente, mox Verbum in utero, mox intra uterum Verbum caro. Et B. Fulgentius in lib. de Fide ad Petrum cap. 18. Firmissimè tene & nullatenus dubites, non carnem Christi sine Divinitate conceptam in utero Virginis priusquàm suscipieretur à Verbo; sed ipsum Verbum Deum suæ carnis acceptione conceptum, ipsamque carnem Verbi Incarnatione conceptam.
units.tr: II. I knew not, &c. The sense is: forgetful, as it were, of myself, I was anxious about this one thing, that I might come to the bride as quickly as possible, and that, meeting her, I should not be outrun even by the swiftest chariots. The Hebrew text has the same sense, which reads word for word, I knew not; my soul set me on the chariots of Ammi-nadib, that is, of the prince of my people. Princes and courtiers, such as perhaps Amminadab was in the time of Solomon, are usually carried in the swiftest chariots. And indeed Christ, the bridegroom of the Church, forgetful as it were of his Divinity and majesty, emptied himself in the fullness of time, taking the form of a servant. So that he might come as quickly as possible from the highest heaven to the Church betrothed to him on earth, and that, the marriage being consummated, he might become one flesh with her, he came from his royal seat and rejoiced like a giant to run the way with incomparable speed. For as Blessed Gregory says in Moral 18, chapter 27: When the angel announced it and the Holy Spirit came, straightway the Word was in the womb, and straightway within the womb the Word became flesh. And Blessed Fulgentius, in the book On the Faith, to Peter, chapter 18: Hold most firmly, and never doubt, that the flesh of Christ was not conceived in the womb of the Virgin without the Divinity before it was assumed by the Word; but that the Word himself, God, was conceived by the assumption of his flesh, and that the flesh itself was conceived by the Incarnation of the Word.

units.la: 12. Revertere, &c. Quasi dicat, Revertens occurre ocyùs, perfectissima mulierum; revertere, inquam, revertere festinanter, ut nos te contemplemur. Nempe sponsus sponsæ absentiam minimè ferens, térque, quatérque eam abeuntem ad se quàm suavissimè revocat. Ecclesiam sibi olim desponsatam Divinis promissionibus & doctrinis insignitam præ cunctis gentibus, & Patriarcharum Prophetarumque miraculis & exemplis decoratam relictâ Dei Lege traditiones hominum sequentem, & post concupiscentias suas abeuntem accurrens Salvator ad se benignè & misericorditer revocat, ut ipsam intueatur, Oculo, inquit D. Th. misericordiæ, miserendo ipsius.
units.tr: 12. Return, &c. It is as if he said: "Returning, come to meet me quickly, most perfect of women; return, I say, return in haste, that we may gaze upon you." The bridegroom, not bearing the bride's absence, calls her back to himself most sweetly, again and again, as she goes away. The Saviour runs to her and calls her back to himself kindly and mercifully: the Church, once betrothed to him, distinguished above all nations by divine promises and teachings, and adorned with the miracles and examples of the patriarchs and prophets, has left God's Law, follows the traditions of men, and goes away after her own lusts. He calls her back so that he may look upon her, with the eye, says St. Thomas, of mercy, by having mercy on her.

units.la: Sulamitis. Id est, Jerosolymitana. Sic autem dicitur speciosa Salomonis sponsa ob insignem formæ decorem, ratione cujus supra v. 3. describitur pulchra, suavis & decora sicut Jerusalem. Pro voce, Sulamitis, multi codices Græci & Latini habent, Sunamitis, ut & Officium Ecclesiasticum Romanenfium habet in communi Virginum. Forte quia Abifag Sunamitis assumta ad calefaciendum Regem David senio confectum, erat, ut dicitur 3 Reg. i.v. 4. puella pulchra nimis, Sunamitides dictæsunt omnes virgines præ cæteris speciosæ & formâ insignes. Sic nos Ciceronem vocamus, qui eloquentiâ præ cæteris pollet. Sic ipse Christus Joannem Baptistam vocavit Eliam, Mat. 17. v. 12. quia spiritu & virtute Eliæ præditus erat. Philo Carpathius pro voce, Sulamitis, vel Sunamitis, solus legit Odollamitis; hàncque vocem interpretatur testimonium in aqua.
units.tr: Shulammite. That is, the woman of Jerusalem. The beautiful bride of Solomon is so called on account of her remarkable comeliness, on which account in verse 3 above she is described as beautiful, sweet and comely as Jerusalem. In place of the word Shulammite, many Greek and Latin manuscripts have Shunammite, as the Roman Ecclesiastical Office also has in the common of virgins. Perhaps because Abishag the Shunammite, taken to warm King David when he was worn out with age, was, as it is said in 3 Kings 1, verse 4, a very beautiful girl, all virgins who were more comely than others and distinguished by their beauty were called Shunammites. So we call Cicero the Roman, who excels others in eloquence. So Christ himself called John the Baptist Elias, Matthew 17, verse 12, because he was endowed with the spirit and power of Elijah. Philo of Carpathus alone, instead of the word Shulammite or Shunammite, reads Odollamite, and interprets this word as a testimony in water.

units.la: CAPUT SEPTIMUM.
units.tr: CHAPTER SEVEN.

units.la: Iterum erumpit sponsus in sponsæ laudes.
units.tr: Once again the bridegroom breaks out into praise of the bride.

units.la: 1. QUid videbis in Sulamite, nisi choros castrorum?
units.tr: 1. What will you see in the Shulammite, except the dances of the camp?

units.la: EXPLICATIO.
units.tr: EXPLICATION.

units.la: 1. QUid videbis, &c. Heb. & Græc. videbitis. Sensus est idem, ac si diceret, Sponsæ pulchritudo instar numerosi exercitûs, & aciei instructæ potentissima est ad quodlibet ferreum pectus molliendum; quia videlicet intuentes non in admirationem tantùm, sed in stuporem convertit. Vide quæ diximus supra cap. 6. v. 9. Certè Ecclesiæ Deo desponsatæ infusa divinitùs pulchritudo, quæ ex multarum virtutum varietate conflatur, intuentium oculos totos ad sui admirationem convertit, & rapit.
units.tr: 1. What will you see, etc. The Hebrew and Greek have will you see. The sense is the same as if he said: the bride's beauty is like a numerous army and a battle line drawn up in order, and it is most powerful to soften any iron heart, because those who look upon her are turned not merely to admiration but to astonishment. See what we said above, chapter 6, verse 9. Certainly the beauty of the Church betrothed to God, poured into her from above and compounded of the variety of many virtues, turns and carries away the eyes of all who see her to wonder at her.

units.la: In Sulamite. Sulamitis interpretatur Pacifica, quòd nomen optimè quadrat in Ecclesiam desponsatam Regi pacifico super omnes reges universæ terræ magnificato. Hinc & Ecclesia toties in hoc sacro Dramate assimilatur columbæ, quæ ab Ovidio Metam. lib. 7. Fabulâ. 12. vocatur Placida, quia ut ait B. Cyrillus Alexandrinus lib. 15. de Adoratione. supremum mansuetudinis fastigium attingit. Vide Commentarium nostrum in Math. 10. v. 16. Hinc & Apostolus monet & dicit in Epistola ad Titum c. 1. v. 7. & 8. Ecclesiæ Episcopum oportere esse benignum, non iracundum. Ad quæ verba Hieronymus : Sciat Episcopus & Presbyter sibi populum confervum esse non servum: reverà nihil est fœdius præceptore furioso : neque vero qui aliquan‐ do irascitur, iracundus est : sed qui crebrò hac passione superatur, torvo vultu, trementibus labiis, rugatâ fronte, effrænatis convi‐ ciis, facie inter pallorem & ruborem variatâ, clamore perstrepens, & errantes non tam ad bonum retrahens, quàm ad malum sævitiâ suâ præcipitans. Appositè hanc in rem Cicero in lib. 1. de Of‐ ficiis : Semper ira procul absit, cum qua nihil rectè, nihil confide‐ ratè fieri potest ; quæ enim cum aliqua perturbatione fiunt, ea nec constanter fieri possunt, nec iis qui adsunt probari.
units.tr: In Sulamite. Shulamite is interpreted as Peaceable, which name fits the Church betrothed to the peaceable King, who is exalted above all the kings of the whole earth. Hence also the Church is so often compared in this sacred drama to a dove, which Ovid in Metamorphoses book 7, fable 12, calls gentle, because, as St Cyril of Alexandria says in book 15 on Worship, it attains the highest pitch of meekness. See our commentary on Matthew 10, verse 16. Hence the Apostle also admonishes, and says in the Epistle to Titus, chapter 1, verses 7 and 8, that the bishop of the Church ought to be gentle, not quick-tempered. On these words Jerome says: Let the bishop and the presbyter know that the people are their fellow-servants, not their slaves. Truly nothing is more foul than a furious teacher. Nor is he who sometimes grows angry quick-tempered; but he who is often overcome by this passion, with a scowling face, trembling lips, a wrinkled brow, unbridled insults, a face shifting between pallor and redness, shouting loudly, and dragging the wandering not so much back to the good as hurling them headlong into evil by his savagery. To the point here Cicero says in book 1 of On Duties: Let anger always be far away, for with it nothing can be done rightly, nothing with due deliberation; for what is done with some disturbance can neither be done consistently nor be approved by those who are present.

units.la: Inchoatam sponsæ laudationem prosequitur spon‐ sus ipsam alloquens.
units.tr: The bridegroom, addressing the bride, continues the praise he had begun.

units.la: 1. QUàm pulchri sunt gressus tui in calceamentis, filia Principis ! Junꝭturæ fœmorum tuorum, sicut monilia, quæ fabricata sunt manu artificis.
units.tr: 1. How beautiful are your feet in sandals, O daughter of the prince! The joints of your thighs are like jewels, the work of the hands of a craftsman.

units.la: 2. Umbilicus tuus crater tornatilis, nunquam in‐ digens poculis : venter tuus sicut acervus tritici, val‐ latus liliis.
units.tr: 2. Your navel is a rounded bowl that never lacks mixed wine; your belly is like a heap of wheat, fenced about with lilies.

units.la: 3. Duo ubera tua sicut duo hinnuli gemelli ca‐ preæ.
units.tr: 3. Your two breasts are like two young roes, twins of a gazelle.

units.la: 4. Collum tuum sicut turris eburnea. Oculi tui sicut piscinæ in Hefebon, quæ sunt in porta Filiæ multitudinis. Nasus tuus sicut turris Libani, quæ respicit contra Damascum.
units.tr: 4. Your neck is like a tower of ivory. Your eyes are like the pools in Heshbon, which are by the gate of the daughter of many. Your nose is like the tower of Lebanon, which looks towards Damascus.

units.la: 5. Caput tuum ut Carmelus. Et comæ capitis tui, sicut purpura Regis vincta canalibus.
units.tr: 5. Your head is like Carmel, and the locks of your head are like purple of the king bound in channels.

units.la: 6. Quàm pulchra es, & quàm decora charíssima in deliciis !
units.tr: 6. How fair you are, and how pleasant, O love, for delights!

units.la: 7. Statura tua assimilata est palmæ, & ubera tua botris.
units.tr: 7. Your stature is like a palm tree, and your breasts like its clusters.

units.la: 8. Dixi : ascendam in palmam, & apprehendam fructus ejus : & erunt ubera tua sicut botri vineæ. Et odor oris tui sicut malorum.
units.tr: 8. I said: I will climb up into the palm tree, and take hold of its fruit; let your breasts be like clusters of the vine, and the smell of your breath like apples.

units.la: 9. Guttur tuum sicut vinum optimum, dignum dilecto meo ad potandum, labiisque & dentibus illius ad ruminandum.
units.tr: 9. Your mouth is like the best wine, worthy to go down smoothly for my beloved, and causing the lips and teeth of those who sleep to speak.

units.la: EXPLICATIO.
units.tr: EXPLICATION.

units.la: I. QUàm pulchri, &c. Id est, quàm elegantiffimo calceamentorum ornatu, ut Principis filiam decet, pedes tui ornantur. Magna pars integri encomii, quod in hoc capite continetur, decorem sponsæ commendat, à comtu potiùs asciti-tio, quàm à natura. Hîc ergo desponsatæ sibi puellæ venustatem sponsus à calceamentis commendat; quomodo & Homerus in Hymno Mercurii matrem ipsius, Maiam scilicet Atlantis ex Pleione Nympha filiam vocat καλλιπῖξλιλον, pulchra calceamenta habentem. De cura autem & elegantia calceorum apertum est testimonium in historia Rhodopidis puellæ venustissimæ, cui dum lavaret, aquila calceum rapuit, illúmque longè asportatum in sinum Psammetichi Regis Ægypti demisit, qui ut fert Ælianus Hist. var. lib. 13. c. 33. miratus pulchritudinem calcei, & fabricationis artem, & concinnitatem, puellam, cujus ille erat, summo labore & diligentiâ quæsitam abduxit sibi copulandam.
units.tr: I. How beautiful, etc. That is, your feet are adorned with the most elegant ornament of sandals, as befits a prince's daughter. A large part of the whole praise contained in this chapter commends the bride's charm as coming from adornment acquired rather than from nature. Here, then, the bridegroom commends the charm of the girl he has betrothed to himself by her sandals, just as Homer in the Hymn to Hermes calls the mother of Hermes, Maia, daughter of Atlas and the nymph Pleione, [καλλίπεδιλον], having beautiful sandals. Concerning the care and elegance of sandals there is clear testimony in the story of the most lovely girl Rhodopis, while she was bathing, an eagle snatched her sandal and carried it far off and dropped it into the lap of Psammetichus, king of Egypt, who, as Aelian reports in Historical Miscellany book 13, chapter 33, admiring the beauty of the sandal, and the skill of its making, and its elegance, sought out with the greatest effort and diligence the girl to whom it belonged and took her away to be joined to himself.

units.la: Pedes Ecclesiæ Deo desponsatæ affectus sunt cordis, quibus ad Deum accedit. Perelegantes, & apti ad hos pedes calcei decor est virginitatis ex B. Hieronymo contra Jovinianum. Est quidem paucorum in Ecclesia virginitas in carne, inquit Aug. in Ps. 147. omnium debet esse in corde. Virginitas carnis corpus intactum; virginitas cordis fides incorrupta. Idem tract. 13. in Joan. Integritas etiam corporis est in Ecclesia, & honorabilius membrum; alia non in corpore, sed omnia in mente servant virginitatem. Quæ est virginitas mentis? Integritas fidei, solida spes, sincera charitas. Itaque ut ait idem S. Doctor Serm. 23. de verbis Domini secundum Matthæum, Tota Ecclesia, quæ constat ex virginibus, & pueris, & maritatis, & uxoratis, uno nomine Virgo est appellata. Unde hoc probamus? Apostolum audi dicentem, non solis sanctimonialibus, sed universæ potiùs Ecclesiæ Dei: Despondi vos uni viro Virginem castam exhibere Christo.
units.tr: The feet of the Church betrothed to God are the affections of the heart by which she draws near to God. The adornment of virginity is a most elegant and fitting sandal for these feet, according to St Jerome against Jovinian. Indeed, virginity in the flesh belongs to few in the Church, says Augustine on Psalm 147, but virginity of the heart ought to be in all. Virginity of the flesh is a body untouched; virginity of the heart is faith uncorrupted. The same in tractate 13 on John: There is also integrity of the body in the Church, and it is the more honourable member; others keep virginity not in the body but in the mind, and all keep it in the mind. What is virginity of the mind? Integrity of faith, firm hope, sincere love. Therefore, as the same holy Doctor says in sermon 23 on the words of the Lord according to Matthew, the whole Church, which consists of virgins, and boys, and married and wed people, is called by one name, Virgin. How do we prove this? Hear the Apostle saying, not to the holy women only but rather to the whole Church of God: I have betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a chaste virgin to Christ.

units.la: * Filia Principis dicitur Ecclesia, quia verè est filia Spiritûs sancti, quem B. Theodoretus hîc Principis vocabulo significatum ait, & idcirco Spiritûs Principalis nomine Psalm. 50. appellatum.
units.tr: * The Church is called daughter of the prince, because she is truly a daughter of the Holy Spirit, whom St Theodoret here says is signified by the word prince, and for that reason is called by the name of Principal Spirit in Psalm 50.

units.la: Gressus. Heb. plantæ, & per synecdochen, pedes.
units.tr: Steps. Hebrew soles of the feet, and by synecdoche feet.

units.la: Filia Principis. Hæc sponsæ appellatio satis indicat eam sic sub habitu pastorali latere, ut tamen semper & Regiam personam, Regiúmque ornatum, ut ipsius natalium splendorem decet, retineat. Junctura femorum, &c. Id est, cingulum, quod est in ambitu lumborum tuorum, æquat magnificentiam cujusvis mundi muliebris, quantumvis affabrè facti & concinnati. Significat autem cœlestis sponsus hac locutione desponsatam sibi Ecclesiam æque ornari omnium concupiscentiarum refrænatione, quâ juxta principis Apostolorum præceptum 1 Pet. 1. v. 13. mentis nostræ lumbi succinguntur, atque mulier speciosa pretiosissimis quibusque ornamentis & summo artificio factis.
units.tr: Daughter of the prince. This title of the bride sufficiently indicates that she lies hidden under a shepherd's garb, and yet always keeps a royal person and royal ornament, as the splendour of her birth befits. The joints of the thighs, etc. That is, the girdle which is around your loins equals the magnificence of any womanly adornment of the world, however skilfully made and finely wrought. By this expression the heavenly bridegroom signifies that the Church betrothed to him is equally adorned by the restraint of all desires, by which, according to the command of the prince of the Apostles in 1 Peter 1, verse 13, the loins of our mind are girded, and a beautiful woman is adorned with the most precious ornaments and works of the greatest craftsmanship.

units.la: Junctura. Heb. [illegible, ~5 letters], quam vocem interpretamur hic cingulum, quo femora, seu lumbi præcinguntur & ambiuntur. Derivatur autem vox Hebraea à radice [illegible, ~3 letters], id est, circuivit. Quia autem cinguli beneficio partes vestium in terram defluentes cum iis, quæ corpus contegant, juxta femora conjunguntur, cingulum sponsæ potuit appellari Junctura femorum. Quin & vox Hebraea [illegible, ~3 letters] non tantum femur sonat, sed & latus, pedem, coxam, lumbos, &c.
units.tr: Joining. Hebrew [illegible, ~5 letters], which word we here render girdle, by which the thighs or loins are girded and encircled. The Hebrew word is derived from the root [illegible, ~3 letters], that is, went round. Because by means of the girdle the parts of the garments that fall down to the ground are joined at the thighs to those which cover the body, the bride's girdle could be called joint of the thighs. Indeed the Hebrew word [illegible, ~3 letters] means not only thigh, but also side, foot, hip, loins, etc.

units.la: Monilia.Heb. [illegible, ~6 letters] à nomine Arabico singulari [illegible, ~3 letters], Jod& Aleph permutatis; ut in [illegible, ~8 letters] ex [illegible, ~3 letters] & [illegible, ~8 letters] ex [illegible, ~2 letters]. Est autem [illegible, ~3 letters] apud Arabes proprie mundus muliebris, ut videre est apud Eutychium Alexandrinum Patriarcham in Annalibus, ubi loquitur de vitulo aureo pag. 106. & in Arabica Paraphrasi 1 Pet. 3. v. 3. A Vulgato interprete hæc vox Arabica hîc & Osea 2. v. 13. redditur monile; cùm autem monile non fit nisi pars ornatus muliebris, synecdochicè per monile, seu monilia intelligendum est quicquid spectat ad mulieris ornatum. Sæpe vox [illegible, ~3 letters] latiùs sumitur Arabicè, & in virorum etiam ornamenta quadrat; unde apud Geographum Nubiensem usurpatur de Nigritis, & de Rege Abutalebo; & apud mox laudatum Eutychium pag. 205. de Rege Josaphat.
units.tr: Jewels. Hebrew [illegible, ~6 letters], from the singular Arabic noun [illegible, ~3 letters], with Yod and Aleph interchanged, as in [illegible, ~8 letters] from [illegible, ~3 letters] and [illegible, ~8 letters] from [illegible, ~2 letters]. Among the Arabs the word [illegible, ~3 letters] properly means women's adornment, as can be seen in Eutychius the Alexandrian patriarch in his Annals, where he speaks of the golden calf, page 106, and in the Arabic paraphrase of 1 Peter 3, verse 3. By the Vulgate translator this Arabic word is rendered necklace here and in Hosea 2, verse 13; but since a necklace is only a part of women's ornament, by synecdoche necklace or necklaces must be understood as whatever pertains to a woman's adornment. Often the Arabic word is taken more widely, and it fits the ornaments of men too; hence the Nubian geographer uses it of the Negroes and of King Abutalebo, and Eutychius, mentioned above, uses it on page 205 of King Josaphat.

units.la: Fabricata sunt manu artificis. Non cujusvis, sed aurifabri, cujus est monilia, torques, annulos, & minuta hujusmodi, quæ ad muliebrem mundum pertinent, fabricare & concinnare.
units.tr: They were made by the hand of the craftsman. Not by just any craftsman, but by a goldsmith, whose work it is to make and fashion necklaces, torques, rings and small items of this kind, which belong to women's finery.

units.la: 2. Umbilicus tuus, &c. Q. d. Est & circa umbilicum tuum gemma non absimilis crateri lunæ instar rotundo, cujus gemmæ pulchritudo & splendor nunquam deficit, quia semper munda est, ut sunt crateres, qui frequenter, inquit Menochius, adhibentur à convivis, ideoque etiam frequenter abluuntur.
units.tr: 2. Your navel, etc. The sense is: "Around your navel too there is a jewel, not unlike a bowl, round like the moon, whose beauty and brightness never fail, because it is always clean, as bowls are, which, as Menochius says, are often used by guests, and therefore are often washed."

units.la: Indigens poculis. Id est, vacuus potionibus, quo sensu & Virg. 1. Georg. dixit,
units.tr: Lacking drink. That is, empty of drinks. Virgil also used the word in this sense in the first book of the Georgics:

units.la: Poculaque inventis Acheloia miscuit uvis.
units.tr: and mixed the Achelous' cups with the grapes he had found.

units.la: Umbilicus, inquit B. Petrus Damiani Serm. 2. in natali Virginum, fragilissima pars corporis est. Quid ergo per Ecclesiæ designatur umbilicum, nisi cœtus infirmorum, atque debilium? Quid vero per craterem, nisi prædicatorum intelligimus ordinem, qui nimirum mirum mirum mentibus auditorum cœlestis doctrinæ vina propinant, eâsque poculis sanctæ prædicationis inebriant? Umbilicus ergo crateri merito comparatur, quia plerumque debilis & infirmus quilibet vas doctrinæ cœlestis efficitur. Qui non indiget poculis: quia cœlestis eloquii non definit irriguus esse fluentis. Unde bene crater hic tornatilis dicitur, torno siquidem quis facilius operatur. Expeditius enim sæpè atque inoffensè in sancta prædicatione discurrunt, qui prædicationis gratiam non suo studio, sed divinitus acceperunt.
units.tr: The navel, says Blessed Peter Damian in Sermon 2 on the feast of the Virgins, is the most fragile part of the body. What, then, is signified by the navel of the Church, except the company of the weak and the feeble? And what do we understand by the bowl, except the order of preachers, who, wonderfully and marvellously, pour the wines of heavenly teaching into the minds of their hearers and make them drunk with the cups of holy preaching? The navel is rightly compared to a bowl, because almost anyone who is weak and feeble becomes a vessel of heavenly teaching. Which does not lack drink, because the stream of heavenly speech never ceases to flow abundantly. Hence the bowl is rightly called "turned," for a turned thing is more easily made. For those who have received the grace of preaching not by their own zeal but from God often run more readily and without stumbling through holy preaching.

units.la: Venter tuus, &c. Id est, pro ventris ornatu habes gratissimum texturæ opus, spicarum scilicet tritici fasciculum liliis septum phrygio opere vesti pulchrè & artificiosè intextum. Per ventrem sponsæ designatur Ecclesiæ fœcunditas, quâ cum Christo mater est populorum. Magnum hujus fœcunditatis & amplum decus est certus prædestinatorum numerus, quos in tempore messis destinato secernendis electis è medio reproborum messores Angeli ligant in fasciculum, ut eos meritis graves in cœlesti horreum deportent veluti triticum, cùm reprobos adinstar palearum leves igni inextinguibili comburendos tradant. Hic electorum fasciculus est vallatus liliis, quia nihil ad custodiendos electos immaculatos ab hoc sæculo fortius, ac firmius est puritate mentis, quâ soli Deo placere appetunt, & displicere timent.
units.tr: Your belly, etc. That is, for the adornment of her belly you have a most pleasing piece of weaving, namely a bundle of wheat ears, enclosed by lilies, woven beautifully and skilfully into the garment in Phrygian work. The belly of the bride signifies the fruitfulness of the Church, by which she is, with Christ, the mother of the peoples. The great and wide glory of this fruitfulness is the certain number of the predestined, whom the angels, the reapers, at the appointed time of harvest bind into a bundle, separating the elect from the midst of the reprobate, so that they may carry them, heavy with merit, into the heavenly barn like wheat, while they hand over the reprobate, light like chaff, to be burned in unquenchable fire. This bundle of the elect is fenced about with lilies, because nothing is stronger or firmer in this world for keeping the elect spotless than the purity of mind by which they long to please God alone and fear to displease him.

units.la: 3. Duo ubera, &c. Post laudata sponsæ ornamenta innatam ipsi pulchritudinem laudare aggreditur amantissimus sponsus. Est autem hic versus expositus supra cap. 4. v. 5.
units.tr: 3. Your two breasts, etc. After praising the bride's adornments, the most loving bridegroom now sets out to praise the beauty that is natural to her. This verse has been explained above, in chapter 4, verse 5.

units.la: 4. Collum tuum, Supple, nitore & candore.
units.tr: 4. Your neck, supply: in brightness and whiteness.

units.la: Sicut turris eburnea. Id est, turriculæ eburneæ similillimum est. Per collum, inquit Menochius, fides Ecclesiæ commodè intelligitur, quæ eboris instar candida, solida, & incorrupta est. Vide dicta supra cap. 4. v. 4.
units.tr: Like a tower of ivory. That is, it is most like a little tower of ivory. By the neck, says Menochius, the faith of the Church is fittingly understood, which, like ivory, is white, solid and incorruptible. See what was said above, chapter 4, verse 4.

units.la: Oculi tui, &c. Quasi dicat, Oculi tui decenter magni, tranquilli & sereni mihi videntur exprimere amplas illas piscinas stabilium & clarissimarum aquarum plenas, quæ sunt ad illam urbis Hesebon portam, quæ appellatur Bath-rabbim, id est, juxta Vulgatum Interpretem, Filia multitudinis, vel quòd juxta hanc portam esset forum perampum & hominum frequentiâ celeberrimum, ut vult Ludovicus Legionensis, vel quia illâ porta ibatur ad vicinam urbem Philadelphiam cui apud Hebræos nomen erat Rabbathammon, ut Masius arbitratur, quod dici posse non negat Legionensis. Oculis sponsæ designatur Ecclesiæ intentio, quæ ample est propter multitudinem operum, tranquilla, quia confidit in Domino, denique serenissima & splendidissima est propter puritatem, quâ illud unum aspicit quod aspiciendum est, & totam se in soliditate æternitatis figit, Ne, ut loquitur B. Greg. Hom. 27. in Evang. si extra fundamentum actionis fabrica ponitur, terra debiscente solvatur. Sunt ergo oculi seu intentiones sanctæ Dei Ecclesiæ amplis, claris, & limpidis urbis Hesebon piscinis similes.
units.tr: Your eyes, etc. As if to say: your eyes, becomingly large, calm and serene, seem to me to express those broad pools of still and very clear water which lie by the gate of the city of Heshbon called Bath-rabbim, that is, according to the Vulgate translator, the daughter of a multitude; either because near this gate there was a very wide market, most crowded with people, as Ludovicus Legionensis thinks, or because through that gate one went to the neighbouring city of Philadelphia, which among the Hebrews was called Rabbathammon, as Masius supposes, which Legionensis does not deny could be said. The eyes of the bride signify the intention of the Church, which is broad because of the multitude of her works, calm because she trusts in the Lord, and finally most serene and most bright because of the purity by which she looks upon the one thing that is to be looked upon and fixes herself entirely on the solidity of eternity. Lest, as Blessed Gregory says in Homily 27 on the Gospel, if the structure of action is placed outside the foundation, it is dissolved as the ground gives way. The eyes, or intentions, of the holy Church of God are therefore like the broad, clear and limpid pools of the city of Heshbon.

units.la: In Hesebon, Fuit Hesebon urbs citra Jordanem in sorte tribus Ruben, in qua urbe olim fuit Regia Sehon Regis Amorrhæorum stagnis, aquisque pulchris abundans. B. Ambrosius in Ps. 118. Serm. 16. Stagna in Hesebon, inquit, quid est, nisi in cogitationibus rationalibus abundantia, quæ est in portis Ecclesiæ, cui merito defertur multitudo doctrinæ, &c. Alludit S. Doctor ad significationem vocis Hesebon, quæ significat cogitationem; quo vocabulo in sua versione usus est Aquila. Hinc B. Theodoret, enarrans præsentem sacri Dramatis locum, ait: Docet sponsus animarum piarum oculos esse veluti piscinas quasdam, quæ divina fluenta suscipiunt, atque exundant perpetuo, propter multitudinem divinorum, quæ illis subinde revelantur, & propter excellentem cognitionem rerum divinarum, &c.
units.tr: In Heshbon. Heshbon was a city on this side of the Jordan, in the lot of the tribe of Reuben, in which city once was the royal seat of Sihon, king of the Amorites, abounding in pools and fine waters. Blessed Ambrose, in Psalm 118, Sermon 16, says: What are the pools in Heshbon, except an abundance of rational thoughts, which are in the gates of the Church, to which the multitude of teaching is rightly brought, etc.? The holy doctor alludes to the meaning of the word Heshbon, which signifies thought; Aquila used this word in his version. Hence Blessed Theodoret, explaining the present passage of the holy drama, says: The bridegroom teaches that the eyes of pious souls are like certain pools, which receive the divine streams and overflow continually, on account of the multitude of divine things which are revealed to them from time to time, and on account of the excellent knowledge of divine things, etc.

units.la: Nasus tuus, &c. Quasi dicat, pulcherrimus nasus tuus non minus addit decoris & ornamenti decoræ faciei tuæ, quàm Libano aspectu gratissimo addit turris illa quæ in ipso est e regione Damasci Syriæ illius, quæ inde Damascena vocatur, Metropoleos pulcherrimæ, maximæ, & fertilissimæ. Sic supra cap. 5. v. 15. gratum sponsi aspectum assimilavit amœno monti Libano, cedris virentibus, innumeris arboribus fructiferis, herbis aromaticis, floribus pulcherrimis convestito, dicens: Species ejus ut Libani. Significat facies intentionem, unde B. Greg. Hom. 4. in Ezech. ficaccipit illud, quod dicitur de animalibus facies eorum & penna eorum extenta desuper. Facies, inquit, & penna extenta desuper describuntur, quia omnis intentio, omnisque contemplatio sanctorum super se tendit, ut illud possit adipisci, quod in cœlestibus appetit. Nam qui bona agere videtur & per hæc non Deo, sed hominibus placere desiderat, intentionis suæ faciem deorsum promit: & qui in contemplatione Dei, non dulcedine beatitudinis satiari appetit, sed doctus videri, ille nimirum intellectus sui pennas desuper non extendit. Faciei igitur Ecclesiæ, id est, sanctis & puris ipsius intentionibus insigne decus addit per nasum, qui odores discernit, designata spirituum discretio, quæ turris Libaniæ instar & alta est, & munita, ut vitia virtutibus superet, atque incursus malignorum spirituum avertat, ut loquitur B. Greg. Hac spirituum discretione, víque discernendi veras virtutes à vitiis, & errores à veritate eget Ecclesia, ut charitatem habens in intentione, habeat & veritatem in electione, sicque gaudeat laudatâ à Domino in Evangelio oculorum simplicitate. Etenim, ut interior oculus, inquit præclarè Bernardus lib. de præcepto & difpenf. cap. 17. verè fit simplex, duo illi esse arbitror necessaria, charitatem in intentione, & in electione veritatem. Nam si bonum quidem diligat, sed verum non eligat: habet quidem zelum Dei, sed non secundum scientiam: & nescio quemadmodum judicio veritatis vera esse possit cum falsitate simplicitas. Volens denique ad veram discipulos instruere simplicitatem magistra veritas: Estote, inquit, prudentes sicut serpentes, & simplices sicut columbæ. Præmisit ergo prudentiam, sine qua neminem satis esse posse simplicem sciret. Quomodo denique vere simplex erit oculus cum ignorantia veritatis? Aut verò vera potest dici simplicitas, quam simplex ignorat veritas? Scriptum est enim: Ignorans ignorabitur. Patet ergo laudabilem illam & à Domino laudatam simplicitatem absque his duobus non esse bonis, benevolentia, atque prudentia: ut oculus videlicet cordis non solum pius, qui fallere nolit; sed & cautus sit, qui falli non possit.
units.tr: Your nose, etc. As if to say: your most beautiful nose adds no less grace and ornament to your comely face than that tower which stands on Lebanon, in the most pleasing aspect, adds, lying opposite Damascus, the most beautiful, greatest and most fertile metropolis of Syria, which is therefore called Damascene. So above, in chapter 5, verse 15, she compared the pleasing appearance of the bridegroom to the pleasant mountain of Lebanon, clothed with green cedars, countless fruit trees, aromatic herbs and most beautiful flowers, saying: His appearance is like Lebanon. The face signifies intention, whence Blessed Gregory, in Homily 4 on Ezekiel, takes that which is said of the living creatures, their faces and their wings stretched upward. The face and the wing stretched upward, he says, are described because every intention and every contemplation of the saints stretches upward, so that it may attain that which it seeks in heaven. For he who seems to do good works and through these desires to please not God but men, lowers the face of his intention; and he who in the contemplation of God seeks not to be satisfied with the sweetness of blessedness but to seem learned, certainly does not stretch the wings of his understanding upward. Thus through the nose, which discerns odours, the discernment of spirits is added as a distinguished grace to the face of the Church, that is, to her holy and pure intentions; this discernment is high and fortified like the tower of Lebanon, so that vices are overcome by virtues and the attacks of evil spirits are turned away, as Gregory says. The Church needs this discernment of spirits, to distinguish true virtues from vices and errors from truth, so that, having charity in her intention, she may also have truth in her choice, and so rejoice in the simplicity of the eye praised by the Lord in the Gospel. For, so that the inner eye, as Bernard admirably says in the book on precept and dispensation, chapter 17, is truly simple, I judge that two things are necessary: charity in intention, and truth in choice. For if it loves the good but does not choose the true, it indeed has zeal for God, but not according to knowledge; and I do not know how simplicity can be with falsehood in the judgment of truth. Wishing finally to teach the disciples true simplicity, the Teacher, Truth, says: Be prudent as serpents, and simple as doves. He therefore put prudence first, knowing that no one can be simple enough without it. Finally, how will the eye be truly simple when it is ignorant of the truth? Or how can that be called true simplicity which the simple one does not know to be true? For it is written: The ignorant will be ignored. It is clear, then, that that praiseworthy simplicity, praised by the Lord, is not good without these two things, goodwill and prudence: so that the eye of the heart may be not only pious, unwilling to deceive, but also cautious, so that it cannot be deceived.

units.la: 5. Caput tuum ut Carmelus.
units.tr: 5. Your head is like Carmel.

units.la: Doctissimus Samuel Bochartus in parte posteriore, de animalibus Scripturæ lib. 5. cap. 9. ex Talmudicis probat purpurariæ piscationis locum in Judæa à scalis Tyriorum usque ad Chaipham & Carmelum patuisse stadiis circiter 230. Tyri Scalarum situm docet Josephus belli Judaici libri secundi cap. 9. ubi Ptolemaidem Septentrionem versus scribit montem habere altissimum, stadiis centum dissitum, quem Scalam Tyriorum vocant incolæ. Ibidem Carmelum legas à Ptolemaide ad Meridiem abesse 120. stadiis. Porrò ad Carmeli radices fuit Chaipha, ut testatur Geographus Nubiensis clim. 3. part. 5. & Rabbi Benjamin in itinerario postquam egit de Accho, seu Ptolemaide pag. 36. & Brocardus in descriptione itineris ab urbe Accho, seu Ptolemaide versus austrum. Tamen, ut advertit idem Bochartus, à Tyri Scalis usque ad Chaipham purpurarum ubique non fuit par copia, sed harum præcipua ubertas circa Carmelum & Chaipham. Eò scilicet videtur referendum quod in Guillelmo Tyrio Chaiphæ vetus nomen fuit Porphyria, ut eadem fuerit quæ Phœniciæ Πορφυρεῶν apud Stephanum ex libro 5. Polybii, tanquam à purpuræ piscatione facto nomine. Præterea 2 Paral. 2. v. 7. & 14. & cap. 3. v. 14. Carmil ponitur inter purpuræ species. Coccum reddunt interpretes, ego purpuræ genus ad Carmelum capi solitæ. Huc facit, inquit Bochartus, quod Carmel, & Argaman, id est, purpura, palàm sunt synonyma, in his Cantici verbis capitis septimi versu quinto, Caput tuum sicut Carmel, & cincinnus capitis tui sicut Argaman, seu purpura.
units.tr: The most learned Samuel Bochart, in the second part of his De animalibus Scripturae, book 5, chapter 9, proves from the Talmudists that the area for fishing purple in Judaea extended about 230 stadia from the Ladders of Tyre to Haifa and Carmel. Josephus, Jewish War, book 2, chapter 9, shows the position of the Ladders of Tyre, where he writes that north of Ptolemais there is a very high mountain, a hundred stadia away, which the inhabitants call the Ladder of Tyre. In the same place you may read that Carmel lies 120 stadia south of Ptolemais. Moreover, Haifa was at the foot of Carmel, as the Nubian geographer testifies (climate 3, part 5), and Rabbi Benjamin in his itinerary, after treating of Acre or Ptolemais (p. 36), and Brocardus in his description of the journey south from the city of Acre or Ptolemais. Yet, as Bochart himself observes, the supply of purple was not equal everywhere from the Ladders of Tyre to Haifa; its chief abundance was around Carmel and Haifa. To this, evidently, should be referred the fact that in William of Tyre the old name of Haifa was Porphyria, so that it was the same as the Phoenician Porphyreon [Πορφυρεῶν] in Stephanus, from book 5 of Polybius, the name having been given from the purple fishery. Furthermore, in 2 Chronicles 2:7 and 14, and chapter 3:14, Carmil is listed among kinds of purple. The translators render it as scarlet; I take it to be a kind of purple customarily caught near Carmel. To this, says Bochart, is related the fact that Carmel and Argaman, that is, purple, are plainly synonyms, in these words of the Song in chapter 7, verse 5: Your head is like Carmel, and the locks of your head like Argaman, that is, purple.

units.la: Comæ capitis tui, &c. Repetit sponsus in hoc hemistichio aliis verbis, quod in priori hemistichio dixerat. Quod non rarum est in Scripturis, maxime in libris Job, Psalmorum & Salomonis. Commendat itaque modo sponsus in præsenti versu fponfæ cæsariem regio ornatu pulcherrimam, eámque assimilat colligaturis florum, ut loquitur Menochius, sericorum, vel laneorum, quæ desinantur paludamento regio texendo, sùntque purpurâ recens fucatæ, posteà, ne dilabantur, firmiter alligatæ in purpurariorum canalibus, ut iterum melius, & penitius tinguntur. Coma capitis sanctæ Dei Ecclesiæ ut purpura est Regis vincta canalibus, quia sicut per caput intelligimus mentem, ut loquitur B. Petrus Damiani Serm. de Sancta Columba, ita per comas capitis non inconvenienter accipimus cogitationes. Sicut enim capilli de vertice prodeunt, ita cogitationes ex mente procedunt. Purpureus vero color, quia sanguinis habet speciem, quid per mysterium, nisi Dominicam innuit passionem? Quid vero canales, nisi sanctorum significant mentes? Sicut enim in canalibus conchyliorum sanguis effunditur, ut in purpureum colorem lana vertatur; sic in sanctorum mentibus Dominicæ passionis cruor assidua meditatione recolitur. Et ita quodam modo pia quælibet anima sanguine tingitur, ut æterni Regis purpuram imitetur. Hoc nimirum modo efficimur Salvatori nostro conformes, ut simus etiam merito postmodum cohæredes.
units.tr: "The locks of your head," etc. In this half-verse the bridegroom repeats, in other words, what he had said in the previous half-verse. This is not rare in Scripture, especially in Job, the Psalms and Solomon. In this verse, then, the bridegroom praises the bride's hair as most beautiful in royal adornment, and likens it to bundles of flowers, as Menochius puts it, of silk or wool, which are woven into the royal mantle, and are dyed fresh with purple, then, so that they do not slip, are fastened firmly in the dyers' vats, so that they may be dyed again more fully and deeply. The hair of the head of the holy Church of God is like the purple of the King bound in the vats, for just as by the head we understand the mind, as Blessed Peter Damian says in his sermon on Saint Columba, so by the locks of the head we may not unfittingly understand thoughts. For as the hair grows from the crown, so thoughts proceed from the mind. But the purple colour, since it has the appearance of blood, what does it signify in this mystery, if not the Lord's passion? And what are the vats, if not the minds of the saints? For just as the blood is poured out in the vats of shellfish so that the wool may be turned into a purple colour, so in the minds of the saints the blood of the Lord's passion is recalled by constant meditation. And so in a certain way every devout soul is dyed with blood, to imitate the purple of the eternal King. In this way we are made conformed to our Saviour, so that we may also deservedly become co-heirs afterwards.

units.la: 6. Quàm pulchra, &c. Sensus est, quis explicet quàm pulchra & venusta sis, ô amoris deliciæ? Cœlestis sponsus Ecclesiam, cujus consuetudine maximè delectatur, vocat amoris delicias, seu, ut habet textus Hebræus & Ixx. amorem in deliciis, seu, ut habet Vulgatus Interpres, charissimam in deliciis, quia ipse de se ait Prov. 8. v. 31. Deliciæ meæ esse cum filiis hominum. Huic Ecclesiæ divinitùs data est pulchritudo, quæ vincat decore famam, gloriam virtute, & reipsa nomen.
units.tr: 6. "How beautiful, etc." The sense is: who can declare how beautiful and lovely you are, O delight of love? The heavenly bridegroom calls the Church, in whose company he takes most delight, the delights of love, or, as the Hebrew text and the LXX have it, love among delights, or, as the Vulgate translator has it, most dear among delights, because he himself says of himself in Proverbs 8:31: My delights were to be with the sons of men. To this Church has been given by God a beauty which surpasses fame in grace, glory in virtue, and reality in name.

units.la: 7. Statura tua, &c. Hoc est, reliquas omnes pulchras fœminas altitudine & proceritate æquè ac pulchritudine & elegantiâ antecellis, atque cum ipsis comparata palmæ victricis instar obtines. Merito autem Ecclesia, cujus conversatio in cœlis est, palmæ comparatur. Est enim, inquit Philo Judæorum disertissimus in lib. 1. de vita Mosis, arborum præstantissima, quæ aspectu pulcherrima, fructum quoque fert optimum, & vitalem vim habet, non in radicibus defossam, ut cetera, sed in summo, quasi cor, sitam in ramorum medio, à quibus circumquaque stipatur, seu Princeps à suis satellitibus. Cujusmodi natura est etiam mentis, quæcumque sanctitatem degustavit. Solet enim hæc sursum spectare, & in sublimibus versari, occupata contemplandis divinis pulchritudinibus, nauci faciens terrena; & hæc lusus reputans, illa siria. Vberatua botrijs. Supple ex versu mox sequente, vineæ. Duo potissimùm sunt indicia, quibus dignoscitur num puella fit dicenda mulier & sponsæ nomine digna; nempe cùm grandior effecta conspicitur staturâ procerâ, ut compertum est; & cùm eidem ubera excreverint, & extumuerint, prout asserit Arist. lib. 7. Hist. animi cap. 1. Ad ista duo indicia exprimenda tales sponsus in præsenti versu adhibet similitudines, ut simul commendet pulchritudinem & corporis proceri, & uberum copia lactis tumentium. Hæc ipsa quoque indicia ad idem affert Dominus Ezech. 16. v. 7. Et grandis effecta es, & pervenisti ad mundum muliebrem : ubera tua intumuerunt. Per ubera sponsæ tumentia designatur gemina Ecclesiæ charitas, seu dilectio, Dei scilicet, & proximi, succo pietatis plena, quæ, ut loquitur B. Greg. Magnus, animam quam possident, vino cœlesti inebriant & nutriunt.
units.tr: 7. "Your stature, etc." That is, you surpass all the other beautiful women in height and tallness, as much as in beauty and elegance, and compared with them you stand like a victorious palm. Rightly, too, the Church, whose conversation is in heaven, is compared to a palm. For, says Philo, the most eloquent of the Jews, in book 1 of On the Life of Moses, it is the most excellent of trees, most beautiful to behold, and it also bears the best fruit and has a vital power, not buried in its roots as other trees do, but situated at its top, like a heart, in the middle of its branches, by which it is surrounded on every side, as a prince is by his bodyguards. Such is also the nature of a mind that has tasted holiness. For it is accustomed to look upwards and to dwell among heavenly things, busy in contemplating divine beauties, counting earthly things as nothing, and regarding these as play but those as serious. Your breasts are like clusters. Supply from the next verse, of the vineyard. There are two chief signs by which one knows whether a girl is to be called a woman and worthy of the name of bride: namely, when she is seen to have grown taller in tall stature, as has been found; and when her breasts have grown and swelled, as Aristotle asserts in book 7 of the History of Animals, chapter 1. To express these two signs, the bridegroom in this verse uses such comparisons, so that he commends at once both the beauty of a tall body and the abundance of the swelling breasts of milk. The Lord himself also brings forward these same signs for the same purpose in Ezekiel 16:7: And you have grown great and have attained to womanly adornment; your breasts have swelled. By the swelling breasts of the bride is designated the twofold charity or love of the Church, that is, of God and of neighbour, full of the juice of piety, which, as Blessed Gregory the Great says, intoxicates and nourishes with heavenly wine the soul that it possesses.

units.la: 8. Dixi ascendam, &c. Persistens sponsus in comparatione palmæ & botrorum ait se animum induxisse sponsæ corporis staturâ pulcherrimæ adhærere, ut continuo ad complexum, & ad osculum ipsius possit currere; sicque fruatur & castissimis ipsius blandimentis sibi quâvis voluptate dulcioribus, & suavitatibus odorum, qui affiantur è facie ejus, non minùs jucundis quàm suavissima malorum fragrantia. Ubera pro blanditiis & aliis sinceri amoris, summæque benevolentiæ indiciis sumi apud Hebræos observatum est supra cap. 1. v. 1. Sumuntur autem botri vineæ hic eodem sensu, quo ibidem vinum, nempe pro quolibet deliciarum genere. Similiter odor malorum usurpatur pro quavis suavitate afflata odoratione percepta, ut supra cap. 1. unguenta optima, & odor unguentorum. Cassiodorus, quem sequitur & venerabilis Beda, ait per palmam, quam Christus ipse se ascensurum dicit; posse intelligi & Ecclesiam, & piam quamque animam, quam supra hortum nominavit, ut in eandem velut in hortum descenderit per gratiæ immissionem, & ut in palmam ascenderit per ejus profectùs & gratiæ augmentum : illius verò apprehendat fructus bonorum operum, atque laborum, quò illos remuneret. Quantò autem Ecclesia, vel pia quæliber anima intimiùs fuerit unita Christo, seu magis profecerit in gratia, tanto uberiùs geminæ ipsius dilectionis ubera incipiunt lac pietatis, &, ut loquitur B. Petrus Damiani Serm. de Invent. S. Crucis, spiritualis lætitiæ vina diffundere, atque tota illius conversationis facies magis incipit odorem cœlestis concupiscentiæ humanarum mentium naribus inspirare.
units.tr: 8. "I said, I will go up, etc." The bridegroom, persisting in the comparison with the palm and the clusters, says that he has resolved to cling to the bride's very beautiful stature, so that he may at once run to her embrace and kiss; and thus he may enjoy her most chaste endearments, sweeter to him than any pleasure, and the fragrances that breathe from her face, no less pleasant than the sweetest scent of apples. That breasts are used among the Hebrews for endearments and other signs of sincere love and the greatest goodwill has been noted above at chapter 1, verse 1. The clusters of the vine here are taken in the same sense as wine there, namely, for any kind of delight. Similarly, the scent of apples is used for any sweetness perceived by the breath of fragrance, as above in chapter 1, the best ointments, and the odour of ointments. Cassiodorus, whom the venerable Bede also follows, says that by the palm, which Christ himself says he will climb, may be understood both the Church and every devout soul, which he named above as a garden, so that he may come down into it as into a garden through the infusion of grace, and climb into the palm through its progress and increase of grace; and he takes its fruit, the fruits of good works and labours, so that he may reward them. But the more intimately the Church, or any devout soul, is united with Christ, or the more it has advanced in grace, the more abundantly the breasts of its twofold love begin to pour out the milk of piety, and, as Blessed Peter Damian says in his sermon on the finding of the holy Cross, the wines of spiritual joy, and the whole aspect of its conduct begins more and more to breathe the odour of heavenly desire into the nostrils of human minds.

units.la: 9. Guttur tuum, &c. Hæc dici de sponsa patet ex pro nomine tuum, quod Hebraicè est pronomen affixum fœminini generis. Sensus est idem, ac si diceret sponsus, Incredibiliter delector suaviloquentia tua, nec solùm delector, sed etiam sine satietate delector.
units.tr: 9. "Your palate, etc." That these words are spoken of the bride is clear from the word your, which in Hebrew is a pronoun attached in the feminine gender. The sense is the same as if the bridegroom said: I am incredibly delighted by your sweet speech, and I am delighted by it not only, but I am delighted by it without satiety.

units.la: Sicut vinum optimum. Quo scilicet nihil jucundius quis bibit ut fruatur voluptate potandi.
units.tr: Like the best wine. That is, the wine one drinks, the most pleasant of all, so that one may enjoy the pleasure of drinking.

units.la: Dignum dilecto meo: Heb. Vadens ad dilectum meum directe. Sensus est idem, ac dum Gallicè optimum vinum familiari epitheto nuncupamus vin d'amis.
units.tr: Worthy for my beloved: Heb. Going straight to my beloved. The sense is the same as when we call the best wine by the familiar epithet vin d'amis in French.

units.la: Labiisque & dentibus illius ad ruminandum. Heb. ad verbum, loquens in labiis dormientium. Sensus est idem, quia hac tota periphrasi nihil aliud intendit sponsus, quàm vini, cum cujus suavitate sponsæ sermocinationem confert, generositatem exprimere ; hanc autem æquè exprimit Vulgata editio, atque textus Hebræus. Solent quippe homines, ut potandi voluptate fruantur, cùm vinum generosum & suave hauriunt, illius hauftulum ore versare, & regustare, quasi linguam, palatum, & dentes illo abluentes, ut simul & suavitate vini oblectentur, & illius odore focillentur. Similiter vinum optimum efficit, ut etiam dormientium labia moveantur, sonum edant, & verba quædam murmurent, seu mussitent ; sensus enim excitat, & animum recreat. Porrò hoc sponsæ encomio significat cælestis Ecclesiæ sponsus ipsius sermones de rebus spiritualibus ac divinis esse quàm dulcissimos, nec dignos solùm, quia à se amantissimo ipsius sponso summâ lætitiâ, certísque & veris summæ suæ in ipsam benevolentiæ indiciis excipiantur, sed etiam quos ille assiduè animo repetat ac ruminetur, ut semperin illis se oblectet.
units.tr: And to his lips and teeth for chewing. Heb., word for word, speaking on the lips of sleepers. The sense is the same, because by this whole periphrasis the bridegroom intends nothing other than to express the excellence of the wine, with whose sweetness he compares the bride's speech. The Vulgate edition expresses this just as well as the Hebrew text does. People who drink fine, sweet wine are accustomed, so that they may enjoy the pleasure of drinking it, to roll the sip around in their mouths and taste it again, washing their tongue, palate and teeth with it, so that they are delighted both by the sweetness of the wine and refreshed by its aroma. In the same way the best wine causes even the lips of sleepers to move, to make a sound, and to murmur or mumble some words, for it stirs the senses and refreshes the spirit. Moreover, by this praise of the bride the bridegroom signifies that the words of the bridegroom of the heavenly Church about spiritual and divine things are most sweet, and not only worthy, because they are received by his beloved with the greatest joy and with sure and true tokens of his supreme goodwill towards her, but also because he constantly repeats them in his mind and chews them over, so that he may take his delight in them always.

units.la: Sponsa.
units.tr: The bride.

units.la: 10. EGo dilecto meo, & ad me conversio ejus.
units.tr: 10. I am my beloved's, and his turning is towards me.

units.la: 11. Veni dilecte mi, egrediamur in agrum, commoremur in villis.
units.tr: 11. Come, my beloved, let us go out into the field, let us lodge in the villages.

units.la: 12. Mane surgamus ad vineas, videamus si floruerit vinea, si flores fructus parturiunt, si floruerunt mala punica : ibi dabo tibi ubera mea.
units.tr: 12. Let us rise early to the vineyards, let us see whether the vine has flourished, whether the blossoms are bringing forth fruit, whether the pomegranates have flowered: there I will give you my breasts.

units.la: 13. Mandragoræ dederunt odorem. In portis nostris omnia poma : nova & vetera, dilecte mi, servavi tibi.
units.tr: 13. The mandrakes have given their fragrance. At our gates are all kinds of fruit, new and old, my beloved, which I have kept for you.

units.la: EXPLICATIO.
units.tr: EXPLANATION.

units.la: 10. EGo dilecto meo, &c. Sponsa dilectissimo sponso in amore respondens, se totam & quæ sua sunt omnia cum summa animi demissione ipsi committit. Ad Ecclesiam est conversio Divini sponsi, ut enim ait præclarè S. Leo Serm. 4. de Nativit. Semper quidem diversis modis, multisque mensuris humano generi bonitas Divina consuluit, & plurima providentiæ suæ munera omnibus retro seculis clementer impertiit; sed in novissimis temporibus omnem abundantiam solitæ benignitatis excessit, quando in Christo ipsa ad peccatores misericordia, ipsa ad errantes veritas, ipsa ad mortuos vita descendit: ut Verbum illud coæternum & coæquale Genitori in unitatem Deitatis suæ, nostræ naturam humilitatis assumeret, & Deus de Deo natus, idem etiam homo de homine nasceretur. Ecclesia vicissim Divino sponso suo adhæret, Christo dilecto suo adhæret, ad ipsumque se convertit, non autem ad delicias, opesque terrenas; itaque eo solo contenta est usurpans illud Ps. 72. v. 25. Quid enim mihi est in cœlo, & à te, id est, præter te, quid volui super terram? Defecit, id est, contabuit, caro mea & cor meum præ desiderio tui, Deus cordis mei id est, cui soli cor meum tribuit cultum & adorationem; cum mundani homines singuli deos suos habeant, quos venerentur? Quemadmodum de gulæ deditis hominibus dixit Paulus Philip. 3. v. 19. quorum Deus venter est.
units.tr: 10. "I to my beloved," etc. The bride, answering her most beloved bridegroom in love, commits herself wholly, with all that is hers, to him in deep humility. The turning of the divine bridegroom is toward the Church. As St. Leo says well in Sermon 4 on the Nativity: "God's goodness has always cared for the human race in various ways and in many measures, and has mercifully bestowed many gifts of his providence on all ages past. But in the last times it has surpassed all its usual abundance of kindness, when in Christ mercy itself came down to sinners, truth itself to the erring, life itself to the dead: so that the Word, co-eternal and co-equal with the Father in the unity of his Godhead, might take on the nature of our lowliness, and God born of God might also be born as man of man." In turn the Church clings to her divine bridegroom, clings to Christ her beloved, and turns to him alone, not to earthly delights or riches. Therefore she is content with him alone, using the words of Ps. 72. v. 25: "For what have I in heaven, and besides thee, what have I desired upon earth? My flesh and my heart faileth, that is, wastes away, for desire of thee, O God of my heart," that is, to whom alone my heart gives worship and adoration. Worldly men, by contrast, each have their own gods whom they venerate, as Paul said of men given over to their bellies in Phil. 3. v. 19: "whose god is their belly."

units.la: 11. Veni dilecte mi, &c, Invitat sponsa sponsum ad loca à tumultibus remota, ut secum res rusticas vel fructûs causâ, vel delectationis invisat, ibique amorem suum experiatur, potiaturque omni bonorum suorum gazâ, ipsi de industria servata. En hujus & duorum sequentium versuum sensus juxta sonum literæ, quo adumbratur sancta mater Ecclesia invitans Christum ad solitudinem cordis sui, ut ibi tempestivè, hoc est, opportunè & magna cum vigilantia simul colluistret secum vineam fidelium, num flores bonorum desideriorum fructus edant actionum sanctarum? Num magna sit spes, ut esse debet, majoris indies progressionis? Num crescant amor Dei & proximi, quæ sunt duo sponsæ ubera, quibus suavissimè pascitur sponsus? An latè fundatur sanctæ conversationis odor? Etenim, ait sponsa, tua dona sunt omnia bona mea, quæ nunc facio, vel quæ olim feci, & omnia refero ad tui laudem, & gloriam, cujus gratiâ sunt facta.
units.tr: 11. "Come, my beloved," etc. The bride invites the bridegroom to places remote from the tumult, so that together they may visit the rustic work of the fields, either for the sake of the fruit or for pleasure, and there she may experience his love and enjoy the whole treasure of her goods, kept purposely for him. Here is the sense of this and the two following verses according to the letter: holy mother Church invites Christ into the solitude of her heart, so that there, in good time, that is, opportunely and with great vigilance, he may tend together with her the vineyard of the faithful. Do the flowers of good desires bear the fruit of holy actions? Is there great hope, as there ought to be, of ever greater progress from day to day? Do the love of God and of neighbour grow, which are the two breasts of the bride, on which the bridegroom feeds most sweetly? Is the fragrance of holy conduct spread widely? For the bride says: all the good things I now do, or have done before, are your gifts, and I refer them all to your praise and glory, for whose sake they were done.

units.la: 13. Mandragoræ. Hcb. דודאים, quod vocabulum designare ramos demonstrat Ravius ex hoc loco collocutorum. Jer.
units.tr: 13. "Mandrakes." Hebrew: dudaim [דודאים], a word which Ravius shows, from this passage of the speakers, designates branches. Jer.

units.la: 2. .V. 1. & 2. que rami dedisse odorem suum dicuntur, cum protruserunt flores vel fructus odoratos.
units.tr: 2. v. 1. & 2. Of these branches it is said that they have given forth their fragrance when they have put forth fragrant flowers or fruit.

units.la: In portis nostris omnia poma. Quasi dicat, non longius proficiscendum est, ut fructus inveniantur. Inter alias amatorias pastorum delicias, inter ardentis desiderii signa clariora, illud unum erat, si poma dilectis suis asservarent. Virgil. Eccl. 1. Mirabar quid mæsta Deos Amarylli vocares, Cui pendere sua patereris ab arbore poma. Tityrus hinc aberat.
units.tr: "In our gates are all manner of fruits." As if to say: there is no need to go farther to find the fruit. Among the other amorous pleasures of shepherds, and among the clearer signs of ardent desire, this one was special: to keep fruit for their beloved. Virgil, Eclogue 1: "I wondered why you, sad, were calling on the gods for Amaryllis, for whom you let the fruit hang from its own tree. Tityrus was away from here."

units.la: Id est, mirabar etiam cui servarentur poma in arbore, neque legerentur; nunc novi amanti Tityro custodiri. Hinc fax Tibullo lib. 1. eleg. 5. Huc veniet Messala meus, cui dulcia poma Delia selectis detrahet arboribus.
units.tr: That is: I wondered also for whom the fruit was kept on the tree and not gathered; now I know it is being kept for the new lover Tityrus. So Tibullus, book 1, elegy 5: "My Messala will come here, for whom Delia will pick sweet fruit from the chosen trees."

units.la: Polyphemus ad Galatheam apud Ovid. 13. Metam. Sunt poma gravantia ramos, Sunt auro similes longis in vitibus uvæ, Sunt & purpureæ, tibi has servamus, & illas.
units.tr: Polyphemus to Galatea, in Ovid, Metamorphoses book 13: "There are fruits weighing down the branches, there are grapes like gold on the long vines, there are purple ones too; these I keep for you, and those."

units.la: Vetera. Alludit ordinario usui, quo semper alieni temporis aut flores, aut poma pluris fiunt.
units.tr: "Old ones." It alludes to the ordinary custom by which flowers or fruit of another season are always valued more highly.

units.la: CAPUT OCTAVUM.
units.tr: CHAPTER EIGHT.

units.la: Pergit sponsa variis testari locutionibus quantopere optet suo frui sponso.
units.tr: The bride goes on to testify, in various expressions, how greatly she longs to enjoy her bridegroom.

units.la: 1. Quis mihi det te fratrem meum sugentem ubera matris meæ, ut inveniam te foris, & deosculer te, & jam me nemo despiciat?
units.tr: 1. Who will give you to me, my brother, nursing at my mother's breasts, so that I may find you outside, kiss you, and no one may now despise me?

units.la: 2. Apprehendam te, & ducam in domum matris meæ: ibi me docebis, & dabo tibi poculum ex vino condito, & mustum malorum granatorum meorum.
units.tr: 2. I will take hold of you and lead you into my mother's house. There you will teach me, and I will give you a cup of spiced wine and the juice of my pomegranates.

units.la: 3. Læva ejus sub capite meo, & dextera illius amplexabitur me.
units.tr: 3. His left hand is under my head, and his right hand embraces me.

units.la: EXPLICATIO.
units.tr: EXPLANATION.

units.la: 1. Quis mihi det, &c. Sensus est, ô utinam mihi modò effes, tanquam fraterculus adhuc fugens ubera matris meæ, & mihi liceret te quocunque loci obvium osculari fine contemtu ? Sic fan�useta Dei Ecclesia libertatem filiorum Dei appetens quàm ardentissimè, simúlque vinculis carnis exolvi, & esse cum Christo, non amplius invitat ad amplexus, ut sub umbris occultatum, aut quasi præ pudore velatum sponsum, sed omni suspicionis timore sublato palàm & coram Angelis Dei, castissimè ut fratrem amplecti, oscularíque percupit.
units.tr: 1. Who will give me, &c. The sense is: "O, that you were mine now, as a little brother still nursing at my mother's breasts, and that I might be allowed to kiss you wherever I meet you, without contempt!" So the Church of God, blessed in its longing for the liberty of the children of God, and eager to be loosed from the bonds of the flesh and to be with Christ, no longer invites the bridegroom to embraces as one hidden in shadows or veiled, as it were, for shame. Rather, with all fear of suspicion removed, she desires to embrace and kiss him openly, before the angels of God, as a brother, in the purest way.

units.la: 2. Apprehendam, &c. Quasi dicat, nunc vero deducam te in domum matris meæ, ut tuo ex jussu ministrabo tibi vinum aromaticum, & multum è punicis meis. Nunc, inquit sancta mater Ecclesia, quamdiu sum in hoc seculo, deducam te in secretum cubiculum mentis meæ per gratiam regeneratæ, ut tres Patres apud Theodoretum interpretantur; ibique hauriam ex te rectam rationem te amandi perfectè, amoribúsque tuis inserviendi, vicissimque tibi amorem meum quasi præstantissimi vini & jucundissimæ potionis poculum propinabo.
units.tr: 2. I will lead you, &c. As if she said: "Now indeed I will bring you into my mother's house, so that at your command I may serve you spiced wine and much of my pomegranate juice." "Now," says holy mother Church, "as long as I am in this world, I will lead you into the secret chamber of my mind, which is regenerated by grace, as the three Fathers interpret it in Theodoret. There I will draw from you the right reason for loving you perfectly and for serving your loves; and in return I will pour out to you my love, as a cup of the finest wine and most pleasant drink."

units.la: 3. Læva ejus, &c. Id est, ibidem sponsus amantissimus me sinu dormientem, complexúque recipiet. Ibidem, ait sancta Ecclesia, caput mentis tollens super sinistram manum vitæ præsentis, & propinquam jamjam æternæ vitæ dextram arripiens, quasi inter sponsi amplexus placidissimè conquiescam.
units.tr: 3. His left hand, &c. That is: there the most loving bridegroom will receive me, sleeping on his bosom, and embrace me. There, says holy Church, lifting the head of my mind above the left hand of present life, and seizing the right hand of eternal life, which is now close at hand, I shall rest most peacefully, as between the arms of the bridegroom.

units.la: Sponsus.
units.tr: The Bridegroom.

units.la: 4. Djuro vos, filiæ Jerusalem, ne suscitetis, neque evigilare faciatis dilectam, donec ipsa velit.
units.tr: 4. I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, that you do not stir up nor awaken my beloved, until she herself is willing.

units.la: EXPLICATIO.
units.tr: Explanation.

units.la: Quæ in hoc versu sunt observanda quoad sensum literalem, vide supra cap. 2. v. 7. illud duntaxat addendum est hoc loco ad hujus versùs cum præcedentibus connexionem, quòd cœlestis sponsus adjuret omnes creaturas, ne sponsam à spirituali somno ullâ vitæ mortalis illecebrâ audeant excitare.
units.tr: What is to be observed in this verse as to the literal sense, see above on chapter 2, verse 7. It is only necessary to add here, for the connection of this verse with those before it, that the heavenly bridegroom charges all creatures that they should not dare to rouse the bride from her spiritual sleep by any allurement of mortal life.

units.la: Sodales sponsæ.
units.tr: The companions of the bride.

units.la: Quæ est ista, quæ ascendit de deserto, deliciis affluens, innixa super dilectum suum?
units.tr: Who is this that comes up from the wilderness, flowing with delights, leaning upon her beloved? ## EXPLANATION.

units.la: EXPLICATIO.

Quæ est ista, &c. Mirantur sodales quòd sponsa præ novo quodam amoris æstu super dilectum suum seipsam quietè dulcissimâ declinans, celerrimè è deserto ascendat Jerosolymam. Mirantur cœlites quòd Ecclesia ex hujus mundi deserto, ubi bonorum omnium est penuria; ad cœlestia gaudia mente & cogitationibus tendat tam illustri ornatu virtutum cum divini sponsi voluntate in omnibus concors; nec ab ipsius beneplacito in ulla penitus rediissentiens.
units.tr: Who is this, etc. The companions marvel that the bride, with a certain new glow of love, resting most sweetly upon her beloved, climbs so quickly out of the wilderness to Jerusalem. The heavenly inhabitants marvel that the Church, out of this world's wilderness, where there is a lack of all good things, strives in mind and thoughts towards heavenly joys, so brightly adorned with virtues, agreeing in all things with the will of her divine bridegroom, and in nothing at all dissenting from his good pleasure. ## The bride speaks to the bridegroom.

units.la: sponsa alloquitur sponsum.
Sub arbore malo suscitavi te : ibi corrupta est mater tua, ibi violata est genitrix tua.
units.tr: Under the apple tree I roused you: there your mother was corrupted, there she who bore you was violated.

units.la: 6. Pone me ut signaculum super cor tuum, ut signaculum super brachium tuum : quia fortis est ut mors dilectio, dura sicut infernus æmulatio : lampades ejus, lampades ignis atque flammarum.
units.tr: 6. Set me as a seal upon your heart, as a seal upon your arm: for love is strong as death, and jealousy hard as the grave; its lamps are lamps of fire and flame.

units.la: 7. Aquæ multæ non potuerunt extinguere charitatem, nec flumina obruent illam : si dederit homo omnem substantiam domûs suæ pro dilectione, quasi nihil despiciet eam.
units.tr: 7. Many waters cannot quench love, nor floods drown it: if a man should give all the substance of his house for love, he would despise it as nothing. ## EXPLANATION.

units.la: EXPLICATIO.

Sub arbore, &c. Initium sui in sponsum amoris memorat sponsa. Primò ait se conciliasse sibi sponsum, & quasi excitasse ad amorem suum sub ipsa arboris umbra, ubi ipsum concepit & peperit mater sua. Ecclesia sibi primò conciliavit Christi amorem per fidem in ipsius Incarnationem, in quaipsum sum concepit & peperit beata, semperque Virgo Maria, corrupta est ac violata mater ipsius Synagoga per peccatum quod admisit ipsum incarnatum recipere nolens.
units.tr: Under the apple tree, etc. The bride recalls the beginning of her love for the bridegroom. First she says she won the bridegroom to herself and, as it were, roused him to love of her under the very shade of the tree where his mother conceived and bore him. The Church first won for herself the love of Christ through faith in his Incarnation, in which the blessed and ever-virgin Mary conceived and bore him; and his mother, the Synagogue, was corrupted and violated through the sin of refusing to receive him when incarnate.

units.la: 6. Pone me, &c. Quasi dicat, Nunc vero enixè te rogo, amantissime & amatissime sponse, ut me inter cor & brachium veluti signaculum firmum ac minimè mutabile constitutam arctissimè complectaris, atque deinceps semper in corde & oculis habeas. Hoc postulat Ecclesia ad altissimam cum divino suo sponso conjunctionem aspirans.
units.tr: 6. Set me, etc. As if she said: "Now indeed I earnestly ask you, most loving and most beloved bridegroom, to embrace me most closely, set between your heart and your arm like a firm seal that is least liable to change, and henceforth always to keep me in your heart and before your eyes." The Church, aspiring to the most lofty union with her divine bridegroom, asks this.

units.la: Quia fortis est, &c. Id est, quia tanta est mei in te amoris flamma, ut ejus violentia inexpugnabiles mortis infernique vires superet; tam ardens est meus in te amor, ut ejus ignis inflammatissimus nec vexationum afflictionumque aquis extingui, nec ulla consolationum aut facultatum quantâvis copiâ eripi, vel obrui potest. Ecclesiæ charitas merito dicta est, ut loquitur Aug. in Ep. 29. ad Hieronymum, fortis sicut mors, sive quia nemo eam vincit, sicut mortem, sive quia in hac vita usque ad mortem est mensura charitatis, sicut Dominus ait: Majorem charitatem hac nemo habet, quàm ut animam suam ponat quis pro amicis suis; sive potius, quia sicut mors animam avellit a sensibus carnis, sic charitas a concupiscentiis carnalibus. Charitatis ardore succensa sancta Dei Ecclesia æmulatur, id est, ardenter exoptat semper charismata meliora æmulatione, id est, zelo Dei, quæ æmulatio est sicut infernus, quia quemadmodum in inferno sapiens ignis, ut ait Minutius Felix in Octavio, membra urit & reficit, carpit & nutrit, sicut ignes fulminum corpora tangunt, nec absumunt; Sic flammeum æmulationis, quæ ex charitate Dei est, ingenium, non damnis pascitur ardentium, sed vitali animorum nutritur incendio. Sacri hujus incendii flagrantissimam flammam in Ecclesia orthodoxa nullæ affiictionum & tribulationum aquæ, nulli voluptatum creaturarum torrentes extinguere aut obruere possunt. Ita est, inquit Bernardus Serm. 79. in Cantica, venerunt flumina, flaverunt venti, & impegerunt in Ecclesiam, & non cecidit, eò quòd fundata esset supra petram: petra autem est Christus. Itaque nec verbositate Philosophorum, nec cavillationibus hæreticorum, nec gladiis persecutorum potuit, aut poterit aliquando separari à charitate Dei, quæ est in Christo Jesu.
units.tr: Because it is strong, etc. That is, because the flame of my love for you is so great that its violence overcomes the unconquerable powers of death and hell; my love for you is so burning that its most inflamed fire can be quenched neither by the waters of troubles and afflictions, nor taken away or overwhelmed by any abundance of consolations or resources. The charity of the Church is rightly called, as Augustine says in Epistle 29 to Jerome, strong as death, either because no one conquers it, as death does, or because in this life the measure of charity extends to death, as the Lord says: Greater love has no one than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends; or rather, because as death tears the soul from the senses of the flesh, so charity tears it from carnal desires. Kindled by the ardour of charity, the holy Church of God is zealous, that is, always ardently desires better gifts with emulation, that is, with zeal for God; and this emulation is like hell, because just as in hell a wise fire, as Minucius Felix says in the Octavius, burns and restores the limbs, seizes and nourishes, as the fires of lightning touch bodies and do not consume them; so the flaming nature of emulation, which comes from the charity of God, is not fed by the losses of those who burn, but is nourished by the living fire of souls. The most blazing flame of this holy fire in the orthodox Church cannot be quenched or overwhelmed by any waters of afflictions and tribulations, nor by any torrents of creaturely pleasures. So it is, says Bernard in Sermon 79 on the Canticles: the floods came, the winds blew, and beat upon the Church, and it did not fall, because it was founded upon a rock, and the rock is Christ. Therefore neither by the verbosity of philosophers, nor by the cavils of heretics, nor by the swords of persecutors could she be, or ever will be, separated from the charity of God, which is in Christ Jesus.

units.la: Non possum hic prætermittere aurea Petri Blesensis verba, queis vim amoris describit in Ep. 34. ad Petrum Minetum consobrinum suum Petragoricensem Episcopum. Fortis, inquit, est ut mors dilectio; cum enim compagem membrorum, animæque & corporis fœdus amicabile mors abrumpat: dilectio è contrario diversas voluntates conflat in unam & in glutine charitatis diversarum rum animarum consolidat unionem. Dilectio absentiæ dimna nau sentit : cùmque diuturnitate temporum pleraque soleant infirmari, dilectio & temporis tractu, & locali distantiâ convalescit.
units.tr: I cannot pass over here the golden words of Peter of Blois, with which he describes the power of love in Epistle 34 to Peter Minet, his cousin and bishop of Périgueux. Love, he says, is strong as death; for when death breaks the framework of the limbs and the friendly covenant of soul and body, love on the contrary unites diverse wills into one, and by the glue of charity binds together the union of diverse souls. Love does not feel the harm of absence; and since most things are usually weakened by the passage of time, love grows stronger both with the lapse of time and with distance of place. ## The bridegroom.

units.la: Sponsus.
8. Soror nostra parva, & ubera non habet: quid faciemus sorori nostræ in die quando alloquenda est?
units.tr: 8. Our little sister has no breasts: what shall we do for our sister on the day when she is spoken for?

units.la: 9. Si murus est, ædificemus super eum propugnacula argentea: si ostium est, compingamus illud tabulis cedrinis.
units.tr: 9. If she is a wall, let us build upon her silver battlements; if she is a door, let us enclose her with boards of cedar.

units.la: EXPLICATIO.
units.tr: EXPLANATION.

units.la: 8. Soror nostra, &c. Quasi dicat, O amantissima sponsa, placet mihi ruum arctissimæ mecum conjunctionis desiderium, sed nisi illud differam, sororculæ nostræ quomodo providebimus in die, quo sermo fiet de ea nuptui tradenda? Placet Christo cœlestis patriæ desiderium in deiponsata sibi Ecclesia, quo cupit dissolvi & esse cum ipso, sed illud ab eodem divino sponso differtur, ut provideat ipsa saluti infirmæ multitudinis suo regimini commissæ, & procuret ei ornatum necessarium ad sui cum eodem Christo conjunctionem nuptialem.
units.tr: 8. "Our sister, &c." It is as if he said: O most beloved bride, I am pleased with your longing for the closest union with me, but unless I postpone it, what shall we do for our little sister on the day when she is to be given in marriage? Christ is pleased by the longing of the Church, his betrothed, for the heavenly fatherland, by which she desires to be dissolved and to be with him. Yet the divine bridegroom himself defers it, so that she may provide for the salvation of the weak multitude committed to her rule, and may procure for them the adornment necessary for their nuptial union with Christ himself.

units.la: 9. Si murus est, &c. Dicit sponsus providendum esse ut sorori tenellæ abundè suppetant ornamenta nuptiis necessaria quæ describit sub duplici similiitudine; una desumitur à muris, qui ut magis decorentur, aut stabiliantur, turres eis, atque pinnæ addi solent egregiâ aliquâ pictura exornatæ: altera desumitur à januæ foribus, quæ vestiri solent tabulis cedrinis. Providendum est, inquit Christus, infirmæ multitudini, ut fortis in fide crescat in charitate cæterisque veris & Christianis virtutibus, quibus decoʼata & munita digna sit quæ copuletur sibi virginum sponso.
units.tr: 9. "If she is a wall, &c."
