The bridegroom says that care must be taken that the tender sister has in abundance the adornments necessary for the wedding, which he describes under a twofold likeness. The first is taken from walls, which, to be more beautifully decorated or made stronger, are commonly given towers and battlements adorned with some excellent painting. The second is taken from the leaves of a door, which are commonly covered with boards of cedar. Christ says that care must be taken for the weak multitude, so that, growing strong in faith and in charity and the other true and Christian virtues, she may be adorned and fortified and so worthy to be joined to the bridegroom of virgins.

units.la: Sponsa.
units.tr: The Bride.

units.la: 10. EGo murus: & ubera mea sicut turris, ex quo facta sum coram eo quasi pacem reperiens.
units.tr: 10. I am a wall, and my breasts are like a tower, since I became in his sight as one who finds peace.

units.la: 11. Vinea fuit Pacifico in Ea quæ habet populos: ra didit eam custodibus; vir affert pro fructu ejus mille argenteos.
units.tr: 11. A vineyard was to the Peaceful One in her who has peoples; he gave it to keepers; each man brings for its fruit a thousand pieces of silver.

units.la: 12. Vinea mea coram me est. Mille tui Pacifici, & ducenti his, qui custodiunt fructus ejus.
units.tr: 12. My vineyard is before me. A thousand are yours, O Peaceful One, and two hundred to those who keep its fruit.

units.la: EXPLICATIO.
units.tr: EXPLICATIO.

units.la: 10. Ego murus, &c. Q. d. Animum induxi facere quod jubes, nempe summo studio, sicut velle te novi, tenellæ sorori nostræ de idoneo nuptiis ornatu providebo; ex quo enim mirum in modum placere cœni sponso, & quasi intimam cum ipso inii conjunctionem, evasi instar muri speciosissimis ac munitissimis turribus ornati, proindeque non parum roboris ac decoris ex me ad sororculam nostram accedere poterit. Asserit Ecclesia se prorsus acquiescere in voluntate divini sponsi, quæ cœlestis patriæ desiderium, quo ipsa exardescit, explere differt propter salutem infirmæ multitudinis; sentit quippe Ecclesia, ex quo indulta sibi misericorditer gratia aspirare & anhelare cœpit ad arctissimam & intimam, quæ in patria est, cum cœlesti sponso unionem, se munitissimam pariter & ornatissimam evasive adinstar muri inexpugnabilis turribus paribus apprimè speciosis ornati, ideóque se posse fortitudine suâ, & geminâ, quâ fervet Dei & proximi dilectione non parum virium & ornamenti conferre infirmæ multitudini, ut cœlestibus nuptiis congruenter ornata ad eas admitratur aliquando.
units.tr: 10. I am a wall, etc. The sense is: I have resolved to do what you command, namely, to provide with the utmost zeal, as I know you wish, a fitting adornment for our tender sister for her wedding. For since I have begun to please the bridegroom in a remarkable way and to enter into an intimate union with him, I have become like a wall adorned with most beautiful and well-fortified towers, and so no small strength and beauty can come from me to our little sister. The Church asserts that she wholly acquiesces in the will of the divine bridegroom, who defers the fulfilment of the heavenly homeland, for which she burns, on account of the salvation of the weak multitude. The Church indeed perceives that, since she began through the grace mercifully granted to her to aspire and long for the closest and most intimate union with the heavenly bridegroom, which is to be had in the homeland, she has become most strongly fortified and equally adorned, like an impregnable wall adorned with equally beautiful towers. Therefore she can, by her strength and by the double love of God and neighbour with which she glows, bring no small power and ornament to the weak multitude, so that they, fittingly adorned for the heavenly wedding, may at some time be admitted to it.

units.la: 11. Vinea, Id est, dives agrorum substantia; ex usu enim Scripturæ hic vinea usurpatur pro omnibus latifundiis, ideo cùm uni vineæ, imò & pluribus simul junctis vineis unus sufficiat custos, hæc vinea multis custodibus dicitur commendata, quasi vix omnes latifundiis tam amplis custodiendis sufficerent.
units.tr: 11. Vineyard, that is, the rich substance of fields; for by the usage of Scripture the word vineyard here stands for all great estates. Therefore, although one keeper is enough for one vineyard, or even for several vineyards joined together, this vineyard is said to be entrusted to many keepers, as if scarcely all of them would suffice to guard estates so large.

units.la: Pacifi o, Id est, Salomoni; amat enim Vulgatus interpres nomina propria per eorum interpretationem explicare, quæ proinde interpretatio, ne pariat obscuritatem, scribenda est principe litera majuscula, ut advertimus in Commentario nostro in Mat. 12. v. 4. Sic statim locum appellatum Baal-hamon per Habentem populos explicavit. Hunc locum parant multi fuisse plagam agri Solymitani, quia Jerusalem dicitur Thren. 1. v. 1. Civitas plena populo, domina gentium, princeps provinciarum.
units.tr: Peaceful, that is, Solomon. For the Vulgate translator likes to explain proper names by their interpretation; and this interpretation, lest it cause obscurity, must be written with a capital letter, as we have noted in our commentary on Matthew 12:4. So too he at once explained the place called Baal-hamon as "having peoples." Many hold that this place was a region of the field of Jerusalem, because Jerusalem is said in Lamentations 1:1: The city that was full of people, is become as a widow: she that was great among the nations, and princess among the provinces.

units.la: Vir affert, &c. Hebraicè & Græcè afferet. Sensus est idem ac fi dicat, Si Salomon per se, conductósque operarios amplissima latifundia sua curare nollet, sed ea vellet aliis elocare, à quovis locationis pretium ipsi offerretur quàm copiosissimum.
units.tr: He brings, etc. In Hebrew and Greek it reads "he will bring." The sense is the same as if she said: if Solomon did not want to look after his very large estates himself, with hired workers, but wished to let them out to others, the highest possible rent would be offered to him by anyone who took them.

units.la: Mille argenteos. Id est, ingentem pecuniæ summam, phrasi notissimâ in sacro textu.
units.tr: A thousand pieces of silver. That is, a huge sum of money, a phrase very well known in the sacred text.

units.la: 12. Vinea mea coram me est. Q. d. Sit quantumvis dives sponsus meus, sint ipsi quantumvis uberrima prædia; ego illa flocci pendo præ ipso sponso, cujus beneplacitum mihi semper præsens ob oculos mentis versatur; ipse, ipse mihi vinea, ipse mihi prædium. Sub metaphora sponsæ maximas sponsi divitias respuentis, dummodò placeat sponso, ipsóque frui possit, inducitur Ecclesia, Q. d. Domini est terra & plenitudo ejus, orbis terrarum, & universi qui habitant in eo; verùm ex omnibus & immensis divitiis ejus quæ sunt sive in cœlo, sive in terra, nihil præter ipsum expeto, ipso solo frui cupio, cujus vultum desiderat universa terra, & cujus voluntati servire, regnare est. Huc facit istud Plutarchi in Problem. Rom. num. 7. Quid est quòd vir ab uxore, uxor à viro dono aliquid accipere prohibetur? An quòd vilissimum benevolentiæ signum donatio sit: dant enim & alieni: idcirco hoc dandi lenocinium ex matrimonio sustulerunt, ut non mercenarium, sed gratuitum, & spontaneum sit totum hoc amare, & redamari? An quòd ab aliis accipiendo, corruptæ alienos admittunt: decorum visum est gratis suos diligere?
units.tr: 12. My vineyard is before me. The sense is: however rich my bridegroom may be, and however abundant his estates may be, I value them as nothing compared with the bridegroom himself, whose good pleasure is always present and before the eyes of my mind. He himself is my vineyard, he himself is my estate. Under the metaphor of a bride who rejects the greatest riches of the bridegroom, provided only that she pleases him and may enjoy him, the Church is introduced as saying: "The earth is the Lord's, and the fulness thereof, the world and all who dwell in it." But out of all his immense riches, whether in heaven or on earth, I desire nothing but himself; I wish to enjoy him alone, whose face the whole earth desires, and to serve whose will is to reign. To this purpose is that passage of Plutarch in his Roman Questions, no. 7: Why is it that a husband is forbidden to receive a gift from his wife, and a wife from her husband? Is it because giving is the cheapest sign of goodwill? For even strangers give. Therefore they removed from marriage this enticement of giving, so that the whole business of loving and being loved might be not mercenary but free and spontaneous. Or is it because those who accept things from others admit corruption from outsiders? It seemed fitting to love one's own freely.

units.la: Mille tui Pacifici. Genitivi casus hæc sunt, & Pacifici, id est, Salomonis, per appositionem Poëtis usitatissimam ponitur ad tui. Sensus hujus hemistichii est: Mille argenteos, quos reddere vinea potest, tibi serva, ô Rex Salomon, & ducentos alios, quos & colendæ vineæ, & custodiendæ soles impendere, operariis conductis retine solvendos: ego enim, ut dixi, te uno, sponse dulcissime, satis dives sum. Satis hinc constat quod supra dixi, custodes hîc non esse eos, quibus vinea locata, sed qui vineam colunt; his enim solvitur labor: illi solvunt redditus. Mentem sponsæ illustrat quod narrat Ælianus lib. 12. Hist. Variæ c. 1. Afpasiam remisisse Cyro juniori pecunias cum muneribus aliis omnibus ad se abipso missis, & subdidisse: Tibi quidem hæc usui esse possunt, qui tantam hominum alis multitudinem, non mihi, qui te unum, sicut ad amorem, sic etiam ad ornatum habeo, & satis habeo. Sic amat Ecclesia sponsum suum cœlestem, sed ipsum solum amat, gratis amat, nec ab illo aliud petit præmium præter ipsum; Qui aliud præmium petit à Deo, & propterea servire vult Deo, carius facit quod vult accipere, quàm ipsum à quo vult accipere. Huic fornicationi contrarius est amor castus. Quis est amor Castus? Amat jam anima sponsum suum. Quid ab illo quaerit, a sponso suo quem diligit? Forte quomodo sibi eligunt homines, aut generos, aut sponsos feminae eligunt? Forte divitias & aurum ejus amat, & fundos, & argentum, & pecuniam, & equos, & familiam, & caetera? Absit! Ille ipsum solum amat, gratis amat, quia in ipso habet omnia, quia per ipsum facta sunt omnia. Aug. in Psalm. 72.
units.tr: A thousand, O Peaceful one. These are genitive cases, and Peaceful, that is, of Solomon, is placed in apposition to thine, a construction very common among the poets. The sense of this half-verse is: keep for yourself, O King Solomon, the thousand pieces of silver which the vineyard can yield, and also the two hundred others which you are accustomed to spend on tilling and guarding the vineyard, reserving them to be paid to hired workers. For I, as I have said, am rich enough in you alone, sweetest bridegroom. From this it is clear enough what I said above, that the keepers here are not those to whom the vineyard has been let, but those who cultivate the vineyard; for it is they who are paid for their labour, while the others pay the rents. The bride's mind is illustrated by what Aelian tells in book 12 of his Varied History, chapter 1: that Aspasia sent back to the younger Cyrus the money, along with all the other gifts he had sent to her, and added: Indeed these things may be of use to you, who maintain so great a multitude of men; but not to me, who have you alone, both for love and for adornment, and I am content with you. So the Church loves her heavenly bridegroom, and loves him alone; she loves him freely, and asks from him no other reward but himself. He who seeks another reward from God, and therefore wishes to serve God, makes what he wishes to receive more precious than the one from whom he wishes to receive it. Chaste love is contrary to this fornication. What is chaste love? The soul now loves her bridegroom. What does she seek from her bridegroom whom she loves? Perhaps as women choose for themselves husbands or sons-in-law? Perhaps she loves his riches and gold, and his estates, silver, money, horses, household, and other things? Far from it! She loves him alone, she loves him freely, because in him she has all things, because through him all things were made. Augustine on Psalm 72.

units.la: Sponsus
units.tr: Sponsus

units.la: 13. Quae habitas in hortis, amici auscultant: fac me audire vocem tuam.
units.tr: 13. O you who dwell in the gardens, the friends listen: cause me to hear your voice.

units.la: EXPLICATIO.
units.tr: EXPLICATIO.

units.la: 13. Quae habitas, &c. Q. d. O dulcissima sponsa hortorum incola, sodales nostri hic nos audiunt; optarem esse alicubi tecum ab omnibus sejunctus, ut dulcissimam summi tui in me amantissimum tuum sponsum amoris indicem vocem liberè me unum audire faceres. Ecclesia dicitur habitare in hortis, quia ad veritatem intimam exculta plantaria virtutum servat. Hanc hortatur sponsus caelestis ut summam suam in ipsum charitatem & devotionem non in clamosa voce, sed in lachrymis & intentione cordis soli scrutatori cordium Deo notis testetur. Hoc autem adimplet Ecclesia etiam in publicis orationibus suis, quia in his soli Deo animarum sponso placere cupit; ut enim ait B. Chrysost. Hom. 19. in Mat. Qui non ideo facit, ut ab hominibus videatur, etsi coram hominibus fecerit, non tamen coram hominibus fecisse videtur. Nam qui facit aliquid propter Deum, neminem videt in corde suo praeter Deum, propter quem facit: sicut artifex eum semper habet prae oculis, qui sibi opus faciendum commisit.
units.tr: 13. You who dwell, &c. The meaning is: O most sweet bride, dweller in the gardens, our companions here are listening to us. I would wish to be somewhere with you, set apart from everyone, so that you might let me alone hear your sweet voice, the sign of your love for me, your most loving bridegroom. The Church is said to dwell in gardens because, having been cultivated towards inward truth, she keeps the plantings of the virtues. The heavenly bridegroom urges her to attest her supreme love and devotion towards him not with a noisy voice but with tears and an intention of heart, known to God alone, the searcher of hearts. The Church fulfils this also in her public prayers, because in them she desires to please God alone, the bridegroom of souls. For, as St. Chrysostom says in Homily 19 on Matthew: He who does not act so as to be seen by men, even if he acts in the sight of men, does not seem to have acted in the sight of men. For he who does something on account of God sees no one in his heart except the God on whose account he acts, just as the craftsman always keeps before his eyes the one who committed the work to him.

units.la: Sponsa.
units.tr: Sponsa.

units.la: 14. Fuge dilecte mi, & assimilare capreae, hinnuloque cervorum super montes aromatum.
units.tr: 14. Flee, my beloved, and be like a roe or a young hart upon the mountains of spices.

units.la: EXPLICATIO.
units.tr: EXPLICATIO.

units.la: 14. Fuge &c. Sponsa annuens petitioni sponsi ait: Facesse igitur hinc ocyus, dilecte mi, tanta celeritate, ut haud absimilis videaris capreae, hinnuloque cervorum supra montes aromatum -urrentibus. Vide quæ diximus supra cap. 2. v. 16. Proripe te, ait Ecclesia sponso suo Christo, & me tecum rape quanta potes celeritate in solitudinem, ut scilicet etiam mediis in urbibus & populis foli Deo placere apperam, & conflatas cum concupiscentiis societates omnino rescindam. Verè enim solitarius est, ut scribit Præclarè B. Clemens Alexandrinus Presbyter. lib. 7. Strom. Qui in civitate habitans contemnit ea quæ in civitate sunt, & quæ alii mirantur, vivitque in civitate tantum in solitudine, ut non locus eum cogat, sed liberum eligendi arbitrium eum justum ostendat. Arnobius junior explicans illud Psalmi 54. Ecce elongavi fugiens, & mansi in solitudine, ait; Si fieri potest, accipiat homo pennas animi in Spiritu-sancto, sicut columbæ descendentis de cælo, & evolet fugiens inimicorum manus; longè vadat, fugiat à peccato, & quasi in solitudine positus, sic nullis curis involvatur humanis. Tunc enim expectat Deum, qui salvat à pusillanimitate spiritus, & tempestate, quíque, ut Augustini in Psalm. 33. verbis utar, habitat lucem inaccessibilem viribus nostris, non muneribus suis. Quia non ad eam potest accedere, ut loquitur idem S. Doctor lib. 2. de actis cum Felice Manichæo cap. 7. nisi cui Deus ipse donaverit ut accedat. Hanc expectantes beatam spem, & adventum gloriæ non secundum quid, verba sunt B. Chrysostomi hom. 5. in ep. ad Titum, sed absolutè & sine comparatione ac naturâ magni Dei, animarum sponsi, & Salvatoris nostri Jesu Christi, juxta præceptum Apostoli Tit. 2. v. 12. Sobriè, & juste, & piè vivamus in hoc sæculo, hoc est, interprete Drogone Cardinali in libro de Creatione & Redemtione hominis tom. 2. Bibl. PP. Sobriè quantum ad nos, juste quantum ad proximos, piè ad Deum. Ut enim præclarè Petrus Blesensis in epist. 132. ad Ernaldum ex Priore Ecclesiæ de Monasteriolo, seu S. Launomari de Monasteriis in territorio Perticensi Dioecesis Carnotensis factum ad annum 1202. S. Launomari Blesensis Abbatem, Ad sobrietatem rerum temporalium moderatio ius pertinet, necessitati satisfaciens, non serviens voluptati. Justitia verò naturalis est, ut non velis aliis facere, quod tibi fieri nolis: & aliis facias, quod tibi fieri velis. Pietas autem testimonio B. Augustini consistit in fide, & spe, & charitate, quâ diligitur super omnia caetus animarum sponsus, qui cœlestium nos nuptiarum participes faciat. Amen.
units.tr: 14. Flee, &c. The bride, assenting to the bridegroom's request, says: Be off then from here quickly, my beloved, with such speed that you may seem not unlike a roe or a young hart running over the mountains of spices. See what we said above on chapter 2, verse 16. Hurry away, says the Church to her bridegroom Christ, and snatch me with you as quickly as you can into solitude, so that I may hasten to please God alone even in the midst of cities and peoples, and utterly cut off the fellowships bound up with concupiscences. For truly he is solitary, as the excellent St. Clement of Alexandria, presbyter, writes in Book 7 of the Stromata: He who lives in a city and despises what is in the city, and what others admire, and who lives in the city in such solitude that it is not the place that constrains him but his free power of choice that shows him to be just. Arnobius the Younger, explaining that verse of Psalm 54, Behold, I have fled far away and remained in the wilderness, says: If it can be done, let a man receive the wings of the spirit in the Holy Spirit, like a dove descending from heaven, and let him fly away from the hands of his enemies; let him go far, let him flee from sin, and, placed as if in solitude, let him not be entangled by any human cares. For then he waits for God, who saves from the faintheartedness of spirit and from the storm, and who, to use the words of Augustine on Psalm 33, dwells in light inaccessible, not by our powers but by his gifts. For no one can approach it, as the same holy Doctor says in Book 2 of the Acts against Felix the Manichaean, chapter 7, unless God himself has granted that he should approach. Awaiting this blessed hope and the coming of glory, not in a qualified way, these are the words of St. Chrysostom in Homily 5 on the Epistle to Titus, but absolutely and without comparison, in the nature of the great God, the bridegroom of souls and our Saviour Jesus Christ, according to the precept of the Apostle, Titus 2:12: Let us live soberly, and justly, and godly in this world; that is, as Drogo the Cardinal explains in his book on the Creation and Redemption of Man, vol. 2 of the Bibliotheca Patrum: soberly as regards ourselves, justly as regards our neighbours, godly as regards God. For, as the excellent Peter of Blois writes in Epistle 132 to Ernald, Prior of the Church of Monasteriolum, or St. Launomarus of the Monasteries in the territory of Perche, of the Diocese of Chartres, made in the year 1202, to Abbot Launomarus of Blois: To moderation in temporal things belongs the sobriety that satisfies necessity and does not serve pleasure. Natural justice is that you do not wish to do to others what you would not want done to you, and that you do to others what you would want done to you. Piety, moreover, by the testimony of St. Augustine, consists in faith, hope and charity, by which the company of souls loves above all the bridegroom, who may make us partakers of the heavenly marriages. Amen.

units.tr: FINIS.
